q Sir G. H. Seymour to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received September 26.) 


(No. 478. Confidential.) 
My Lord, Si. Petersburgh, September 13, 1853. 
,.. YOUR Lordship will not fail to have observed that Count Nesselrode 
mM (except on the occasion of his communicating to me his last despatch to Baron 
at Meyendorff) has manifested repugnance to speaking to me of the evacuation of 
is the Principalities, or to listening to anything which I might have to say on the 
% subject. 
f , The subject, and those connected with it, he has indeed avoided in a marked 
if manner.

Sir G. H, Seymour to the Karl of Clarendon.— (Received September 26.) 


(No. 486, Confidential.) 
My Lord, St. Petersburgh, September 16, 1853. 

IF the Turks have not been ill advised when they determined upon reect- 
ing, or (which comes nearly to the same thing) upon altering the Projet de 
Note recommended to their adoption by the Representatives of the Four 
Powers, there must be an identity between Turkish and MTussian interests, of 
which no one had suspected the existence. 

Certain it is that no course more agreeable to those of the Emperor's 
advisers, who would recommend the adoption of extreme measures against 
Turkey, could have been devised than that which has been taken by the Porte ; 
and none, | may add, could be less calculated either to stimulate the exertions 
of sincere friends, or to guard against the falling off of those less devoted to the 
cause of Turkey, who for a time found themselves (probably to their great 
concern) in opposition to the views of Russia. 

As I have already had the honour of stating to your Lordship, the language 
of the Russians, even of those habitually the most moderate, is that concession 
has been made hitherto only on the side of the Emperor, and that it has already 
been carried to its extreme limits, 

To this they add, that the Vienna Projet de Note, besides being drawn up 
by the Plenipotentiaries of the Four Powers, derived an additional sanction by 
having been referred to London and Paris, where it received some amendments, 
ind that under these circumstances it must be considered as offering that 
amount of satisfaction to which the Emperor is fully entitled, even in the 
opinion of England and Franee. 

| do not then hesitate to state to your Lordship that had he remuined at 
lis own eapital, His Imperial Majesty would not have abated an iota of these 
pretensions, which he considers to haye received the sanction of the Allied 
Governments. 

It remains to be seen whether His Majesty will show himself more pliant 
in Germany, where he will be brought into contact with those whose friendship 
he so highly values, and where he will perhaps hear those traths which in his 
own country are never allowed to reach him. 

Supposing His Imperial Majesty to be induced to lend himself to the modi- 
fications proposed by the Turks, or to some of the same nature, all for the 
present will be well; in the contrary event 1 trust your Lordship will pardon me if 
L express the necessity which I feel would exist for urging the Turkish Govern- 
ment to adopt those terms which in the opinion of the Allied Governments it 
was considered might be safely subseribed to by them. 

It may be presumptuous in me to pronounce an opinion, but it appears to 
me that a point of very great importance has been overlooked by the Sultan's 
Government. They have failed to perceive that less fivourable terms of com- 
position prepared by the Four Powers, and accepted in deference to their advice, 
are more atlvantageous to them than would be better conditions if settled by 
themselves, 

In the one case they have a right to look to the Four Allies for protecting 
them aguinst any evil consequences which may arise from their own work ; in 
the other they may be lef’ by some of their nominal friends to extricate them- 
selves as best they can from anny fresh difficulties which nay come upon them. 
The point would be one of great importance in the case of any Government: 
it is peculiarly momentous with regard to one which must be kept up by the 
exertions of its friends, or which will cease to have any existence, 

1 am aware that diplomatic agents are accused of being too frequently 
tinged with the opinions of the Court at which they reside, and unconsciously | 
may be open to the reproach; I would nevertheless take the great liberty of 
observing to your Lordship that it appears to me that it would be a serious 
misfortune were we to take our stand against Russia upon any difficulty con- 
nected with terms of arrangement to which we ourselves have been partics, ond 
that all our energies should be exerted towards guarding (it may be hoped in 


aa 


4 


concert with our allies) against those future encroachments upon a defenceless 
neighbour, which it is probable will be continued by Russia a8 occasion may 
Server 
Such a bulwark might be constructed when the political gale has spent 
‘taclf, but is not to be undertaken while so much swell still prevails. 
L have, &e. 


(Signed) G. H. SEYMOUR.

My Lord, St. Petersburgh, September 16, 1853. 

RY the arrival of the messenger Blackwood I have been put in possession 
of your Lordship’s despatches down to No. inclusive. 

1 am sorry to say that from some inadvertency Count Nesselrode left 
St. Petersburgh without calling to mind that it had been settled that I was to 
sce him before his departure ; 1t appears, however, that he held a conversation 
with General Castelbajac which is not without interest. 

The French Envoy has received (amongst others) two despatches. from his 
Government, the one expressive of great regret at the non-acceptance by the 
Sultan of the Vienna note; the other stating that the advance of autumn renders 
“+ necessary that the fleets should be prepared to seek more secure anchorage 
than is offered by Besika Bay, and directing General Castelbajac to ascertain 
what would be the feelings of the Russian Cabinet if they were ta enter the 
Dardanelles. 

To obtain this information my colleague has addvessed himself, as he has 
been obliging enough to inform me, to Count Nesselrode himself. 

Upon my expressing a hope that this reference had not been made in an 
apologetic form, General Castelbajac observed that I might feel quite easy upon 
that point; that he had said to Count Nesselrode, ‘I had been directed to 
sound you, now I take upon myself to consult you more openly; 1 do so 
hecause, while we should have had no explanations to give of our movements it 
the Emperor had maintained his reserve with respect to the Principalities, we 
can show more confidence now that His Majesty has made known through the 
despatch addressed to Baron Meyendorif on. the 27th ultimo, his intention of 
giving orders for thelr evacuation as soon as a Turkish Plenipotentiary shall 
have arrived here with the note which His Majesty lad been led to expect.” 

There appear to have been two conversations in which this subject was 
approached, When the first took place Count Nesselrode had not seen the 
Emperor, and could not speak of his feclings; at the second, as I learn from 
my colleague, the Chancellor gave him to understand that no great objections 
would be entertained by His Majesty to the entry of the fleets ito the Darda- 
nelles, if it were clear that this movement bad a nautical and not a political 
character. 

Having again observed that I would not conecal from General Castelbajac 
that my feelings would have led me to deprecate anything like an appeal to the 
forbearance of the Emperor upon this question ; he replied that | might dismiss 
all misgivings, as he had explained clearly that it was only an approach to 
confidence and conciliation on the part of the Emperor which had enabled him 
to make advances in the same direction. 

A statement which is worthy of attention was made by Count Nesselrode 
vn the course of this conversation; some allusion having been made to the 
future, respecting which so much uncertainty prevails still, his Excellency 
remarked that one point was at least certain, that no military operation could 
he undertaken during the winter, “here,” he said, “ we are met by a physical 
impossibility.” 

| will only add that my French colleague requested me to consider the 
communication Which he had made to me as strictly confidential, as he had no 


authority to open himself to me upon this subject,

Lord A. Loftus to the Earl of Clarendon. —(Received September 26.) 
(No. 5.) 
My Lord, Berlin, September 23, 1853. 


IN an interview I had this morning with Baron Manteuffel his Excellency 
‘nformed me that he had just received a telegraphic despatch from Count Arnim, 
the Prussian Minister at Vienna, dated yesterday afternoon, stating, that “ Lord 
Westmorland had read to the Conference a telegraphic despatch, according to 
which the English Cabinet approves of the declaration; but says, that as the 
Cabinet of Russia, according to its last despatches, did not interpret the Vienna 
note as the British Government did, they could no longer counsel the Porte to 
accept the Vienna note.” 

His Excellency seemed much surprised at this intelligence, and was evidently 
anxious for some explanation of the despatch which Lord Westmorland had 
received from your Lordship, and which he had communicated yesterday to the 
Conference at Vienna. As his Excellency informed me that he was about to 
communicate this telegraphic despatch to the King. | deemed it of importance 
that his Excellency should be enabled to convey to His Majesty a correct view 
on the subject, and I judged it would be in accordance with your Lordship’s 
wishos that | should communicate, confidentially, to Baron Manteuffel, any 
information which would relieve his mind of doubts or prevent false deductions. 

Your Lordship’s despatch No. 308," to the Earl of Westmorland (which J 
received yesterday under flying-seal), enabled me to give the following explana- 
tions to Baron Manteuffel; but 1 was careful in not giving to this statement the 
character of an official communication. 

L commenced by stating to his Excellency, that he had been aware of the 
moderate and conciliatory course which Her Majesty’s Government hud pursued 
from the commencement of this tedious and dificult negotiation ; that Her 
Majesty's Government had had deeply at heart the pacific solution of the 
differences between Russia and ‘Turkey in a manner consistent with the honour 
of the Sultan and the independence of Turkey; that with this view the note 
drawn up at Vienna had been recommended to the acceptation of the Porte; 
and further, that the modifications to that note which had been proposed by 
Turkey, had been considered as unimportant, and as bearing the same imterpre- 
tation as contained in the Vienna note; whilst Her Majesty's Government in 
adopting these views had placed confidence in the declaration which the Emperor 
of Russia had repeatedly put forth, viz, that he sought for no new right and no 
increase of power in Tirkey. IT then observed to his Excellency, that the 
reasons put forth by Count Nesselrode in his despatch to Baron Meyendorff tor 
the rejection of the modifications proposed by Turkey, were of a nature to 
awaken fears that the interpretation of the Vienna note was viewed otherwise by 
Count Nesselrode than by the framers of that note, and that Russia seemed to 
put a different construction on the terms of that note than the one entertained 
by Her Majesty's Government. 

| remarked to his Excellency, that the object which the Four Powers. have 
been labouring to attain, 18 to establish, both now and hereafter, permanent 
friendly relations between Russia and Turkey, and that it was obvious that the 
interpretation of the note, which was to be considered as the basis of reconcilia- 
tion, should be one and the same; that it should bear the same sense in the 
opinion of both parties, and that it was highly Nip ee that no difference of 
interpretation should hereafter arise which might lead to fresh disputes. His 
Excellency would, therefore, doubtless acknowledge that in the interest of peace 
it was most desirable, nay, of paramount importance, that all cnuse for future 
misunderstanding should be avoided, and that for this purpose it was impera: 


* See Part 1, p. d34. 


6 


tively necessary that any doubts which might be entertained by cither party as 
to the interpretation of this note should be cleared up, and that it was pei 
that this understanding should be arrived at previous to its signature by Turkey. 

I added, that after the repeated declarations of the Emperor of Russia that 
he seeks no new right and no further extension of power in'Turkey, it might confi- 
dently be hoped that His Imperial Majesty would not hesitate to give those 
assurances which would quiet the present fears of Turkey, and which, if happily 
the present differences were adjusted, would tend to consolidate on a firmer and 
surer basis the future friendly relations of the two States. 

His Excellency listened carefully to my observations, and, without expres- 
sing any decided opinion, seemed to assent to the justice of the views | had 
exposed. | 

His Excelleney was good enough to give me a copy of the telegraphic 
despatch, which I have the honour to inclose to your Lordship herewith, in 
original and in translation. 

I trust your Lordship will approve of my having made this communication 
to Baron Manteuffel, as well as of the substance of my observations. 

I have, &e. 
(Signed) AUGUSTUS LOFTUS.

that the Turkish moditications of the Vienna note had been rejected by the 
Cabinet of St. Petersburgh, and stating the grounds upon which that decision 
was founded. 

These despatches would appear to preclude the hope of an amicable arrange- 
ment between Russia and Turkey, and as their effects may consequently be 
disastrous to Europe, they have received the serious attention of Her Majesty's 
Government ; aa T shall now proceed to state the opinion that has been 
formed of them with reference to the intentions of the Conference of Vienna in 
framing the note, to the motives of the Otteman Government in proposing 
amendments, and to the repeated declarations of the Emperor that he desired no 
new right nor any extension of influence in Turkey. 

In his first despatch Count Nesselrode alludes. to the terms on which the 
note had been accepted at St. Petersburgh, and the understanding that if any 
changes were introduced at Constantinople, the Russian Government would be 
at liberty to withhold its assent. 

The Russian Government had of course a right to make this condition, or 
to suggest amendments to the note. The Turkish Government possessing 4 
similar right, exercised it by proposing certain modifications. ‘The Conference 
had no power to impose the note on cither party: its position was that of a 
mediator endeavouring to do equal justice to both parties, and its intention was 
to guard the honour and independence of the Sultan, and secure to Russia 
what she was entitled to claim, bat no more, viz., the maintenance of existing 
Treaties, and the statws quo in matters of religton. The Conference, therefore, 
could not refuse to entertain the modifications of the Porte, although regretting 
the loss of time which they occasioned. They were not looked upon as altering 
the sense of the note, nor at variance with the intentions of the Goaference: and 
they were unanimously recommended to the acceptance of the Russian Goyern- 
ment, the Russian Minister at Vienna, it is understood, concurring in the 
recommendation. 

They have been rejected, but the Russian Government did not take its 
stand upon the condition on which the note had been necepted, Viv. that of no 
change being made, but has fully entered inta the objections to which it con- 
sidered the modifications were liable, and which showed that inferences were 
drawn from the note, and claims were to be established by means of it hereafter, 
altogether inconsistent with the views and intentions of the Four Powers, 

The frankness of this proceeding on the part of the Russian Government, 
and the determination that its intentions should not be misapprehended, are doubt- 
less ey pene but on the other hand Her Majesty’s Government feel, that 
even while retaining their own original interpretation of the note, it would 
now be highly dishonourable to press its acceptance on the Porte, when 
they have been duly warned by the Power to whom the note. is to be addressed, 
that another and a totally different meaning is attached to it by that Power, 
And even if this were not dishonourable, it would be in the highest degree 
impolitic for the reasons stated in Count Neaselrode’s first despateh with refer- 
ence to admitting of any amendments, viz., that the Emperor would expose 
himself “to renew political relations with Turkey under unfavourable auspices, 
whieh would deprive them of all solidity for the future, and inevitably bring 
about a fresh ad more decided rupture.” 

Her Majesty's Government earnestly desire to see the relations between 
Russia and the Porte re-established on a friendly and permanent footing, and 
they consequently can be no party to.an arrangement which the Cubinet of 5t. 
Petersburgh has shown would frustrate the object which they have at heart. 

Count Nesselrode declares that the modifications are by no means so insig- 
nificant either in their spirit or their “ arriére pensées,” as might at first sight 
be supposed ; but he appears not to be aware that this declaration goes far to 

C 


10 


justify the Turkish Government in proposing them; and his Excellency 
altogether fails to show by what right, or in reparation of what injury Russia 
claims admissions and concessions from the Sultan, who is unwilling to make 
them, and whose independence Russia, together with the other Powers of 
Europe, have determined to respect, 

With regard to the first objection in Count Nesselrode’s note, I have to 
observe, that the Conference at iednn: in adverting to the active solicitude at 
all times displayed by the Emperor of Russia for the maintenance of the privi- 
lezes and immunities of the Greco-Orthodox Church, simply intended to record 
the anxiety which every Sovereign must feel for the welfare in a foreign country 
of the religion he himself professes ; but the Conference by no means intended 
to affirm that the immunities and privileges in question were solely due to the 
solicitude of the Emperors of Russia ; and the Porte is justified in asserting that 
many of these privileges are of a date anterior to the existence of diploimatic 
relations between the two countries. 

Count Nesselrode alludes to other grievances, but specifies none except 
that regarding the Holy Places, which has been satisfactorily settled ; nor have 
any other grievances connected with religious matters at any time been put 
forward by Russia, and it was not for the Conference to assume the existence of 
wrongs of which they had no knowledge. . 

But Count Nesselrode asks, where then was the object of Prince Men- 
chikoff’s mission 2—and the answer to that is the assurance repeatedly given, 
that it was to settle the question of the Holy Places, and to obtain a guarantee 
for its not being again disturbed, “'bat question has been settled to the satis 
faction of all parties, and the Vienna note contains a guarantee against which 
Russia raises no objection. 

The modifications proposed by the Porte with reference to the Treaty of 
Kainardji appeared to Her Mtajest 's Government wholly uncalled for, until they 
read the objection made to it by Count Neaselrode’s note. Her Majesty's 
Government considered that the stipulations of the Treaty of Kainardji, and the 
maintenance of religious privileges, had been disconnected in the note in a 
manner not to be mistaken, and indeed this ts admitted by Count Nesselrode ; 
hut the Russian Government, while disclaiming all pretension to exercise a 
Protectorate, yet affirms that all these religious privileges and immunities “are 
direct consequences of the ‘Treaty, which was doubtless a solemn engagement 
taken by Turkey towards Russia; and the fulfilment of that engagement, but no 
more, it was the object of the Conference to secure. By Count Nesselrode’s 
interpretation of the note, however, Russia would, under the seventh Article 
of the Treaty, be entitled to superintend all these privileges and immunities, 
which are of that peculiar character that she would be constantly able, if so 
minded, to interfere between the Sultan and his subjects; and thus the religious 
Protectorate, which is abjured, and the new rights and extended influence, which 
are equally disclaimed, would be established, 

It is supertiuous to say that no such intention was entertained by the 
Conference; nor can the ‘Treaty of Kainardji, by any subtlety of reasoning, be so 
construed, By the seventh Article of that ‘Treaty, the Porte promises to protect 
the Christian religion in all its churches throughout the Ottoman dominions ; 
but by the same Article the Mimsters of Russia are permitted to make repre- 
sentations in favour of a new church and its ministers; and this clause would 
have been wholly unnecessary if Russian diplomacy had also been allowed to 
muke representations on every matter connected with religion, If the Article 
hore the sense that Count Nesselrode now seeks to attach to it, and if the two 
Contracting Parties had been agreed upon it, it is reasonable to suppose that at 
the signing of the Treaty a stipulation so important as that of maintaining the 
privileges and immunities of the Greek Church would not have been omitted. 

‘The third objection raised by Count Nesselrode is even more than the two 
which precede it at variance with the intention of the Conference, which assuredly 
was not that the Sultan should enter into an engagement with Russia, to 
concede to the Greek Church all such advantages as might be granted to other 
Christian denominations, but only those advantages which were conceded to 
communities who, like the Greeks, were Ottoman subjects. . 

The spiritual head of the Roman Catholics in Turkey, as elsewhere, 15 a 
foreign Sovereign; and if it pleased the Suitan to enter into a Concordat with 
the Pope, conferring privileges upon Roman Catholics not subjects of the Porte, 


li 


surely that ought to confer no right upon the Emperor of Russia to claim all 
the benefits of that Concordat for the Greek community, subjects of the Porte, 
whose spiritual head, the Patriarch of Constantinople, is also a subject of the 
Sultan. 

No Christian community being subjects of the Sultan would have any right 
to participate in the privileges and advantages that the Sultan might confer upon 
Russian convents, ecclesiastics, or laymen, such, for example, as the Russian 
church and hospital about to be built at Jerusalem ; and in the same manner 
the Greek community, consisting of many millions, would have no right to 
participate in advantages granted to foreign convents or ecclesiastics, and which 
might not, for many and obvious reasons, be fitting for a Christian community 
subject to the Porte. 

In fact, if the Sultan has at any time, in the exercise of his sovereign 
authority, conferred religious privileges upon 1 community not subject to him; 
or if he at any future time should think proper to do so, Count Nesselrode 
claims that Russia should have a right to demand that several millions of Greeks 
who are subjects of the Porte should at once be placed upon the footing of 
foreigners, and should enjoy, through the intervention of Russia, all the advan- 
tages which the Sultan, for reasons of which he is the only competent judge, 
may have granted to such foreigners. 

How such a claim can be reconciled with the professed desire for the 
maintenance of existing Treaties and the strict status quo in religious matters, it 
‘s not for Her Majesty’s Government to explain; but they consider that it 
exhibits a total disrezard for the feelings and interests of the European Powers, 
who, in common with Russia, have declared that they will uphold the independ- 
ence of Turkey, and who cannot therefore see with indifference that Russia 
should thus surreptitiously seek to obtain a virtual Protectorate over the Chris 
tian subjects of the Porte. And with respect to Count Nesselrode’s supposition, 
that some new privilege, not mentioned in the recent firmans, might be granted to 
the Roman Catholic establishment in Palestine, to the prejudice of the native com- 
nvunities, his Excellency appears to have overlooked that by the Vienna note the 
Porte engages that no change shall be made in the order of things lately esta- 
blished at Jerusalem, without previous communication with the Governments of 
Russia and France. 

I have now fully stated in what spirit and with what intentions the Vienna 
note was framed; but in interpreting it as Count Nesselrode has done, by his 
objection to the modifications, his Excellency not only does not prove, but he 
does not even advert to any obligation by which the Porte is bouml to make 
concessions utterly irreconcileable with its independence. But Her Majesty's 
Government are compelled to consider that the claims put forward by Russia 
are equally irreconcileable with the assurance that no extended power or influ- 
ence is sought in ‘Turkey, ‘They deeply regret that such claims should have 
been made; for even were they successful, they would be useless to Hussia 
if she sincerely desires the independence of the Ottoman Empire; but under any 
cireumstances they must produce feelings of suspicion and distrust on the part 
of the Porte; and differences between the ‘Two Powers will thus in future, as of 
late, be a source of anxiety to Europe, and expose the general peace to constant 
danger of disturbance. 

You will communicate this despatch to Count Nesselrode, or to M. de 
Séniavine, should Count Nesselrode be still absent, and also give him a copy. 


lam, &e. 
(Signed) CLARENDON.

The foundation upon which you rest your right to make this inquiry 18 the

not to admit, and the other Contracting Powers not to send ships of war, not

Russian soldier entered the Danubian Principalities, and from that moment the 
Sultan had a right to invite the British squadron into the Straits, and Her 
Majesty's Government had a right to send the British squadron mito, and if 
necessary, through those Straits. a. 

It is true that on entering the Principalities war was nat declared by 
Russia, but a country whose territory is forcibly invaded and retained in contra- 
vention of a special Treaty engagement, for the purpose of compelling it to 
submit to conditions which it considers incompatible with 1s political indepen- 
dence, whose functionaries are forbidden to hold intercourse with its Government, 
and whose tribute ts suspended,—that country cannot consistently with inter- 
national law or usage, or with commen sense, be considered at peace with the 
Power that so acts towards it; and I repeat, therefore, that Irom the day on 
which the Principalitics were occupied, the Treaty, in accordance with its own 

rovisions, has been suspended, and it rested with the Sultan and with Her 
Majesty's Government to determine at what time, and for what purposes, the 
British squadron should enter the Dardanelles. a Sace

obstacles to the work of conciliation, but exclusively trom apprehension of local 
dangers to British life and property ; his proceedings have been entirely approved 
by Her Majesty’s Government, who, with the same object in view, have instructed 
him to send for the whole of the squadron. "

My Lord, St. Petersburgh, September 23, 1853. 
THE messenger Robins arrived at St. Petersburgh on the 20th instant, and 
{am thus in possession of your Lordship's despatches down to No, 208 inclusive. 
With rabrancs to your Lordship's, No. 203, which reached me on the Lath 
instant, your Lordship will have learned the circumstance which revented my 
expressing to Count Nesselrode the earnest hope entertained by Ter Majesty's 
Government that the modifications proposed by the Porte to the Vienna note 
may receive the Emperor's assent. 


13 


I regret not having had an opportunity of making known this wish in your 
Lordship's name; but the attempt to change the Emperor's decision would, 1 
am convinced, have been made in vain. 

This, | would state to your Lordship, is likewise the belief entertained by 
the Prussian and French Ministers; while as to the hopes that were to have 
been expressed on the part of the Austrian Cabinet, that the Emperor would 
not withhold his approval of the Turkish alterations, these hopes have, as I 
understand, been made known in a feeble tone. 

The French and Prussian Envoys, and, 1 believe, the Austrian Chargé 
d'Affaires, lay great stress upon the forward position taken up by the Emperor 
in the two Circulars and the Manifesto, upon the abatement subsequently made 
in the Imperial pretensions, and upon the difficulty which a fair regard for his 
own interests would place in the way of much further concession on the part of 
His Imperial Majesty. 

i would take the liberty of stating to your Lordship that the impression 
left upon my mind by the conversations which I held with the Chancellor, and 
by the hasty perusal of the despatch of Siicuier 7 t0 Baron Meyendorff, which was 
placed in my hands, is that the Emperor, by refusing the Turkish amendments, 
was not to be understood as closing the door against arrangement or negotiation, 
but as declining to concede to the Sultan a faculty which he himself had not 
exercised, as considering his assent to the Vienna note cancelled so soon as the 
Sultan’s refusal to agree to it became decided, and in this manner as reserving 
to himself perfect freedom as to the future course of diplomatic action. 

Unfortunately the warlike disposition manifested by the Turks, together 
with the idea which has been encouraged by the public press of the Emperor's 
consent having been extorted from him under pressure, are certain to increase 
the difficulty of obtaining concessions on the side of Russia; and the chances 
of a favourable issue are further diminished by the belief indulged (as 1 know 
upon certain grounds) by the Russian Cabinet of its being impossible that the 
Turkish armies should hold together until the spring. 

T have, &c. 
(Signed) G. H. SEYMOUR.

No. 17. 
Sir G. H. Seymour to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received October 2.) 


(No. 498. Confidential.) 
My Lord, St. Petersburgh, September 24, 1853. 


THE Marquis de Castelbajac has been kind enough to read me a despatch 
dated the 13th instant, which he received yesterday from Paris. He requested 
me to consider the communication as confidential. 

The despatch struck me as being an important one, as it appears to esta- 
blish that France does not consider herself pledged to any particular course by 
the projet de note assented to by the Emperor and refused by the Porte, and 
that in the event of the existing difficulties not being surmounted, she regards 
herself as free to follow that course which she shall consider suited to her interests 
and to those of Europe. 

At the same ane M. Drouyn de Lhoys manifests his deep regret at the 
Sultan’s refusal, and expresses his intention of urging the Porte to reconsider 
what he considers an imprudent resolution, Seve eee . 

He accordingly incloses a projet de note, which it is his wish should be 
addressed by the four missions at Constantinople to Reshid Pasha, in which, in 
friendly but energetic terms, he is called upon to recall a hasty determination, 
and to subscribe to terms which the Powers interested in the independence of 
Turkey have, ina very friendly spirit, judged it expedient to press upon his 
acceptance. 

I have, &c. 
(Signed) G, H, SEYMOUR.

Lord A, Loftus to the Earl of Clarendon.—{Received October 2.) 


(No. 12.) | 
My Lord, Berlin, September 27, 1853. 


IT may not be without interest to your Lordship to learn the feeling of 
publie opinion, and of the public press, in this country, at the proses TaneD 
when so important a change has taken place in the complexion of Eastern 
nT am happy to report to your Lordship, that [have learnt from persons 
capable of forming u correct opinion on these mutters, that the great mass of 
Asse men, persons of the commercial and industrious classes, and of that 
influential class here termed the bureaucratic, view with alarm the aggressive policy 
of Russia, and are opposed to her ambitious designs in the East ; and it is a 
duty further to add, that they have hitherto viewed the moderation which 


17 


has been evinced by the Western Powers towards Russia with surprise and 
regret. 

The higher classes of the nobility, and more especially of those immediately 
attached to the Court, are, on the other hand, devoted to the Emperor and to 
Russian interests. ‘These inclinations are accounted to me as possibly owing 
their origin in gratitude for favours already conferred, or in expectation of future 
distinctions; whilst, lam led to believe, that continual alarm of revolutionary 
changes inspires them to look to the Emperor of Russia as Europe's surest 
bulwark against the inroad of democratic principles. 

| am happy to inform your Lordship, that since the publication of the 
Russian objections to the Turkish modifications, the whole Berlin press, with 
one exception, strongly denounces the policy of Russia, and represents in its true 
light the ambitious projects she has in view. 

The one exception to which I allude is the *“ Kreuz Zeitung," which, until 
an article appeared in to-day’s newspaper analysing the armies of Russia and 
Turkey, and their respective chances of success in the event of war, has main- 
tained a profound silence on Eastern affairs, and has abstained from inserting any 
leading articles in matters of foreign policy.

Lord A, Loftus to the Karl of Clarendon.—(Received October 2.) 


(No, 13. Confidential.) 
My Lord, Berlin, September 27, 1853. 

I WAITED on Baron Manteuffel this morning, when his Excellency 
informed me that he had received a telegraphic despatch from the Chevalier 
Bunsen, stating that in consequence of a communication from the Grand Vizier, 
the English and French Ambassadors had called up from Besiea to Constan- 
tinople four war-steamers, for the protection of the subjects of their respective 
states. I] confirmed to his Excellency this intelligence, adding that it was 
possible that the combined fleets might shortly follow; and I took occasion to 
observe to his Excellency, that in such event the presence of the English fleet at 
Constantinople must not be construed in any sense but in that of supporting 
the Sultan and protecting His Majesty's subjects in case of need. I took this 
precaution in order that this step might not be viewed as a measure to coerce 
the Sultan into the aceeptation of the Vienna note. 

On inquiry I found that his Excellency had received no report from Count 
Arnim, which he accounted for by the absence of Count Buol from Vienna. 
In reply to a further inquiry whether Count Arnim had repaired to Olmiitz 
with his other colleagues, his Excellency replied in the negative, adding that he 
was very glad he had not done so, I then asked his Excellency what instruc- 
tions he had addressed in the present altered circumstances of the Eastern 
Question to the Prussian Ministers at Constantinople and Vienna: he replicd 
that he had forwarded no new instructions to Baron Wildenbruck since that 
reported in Lord Bloomfield’s despatch No. 339 of the 27th ultimo, in which he 
had been directed to press on the Porte the acceptation of the Vienna note: 
that since I had last seen him, he had only instructed Count Arnim (in the 
event of no new arrangement being concluded at Olmiitz), to propose to the 
Conference at Vienna “to communicate to Russia and the Porte the declaration 
which had been previously agreed upon,” and which his Excellency seemed to 
think would be viewed as bearing a satisfactory assurance to Turkey ; while it 
could not but be distasteful to Russia, That was the only plan which he could 
devise for alleviating the present difficulties, 

[ observed to his Excellency, that since Russia had expressed her objections 
to the Turkish modifications, and in opposition to the sentiments of the Con- 
ference, had declared them to be of importance, it appeared to me that it 
became the dignity of the Conference, who had framed the note, to express their 
own interpretation of it, and in failing to do so they could scarcely call upon 
the Porte to accept it, In this sense, perhaps, some such proposition as his 

D 


1s 


Excellency proposed might be productive of good, as it would place on record 
the sense aud spirit in which the Vienna note had been framed His Excellency 
then said, “What can we do? To ask the Emperor to accept the modifications 
would be illogical; we have no grounds for doing so.” I rejoined that “ the 
very fact of the misinterpretation of the note by Russia offered sufficient grounds 
for that misinterpretation to be cleared up, and that there was the same reason 
now to disapprove of the objections raised by Russia to the modifications, as 
there had been at the commencement to censure the views put forth in Prince 
Menchikoff’s demands.” 

Before taking leave of his Excellency, 1 inquired what were the intentions 
of the Prussian Government under existing circumstances, and what line they 
would pursuc? 

I remarked to his Excellency, that His Majesty had lately expressed to 
Lord Bloomfield his desire to act in concert with England on this question ; that 
the position of Prussia entitled her to exercise a great moral influence ; that it 
behoved her to maintain her independence of action, and not to be carried in 
the wake of Russia; and that | hoped she would remain free and unfettered to 
pursue that course which her own interests dictated. 

His Excellency replied that His Majesty still maintained the same desire 
to act with Englund; that it was difficult for Prussia to move further in this 
matter: and that it was clearly her policy to hold aloof, as far as she was able, 
and to await the moment when perhaps her offices might be of service; in 
short, he said that Prussia would endeavour to remain as neutral as possible, and 
keep watch over her own internal safety, 

I did not further press his Excellency on this point. 1 inquired, however, 
if he was informed what course Austria was likely to pursue. His Excellency 
replied that he could not say, but that he knew that the occupation of the 
Provinces weighed heavily on her. 

In conclusion, I have the honour to state that my general impression from 
what fell from his Excellency at this interview is, that he foresees that hostilities 
in the East are unavoidable; that it is the wish of the Prussian Government to 
maintain a strict neutrality, but that no decision has been taken by His Majesty 
or will be taken, until after the Conference at Olmiitz, 1 may likewise remark 
confidentially to your Lordship, that I observed that his Excellency is imbued 
with fears lest an European war should arise out of these Eastern difficulties, 
and that to these fears may be somewhat attributed that ardent desire for 
neutrality which has ever been @ marking feature of Prussian policy. 

I have, &e. 
(Signed) AUGUSTUS LOFTUS.

given by His Imperial Majesty the Emperor of Russia, to the effect that His 
Majesty usks only for a general guarantee of the immunities already granted 
to the Greek Chureh, and for nothing which could in any way prejudice the 
independence or rights of the Sultan, or which would imply a desire to interfere

in all matters appertaining to the ‘ Orthodox Greek Church,’ and the promise to

quent to the present the Sultan may be disposed to grant to any other denomi- 
nations of Christians.” 

This claim, aa your Lordship will observe, is very different from that 
implied in the interpretation which has been given to the paragraph in the 
Vienna note, objected to by Reshid Pasha as conferring upon several millions 
of the subjects of the Porte religious privileges granted at different times to the 
subjects of other Powers residing within the Ottoman territory. _The pretension 
now put forward is only that in future if any additional immunities are granted 
to Christians of any denomination, they shall not be withheld from members of 
the Greek Church; it is therefore prospective in its operation, and as such it is 
not believed that it ought to be considered in any way a condition onerous to 
the Porte, or untitting for it to grant. 

It is the ylection of Count Nesselrode to imstruct the various Represen-

My Lord, Paris, Oclober 4, 15538. 

ON ante last, the 30th ultimo, M. Drouyn de Lhuys received a tele- 
graphic despatch from Vienna, stating that a fresh proposition for the settlement 
of the Eastern Question had been sent from Olmitz, for the consideration of 
the Cabinets of London and Paris. In mentioning this to me M. Drouyn de 
Lhuys added, in reply to a question which I put to him, that he did not know 
the exact tenour of the proposition, but he seemed inclined to augur favourably 
of it, as he had been told that it was based on the declaration which your Lord- 
ship, on learning the rejection by Russia of the Turkish modifications of the 
Vienna note, had proposed should be made by the Conference of Vienna, in 
order to induce the Porte still to sign that note, a proposal to which the Cabinet 
of Vienna had not then given its assent, I thought it necessary to remind 
M. Drouyn de Lhuys that, when your Lordship made that proposal, the motives 
which induced Russia to refuse the modifications had not been made known, and 
that the whole ‘question had assumed a very different aspect now that Russia 
had so petty declared the interpretation which she gave to the work of the 
Vienna Conference. 

On Sunday M, de Hubner made the communication which M. Drouyn de 
Lhuys had been led to expect, and he left with his Excellency copies of the note 
which it is proposed that the Representatives of the Four Powers at Constanti- 
nople should address to the Porte, and of Count Buol’s despatch urging the 
French Government to adopt this course. As your Lordship must be in posses- 
sion of these papers, | need not attempt a description of them. M. Drouyn de

produced by it upon my Government, any observation | made must not he 
considered as carrying with it official weight. 

There were, I said, several points to be considered; the nature of the 
declaration, the value of it; and, supposing these to be resolved satisfactorily, 
the time and manner of making it known to the Porte. With regard to the 
nature of the declaration, it seemed to me that we were required to give 
assurances as coming from Russia, of which we had no official knowledge, while 
care had been taken to make us well and officially acquainted with a [Russian 
document of a very different character and meaning, In fact, the declaration 
would rather convert us into advocates for Russia than recognize us as friends 
of the Porte. With respect to its value, there were no doubt yaluable admis- 
sions apparently made by Russia, but the fourth paragraph scemed to me so 
obscurely worded, that its meaning might be doubted. The first part of it 
which explained the status quo, was satisfactory enough, Tt was clearly laid 
down that nothing was asked for the Greek community which was not enjoyed 
by other Christian communities, subjects of the Porte. But the latter part, 
which regarded the future, was not so clear, for then the stipulation ran in 
favour of concession to the Greeks of all privileges which might hereafter be 
granted to other Christian rites. No mention was here made of Christians, 
subjects of the Porte; and as this wasa point on which the Ottoman Govern- 
ment was peculiarly susceptible, the paragraph would hardly prove satisfactory 
to them. However this, as well as other objections which I had ventured to 
signalise, admitted of correction. But then came the question, would the Porte, 
after all that had happened, and with the knowledge, which no doubt the Turkish 
Ministers possessed, of the interpretation given by Count Nesselrode to the 
Vienna note, would the Porte be satisfied with this declaration on the part of 
the Conference? And, if she was not, how far would the two Governments le 
prepared to go in combating the Porte’s continued objections to sign the Vienna 
note? I felt certain, I said, that Her Majesty's Government would not go the 
lengths recommended by Count Buol, or abandon the Porte to her fate, because 
she maintained a right to have an independent opinion respecting an engagement 
so important as that into which she was called upon to enter. lasked M. Drouyn 
de Lhuys whether the Emperor had considered this part of the question, and 
the position in which the two Governments would find themselves, if, with their 
fleets before Constantinople, they pressed the acceptance of the Vienna note 
upon the Porte, and the Porte persisted in her refusal, and war was the conse= 
quence? M, Droayn de Lhuys replied that he certainly had not put the 
question categorically to the Emperor, but that he felt (and he had stated as 
much to M. de Hubner) that France could not abandon Turkey, because she 


a 


26 


took her own view of her own interests, while the act of aggression on the part 
of Russia remained the same; and he added that the general tenour of the 
observations which had fallen from the Emperor, in the course of these long 
negotiations, would lead him to suppose that His Majesty entertained the eame 
opinion. 

At the end of a long conversation, M. Drouyn de Lhuys seemed inclined 
to think that the Cabinets of Paris and London might reply to the Austrian 
proposal, by saying that they had no objection to submit it to the Porte, and 
recommend the Ottoman Ministers to examine it and see whether they could 
not find in it assurances sufficiently explicit to enable them to sign the Vienna 
note, and the two Governments might reserve to themselves, as indeed Austria 
herself had done, perlect liberty of action, should the Porte persist in: her 
refusal.

The Earl of Clarendon to the Earl of Westmorland. 
(No. 326.) 


My Lord, Foreign Office, October 5, 1853. 

COUNT COLLOREDO has placed in my hands a despatch from Count 
Buol, in which he refers to the effect produced on the Cabinets of London and 
Paris by the confidential communication made by the Cabinet of St. Peters- 
burgh in support of its rejection of the modifications required by the Porte in 
the Vienna note, and to the explanations which the British and French Govern- 
ment have considered indispensable, in consequence of the interpretation given 
to that note by the Government of Russia. 

Baron de Bourqueney, at the moment of Count Buol’s departure for 
Olmutz, received instructions to invite Count Buol to declare, in conjunction 
with the Representatives of the Three Powers, the true sense of the Vienna 
note to be apposed to the interpretation put upon it by Count Nesselrode ; and 
although Count Buol could not entirely agree to this proposition, he availed 
himself of the oceasion afforded to him in his interview with Count Nesselrode 
to devise some means of giving renewed action to the Conferences which had 
been for the moment paralysed. 

The explanations of Count Nesselrode have confirmed Count Buol tn the 
conviction that Russia does not aim at any interference in the internal affairs of 
the Ottoman Empire, and that the demands of the Emperor of Russia do not 
involve anything derogatory to the sovereign rights of the Sultan. And Count 
Buol regards the declaration of this conviction as it is embodied in the inclosed 
projet de note to be the exact and authentic expression of the meaning of the 
Emperor of Russia, the more especially as His Imperial Majesty has seen and 
approved this note as expressing his real intentions; and Count Buol is of 
opinion that the proper method of offering a guarantee against any false inter- 
prea) being put on the Vienna note, and of overcoming the seruples of the 
*orte, would be to make known these intentions by a simultaneous declaration of 
the Representatives of the Pour Powers. 

The Austrian Government is ready to authorize the Internuncio at Con- 
stantinople to make the declaration contained in the annexed propel de note as 
soon as his colleagues shall have received a similar authority from their Govern- 
ments, and shall have been assured that the presentation of this note will be 
followed by the immediate signature of the Vienna note, and its transmission by 
an Ambassador to St. Petersburgh, 

Count Buol hopes that this projet\de note is calculated to effuce the 
impression produced on the English and French Governments by the last com- 
murieation from the Russian Government, and is of opinion, that as the 
Cabinet of Russia disavows all intention of interference in the internal affairs of 
‘Turkey, and gives a more satisfactory definition of the rights which 1t wishes to 
sce guaranteed, as well as an unconditional adherence to the projet de note, the 
objections to the Vienna note appear groundless. Tt appears to Count Buol ta 
be of great importance to adhere to the Vienna note, notwithstanding the difh- 
culty of getting it accepted at Constantinople, and he hopes thut the resistance 
of the Ottoman Government will give way before the united and energetic 
representations of the Four Powers. Should it he otherwise, and should the 
Porte obey the dictates of impulse rather than the advice of its friends, such 
conduct would lead the Austrian Government to suppose that the Porte has 
decided to adopt a course Which Austria is not inclined to follow. 

But the Austrian Government does not anticipate the oceurrence of such 
an extremity, if the Porte is made to understand that should it remain deaf to 
the representations of its allies, it will lose all title to their support, Nothing 
would have more effect, in the opinion of the Austriun Government, in making 
the advisers of the Porte aware of the dangers to which the Ottoman Empire is 
exposed, than language held by the maritime Powers proportioned to the gravity 
of the occasion, If the Porte should push their blindness so fir as to desire to

to declare openly to the Porte that it will be reduced to the complete isolation of 
which it can easily foresce the consequences,

The Earl of Clarendon to the Karl of Westmorland. 
(No. 327.) 
My Lord, Foreign Office, October 4, 1853, 

COUNT COLLOREDO has communicated to me 1 confidential despateh 
from Count Buol, stating that the impression which his interview with Count 
Nessclrode has left on his mind, resolves itself into’a conviction that Russia 
sincerely desires a pacific solution of her differences with the Ottoman Empire, 
but that having advanced too far to recede, she cannot forego the engagements 
ro which she is pledged without having obtained her demands, which, circum- 
scribed as they are by the sollicitude of the Four Powers within just limits, the 
Ottoman Porte could accede to without prejudice to its honour or interests, 

If the note, the project of which is inclosed in my despatch No, 326, is 
agreed to by the Mediating Powers, and supported at Constantinople with that 
energetic unanimity which 1s the indispensable condition of success, it will, in 
Count Buol’s opinion, be possible to re-establish harmony between the contend- 
ing parties, and consequently to secure the evacuation of the Principalitics before 


29 


tlie winter renders that evacuation very difficult, if not impossible, and Count 
Buol urges the necessity of acting with promptitude, 

Count Buol then alludes to the decision of the Representatives of Great 
Britain and France at Constantinople, to call up a portion of the fleets anchored 
in Besika Bay ; and states that the Cabinet of Russia have no present intention 
of raising a question on this subject. 

Count Buol points out that whatever may be the international question to 
which the appearance of the English and Trench vessels before Constantinople 
may give rise, a powerful weapon is placed in the hands of the two Powers, and 
one which, according to the use made of it, will tend either to facilitate or to 
obstruct the solution of these differences. Count Buol is convinced that Her 
Majesty's Government cannot but recognize the importance of taking from the 
fanatical party all pretence of regarding the presence of the foreign ships of war 
as an encouragement given to their schemes, and considers that if the Repre- 
sentatives of Great Britain and France know how to tuke advantage of the naval 
forces at their disposal, to strengthen the eredit and influence of the moderate 
advisers of the Porte and the friends of peace, and to free fhe Sultan from the 
influences which endanger his freedom of action, they offer by such an attitude 
the best justification of the step they have thought soe As adopt.

(Signed) CLARENDON.

No. 36. 


The Earl of Clarendon to Lord Cowley, 
(No. 403.) 


My Lord, Foreign Office, October 7, 1853. 

ON the 4th instant Count Walewski informed me that the assurances 1s 
to the intentions of Russia contained in Count Buol’s project of note appeared 
eatisfactory to the French Government, who were prepared, with the concurrence 
of Her Majesty's Government to agree to the signature of that note by the 
Four Representatives at Constantinople; and that it should be offered to the 
Porte in exchange for the note originally sent from Vienna, 

I told Count Walewski that Count Buol’s despatch and project of note had 
not yet been considered by the Cabinet, but that I knew enough of the opinions 
of my colleagues to assure his Excellency that Her Majesty's Government 
could not concur in a measure which they must know beforehand would be 
useless, and which would not be justifiable even if it were not useless. 

It was unnecessary, I added, now to revert to the nature of the modifica- 
tions proposed by the Porte. The Porte had a right to make them; we had 
recognised that right, and the Turkish Government was pledged not to accept 
the note without them. It would therefore be imprudent on the part of the 
English and French Governments, and unfair towards the Porte, to offer advice 
in favour of the Vienna note, which must beyond all doubt be rejected. 

I desired moreover to observe that if we accepted Count Buol’s project 
of note, we should at once admit that the assurances given on the part of Russia 
were complete and satisfactory, that the Emperor had offered sufficient guarantees 
of his intention, and that no further resistance to his demands on the part of 
the Porte could be sanctioned hy our respective Governments ; but a despatch 
from the Austrian Government containing these assurances (supposing them to 
be satisfactory, which I was far from admitting) would offer no real security to 
the Turkish Government, and would not neutralize the despatch of Count 
eee which disclosed the views of Russia, and justified the fears of the 

orte. 

The proposed collective note would, therefore, as a matter of course, be 
refused, and the position of the English and French Governments would then be 
false and embarrassing, 

Count Walewski concurred in these views, which, he said, he should 
immediately submit to the consideration of his Government; and in the mean- 
while he requested me to give no definitive answer to Count Colloredo. 

Count Walewski yesterday informed me, that his Government had renounced 
all idea of again recommending the Vienna note to the Porte, and his Exeellency 

laced in my hands a despatch from M. Drouyn de Lhuys, copy of which 1s 
lerewith inclosed, stating the course which the Government of the Emperor 
proposes fo pursue, 

This despatch whieh in substance is similar to that of your Excellency’s, 
marked No. 740, has been attentively considered by the Cabinet ; and T have to 
inform your Excellency, that the views of Her Majesty's Government coinctle 
generally with those of the French Government. 

It is to be hoped that the combined fleets are now at Constantinople, and 
prepared to act in defence of the Sultan; but it is to be borne in mind, that our 
information as to the actual state of things there is confined to a telegraphic 
despatch of the 26th ultimo, announcing that the Supreme Council had deter- 
mined in favour of war, but had left the declaration of war, and the mode of 
carrying it on, to the Sultan and his Ministers; and it therefore appears advisalile 
to Her Majesty's Government, that general instructions should be given to the 
Ambassadors and Admirals to employ the combined fleets in whatever manner, 
and at whatever place, they may think necessary for defending the Turkish 
territory against direct azsression, If the Russian fleet were to come out of 
Sevastopol the fleets would, a5 a matter of course, pass through the Bosphorus, 
but a descent, such as that contemplated by M Drouyn de Lhuys, upon a place 
now so strongly fortified as Varna, and which the Turkish fleet could of itself 
effectually protect, appears very improbable; and Her Majesty's Government 

F 


4 


consider therefore, that at the present moment, and in the absence of precise 
‘nformation, it would be expedient that the flects should be stationed at 
Buyakderé, as the point from which they eould most readily be employed for the 

rotection of Constantinople, or of any other part of the Sultan’s dominions which 
might be in danger of-attack, The fleets would thus be in the position desired 
by the French Government, of waiting, without seeking, for the occasion of 
performing their duty ; they would neither assume the aggressive attitude which 
they ought not to have, nor expose the interests which it is our object to 
protect. 

Lam, &c. 

(signed) CLARENDON,

No. 37. 
Sir G. H, Seymour to the Earl of Clarendon —(Received October 7.) 
(No. 502.) 
My Lord, St. Petersburgh, September 25, 1853. 


ALTHOUGH a great variety of opinion exists with regard to Turkey and 
her relations towards Europe, there are certain points upon which I believe all 
rational men of all parties and nations are agreed, 

All admit that the power of the Turk ts diminished and diminishing ; that 
of Russia much increased and on the mnerease; that the policy of Russia has 
heen ever that of encroachment upon her declining neighbours; that if carried 
on much longer this system must end in the total destruction of the weaker of 
the two; and, above all, that from circumstances that are known to every one, 
the whole of Europe, with the exception of this country, are deeply interested 
in the preservation of the Ottoman Empire within the limits that remain to it 
after a long series of aggressions. 

These data lead, it appears clear, to the conclusion either that Turkey will 
be saved through the goodwill and the good offices of Europe, or that her doom 
is clearly fixed. 

If this be admitted, it follows that the only course to be pursued with 
regard to Turkey is that te never should be permitted that her differences with 
her eternal enemy should be settled with her alone, but that they should be 
submitted toa general council of the Great Powers, whose competency rests 
upon the general nature of the interests for which they have to rovide. 

In the case of the late demands made upon the Porte by Prince Menchikoff, 
a precedent hud been established which, if its value had been justly appreciated, 
might have given very ‘nereased stability to the Ottoman power. 

The Emperor calls for a note to which he was certainly in 10 ways 
entitled, and calls for it in 50 imperious a tone that it signified that not the 
slightest alteration even in its text will be admitted. . 

The demand is objected to by the Sultan, and upon being laid before the 
Great Powers, is modified to such an extent as in their opinion to take away all 
danger from compliance ; when at the eleventh hour the award is put aside, not 
by the party against which they had come forward, but by that in whose behalf 
they were prepared to exert themselves strenuously. 

Had the differences between the Emperor and the Sultan been left for 
settlement by an Act to be agreed upon between their two Cabinets, the respon- 
sibility would have reated with the Porte, while the power of interpreting that 
Act would have remained with the stronger of the Contracting Parties, who, as 
has been seen by the construction which they place upon the Treaty of 
Kainardji, are not ‘backward in founding very extensive demands upon very 
alight grounds. 

With a note prepared by the Allied Governments, and by their advice 
signed hy the Sultan, the case would be widely different. 

‘Those who drew up the instrument would best know the value which they 
intended to attach to it; those who tendered this advice to the Sultan had by 
ao doing contracted the engagement of providing that its effects should prove 
salutary. 

ia word, less favourable conditions obtained by the Porte at the hands of 
the Great Powers would have been more to her ultimate advantage than any,

I THINK it right to state to your Lordship, with reference to your 
despatch to Lord Westmorland of the 20th instant, No. 408, that neither 
myself nor the French Minister are acquainted with the despatch to Baron 
Meyendorff, explaining the interpretation put by the Russian Government upon 
the note prepared for the signature of the Porte at Vienna, The despatch 
which I read, as far asa very hurried perusal of it enables me to speak of it, 
dwelt rather upon the objections entertained by the Emperor to allowing amy 
alterations of a note to which he had acceded in its original form, than upon the 
nature of the proposed modifications themselves. 

Your Lordship will readily anderstand that I have very little intelligence to 
offer you which may tend to ero light upon the involved question upon which 
public attention is almost exclusively fixed, the fact being that all Cabinet 
messengers have received orders to proceed with their despatches to Warsaw. 

One only circumstance has come to my knowledge, which 18 deserving of 
mention, and the more so 45 it may entirely alter the situation of Eastern 
affairs. 

A letter from Odessa, dated the 19th instant, acquaints the Freneh Mission 
that six steamers, three English and three French, have been detached from the 
combined fleets, and have arrived before Constantinople for the purpose of 
affording protection to the Sultan and to the Christian po ulation, both m some 
danger from the warlike and fanatical spint which prevails in the capital ; while 
according to accounts which have been received from the same port by M. de 
Séniavine, five vessels of each fleet are now anchored in the Bosphorus, 

It may be well that I should observe to your Lordship that a reference to 
my correspondence will show that [ had taken various opportunities for pointing 
ont to the Russian Government that an appeal made to over-excited religious 
feelings in this country would be tolerably certain to light up a corresponding 
flame in Turkey, whilst for some time past it hus been the abject of the Russian 
Cabinet to exhibit the fanaticism and violence observable among the ‘Turks as 
the natural consequences of the injudicious support which their resistance to 
very legitimate demands had met with from the English and French Govern- 
ments.

Lord A. Loftus to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received October 7s) 


(No. 21, Confidential.) 
My Lord, Berlin, October 5, 1859. 


THE intended visit of the Emperor of Russia to the Prussian Court, as 
reported in my previous despatch, is an event of perhaps more striking import- 
ance than the precipitate visit of His Prussian Majesty to Warsaw, and is caleu- 
lated to impress the uninitiated with an opinion that a cordial alliance has been 
voneluded between the two Monarchs. 

The devotees of Russia will not certainly fail to describe this event in the 
most glowing terms, and to imbue the public mind with the conviction that in 
the face of passing events the three northern Courts are intimately allied in 
mutual support and for mutual protection. 

The union of the three Sovereigns at Warsaw has, no doubt, been intended 
by the Czar as a eounter-demonstration to the appearance of the allied fleets at 


Constantinople, and may ‘deed momentarily succeed in imposing on the eredu- 
Jous and timid sensibilities of the public mind, 

Hhore ia no doubt entertained but that the Emperor has in view to resusci- 
tate the Holy Alliance, and that no efforts have been or will be spared on his 
par to inveigle His Prussian Majesty into some treaty or arrangement with 
Lassi. 

Your Lordship will have remarked that His Prussian Majesty was neither 
attended to Wursaw by any member of his Ministry, nor even by any person of 


hia household of a political tendency. All possibility, therefore, of signing any 
positive engagement was frustrated. | 
1 am privately and confidentially informed from an authentic source that 


_ the nation, that internal disorders would soon be added to hero

the Emperor of carrying through this scheme was to accompany the King here, 
for the purpose of endeavouring, with the aid of the Queen and the Court party, 
to gain over Baron Manteuffel; and in defwult of this, to resort to any other 
means by which he might attain this object. 

It is therefore of the highest importance that I should inform your Lordship 
and it is with the greatest satisfaction that | am enabled to do go, that Baron 
Manteuffel is steadfastly resolved and determined to oppose to the utmost an

The policy of Prussia in the present crisis is evident and unmistakeable. 
She has nothing to gain by an alliance with Russia, She has everything to risk 
and to lose. Her finances would not allow her to engage in war, except at great 
sacrifice; her commerce and her industry would be ruined. She might be 
dragged into costly and deadly strugeles in Hungary, Italy, and even Poland 
from which she could reap no future compensation ; whilst the alliance with 
Russia would be so anti-national, so unpopular, and would wei rh so heavily on 

. | ther misfortunes, 

On the other hand, her natural alliance is with England. It is dictated by 
two great principles, which in the present day are all-powerful. First, that of 
supporting Protestantism, and the furtherance of civil and religious liberty ; and 
secondly, by the community of commercial and material interests. 

__ At the present conjuncture, when the success of the Emperor's schemes 
might produce the gravest consequences, I have taken every means in my power 
through influential friends of Baron Manteuffel, to convey to him the vital 
importance to Prussia of separating herself from Russian policy, of maintaining 
her neutrality. The strongest arguments have been laid before him, and I have 
the conviction that he will submit them to the highest quarter. I conceive that 
at the present moment all that we can ask of Prussia is neutrality, Our gain 
will even be considerable in keeping her detached from Russia. Of a successful 
issue In this respect I have no doubt, so long as Baron Manteuftel can hold his 
position; and at this present critical moment, and on a question in which be 
would be supported by public opinion, his secession from office would be too 
dangerous and embarrassing an object for his opponents to aim at.

No. 42. 
The Earl of Westmorland to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received October 7.) 


(No. 363.) 
My Lord, Vienna, October 4, 1853. 

| TRANSMITTED to your Lordship, the day before yesterday, the two 
telegraphic despatches which had reached me from Lord Stratford de Redcliffe, 
dated Constinenopls; the 25th and 26th ultimo, the last of which contained the 
important intelligence of the decision in favour of a declaration of war against 
Russia, which had been adopted by the Great Council of the Ottoman Empire. 

T communicated this intelligence to Count Buol, who had not as yet 
received it from the Internuncio, although from his previous despatches he was 
prepared to expect it. | 

Fully aware of the gravity of such a decision unanimously adopted by the 
Divan, Count Buol still did not consider it as precluding all hopes of a peace: 
able arrangement. He looked upon the statement in Lord Stratford’s despatch 
“that this decision had been taken notwithstanding the efforts of the Represen- 
tatives of the Four Powers, and more particularly of his own,” as affording some 
reason to expect that the counsel of the Sultan’s allies might still have weight in 
preventing immediate hostilities, an expectation which was fortified by the 
decision of the Council that the declaration of war, and the measures to be 
adopted, were to be left to the Sultan. 

Count Buol expressed his anxious hope that the united action of the Four 
Powers would be employed to obtain this object, and should a term he fixed (as 
reported by M. de la Cour) for the evacuation of the Principalities previous to 
the commencement of hostilities, he thought that the time so gained might be 
taken advantage of to present to the Government of the Sultan the project of 
declaration submitted for your Lordship’s approval, and which had received the 
sanction of the Russian Government, 50 8 to induce the ‘Turkish Ministers to 
pause before they brought upon their country the incalculable evils and dangers 
inseparable from a state of war. 

Count Buol reiterated his conviction, that the statement contained in that

Sir, Foreign Office, October 6, 1853. 

BARON BRUNNOW called upon me yesterday to inquire whether any 
decision had been taken by Her Majesty's Government upon Count Buol’s 
despatch, which, as he learned from Count Nesselrede, was to be communicated 
to me by Count Colloredo. 

In reply, 1 told Baron Brunnow that no final decision could be taken on 
that despatch until it had been submitted to the Cabinet ; but in the meanwhile 
I should not hesitate to ‘aform him that, under no circumstances would Her 
Majesty’s Government recommend the Turkish Government now to accept the 
Vienna note: Ist, because it would be useless, as the Porte had determined not 
to accept it without modifications 5 and 2ndly, because a despatch from the 
Austrian Government, containing assurances a5 to the intentions of Russia, 
could not, in the eyes of Her Majesty's Government, neutralize the despatch of 
Count Neaselrode, in which those intentions were disclosed in a manner to leave 
no doubt as to the interpretation that would hereafter be put upon the Vienna 
note by Russia. 

I added that, assuming that Russia only asked what she had a right to 
claim, and what, consequently, Turkey was prepared to concede, it appeared 
ineredible that all Europe should be kept in a state of suspense and excitement 
respecting a form of words which, under the circumstances, 1 assumed ought to 
present no difficulty whatever; but that no settlement of differences was possible 
by notes requiring explanations, and accompanied by vague assurances, 

Baron Brunnow subsequently alluded to the letter he had received from 
me, and begged | would receive a remark he was about to make with the same 
friendly spirit and sincere desire to avoid misunderstanding between our Govern- 
ments in which it was offered ; and he then, after reciting the passage in my 
letter respecting the right of the British fleet not only to enter the Dardanelles, 
but to pass through the Straits, said, that if the British fleet entered the Black 
Sea, it might be regarded by the Russian Government as a serious proceeding, 
that would impart a new character to the question at issue. But Baron Brun- 
now again requested me to understand that he had no instructions from his 
Government on the subject, and had merely wished to record his own opinion. 

I suid that the passage of the letter to which he referred was a statement 
of the right possessed by Her Majesty's Government in consequence of the 
occupation of the Principalities by Russia, and the suspension of the Treaty of 
1841+ and that the manner of exercising that right would depend upon cireuin- 
stanees into which I should not then enter, 88 he had received no instructions 
from his Government to make the inquiry, and had confined himself to giving 
his own opinion in a tone and spirit that were unobjectionable, 

Baron Brunnow informed me that ‘t would be his duty to send a reply to 
my note, but he hoped it would not render a rejoinder necessary, a5 he chou 
regret that the correspondence was prolonged, I said that would entirely 
depend upon the nature of his reply.

My Lard, Foreign Office, October 8, 1853. 

IN my despatch No, 326, I stated to you the substance of a despatch from 
Count Buol, which had been communicated to me by Count Colloredo, and 
which contained a project of note to be signed by the Four Representatives at 
Content? and delivered in exchange for the original note sent from 

jenna. 

Your Lordship will express to Count Buol the regret of Her Majesty's 
Government at being unable to concur in a measure to which the Austrian 
Government attaches so much importance, but which Her Majesty's Govern- 
ment are convinced would be attended with no other result than fresh disap- 
pointment and further loss of time. 

The Turkish Government have declared that they cannot accept the 
Vienna note without the modifications, which they had a pertect right to pro- 
pose, and which were adopted by the Conference, but which were unfortunately 
rejected by the Cabinet of St, Petersburgh. Her Majesty's Government know, 
therefore, that it would be useless to recormmend the note in ita unaltered form ; 
and they know, moreover, that it would be dishonourable to do so with refer- 
ence to the interpretation put upon it by Count Nesselrode’s despatch to Baron 
Meyendorff, which the project of note now proposed by Count Buol would not 
neutralize, nor would it afford any real security to the Porte. 

Her Majesty's Government will not doubt that the assurances contained in 
that note were given with a desire to remove the apprehensions felt by the 
Turkish Government; but there is reason to fear that by such means the object 
desired will not be attained, for the note appears to adopt the sense in which 
Russia persists in construing the Seventh Article of the Treaty of Kainardji, and 
thus, by maintaining that the privileges and immunities of the Greek Church have 
been conferred in consequence and in fulfilment of that Article, to assume u 
protectorate over the Greek subjects of the Sultan. 

But the Seventh Article, by which the Sultan promises protection to. the 
Christian religion in all its churches, confers no protectorate upon the Emperor 
of Russia. A new right is therefore sought, and it is one that the Sultan, with 
due regard to his independence, cannot coneede, The Emperor of Russia, how- 
ever, disclaime all desire of nequiring any new right, and it is impossible there- 
fore to comprehend why # point that could so easily he made ee should so 
perseveringly be left in doubt. : 

Count Buol’s note renews the assurances that are to be found in the 
circular of Count Nesselrode, that tne Emperor asks nothing contrary to the

My Lord, Berlin, October 7, 1853, 
THE messenger Webster delivered to me this day, at 2 o'clock F.M., your 


Lordship’s despatches to No. 12 inclusive. 

After hastily perusing them, I waited on Baron Manteuffel, and was 
fortunate to have a few moments’ conversation with his Excellency previous to 
his departure for Potsdam, to receive His Prussian Majesty and the Emperor of 
Russia. 

His time was too limited (and more particularly as his Excellency is not 
conversant with English) to allow of my communicating to him in ertenso (im 
obedience to the instructions contained in your Lordship’s despatch No. 11) the 
despatch No. 222, which your Lordship had addressed to Sir H. Seymour, 
pourtraying with such force and clearness the grounds on which Her Majesty's 
Government could no longer counsel the Porte to accept the Vienna note, when 
I expressed to his Excellency the absolute necessity, under the present altered 
circumstances, of devising some fresh mode of arrangement, 

His Excellency said that if the Porte persisted in her refusal to sige the 
note without modifications, he did not well see how Russia could accept the 
note with modifications, and that in this case the Vienna note would become a 
dead letter. 

L stated to his Excellency that the declaration oat proposed to be given 
to Turkey as an equivalent for her modifications, offered no guarantee for the 
future, on the part of Russia; that the Russian name would pass down to 
posterity in indelible characters ready to be produced as a living document on 
any favourable occasion, whilst the declaration of the Four Powers, after having 
undergone a tardy conception and a hurried birth, would, unless duly signed and 
ratified by the Russian Government, bear no stamp of legul value; that it might 
hereafter be subjected to as dubious a construction as had now been offered to 
the Vienna note. 

I further remarked to his Excellency that there was no. use in discussing 
this point further, for the Porte positively would not sign the note as if now 
stood, and therefore if any amicable arrangement was to be attained, it must be 
sought for through another channel, 

I then read to his Excellency with emphasis the instructions embodied in 
your Lordship’s No. UI. 

[ could perceive that his Excellency was impressed with the decisive tone 
of your Lordship’s despateh, but he did not offer any further remark. 

T have, &c. :
