Lord A. Loftus to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received October 10.) 


(No. 26. Confidential.) 
My Lord, Berlin, October 7, 1553. 

I WAS anxious to profit of the few moments of my interview with Buron 
Manteuffel this day to impress him deeply with the grave importance to Europe 
and to his own country of the interview which his Excellency would shortly 
have with the Emperor of Russia; and | thought it my duty to express to him 
my conviction that attempts would be made to induce him to enter into pro- 
mises or engagements which would materially change the system he had 
hitherto expressed his intention to pursue, and prove of the most disastrous 
consequences to the pment and future interests of Prussia. 1 repeated to him 
again the arguments I had used in favour of Prussia maintaining an independent 
line, as reported in my No, 21, and the danger that must result to her from an 


47 


alliance with Russia, and I quoted to his Excellency the words of the Great 
Frederic, “ that the quarter from which Prussia has most to fear was Russia.” 

His Excellency listened with attention, and I could well perceive 18 per- 
fectly prepared to withstand any attempt that may be directed against him. He 
seems to place reliance on the King, and to be assured that His Majesty will 
remain steadfast to the policy he was pursuing, and to the views he has so often 
expressed. It must also be borne in mind that the King has personally since 
1848 no great feeling or predilection for the Emperor Nicholas. 

Baron Manteuffel remarked to me that there was only one idea which 
appeared to weigh on His Majesty’s mind: it was the continual fear of France 
and French invasion. 

I told his Excellency that this fear ought rather to bind him more closely 
to England ; that in the event of war his greatest security would be in not allying 
himself with Russia. 

Baron Manteuffel told me in the most resolute manner that they would 
never get him to sign any engagement with, or make any promises of whatever 
nature to, the Emperor of Russia. . 

I trust, my Lord, that in lieu of having achieved a victory, His Imperial 
Majesty will quit the Prussian capital with having sustained a moral defeat, the 
greater for having sought his end in person. 

[have the honour to inclose to your Lordship an article in original and 
translation from the Kreuz Zeitung,” \the Russian organ,) with respect to the 
visit of the Emperor of Russia, at the end of which is very ambiguously 
expressed a doubt that it will attain any political object. 

His Imperial Majesty will remain at Potsdam until Monday next, and will 
return on the morning of that day to Warsaw. 

[ shall hope on Tuesday to be informed of what has passed at Warsaw and 
here, and shall not fail to report to your Lordship all details of interest and 
importance. 

L have, &e, 
(Signed) AUGUSTUS LOFTUS,

Lord Stratford de Redeliffe to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received October 12.) 


(No. 277.) 
My Lord, Therapia, September 25, 1853. 

ON the morning of the 22nd instant T received from the Earl of Weatmor- 
land a telegraphic despatch dated the 16th; a copy of it is inclosed herewith. 
It informs me of what had ocurred in the conference at Vienna subsequently 
to the arrival of a negative answer from Russia, and to the receipt of your 
Lordship's instruction thereon to Lord Westmorland. ‘That instruction in its 
application to me was neutralised by Count Buol’'s declaration respecting 
ML Drouyn de Lhuys’ note, and by Lord Westmorland’s reference to your 
Lordship for fresh instructions, all collective action being found, as he allirme, 
impossible for the time at Vienna. 

The messenger with your Lordship's despatches to the 8th, arrived on the 
afternoon of the 22nd. 1 have nothing to acknowledge on the subject of the 
pending difference, except the correspondence with the Courts, communicated 


in copy. 

hy colleagues of Austria, France, and Prussia have received telegraphic 
despatches from Vienna, announcing the tutal refusal of the Porte’s modifications 
by Russia, and recommending anew the acceptance of Count Bual’s note 
without amendments, The idea of Austria and Prussia appears to be that the 
Porte should send its acceptance by an ‘Ambassador to Olmiitz, in the hope that 
the Emperor of Austria being there with the Emperor Nicholas, His Majesty 
might prevail upon the latter to evacuate the Principalities at once, and remove 
the Porte's distrust by satisfactory assurances. 

The Ottoman Ministers, on the other hand, persist in their previous 
determination. ‘They continue to attach a vital importance to the modifications 
of the Austrian note demanded by their Government ; and notwithstanding 
various rumours of successful intrigue and of a change of counsels, sometimes 
at the Seraglio, sometimes at the Porte, their intentions, since they received from 
the Sultan's Ambassador at Vienna # confirmation of the Russian negative, 
assume more and more a character of resistance even to war, 

My impression is, that they have it in contemplation to address a direct 
summons to Prince Gortchakott for the evacuation of the Principalitics by the 
troops under his command, allowing @ certain term for compliance ; that, in case 
of refusal on his part, they will order an ‘neursion of the side of Georgia, anc 
also perhaps an attack on the Russian gun-boats on the Danube, if not an 
attempt beyond. It 18 also, L suspect, 1m contemplation to lay an embargo on 
the Russian shipping, to send assports to the Nussian Consuls and agents 
remaining in Turkey, and to exp ain these proceedings to the nation and foreign 
Powers hy means of a public manifesto. . 

It cannot be necessary for me to assure your Lordship, that | have not 
waited for fresh instructions in order to check these tendencies by adimonishing 
the Porte of their perilous consequences, by repeating the former advice of Her 
Majesty's Government as to the acceptance of Count Buol’s note, and by holding 
out the prospect of guarantees affording more security than the proposed modifi- 
«itions of that note, Unfortunately, for the admission of your Lordship’s 
arguments, the importance attached by the Porte to its own view of the 

uestion has derived additional strength from the indifference shown to its 
ultimatum, from the silence maintained by the allied Powers with respect to its 
protest against the Russian occupation of the Principalities, from the expensive 
preparations which it has made for war ; and, finally, from the excited state of 
mind prevailing among the Mussulman population, and more especially among 
the religious classes and corporate tradesmen of the capital. 

Yesterday morning, to my surprise, and, indeed, to that of every one not 
in the secret, the Sultan, whose firmness had been doubted of late, commanded 
the attendance of his principal Ministers at the palace; and, after establishing 
in their presence the facts of the refusal of the Porte’s amendments by Russia, 
and the Porte’s determination not to give them up, directed a mecting of the 
General Council to be called for this day. 


53 


According to the ‘nformation which has reached me, I have reason to 
believe that war in principle will be the result of its deliberations, and that an 
actual declaration of war will be delayed awhile in order to afford time for some 
additional preparations, and for giving effect to some auxiliary measures that 
cannot be dispensed with, It is reported that about 100 individuals are 
invited to the Council, and that among them is an unusual number of the Ulema. 

Lhave now to state, with respect to me and my colleagues, that much 
embarragsment has arisen from the want of any positive instructions, owing, 
apparently, to some unexplained accident in the case of the Austrian and 
Prussian Ministers, for whom despatches of the 13th instant have been officially 
announced, and to distance, no doubt, and to consequent slowness of communi- 
cation, with respect to the French Ambassador and myself. 

The day before yesterday, on the receipt of telegraphic despatches from 
Vienna of the 17th, the Austrian, French, and Prussian Representatives had a 
separate meeting at Pera, and | was informed that they intended to meet again 
in the same manner, and, when agreed amon themselves, to seek 8 conference 
with me. A passage in Lord Westmorland’s telegraphic despatch to your 
Lordship of the 16th, sugested, at the same time, a suspicion of something like 
‘ntimidation to be employed by M. de Bruck in support of Count Buol’s note, 
and its unconditional acceptance by the Porte. 

I thought it best to meet these appearances at once with becoming frank- 
ness. I told M. de la Cour that I would not consent to a conference in which 
| should stand on any other than equal terms with him and our colleagues. 
received in reply from his Excellency a solemn assurance that there was no 
truth whatever in the report which had reached me of a separate understanding 
between them. I also gave M. de Brack distinctly to understand that, far 
from taking part in any language of an intimidating tendency towards the Porte 
under present circumstances, | should feel it my bounden duty, in the absence 
of instructions, to mark my repugnance fo By such mode of proceeding by a 
total separation from those who adopted it, Baron de Bruck admitted that the 
passage, which T had pointed out to him in Lord Westmorland’s report, might 
fairly warrant an unfavourable inference, but that he expected nothing of the 
kind from his Court, and certainly was not authorized as yet to employ any 
language of an intimidating character. He stated, however, that he had instruc- 
tions to complain of the treatment experienced by Christians in Bosnia, and to 
remonstrate against the employment of refugees in the Turkish arnw. 

It is obvious that representations of this kind may be addressed with 

rfect fairness and in no unfriendly apirit to the Porte; but it is also evident 
that much depends upon the tone which is given to them, and upon the extent 
to which in the sequel they my be carried, 

This morning, at an early hour, the three Representatives came in a body 
to my house. After the explanations which had taken place J received them 
with confidence, and raised no further question as to their intentions, Having 
learnt, the evening before, that o General Council was to take place at the 
Porte to-day for the purpose stated to your Lordship, | had already prepared a 
letter to Reshid Pasha, with the twofold view of making another attempt in 
favour of delay on the ground of our expected instructions, and of diverting the 
Porte, if possible, from its ‘nelination to substitute a hostile attitude for any 
further endeavour to attain its object by means of the Four Powers. The dra 
of my letter was founded on such indications of your Lordship's views as I could 
extract from the imperfect or unofficial elements within my reach; and [ tried 
to make it as impressive in admonition and as attractive in point of assurances 
as 1 could possibly venture to do without exposing myself to the hazard of being 
disavowed by Her Majesty’s Government. 

Being thus prepared, and time being as precious as the circumstances were 
urgent, I declared without reserve, but with every consideration for my col- 
leagues, that, if they would unite with me, | was ready to send in the proposed 
letter; but, with the exception of mere verbal alterations, that, if they were not 
at liberty to go 80 far, | should m self abstain from addressing the letter to 
Reshid Pasha, ‘To prevent mistakes, } read to them the whole of Lord 
Westmorland’s telegraphic despateh of the 16th. 

The French Ambassador cealaved at once that he accepted the letter without 
veaetve, ‘The Internuncic aud M. de Wildenbruch, after much hesitation and 
sincere endeavours, I believe, to overcome their scruples, declined to follow him, 
unless the declaration, constituting & future guarantee for the Porte, and sent

with your Lordship’s concurrence to M. de Bourqueney, were withdrawn, Such 
a mutilation of this essential point of my letter could not possibly receive my 
assent, the more so as the guarantee in question had been recommended by your 
Loree and ree Se to a ste proposed with the view of turning the 
™m 1 e propensities, and obtaining, against eve robabilits 
more chance for a pacific aeilemient ee a pallies 
_ ‘The issue of the meeting was that the French Ambassador decided on

My draft of the letter is inclosed herewith in copy, and the alteration 
adopted by the Austrian and Prussian Ministers is annexed to it for your Lord- 
ship's more complete information. 

It remains for me to explain the course which I subsequently adopted for 
the BUpoes of uniting a proper degree of consistency with the exigencies of the 
case. 1 addressed an instruction to M. Pisani explaining the circumstances 
which had just occurred, and inclosing to him a copy of the above-mentioned

é letter. 
____L hope to have made by this simple expedient as much impression on the

No. 64. 
Lord Stratford de Redcliffe to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received October 12.) 


(No. 279.) 
My Lord, Therapia, September 26, 1853. 

YOUR despatches to the [Sth instant, forwarded from Marseilles in Her 
Majesty's steam-ship “Triton,” reached me in the night, and at an early hour 
this morning | waited on Reshid Pasha, intending, with their assistance, to make 
yet another effort in favour of peace. | 

The General Council, in its sitting of yesterday, had not come to an 
‘revocable decision. Jt wag to meet again to-day, and there still existed a bare 
possibility of its being induced to follow a less precipitate course, 

With this last chance in view, I brought the whole purport of your Lord- 
ship’s instruction No. [84 under his Highness's consideration. I apps him 
of the friendly and attentive manner in which the Porte's modifications had 
been examine by Her Majesty’s Government, and of your Lordship’s deliberate 
conviction that they make no real addition to the securities implied in the terms, 
and particularly in the spirit, of Count Buol’s note. 1 painted in strong colours 
the danger to which the Porte would expose itself by staking its resources 
single-handed against those of the Russian Empire. 1 made no secret of those 
circumstances which, operating generally throughout Europe, and more parti- 
cularly at this moment in France, forbid the Porte to look with any degree of 
confidence to active cooperation from without. Admitting the BEEP eee and 
effective enersy which had been displayed in preparing for the worst, I reminded 
the Ottoman Minister of the several obvious deficiencies, especially in point of 
finance, under which the Porte would have to labour in # hostile contest with 
Russia. 1 did not conceal from him our opinion that, even if the allied 
squadrons were to appear in the Black Sea, they could not be expected to afford 
any effectual aid, either for impeding the progress of an invasion in Bulgaria, or 
for compelling the Russian army to evacuate the Principalities, 

With respect to the proposed means of arrangement I said that, although 
the Porte might feel a natural reluctance to sign the Vienna note unaltered, 
after its declared resolution to that effect, [ was convinced that, if the Porte’s 
interpretation of the doubtful passages in the note were formally placed under a 
ruarantee, as expressed in the terms transmitted from London and Paris to 

Tienna, and were communicated to the Cabinet of St. Petersburgh as being 
adopted by the Four Powers engaging themselves thereby towards the Sultan’s 
Government, the Porte would in reality be secured against every danger con- 
nected with the note, and enjoy in a great measure that kind of guarantee for the 
future which it had sought under a form difficult, if not impossible, to concede. 

| gave the Pasha, in conclusion, # transcript of the guarantee which I had 
described, and, finding myself more at liberty since | came into possession of 
your Lordship’s instructions, | signed officially the letter which I had prepared 
the day before, as your Lordship knows already, for joint communication to 
Reshidt Pasha. | Bs 

Providing at the same time for the almost certain contingency of a decision 
in favour of war, | implored his Highness to prevail, if possible, on the Council, 
even should it adopt he principle of going to war rather than accept ihe Vienna 
note, so far, at least, to suspend the application of that principle as to allow 
time for one more appeal to the Four Powers on the basis of their concurring to 
munrantee the Porte's interpretation of the note. 1 could not, on this sup- 
position, dispute the necessity of fixing a term, perhaps even a short one, for 
receiving an answer from Vienna; but there was so evident an advantage in 
keeping open a door, even partially, for the chances of settlement by nego. 
tiation, that I was urgent with the Ottoman Minister to place my suggestion 
before his colleagues and the Council in its most favourable ight. 

Reshid Pasha assured me that he would act in the manner I requested ; 
but he held out a very slender prospect of success, and it was evident on the 
whole that although he admitted the truth of my remuarks, and was not insensible 
to the danger in prospect, he considered the decision us virtually taken, and the 
popular feeling so strongly pronounced, as to leave the Government no safe or 
satisfactory course to pursue but that of resistance by force of arms. 


57 


_, - did not leave the Pasha till it was time for him to repair to the Council 
The decision of that Assembly, which comprised at its second meeting upwards 
of one hundred and twenty members, appears to have corresponded entirely 
with my anticipations. The Vienna note has been universally rejected as 
inadmissible without the required modifications, and a recourse to war has been 
declared indispensable ; the time and circumstances of its declaration, together 
with such measures as are to accompany it, being left to the discretion of the 
Ministerial Council, confirmed by the Sultan's authority. 

Reshid Pasha, in conveying this decision to my knowledge, authorised 
M. Pisani to assure me that he had submitted my letter, together with: those 
of my three colleagues, and also my separate suggestion of the morning, to the 
Council’s deliberate consideration. As it appears that his Highness addressed 
the assembly at no inconsiderable length, | cannot doubt his having done full 
Justice to my argument in support of your Lordship’s views, and it only remains 
forme to regret that the force of circumstances and the strength of public 
opinion have made it necessary for the Porte to maintain its consistency at 
every hazard on the side of Russia, and in opposition to the counsels of those 


who, no doubt, have the welf 1 i Turki i 
‘ are and independence of the Turkish empire 
sincerely at heart. " oe

My Lord, Therapia, September 27, 1853. 

__ THE Prussian Minister sent me a message this afternoon by his Secretary 
of Legation, suggesting the notion of a direct appeal to the Sultan on the part of 
the Four Representatives, before His Majesty is committed to a formal confirma- 
tion of the decision taken yesterday by the General Council. a rare 

I replied that with every wish for peace, and acting under a strong sense of 
responsibility, l could not perceive the slightest chance of any success Lo result 
from the proposed step. Were the Sultan, I observed, to comply with “our 
adviec, he would thereby expose himself to no small degree of embarrassment 
und even of danger. The order to summon a General Council had emanated 
directly from the Throne, and the resolutions submitted by that Assembly for 
His Majesty's epproval lad been wnanimously adopted in accordance with the 
opinion of the Mussulman publie. The Sultan could not, therefore, accede to 
our representations without placing himeelf in flagrant opposition to the chick 
notahilities of his empire, who had expressed the national sentiment, and also in 
contradiction virtually of his own deliberate act, We, on the other hand, if we 
had the advantage, which we had not, of being agreed in our language, could 
only hold out to His Majesty a vague prospect of guarantee to make up for the 
ucceptance of a note unanimously condemned, whether right or wrong, by the 
Council as dangerous and humiliating to the Porte. Compliance might save 
him from the immediate perils of war, but only at the risk of disturbin the 
public tranquillity, and finally of losing both bis throne and his life, se 

I learnt from M. de Wildenbruch’s messenger that Baron de Bruck had

exertions, many weak points to guard, or deficiencies to supply. Among the

Pasha, there is reason to suspect that the class of staff-officers is far from being 
effective. The Porte looks abroad for the means of supplying this deficiency ;

will probably be kept in the back ground out of deference to the former of those 
Powers, | know not where, except in England or France, the Porte is likely to

Inclosure in No. 68.. 
M. E. Pisani to Lord Stratford de Redcliffe. 


My. Lord, Therapia, September 24, 1850. 

I HAVE the honour to report that M. de Steind! called on Reshid Pasha 
to tell him that Baron de Bruck requested that the General Council should be 
porcone until Wednesday or Thursday; that your Lordship and M. de la 

our, whom the Internuncio had seen this morning, also concurred in the same 
opinion, and that he was instructed strongly to advise the acceptance of the 
Vienna note “ purement. et simplement.” 

To this Reshid Pasha replied, that he had not in his power to defer the 
meeting of the General Council any longer, since he received peremptory orders 
from the Sultan that the Council should not be delayed any further, amd 
assembled for to-morrow, Sunday. He asked M, de Steind! whether Baron de 
Bruck had any communication to make to the Porte, or whether it was merely 
to urge them to accept the note? M1. de Steindl’s answer being that he had no 
new proposal and confining himself to what he had already stated, his Highness 
observed to him, that he was authorized to tell Baron de Bruck that from the 
Sultan down to the last Turk, all were firmly resolved to run the risk of being 
annihilated rather than sacrifice their independence and sovereign rights by 
acceding to the proposed note, That even supposing, said he, that cuarintees 
will be offered to us, those guarantees will never be of a nature to safeguard our 
sovereign rights, and prevent Russia from directly interfering in our internal 
affairs. 

M. de Steindl having told Reshid Pasha that Austria entertained appre- 
hension that the Porte might turn to account the national feeling, and give the 
character of a holy war, his Highness said, that far from contemplating any such 
idea, the Porte was most careful to declare, both verbally and in writing, that if 
she was compelled to fight she would do so for the saered rights of the 
Sovereign and the independence of his Government ; whereas Russia did not fail 
to proclaim to the world that she was to undertake a holy war against Turkey, 
and made all sorts of publications to rouse the national fecling against us, 

M, de Steindl having brought the conversation about the refugees said, 
that he understood they were to be enlisted in the Turkish army, and that if 
such were the case Austria would be exceedingly displeased with such proceed- 
ing. Reshid Pasha returned for answer, that the Porte 1s certainly at liberty to 
employ any one and any means against Russia; but he could assure him, mean- 
while, that the Porte will be cautious to avoid doing anything which might be 
disagreeable to Austria; and as long as Austria will behave as a friendly Power 
towards ‘Turkey, she might depend upon the good faith and good will of the 
Porte to abstain from giving umbrage to a neighbouring and friendly Power; but 
in the contrary case she will be free to act according to circumstances, 

I have, &e. 
(Signed) ET. PISANI.

Lord Stratford de Redcliffe to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received October 12.) 


(No. 287. Confidential.) 
My Lord, Therap, October 1, 1854. 

LAST night 1 sent to apprize the French Ambassador of my intention to 
forward despatches to-day by way of Marseilles, and to offer to take charge of 
his Excelleney’s correspondence. 

This morning | learn that he went at an early hour to Reshid Pasha, of 
whom he inquired what object T had in sending off a vessel with despatchies. 
The Pasha naturally replied that he supposed I meant to send an account of 
the Porte’s decision, which did not satisly M. de la Cour, who remarked that 1 
had already written on that subject. by the telegraph. 

I beg to observe that my object in writing by express is to afford your 
Lordship full information of the state of affairs at this juncture, which I could 
not do by telegraph, and to submit my ideas as to the only perceptible modes 
of still avoiding the calamities of war. 1! have also to express my regret that 
M. de la Cour should not have shown more confidence in me than to go toa 
reac wy in search of information which | would cheerfully have given to him 
myself. 

: It appears that the French Ambassador expressed to Reshid Pasha his 
persuasion that the Porte intended to close every door to negotiation, and that 
the Pasha assured him of the Porte’s continued willingness to re-open nego: 
tiations, and to accept any proposal consistent with its sovereign rights and 
independence. His Highness added that France having originated the religious 
discussion, was bound more than any other Power to assist the Porte in case 
of need, both morally and materially ; he went on to express ® similar reliance 
on the friendly and consistent sentiments of England, intimating, in reply to 
M. de la Cour's inquiries, that he did not reckon on similar proofs of friendship 
from Prussia and Austria, the latter Court especially being unwilling, as he 
conceived, to displease the Emperor of Russia. 

I have, &e. 
(Signed) STRATFORD DE REDCLIFFE.

No. 78. 
Sir G. H. Seymour to the Earl of Clarendon.—( Received October 12.) 


(No. 510. Confidential. 
My Lerd, St. Petersturyh, October 4, 1853. 

WITHOUT stating that his information was received either from previous 
conversations with the Emperor or with Count Nesselrode, the Prussian imister 
has acquainted one of my diplomatic colleagues that hitherto it had been His 
Imperial Majesty’s intention to take upon himself the expense of the occupation 
of the Principalities: but that in the event of the Porte persisting in their 
refusal to sign the Vienna note, he will order an advance of fresh troops into the 
Principalities ; will throw the whole expense of his armaments upon the Sultan ; 
and will not withdraw his armies until the uttermost farthing of this sum, what- 
ever may be its amount, shall be paid. 

I have no hesitation in saying that this resolution is very much what is to 
be expected from a Sovereign as impatient under any contradiction of his will as 
the Emperor Nicholas; but, at the same time, the doubt crosses my mind 
whether General Rochow may not have spoken of a decision which he considers 
probable as one which has actually taken place. 

My Prussian colleague bas the failing of being a little too Russian in his 
feelings and sympathies, and, if Tam not unjust by him, would be well pleased 
to hold the language which would be the most likely to promote the objects 
wihch the Imperial Cabinet have in view. 

I have, &e. 
(Signed) G. H. SEYMOUR.

HER Majesty's steam-ship © Caradoc” being on the point of starting, by 
the Admiral’s order, for Malta, with the view of catching the Indian liome-bound 
mail, I was preparing to avail myself of the opportunity when your Lordship's 
despatches to the 24th instant arrived. A hasty perasal of the correspondence 
has absorbed so much of the short time at my disposal that, I can only forward 
the important papers which I have this moment received from the Ottoman 
Secretary of State for Foreign Affairs. ‘They consist of an explanatory declara- 
tion or kind of manifesto addressed to the Four Re yresentatives, a summons to 
be addressed by Omer Pasha to Prince Gortchakoff, and an official note accom- 
panying these two papers. 

The originals are in Turkish, the French translations transmitted herewith 
were sent to me from the Porte. The English translation of the note was made 
by Mr. Alison. 

My previous correspondence will have prepared your Lordship for this 
decisive communication. 

M. Pisani informs me that the papers now forwarded have received the 
Sultan's formal sanction ; and that the letter for Omer Pasha will be transmitted 
to Shumla early to-morrow morning. 

I learn, moreover, on the same authority, that the Sultan has directed 
Reshid Pasha to apply to the French Ambassador and myself by note for the 
ugsistance of the respective squadrons.

Lord A. Loftus to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received October 15.) 
(No. 32. Seeret and Confidential.) 
My Lord, Berlin, October 11, 1853. 

| WAITED by appointment on Baron Manteutfel yesterday morning, and 
found his Excellency cheerful and gay, contrasted with the thoughtful and pre- 
occupied mood which he had evinced at my last interview. His Excellency 
expressed himself as feeling relieved of a heavy weight, and as breathing more 
freely since the Emperor of Russia's departure. 

His Excellency informed me that all had ended as he had previously hoped, 
and that he had undergone a severe and heavy pressure. 

He stated to me that in his first interview with the Emperor, His Imperial 
Majesty was much excited and had used harsh terms (des termes outrées), in 
which Prussia had come in for her full: share. The Emperor stated to his 
Excellency that “ his last rouble and his last man were and would be at Prussia’s 
disposal,” and inquired what he could expect in return? Baron Manteutfel 
ruplied that Prussia was not in want of either; that her interest: demanded that 
she should remain neutral; that it was impossible for her to sacrifice her position, 
and to act in concert or alliance with Russia in the Oriental question ; and that 
in preserving a neutral course, Prussia hoped she might be the better enubled to 
tender her impartial good offices in the cause of peace. 

Along conversation then ensued, which his Excellency supported by arguin 
aie impossibility of Prussia being brought to cooperate in any manner wit 

ssi. 

1 inquired of Baron Manteuffel whether any direet proposition in writing in 
the shape of a Protocol or Convention had been submitted by the Emperor. 
He replied, with some degree of vagueness and hesitation, © qu'il n'y avait pas 
un papier précisement sur la table.” 

In the course of further discussion the Emperor said, ** Voili les flottes 
qui sont entrées dans les Dardanelles, Est-ce que vous souffrez ainsi une 
‘afraction du ‘Traité de 1841?" Baron Manteutfel reminded His Imperial 
Majesty that Prussia had likewise witnessed the occupation of the Danubian 
Principalities. 

The interview. lasted some hours, during which His Imperial Majesty 
appears to have exhibited great warmth of temperament occasioned by disap- 
pointment, 

Baron Manteufiel was firm and resolute in refusing to enter into any engage- 
ment present or future, or give any promise to the Emperor of the support of 
Prussia; and Jam led to believe from another souree that his Excellency openly 


71 


stated to the Emperor in the presence of the King that he would resign his 
portfolio rather than act in opposition to his duty and his conscience. 

On the following day, previous to the Emperor's departure, Baron Man- 
teuffel had again a protracted audience of His Imperial Majesty, when they 
were closeted alone. 

Baron Manteuffel informed me that on this occasion the Emperor was more 
calm, and assumed a different tone; His Imperial Majesty seemed to evince an 
indifference whether Prussia would act with him or not, hinting that it was of 
no moment to him, and that he had more the interests of Prussia at heart; but 
that for himself, were he to exhaust the last rouble in his ‘Treasury, he would 
fight alone. 

Baron Manteuffel further informed me, that in conversation the Emperor 
had stated that he should not attack the Turks—that he should act on the 
defensive ; but he seemed to expect that they would he the first to attack him in 
the provinces. : 

His Imperial Majesty likewise remarked to his Exeelleney: © Je viens de 
recevoir dea nouvelles de Constantinople du 90. Il n'y avait pas encore eu 
une déclaration de guerre ; voyez comime vos nouvelles sont fausses.” 

His Imperial Majesty appears to have used and fruitlessly exhausted all 
his immense power of captivation and menace; whilst Baron Manteuffel stood 
unflinchingly stedfast and determined. Prussia may indeed be proud that at 
so eventful a moment she was possessed of a Minister who had the courage, 
firmness, and straightforward honesty to face the Czar of Russia, and to resist 
manfully counsels and demands which were incompatible with the interests and 
safety of his country. 

Baron Manteuffel informed me that he could evidently Nears that the 
Emperor was desirous of peace. His Imperial Majesty stated that having once 
accepted the Vienna note, he could make no further advance ; but his language 
and manner seemed to imply that he was open to receive any propositions 
from other quarters, and the impression I gathered from what fell from Baron 
Mantenffel is that His Imperial Majesty almost invited them, 

Having been privately informed from a eredible source that the Emperor 
had-urged the King to send a corps Warmée into Poland, in case it should be 
necessary, in the event of war, for Russia to move the second corps into Podolia 
or elsewhere, and that klis Majesty had refused to lend himself to any eventualities : 
I inquired of Baron Manteuffel whether any particular allusion had been made 
by the Emperor to Poland, His Excellency replied with some hesitation, that no 
epecial allusion had been mate, further than that the Emperor had remarked 
that he knew attempts would be made to raise a rebellion there, but that he 
had force enough to quell it. 

Baron Manteuffel also told me that nothing of a political nature had been 
actually under discussion at Warsaw, and that the Eiperor had only read to 
the King a vast number of despatches and private correspondence from Princess 
Lieven and others at Paris. 

Your Lordship will doubtless perceive that the aim the Emperor had im 
view was to poison the King’s mind against France and to excite his apprehen- 
sions of her. 

In closing this report, | may be permitted to observe to your Lordship that 
on & subject of 50 grave and so confidential a nature as the interview between 
the Emperor of Russia and Baron Manteuffel, I found his Excellency naturally 
disinclined to divulge more than was sufficient to place his conduct In its true 
light, and that | consequently was cautious not to press inquiry on his 
Excellency indelicately. 

1 am inclined to believe that his Excellency is anxious not to create any bad 
feeling with Russia by unnecesss ily displaying in too open terms the failure of 
the Emperor of Russia s viait. 

The Prince of Prussia was at Potsdam during the eon aga atay there, and 
Lum informed, from a private source, strongly supported the views and policy of 
Baron Manteuffel. 

On taking leave of his Excellency he begged me to convey to your Lord- 
ship his assurance that no promise or engagement of any kind had been given 
to the Emperor; and he further expressed a wish that what he had related to 
me should be considered as strictly secret and confidential, 

I have, &c.

My Lord, Berlin, October 12, 1853. 

| HAVE not failed to execute the instructions contained m your Lordship's 
despatch No, 12 of the Sth instant, and to convey to Baron Manteuffel the 
favourable light in which your Lordship had received his idea of renewing the 
negotiation on the Eastern question in London; and | am specially charged by 
his Excellency to express his thanks to your Lordship, for the good reception 
which hig proposition had met with. 

Lhave had some conversation with his Excellency on that subject both on 
Monday lust, previous to his taking Her Majesty's decision, and again this 
morning. 

On the former occasion his Excellency informed me that he was of opinion 
that, under present circumstances, the Vienna note was no longer applicable, and 
that some new arrangement on another basis must be sought for, His Excel- 
lency seemed further of opinion, that nothing more could be expected from the 
Vienna Conference. ‘These feelings appeared to me to strengthen his convic- 
tion that a pacific arrangement was only now to be attained in London. 

Since his interview with the Emperor of Russia, his Excellency is the more 
‘clined to the idea thut some effort in. the above sense should be made in 
London, as he is persuaded that the Emperor is desirous of a pacific solution. 

Baron Manteuffel informed me to-day that he had submitted the question 
to His Majesty, who had consented, after many objections to the adoption of 
his proposal. It has been, therefore, agreed, that the Chevalier Bunsen shall be 
instructed to enter upon the subject confidentially with your Lordship, and he: 
will be furnished with instructions to this intent. 

| inquired of his Excelleney what was the precise nature of the proposition 
which he intended tomake, His Excellency replied, that as he was anxious to 
avoid any severe scrutiny or misrepresentation of his views at the outset, he 
should merely propose as preliminaries: 

Ist, ‘That a pacific settlement should be sought to be attained by means of 
negotiation. 

2ndly. That the whole question of differences between Turkey and Russia 
should be settled from beginning to end on a firm and permanent basis. 

On my inquiry his Excellency seemed to consider that the broad haais 
which he assumes, would imply the annulling of all ‘Treaties existing between 
Russia and Turkey, and the adoption of a frost one which would stand in their 
place. He stated that, in his opinion, there should be an end of everything ab 
antiquo, and a thorough new settlement de novo, 

T remarked to his Excellency that this was a difficult, but perhaps not a 
hopeless undertaking, and that, in this enlightened age of civilization, when all 
nations were desirous of peace, there ought to be no reagon for despairing of 
obtaining, by peaceful negotiation, that complete resettlement which must be the 
inevitable result of a war. 

T inquired of his Excellency, whether any knowledge of these intentions 
had been communicated to the Emperor of Russia. His Excellency replied, 
that a negotiation in London had been mentioned to His Imperial Majesty, but 
the Emperor hastily broke off the conversation, remarking that London was to 
him the least desirable place; but that if a sutiafuctory arrangement could be 
presented he would certainly accept it, from whatever quarter itcame. Daron 

Janteuffel replied to the Emperor, that as the greatest difficulty was offered in 
London, it was there that it could be solved with the greatest fucility. 

His Imperial Majesty also expressed a wish, that whatever arrangement 
might be come to should be first presented to, and accepted by the Porte, as he 
could not again subject himself to the treatment he had received from Turkey 
with respect to the Vienna note. 

His Imperial Majesty, however, eaid that his impression was, that the 
Maritime Powers were bent on making war against him, in which ease he could 
not hold back from it, 7

He told me he would have given me a copy of the memoir he had submitted

No. 86. 
Sir G. H. Seymour to the Earl of Clurendon.—(Received October 15.) 


(No. 514. Confidential.) 
My Lord, St. Petersburgh, October 6, 1853, 

1 HAVE the honour to acknowledge the receipt of your Lordship's 
despatch of the 27th ultimo, No. 218, containing the copies of three despatches 
relating to the departure of the British and French fleets from Besika Bay to 
Constantinople, 

Your Lordship will I trust pardon me if I express the great satisfaction 
which I feel at learning that appearances at that capital have been such as fully 
to justify a disregard of the Convention of 1641, even sup sing the justification 
not to have been preceded by the forcible entry of the I ussian troops into the 
Sultan’s dominions. 

As | have taken the liberty of stating to your Lordship on more than one 
occasion, I have been very desirous that the unhappy differences between 
Turkey and Russia should be decided by the submission of both parties to an 
award of the Allied Powers; but fromthe moment that it became clear that this 
was accepted by the one in a sense favourable to a continuance of those 
encroachments by which the peace of Europe would be endangered, it becomes 
of the utmost importance that such barriers as English and French fleets should 
be opposed to Russian ambition. 

In saying this, 1 would beg to remark that | have no reason to change the 
opinions which I have frequently submitted to your Lordship as to the 
Emperor’s views. 

Now, as before, | believe that His Majesty began this deplorable quarrel, 
and even took military possession of the Principalities, neither with the idea of 
overrunning the rest of Turkey, of adding to his already overgrown possessions, 
or of involving himself in disputes with his allies; but 1 cannot doubt that His 
Majesty entertains most exaggerated ideas as to the influence to which he 1s 
entitled in the country of a feeble but independent Sovereign ; and that the time 
is fully come when some demonstration must be made which will have the effect 
of showing where the limits to his authority are traced, the passage of which 
constitutes a trespass as well upon Europe as upon Turkey. 

As L have several times taken the liberty of remarking to your Lordship, 
the Emperor is, 1 believe, less opposed than is commonly thought to the 
existence of Turkey; but the independence of Turkey is an idea very foreign ta 
his thoughts, and it is one to which it is very important that he should be 
brought to reconcile himself. 

I have, &c, 
(Signed) G, H. SEYMOUR.

My Lord, Foreign Office, October 15, 1853. 

1 APPROVE of your having forwarded to me by the extra messenger

The Chevalier Bunsen, in his interview with me this morning, did not 
allude to the project for settling the differences between Russia and Turkey, 
that was mentioned to your Lordship by Baron Manteufel, as reported in your 
despatch No. 36 of the 12th instant; but he asked me what course Her Majesty's 
Government intended to pursue. 

I told the Chevalier Bunsen that it was proposed to draw up a fresh note, 
together with a Protocol, founded upon the Treaty of 1841, which should be 
forwarded immediately to Constantinople with a strong recommendation to the 
Porte to accept the note, but not precluding such modifications as might be 
agreed upon between the Representatives of the Four Powers and the Turkish 
Government, 

| have to observe, however, that an arrangement of this nature may not be 
practicable, nor indeed would it he sufficient in the event of war having heen 
formally declared, and hostilities commenced between the Two Powers. An 
instrument more formal than a note would then be required for placing their 
relations upon a permanent and satisfactory footing, and future doubts and 
disputes should be euarded against by a Treaty. 

Baron Manteuffel, to whom your Lordship is instructed to communicate 
this despatch, will see that the views of Her Maissty's Government coincide 
with those which he expressed to your Lordship. 

But Her Majesty's Government do not disguise from themselves that the 
assent of Russia to a new and permanent form of arrangement is not to be 
reckoned sib The views which His fmperial Majesty is known to entertain 
with regard to the approaching and inevitable dissolution of the Ottoman 
Empire; the policy towards ‘Turkey that he has of late pursued, and seenis 
determined to persist in; together with the indisposition he has always Mmiltli- 
fested to admit of foreign ‘aterference in the relations between [Russia and the 
Porte, while they render the settlement of those relations upon a new and equit= 
able footing most desirable for the future peace of Europe, yet at the sume time 
make His Faipertal Majesty's acquiescence in any few arrangement not impro- 
bable, But on the other hand, it is to be borne in mind that unless: the result 
of war was favourable to Turkey, she would have no claim to depurt from 
‘Treaties by which she has so recently declared herself to be bound, 

The difficulties by which the whole question 1s atill beset, and the compli- 


 eations which unavoidably arise from the distances which separate the contending 


Powers and those whieh are willing to mediate between them, and the failure 
which, from various causes, has attended the Conference at Vienna, induee Her 
Majesty’s Government to give their entire assent to the proposal of the Prussian 
Government, that the negotiation should hencefarward be carried on im London. 

Baron Manteuffel informed your Lordship that the Emperor of Russia had 
expressed his repugnanee to the proposal, and had declared that to him Lonidon 
would be the least desirable place for conducting the negotiation. Butat any 
conference held here the interests of Russia would be fully represented : and 
His Imperial Majesty is no more justified in doubting the perfect impartiality of 
Her Majesty’s Government than he is in expressing his belief, as reported to

Lord Cowley to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received October 17.) 
(No. 763. Confidential.) 


My Lord, Paris, October 16, 1853. 

M. DE BOURQUENEY is Jed to think from a telegraphic communication 
dated the 6th instant which he has received from M. de la Cour, that an 
attempt will be made by the Porte to induce the English and French Ambas- 
sadors at Constantinople to enter into a Convention, binding them to employ 
the naval forces of the two countries placed at their disposal in support of any 
hostile measures it may please the Turks to take against Russia, as the price of 
the admission of those fleets within the Dardanelles. 

When the intelligence first reached M. Drouyn de Lhuys, he appeared much 
annoyed that M. de la Cour had asked for instructions how to act should this 
demand be made, With that want of forethought and neglect of consequences 
which too often characterize French proceedings, he appeared to think, without, 
however, directly avowing it, that the admission of the fleets into the Bosphorus 
should be secured on any conditions. In a conversation, however, which I had 
with him yesterday, he showed that he had reflected upon the inconvenience to 
which a Convention, such as had been hinted to him, would expose the two 
Governments, 

The only answer returned to M. de la Cour has been the laconic one, 
“ Puites entrer les flottes.”

No. 96. 


Lord A. Loftus to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received October 18.) 


(No. 42.) 


My Lord, Berlin, October 15, 1853. 

I WAITED on Baron Manteuffel this morning, and inquired from him 
whether he had received further intelligence concerning the proposition reported 
in my despatch No. 34 of the 12th instant, which had been expected from 
Vienna, and to which Count Crivelli, the Austrian Chargé d’ Affaires, and Baron 
Budberg, the Russian Minister, has referred in conversation with his Excellency. 

He replied that Count Cravelli had informed him, that he had received the 
despatches: he had expected from Vienna, but there was no mention in them of 
any new proposition. His Excellency was ut a loss to explain this circumstance, 
and the more so, as his Exeellency told me that there could be no doubt that 
the proposition, as stated in my despatch No. 34, had been under the considera- 
tion of Count Buol and Baron de Meyendorff, for the Emperor of Russia, when 
here, had referred to it in conversation with him, and had even informed him of 
the nature of the arrangement which was to be proposed. 

My own suspicion is, that it was a plan got up by Russia in order to seduce 
the support of Austria and Prussia, and thus to separate them from the Western 
Powers. ‘This plan may have been counteracted by the failure of the Emperor's 
designs on Prussia, and the proposition may have, accordingly, been abandoned 
as ape 

eing on this topic of distrust of Russia, | warned his Excellency against 
Prussia being entrapped to give her adhesion to proposals emanating from 
Vienna. His Excellency informed me, without hesitation, that he would never 
be carried so far, and that he would give no reply to any proposition without 
first consulting with the English Government.

No. 105, 
Lord Stratford de Redcliffe to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Recewed October 19.) 
(No. 290.) 
My Lord, 


Therapia, October 5, 1853. 

rT is very desirable for your Lordship to have the means of judging how 
far the Porte may be swayed by other than urgent and indispensable motives, in 
bringing its differences with Russia to the immediate hazard of war. The prac- 
tical importance of such knowledge in the present stage of the question may 
perhaps lie open to doubt; but still it is natural for your Lordship to seek a 
clear view of the subject; and it would be satisfactory for all who depreeate the 
disasters of war to find that the Sultan's Ministers have not given way to 
groundless fears or to illusive speculations. On these points I can, however, 
add but little to what your Lordship has been able to derive from my precedin 
correspondence and the language of the Sultan’s Minister in London, Allowing 
the assertions on one side to be neutralized hy the suspicions entertained on the 
other, conjecture and inference are all I have to offer. 

It must be admitted that the Porte has had reason to derive an increase of 
courage from circumstances which have occurred since the departure of Prince 
Menchikoff, She has seen the Four Powers acting together on her behalf; she 
has heard the voice of all Europe condemming her adversary ; she perceives that 
the public sentiment of England and France is almost universally in her favour ; 
she fais from all sides that the occupation of the Principalities by Russia con- 
stitutes acase of war; and she has not only put herself intoa state of respectable 
defence, but she has sppenlee with perfect success to the zeal of her Mussulman 
and to the loyalty of her Christian subjects, 

The effect. of these successive encouragements can hardly have failed to 
raise her confidence and to strengthen her resolution. Even on the first presenta- 
ion of Prince Menchikolfs ultimatum, the general feeling was one of resistance 
to his pretensions. There was indeed a visible abundance of desire and endeavour 
to avoid an extreme course; but the point at issue, namely, the exercise of 
Russian influence by means of a recognized right to interfere in the management 
of Greek ecclesiustical affairs, was stoutly rejected, and the dangers officially 
intimated as likely to follow on the breach of diplomatic relations between Russia 
and Turkey were braved deliberately by the Sultan and his Government, 

Motives to a decided course of action have also sprung naturally from 
another source, or rather from the same taken in a different point of view. 
Large armies and powerful squadrons cannot be collected anywhere without 
exciting strong feelings among the people, and proclamations enlisting the hearts 
ofall ina cause of common interest must necessarily bring out that popular 
spirit and national will which few Governments can entirely control, and which 
no Government can afford to throw away or to chill by unseazonable disappoint- 
ment, ‘The personal sacrifices attendant on military preparations opposed to 
suich a neighbour as Hussia, the increased pressure of taxation, and the enormous 
expenses devolving unavoidably, with much alarm and anxiety, on the State,' | 
must also have had their effect in producing an eager and impatient desire to’ 

O2 


— Se 


=) 8) 


reach somie kind of final result. ‘The Turks must naturally long to change 
their present irksome position, and to put away the yexation aud disgrace of 
acquiescing indefinitely in a forced occupation of two of their largest provinces 
by foreign armies. There may be some degree of excitement in the feelings 
thus called out; but while the Sovereign and his Government, in sympathizing 
with their people, must take the public opinion into their account, they have 
also substantial reasons of policy to plead in their justification, Such exertions 
as they have been making since the retirement of Prince Menchikoff tend more 
and more, as they are prolonged, to exhaust the resourees of the Empire, and to 
render any future assertion of its independence, however great may be the 
necessity, difficult and almost hopeless. It can hardly be matter of surprise that 
auch a concurrence of excited feelings and reasonable motives should have pro- 
duced a ferment among the fanatical, but not on that account the less influential, 
classes of the capital; that a sympathising pay should have been formed in the 
Ministry ; and that all should have relieved themselves from individual respon- 
sibility by gathering round the throne, and resorting, in failure of other hopes, to 
their own imperfect yet self-dependent means of relief. 

(tis clear that there would have been imminent danger, under the cireum- 
stances, in taking any other course, and the more pacific members of the 
Cabinet appeared as little disposed as able to make head against the general 
determination. Reshid Pasha, and others of his ability and experience, cannot 
be ignorant of the peril to which they expose their country by engaging single- 
handed in a war against Russia, ‘They may reckon to certain degree upon 
the chances of eventual assistance from England and France; but they have 
been too often admonished by me and my colleagues of the precarious natare 
of such expectations to entertain them as justifiable reasons for entering upon a 
war policy. My impression is that their motives for going to war are such as | 
have described above, and that they indulge the hope of succour from abroad, 
upon the same principle that when a ship is on fire the seamen throw themselves 
overboard, and take their chunce for struggling with the waves until they are 
picked up by some other vessel already in sight. 

Notwithstanding all this, an inference of opposite tendency may possibly 
be drawn from the Porte’s conduct in the late negotiations. The Turkish 
Ministers may be thought to have shown a want of readiness to close with fair 
terms of accommodation, by making unnecessary objections, by shifting their 
grounds, or by acting with gratuitous slowness, | 

On these several points | cannot hope to offer your Lordship any fresh 
information. If there be some appearances respecting them to justify a 
suspicion that the Porte has looked at times: rather to the camp than to the 
Cabinet for a solution of its differences with Russia, they cannot in fairness be 
separated from the difficulties and complications of the nvatter in hand, or from 
the peculiarities which still prevail here in the habits of thinking, the modes of 
transacting business, and the processes of communication. ‘There is much, no 
doubt, to disapprove, and even to complain of, in the Porte’s habitual relations 
with Christendom; but the manner, at once firm and conciliatory, with which, 
on the whole, she has proceeded under circumstances of unusual provocation 
and unjust aggression, adhering to her rights in-a spirit of independence, and 
accepting humiliations in deference to the counsels of her allies, ought surely ta 
pass to her credit and entitle her to indulgence, If she asked at one time for 
the guarantee of the Four Powers as a supplement to the terms which alone she 
considered safe and honourable, she has since evinced a willingness to desist 
from that condition. She had previously declared her readiness to subscribe the 
Vienna note; not, indeed, without modifications, but with such as their allies 
have judged to be reasonable in substance, though superfluous in form, and 
which they have strongly recommended to the acceptance of the Emperor 
Nicholas. 

At all events, my Lord, whatever circumstances may in reality have turned 
the scale fram peace to war, | am slow to believe that the Turkish Ministers are 
acting froma political preference for the latter course. It is more natural and 
reasonable to suppose that they are not plunging wantonly into hostilities under 
the influence of any unreflecting passion; butthatin despair, however mistakenly, 
of securing what they conceive to be essential to the sovereignty and independence 
of the Porte, and fearful of a popular revolution, together with the exhaustion 
of their available resources, they have resorted courageously, though reluctantly, 


89 


to the only remaining chance, as they imagine, of at least saving their honour, if 
they do not succeed in anything else. 

There is, no doubt, some rashness in deciding on such a course ; but-a 
more timid line of policy would, in their estimation, have dangers of its own, 
without offering a permanent escape from those of war. The Sultan and his 
Ministers cannot be blind to a truth which is obvious to every one. They 
must perceive that their hold upon the sympathies of any auxiliary Power is one 
which has its origin in the sense entertained by that Power of its own interests. 
Temporary circumstances may produce an exceptional effect; but in their very 
natural and reasonable anxiety to elude the grasp of Russia, they can hardly be 
blamed for looking with hope to the adverse interests and corresponding policy 
of England and France. 

T have, &e. 
(Signed) STRATFORD DE REDCLIFFE.

Lord Stratford de Redcliffe to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received October 19.) 
(No, 291.) 


My Lord, Therapia, October 5, 1853. 

A SPIRIT of self-deyotion, unaccompanied with fanatical demonstrations. 
and showing itself among the highest functionaries of the State, bids fair to 
give an extraordinary impulse to any military enterprise which may be under- 
taken against Russia by the Turkish Government, , 

The Sultan has given his reluctant consent to the negotiation of a loan, 
The corps of Ulema are preparing, a8 it is currently reported, to advance a 
considerable sum in support of the war. The Grand Vizier, the Minister for 
Foreign Affairs, and other leading members of the Administration, have resigned 
a large proportion of their horses for the service of the artillery. [Keinforee- 
ments continue to be directed towards the Danube and the Georgian frontier. 
Several steam-frgates are to be sent almost immediately into the Black Sea. 
In short, it is evident that, if hostilities commence, they will be prosecuted in a 
manner to test the strength of the contending parties, and to leave on the one 
side or on the other deep and durable traces of u truly national struggle. ‘That 
the chances are greatly in favour of Russia, when we look to the final result, 
can be doubted by few, unless the assistance of the maritime Powers be given 
to Turkey with that degree of frankness and cordiality which passing circum- 
stances may render difficult, but which more lasting interests would seem even- 


tually to require. I have, &e,

Lord Cowley to the Earl of Clarendon. —(Received October 19.) 
(No. 768.) 


My Lord, Paris, October 18, 1853. 

M. DROUYN DE LHUYS informed me yesterday that he should direct 
Count Walewski to consult your Lordship as to the propriety of asking the 
Forte's permission to garrison the Castles of the Dardanelles during the presence 
of the combined flects within those Straits. The French Minister appears to 
have been led to this idea by two considerations: Ist, the danger to which the 
fleets might be exposed should the fanatical party, whose only creed was hatred 
to Christians. in general, gain the upper hand in the councils of the Sultan ; 
Qnd, the possibility of the Russians undertaking a winter campaign, and 
advancing on Constantinople through Servia, a plan which M. Drouyn de Lhuys 
has been given to understand is or has been in contemplation. But a successful 
operation of this nature might place the Russians between Constantinople and 
the Dardanelles, and give them the command of those Straits, He thought, 
therefore, that it would be prudent to guard as far ag possivle against these 
contingencies. é 

Tobserved that I thought it very unlikely that the Turks would divest 
themselves even momentarily of the absolute command of the forts at the 
Dardanelles; but as the matter has been referred to your Lordship, I did not 
discuss it further. 

| have only to add that M, Drouyn de Lhuys did not seem to contemplate 
sending troops for the gurrison of those places, should it be agreed on all sides 
that such @ measure was desirable, He appeared to think that the Admirals 
had sufficient. means at their disposal to undertake the defence of them, 

I have, &e. 
(Signed) COWLEY.

No. 122. 
The Earl of Clarendon to the Earl of Westmorland. 


(No. 346.) 
My Lord, Foreign Office, October 25, 1853. 

YOUR Lordship's despatch No. 376 of the 15th instant has been received 
and laid before the Queen. 

Her Majesty’s Government learn with sincere satisfaction that the desire of 
the Cabinet of Vienna to co-operate with them for the maintenance of peace has 
undergone no change; and your Lordship will inform Count Buol that that 
desire is fully reciprocated on the part of Her Majesty’s Government. 

The report of your Lordship’s conversation with Count Buol was confirmed 
by a despatch from his Excellency, which Count Colloredo has placed in my 
hands, anda copy of which is herewith inclosed.* 

Count Buol appears to consider that the present moment is not Spporany 
for taking any further steps upon the momentous question at issue, and that it 
would be desirable to wait until the views of the Emperor of Russia are known 
upon the declaration of war by the Turkish Government. ; 

Her Majesty’s Government, however, have arrived at a different conclusion, 
and, in the belief that an opening was still left for negotiation, Her Majesty's 
Ambassador at Constantinople was instructed, a few days ago, to use his efforts 
to prevent the commencement of hostilities. Her Majesty's Government are, 
therefore, on every account bound to give effect to their intentions with the 
least delay possible, and I accordingly inclose to you the copies of two notest 
which you will submit to the consideration of Count Buol, and carnestly 
recommend for the adoption of the Austrian Government. 

The first is founded upon the Treaty of 1841, and refers to the assurances 
repeatedly given by the Cabinet of St. Petersburgh, and recently renewed at 
Olmiitz, as well as to the assurances that on various occasions have been 
received from the Porte. It is hoped that this note will be signed by the 
Representatives of the Four Powers at Constantinople, recommending to the 
acceptance of the Porte the note which has been framed with due regard for the 
honour and independence of the Sultan, while the maintenance of existing 
engagements between Russia and Turkey, the spiritual privileges of the Greek 
Church, and the guarantee respecting the holy places, are provided for in strict 
accordance with the assurances of the Cabinet of St. Petersburgh as to what was 
really desired of the Porte. 

Your Lordship will, however, see by my despatch No. 235 to Lord Strat- 
ford, of which a copy is inclosed, and which you will also communicate to Count 
Buol, that Her Majesty’s Ambussador is at liberty to admit of such modifications 
to this note as to himself and his colleagues may appear reasonable, and which 
ak not be of acharacter to preclude the acceptance of the note by the Emperor 
af Russia. 

Her Majesty's Government consider this to be just, because the Turkish 
Government are the only competent judges of the form of note they can properly 
assent to; and it is indispensable, in order to avoid the error committed on a 
former occasion, which the Emperor of Russia, no less than the Sultan, has a 
right to expect shall not again be repeated ; and that no proposal shall be made 
oe His Imperial Majesty which has not previously been agreed to by the 

rie.

My Lord, Berlin, October 22, 1853. 

BARON MANTEUFFEL privately informed me to-day that a copy of a 
despatch from Count Nesselrode to Baron Meyendorif has been communicate 
to him by the Russian Minister, in which the thanks of the Russian Govern- 
ment are expressed for the attempts which Austria had made at Olmutz for a 
pacific arrangement in the Bastern differences. Reference was therein made to 
the propositions which Count Nesselrode had talked over with Count Buol, 
relating to a direct arrangement being entered into between Russia and Turkey. 
The Chancellor expresses his opinion that such arrangement is the only one 
now left for a peaccable solution, and he directly refers to an Envoy being sent 
by ‘Turkey to negotiate directly with the General commanding, Prince 
Gortehakotf, 

In as far as 1 could learn, hopes of such an arrangement had not been 
entirely abandoned on the part of Russia; for General Rochow, the Prussian 
Minister at St. Petersburgh, in a despatch received only this day, refers to it, 
although news must have been then received at St. Petersburgh of the declara- 
tion of war by Turkey. 

Baron Manteuftel appeared to attach but little importance to this mode of 
pacification.

No. 125. 
Lord A. Loftus to the Karl of Clarendon.—\ Recetved October 25.) 


(No. 5). Confidential.) 
My Lord, Berlin, October 22, 1853, 


AT an interview with Baron Manteuffel this day, his Excellency informed 
me most confidentially that M. Crivelli, the Austrian Chargé d'Alfuires, had 
communicated to him a proposal on the part of his Government that a statement 
of the differences pending between Russia and Turkey, with a report of the steps 
which have been adopted by Austria and Prussia towards a pacification, should 
be laid before the Germanic Dict, and that Germany should pronounce through 
their common organ, their determination to maintain neutrality. | 

His Excellency had not yet informed His Majesty of this important com- 
munication. He seemed indisposed to partake of the Austrian view, although he 
appeared to receive with sntisfiction this proof of the neutral line which the 
Austrian Cabinet would pursue. He informed me that he had as yet tuken mo 
decision as to the reply he should make. He thought, however. o acceding to 
the wish that a report oa the Oriental question should he luid before the Diet, 
but wished that no opinion as to the course to. be pursued should be expressed 
by that body. | 

I remarked to his Excellency that it appeared to me the step he was about 
to take might establish a dangerous precedent for Prussia, and be productive of 
grave consequences to her hereafter, Prussian had on the present ovcasion 
assumed that independent line which became a great Power, and her policy was 
based on the public opinion of the nation in ‘ecoummunity with their naterial 
interests: that it would not now be in consonance with her dignity to renounce 
the important place she held in Europe into the hands of a federal body amongst 
whom Austria held the first place, and perhaps might assume the directing lead ; 
that the jurisdiction of the Germanic Diet had been (us far as | was aware) 
generally confined to matters of purely German interest; and that jreat 
Huropean questions, such as the Oriental question, ought to be treated solely by 
the great Cabinets of Europe, I therefore represented to his Excellency that it 
would be, in my opinion, unwise in Prussia to recognize the principle even of 


pe~ JD, 


102 


submitting to the Germanic Dict any report whatever relating to the Oriental 
question, and that the safest as well as the wisest course to pursue, would be 
simply to reply that in the opinion of Prussia the Oriental question was not of 
that political or internal nature on which a decision of the Diet should be 
called for. 

His Excellency, on consideration, agreed with the views and the opinions I 
had expressed, and told me that it would be his endeavour to act in consonance 
with them. He‘could not, however, distinctly state whut reply he should make 
until he had submitted the question to His Majesty’s decision. 

1 trust that the opinion which I have expressed to Baron Manteuffel on 
this subject will meet with the approbation of Her Majesty’s Government, 

have, &c. 
(Signed) AUGUSTUS LOFTUS.

My Lord, Berlin, October 22, 1853. 


IN conformity with the instructions contained in your Lordship's despatch 
No. 23, | expressed to Baron Manteuffel this day the thanks of Her Majesty's 
Government for the communication relating to the Emperor of Russia's visit to 
Berlin, which had been made to your Lordship by the Chevalier Bunsen ; and 1 
did not fail to congratulate his Excellency, in the name of Her Majesty's Govern- 
ment, upon the suceess which his wisdom and firmness, 1 position of more 
than ordinary difficulty, had attamed. 

His Excelleney begged me to return his thanks to your Lordship, and 
appeared much pleased at the confidence evineed towards him by Her Majesty's 
Government. 

L afterwards read to his Excellency your Lordship’s despatch No. 25; and 
his Excelleney was happy to learn, both from the Chevalier Bunsen and from 
your Lordships despatch, that the views of Her Majesty's Government coincide 
with those which he has expressed. It is his Excellency's fervent hope that the 
endeavour which is now making in London will meet with a successlul result. 

1 then informed his Excellency, after reading that part of your Lordship’s 
despatch relating to the intimacy and confidence subsisting between the Cabinets 
of England and France, that it was indispensably necessary that he should 
‘form the French Minister and his Government of the views of the Prussian 
Government, and of bis wish that some species of negotiation should be entered 
wpon in London, His Excellency told me that he had already signified this 
project to the French Government through Count Hatateldt, and that he had 
received in return a telegraphic despatch from him, stating that the proposal had 
been favourably received. He agreed that it would be ailvisable now to commu- 
nicate freely with the French Minister, and he assured me that he would not 
fail so to do. His Excellency at the same time requested that the project of a 
negotiation in London might be kept secret from other quarters, as he consi- 
dered that if it was prematurely divulged, considerable difficulties might be 
interposed, 

I have since seen M. de Moustier, the French Minister, who has informed 
me that Baron Munteuffel had opened to him on this subject; and I have 
likewise communicated to him the mode of pacification which Baron Manteuttel 
had in view, 

I have again to assure your Lordship that the most perfect unity and 
cordiality exist: between M. de Moustier and myself; and it shall be my duty 
to communicate with him unreservedly on the subject of Oriental affairs,

My Lord, Vienna, October 18, 1853. 
THE Turkish Ambassador at this Court received on Friday last the 
copies of the summons to be addressed by Omer Pasha to Prince Gortchakoff, 
and of the manifesto of the Sultan to his subjects, and he immediately commu- 
nicated them to Count Buol, ‘the latter stated to me that although he deeply

Sir G. H. Seymour to the Earl of Clarendon.—( Received October 25.) 


(No. 590. Seeret and Confidential.) 


My Lord, St. Petersburgh, October 14, 1853. 

TO judge of the alteration in the pretensions of Russia, since the com- 
mencement of her unhappy quarrel with the Porte, it is of some interest to 
compare the terms of the projet de note, of which a copy was’ inclosed to Lord 
Westmorland, in your Lordship’s despatch No. 826, with the language held to 
me by the Emperor, as reported in my secret despatch No 268 of the lst May. 

If at that time His Majesty had deigned to listen to my suggestion, a note 
of the kind now proposed by the Austrian Cabinet would have been unnecessary, 
and long months of painful anxiety, destined perhaps to be followed hy much 
greater misfortunes, would have been avoided. 

It may be in your Lordship’s recollection that, as recorded in my despatch 
of the lst May, I took the liberty of saying to the Emperor: “If your 
Majesty is correct in stating that no fresh rights are sought for the Imperial 
Government, the objections entertained towards the note presented for the 
Porte’s acceptance and signature must turn upon a matter of redaction ; allow 
me then to inquire whether there will be any objection to such an alteration in 
the terms of the note as shall leave a simple confirmation of old rights and 
preclude the possibility of any new ones being claimed.” 

His Majesty's refusal to comply with a suggestion fully warranted by his 
own declarations, as well as those of his ministers, too correctly shadowed out 
those difficulties in which Europe has ever since been involved, — 

I have, &e. 
(Signed) G. H. SEYMOUR,

protest entered by Baron Brunnow against the entry of Her Majesty's ships of 
war into the Dardanelles, but bad refused all credence to the statement. 

Until the receipt of your Lordship’s No. 225 and its two inclosures, it 
appeared to me hardly possibly that the condition in which Turkey has been 
sliced should be considered by any one as such as to leave her under those 
obligations which are notoriously contingent upon a state of peace, and still less

one Power to invade and occupy large portions of the Turkish territory, contrary 
to the will and interests of the Sultan, an illegality would be committed if the

and possibly in the interests of His Highness.

Sppeared ta me to have been often called for in the course of the late nego-

as offering a guarantee for the proper use of powers with which he might be

Such weight, | said, as may be given to personal character may well be 
allowed to that of the Emperor; but in affairs between States, as in those between 
individuals, it is the character of the agreement and not of the person which is 
to be considered: the stipulations to be undertaken by Turkey are those which 
are to be binding on her not only during the reign of the Emperor Nicholas but 
under those of His Majesty's followers on the Throne. 

Count Nesselrode wished that he could feel certain that the existence of 
unjust suspicions had not been betrayed of late, and added that, although grieved 
to- say so, he would not conceal from me his apprehension that it was the settled 
purpose of Her Majesty's Government to humiliate Russia. I might be assured 
that under no possible circumstances would humiliation be submitted to by the 
Emperor, 

If, I replied, this feelmg exists | am glad you have expressed it, for I 
ean declare to you, before God, in case such an asseveration be necessary, that 
your suspicion is unjust; no, | continued, you may be very certain that no 
disposition, however slight, exists with us to humiliate either Russia or the 
Emperor, or even to deprive Russia of any portion of her just influence ; but, if 
you will a wish is felt and a resolution 13 eben not to admit claims which Her 
Majesty’s Government consider that Russia is not entitled to make. 

Beyond this, | continued, I am willing to admit that Her Majesty's Govern- 
ment, although as anxious as at the outset for the continuance of peace, is intent 
upon that peace being of a durable kind; if it is desired to make only such an 
arrangement as would but stave off war for a few months, Her Majesty's Govern- 
ment care very little whether the storm breaks now or a little later: in fine, M. le 
Comte, T entreat of you to dismiss from your mind a suspicion which is 
unworthy, and which lias not a shadow of foundation. 

The Chancellor wished that it were in his power to set his mind ut ease ; 
but observed, that the fecling which he attributed to Her Majesty’s Government 
was common to all England. How, he would ask, was it possible that such 
hostility should be felt throughout all classes against Russia? 

I thought the feeling admitted of an easy explanation; the English public 
had been led to believe, in the spring, that the ¢lifferences between Russia and 
Turkey were to be immediately arranged; they suw no approach to agreement ; 
they considered the independence of ‘Turkey in danger; the whole community 
suffered, every man in his own interests, and it could not be wondered at if, at 
last, any measures were desired by the public which should put an end to prolonged 
uncertainty. 

Count Nesselrode proceeded to speak with much feelmg of the horrors of 
war i general; particularly of war between, two powerful countries--two old 
allies like England and Russia—countrica which, whilst they may be of infinite 
use to one another, possessed ench the means of inflicting great injury upon its 
antagonist; and ended by saying, that if for any motives known to him war 
should be declared against Russia by England, it would be the most unintel- 
ligible and the least justifiable war ever undertaken, | 

At the conclusion of some conversation to which this observation gave rise, 
the Chancellor said, “In a few words our position 1s this: war has been 
declared against us by Turkey; we shall, in all probability, issue no counter 
declaration, nor shall we make any attack upon Turkey; weshali remain with 
folded arms, only resalved to repel any assault made wpor 1s, whether in the 
Principalities or on our Asiatic frontier, which we lave been reinforcing: 50 we 
shall remain during the winter, reudy to receive any peaceful overtures which, 
during that time, may be made to us by Turkey 3 that is our position,” 

L observed, that I thought the position a worthy one; and thot I need 
hardly add, how sincerely I desired that the negotiations carried on by ‘Turkey,

which, like Her Majesty's Government, | deeply deplored.
