My Lord, Foreign Office, October 27, 1853. 

SOME days ago Count Colloredo read to me a despatch from Count Buel 
respecting the infraction of the ‘Treaty of 1841 on the part of Her Majesty's 
Ambassador at Constantinople, when in the month of September two vessels of 
war had entered the Dardanelles at his request ; and that without intending to 
enter any idle discussion upon the subject, Count Buol could not avoid 
expressing his regret that some previous communication had not been made to 
Austria and Prussia, who were parties to that Treaty. 

[ told Count Colloredo that Count Buol did not seem to to have acted 
upon his intention, because by writing a despatch which was to be read he did 
enter into a discussion, and that discussion was certainly an idle one, for there 
had been no infraction of the Treaty, as the Porte had ceased to be ina state of 
al with Russia from the moment that the first Russian soldier crossed the 

ruth. The Treaty of 1541 was accordingly suspended, and foreign ships of war 
were no longer prohibited from entering the Dard : 
the Straits, and as this state of things arose from the acts of Russia it was to the 
Cabinet of St. Petersburgh, and not to Her Majesty’s Government, that the 
remonstrances of Austria should have been addressed. Count Colloredo declined 
to give me a copy of Count Buol’s despatch.

No. 142. 
Lord A. Loftus to the Earl of Clarendon.—( Received October 29.) 


(No. 56. Confidential.) 


My Lord, Berlin, October 25, 1853, 

WITH reference to my despatch No. 51 of the 22nd instant, marked Con- 
fidential, reporting to your Lordship that a proposal had been made by the 
Austrian Chargé d’Affaires to Baron Manteuffel to the effect that a declaration of 
the neutrality of Germany in the differences between Russia and Turkey should 
be pronounced by the Germanic Diet, Baron Manteuficl informed me con- 
fidentially this morning that General Prokesch was to arrive here this evening or 
‘nthe course of to-morrow to urge this matter on the Prussian Government, 
and to press for an immediate reply. His Excellency did not look forward with 
much satisfaction to this visit, as he had not had sufficient time to lay before His 
Majesty the great importance which such a step would involve, and he seemed 
to fear the effect which Baron Prokesch’s power of persuasion might have on 
the King, who was personally disposed to entertain favourable views to any col- 
lective action of the Germanic Confederation. 1 repeated to his Excellency the 
dangers which in my opinion would result to Prussia hereafter if on this occasion 
she recognised the principle of submitting the direction of her policy on great 
European questions into the hands of the Germanie Diet; that it would 
establish a precedent which would infallibly fetter her future freedom of action, 
and place her on a line with the smallest of the German Principalities ; and that 
it would be virtually delivering into the hands of Austria the lead and decision on 
all future questions of her foreign policy, and be placing her in a subservient 
position to Austria, 1 remarked to his Excellency that in the present con- 
juncture Austria and Prussia were the German Powers most interested in the 
Oriental question, and that their separate declaration of neutrality would be 
sufficient guarantee to the smaller German States that German interests would 
not be endangered by any eventualities to which the Bastern question was likely 
to give rise. 

Hlis Excellency expressed himself as entirely coinciding with these opinions, 
and told me that he should represent the question in this light to His Majesty. 


He informed me confidentially that he had spoken with the Prince of 


Prussia on the subject, and that His Royal Highness had strongly expressed his 
opinion against the adoption of the course proposed by the Austrian Govern: 
ment. 

His Expelienty seemed to be perfectly aware of the object of the Austrian 
Government in making this proposal, and equally determined in his own mind 
not to give effect to it. 

His Excellency further informed me that he should accompany the King 
to-morrow on a shooting excursion, which he had not previously intended to 
do, and should not return to Berlin until late on Thursday evening. Ele will 
thus elude the pressing demands of Baron Prokesch, and he evidently hopes in 
the meantime that a decision wil be taken by His Majesty of declining the 
invitation of the Austrian Government, in conformity with the views and 
opinions which I have had the honour to report to your Lordship. 

It is probable, however, that the Prussian Government will assent to a 
communication being made to the Diet, stating the policy of neutrality on the 
Eastern question which the two German States intend to pursue, and their hopes 
that a pacific solution may yet restore peace between the contending parties,

the independence of Prussia and her freedom of action should not be in the

I have taken care to state to Haron Manteultel that 1 am without any 
‘nstructions from Her Majesty’s Government on this subject, and that he must 
solely accept what I have expressed to him as the expression of my private 
opinion. 

: I trust your Lordship will approve of the advice which | have tendered ot

T HAVE held an interesting conversation with Count Orloff since his return

tn a friendly manner. ‘To speak the truth, great faults have been committed on

moment it had been contemplated, you had been sent in Prince Menchikoft’s 
place to Constantinople, all that has occurred there would have been avoided.” 

And I really believe you are right,” rejoined Count Orloff. “1 know you 
English; L have negotiated with you; and | know you are to be trusted. 1 
believe, too, that you have a certain confidence in me. Menchikoff is unques-

Sir J. Milbunke to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received October 29.) 


(No. 78.) 


My Lord, Munich, October 23, 1853, 

THE Emperor of Austria has quitted Munich on his return to his own 
capital, 

The language of His Imperial Majesty in regard to the policy of Austria on 
the Turkish question has given much satisfaction here, and has inspired fresh 
hopes as to the possibility of still averting a catastrophe in the Hast, or, at any 
rate, should a collision between Russia and Turkey be unavoidable, of preventing 
the extension of the war beyond the narrow limits of the provinces of the latter 
Power. 1 have been informed that the Emperor's aide-de-camp, Count de 
Griinne, took an opportunity of explaining to M. Von der Plordten, in a long 
confidential conversation, the position which the Austrian Government had been 
compelled to take in the present conflict; and he seems also to have let fall 
some hints as to the attitude which it might hereafter assume in the event of the 
complications becoming mere serious. On the latter point he is reported to 
have said that the suppasition that the efforts made by the Emperor of Russia 
at Olmiitz and Warsaw to engage Austria to anything beyond the observance of 
neutrality had been successful, was altogether erroneous; and he gave it to be 
understood that although the Emperor considered himself to owe to the 
Emperor of Russia a lasting debt of gratitude, which imposed a certain degree 
of restraint upon him, it was only under the conviction that the latter would 
continue to limit himself to what are termed his present moderate demands, that 
this declaration of neutrality had been made, All the endeavours of the Imperial 
Government, Count de Grinne observed, would be directed to maintaining this 
position, so long at least as nothing should occur to menace the integrity of the 
Ottoman Empire. What change of policy, or attempt on the part of Russia ta 
agerandize herself at the expense of Turkey might render expedient, it was 
impossible to foresee at the present moment; but under no circumstances would 
Austria enter into any combination against those Powers which had imposed 
upon themselves the task of aiding the Sultan under such a contingency. ‘This 
account of what passed between Count de Griinne und M, Von der Pfordten, 
was given to me by one of my colleagues, to whom it had been repeated by 
M. Von der Pfordten himself, and to a certain extent was confirmed by a subse- 
quent conversation | had with his Excellency on the subject. He informed me 
that His Imperial Majesty lad twice spoken with him on these matters, and 
after reviewing at some length the possible eventualities which might arise out 
of a war between two such powertul States, had finally completely reassured 
him by stating that whatever turn affairs in the East might take, he was 
determined to observe the strictest neutrality. 

Upon hearing this, | naturally inquired upon what conditions this attitude 
of neutrality had been secured; and whether Austria would be disposed to 
remain & passive spectator of the permanent establishment of Russia along +o 
extensive a partion of the banks of the Danube as that whieh forms the Watla- 
chian frontier; making at the same time some observations on the eflvets whieh 
such a proceeding would be likely to produce on the commercial interests ot 
those countrics of Germany which ate traversed by that river. 

M. Von der Pfordten, who appears to have been converted to the doctriie 
of the Greck propagandists relative to the impending dissolution of the Turkish 
Empire from internal decrepitude, did not seem much to relish the notion of an 
appropriation of the Danubian provinces by Russian, of which, however, he 
assured me the Emperor of Austria cntertained no sort of apprehension, though 
he admitted that the seizure of them would form one of the two cases which 
would justify Austria in quitting her preseribed neutrality; the other was the 
eventuality of an attack on her Halian provinees, which 1 agreed with him in 
thinking not very imminent in the actual state of European polities. His 
Excellency talked a good deal about the formation of a Christian community 
under the name of a Byzantine Empire, with Constantinople for its capital, in 
the place of the Turkish rule, which 1s sa netieS to be on the eve of disappearing

from the continent of Europe; but when I pressed him for his ideas as to who 
would be a proper Sovereign to place on such an uncertain throne, he hesitated 
fo name the only one who was undoubtedly in his thoughts, but who would 
probably be more unfit than any other, in every point of view, to be intrusted 
with the re-organization of a State of such magnitude. 

'To this country, whose system of policy has of late years approached as 
nearly as circumstances would permit to that of Austria, the explanations of 
His Imperial Majesty have praved peculiarly tranquillizing ; for they have had 
the effect of relieving the public mind from a load of dread whieh has weighed 
upon it ever since the commencement of the dispute, that the proximity of 
Austria to the scene of action must, sooner OF later, involve her in the struggle; 
and in-such case it does not require the exercise of much penetration to discover 
that the other States of the Contederation would have an infinitely small chance 
of escape from participating in ‘also, Of all this danger the statesmen of this 
part of Germany were fully sensible, and consequently great is their joy at the 
prospect of the respite which the proclaimed neutrality of Austria holds out to 
them. ‘This Government in particular has given utterance to its feelings of 
satisfaction ina pompous and somewhat absurd article m its semi-official organ, 
‘a which the sole credit of preserving the peace of Europe during the present 
crisis is given to Germany. 

The east and the west of Europe, it says, threatened to engage In a8

wis placed in the bands of Germany, and it is placed in good hands as all 
Europe must allow. Germany and Austria, united as they are, possess the 
peer to decide all Buropean questions. Without them nothing can happen in 

Surope; and that nothing can be attempted against them, it will suffice to 
abaerve that they have more than adequate means of repulsing any impertinence 
that may be essayed, from whomsoever it may come, but which is not to be 
apprehended so long #s they remain true to themselves, seu nothing 
further than respect for their rights secured to them hy existing Treaties. 

There ig much more in the same strain, but 1 hardly deem it worth while 
to take up your Lordship’s time with any additional extracts.

Lord A. Loftus to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received October 31.) 


(No. 58. Confidential.) 
My Lord, Berlin, October 28, 1653. 


BARON PROKESCH, the President of the Dict, has arrived at Berlin, 
and had a lengthened interview this day with Baron Manteuftel. ; 

His Excellency informs me confidentially that Baron Prokesch lias submitted 
to him a project (which 1 have already had the honour to announce to your 
Lordship in my despatch No. 56 of the 25th instant), proposing to the Prussian 
Government to join in addressing a collective report to the Germanic Diet on 
the Oriental question, and to invite a declaration of neutrality on the part ot 
the Germanic Confederation, should war unfortunately arise out of the differ- 
ences between ‘Turkey and Russia, His Exeelleney seemed to think that it was 
not the intention of Austria to submit this proposal to that body asa subject of 
deliberation, but merely as a communication of the policy which Austria and 
Prussia intended to pursue in this question, and as an invitation for the collective 
assent of the other German States, = i | 

Baron Manteuffel expressed to me his conviction that one object Austria 
had in view by this measure was to give assurance to the commercial and finan- 
cial world, for he was aware of the great financial embarrassments tinder which 
she was now labouring; and he conceived that a positive assurimece of neutrality 
expressed by the Germanic body would enable her to concert temporary 
measures of relief with greater facility and on more favourable terms. 

Baron Prokesch informed Baron Manteutlel that even if Prussia declined to 
to accede to a joint representation to the Dict, Austria would not be deterred 
from it, and would inform the Diet of the steps which shie had taken for the 
attainment of a pacilic solution, and of her present determination to mamtain a 
perfect neutrality in the event of open hostilities being resorted to by the 
contending purties, | 

In addition to the views and opinions which I had already expressed to tis 
Excellency against adopting this course, [was enabled now to add that, in conse- 
quence of the new propositions which 1 lind submitted to his Exeelleney this 
day, any such declaration of the Dict would he ill-timed and wnicalled for, 

It is evident to me that his Excellency disapproves of this proposal con- 
veyed through Baron Prokesch: and I feel confident that an evasive if not oo 
purely negative answer will be given by the Prussian Goverment. 

| have, &e. 
(Signed) AUGUSTUS LOFTUS.

No. 153. 
Lord A. Loftus to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received October 31.) 
(No. 59.) 
My Lord, Berlin, October 28, 1853. 

THE messenger Poignand delivered to me yesterday your Lordship’s 
despatches to No. 32 inclusive, 

As Baron Manteuffel did not return to Berlin till a late hour last evening, 
I was unable to see him until this morning, when I had an interview with his 
Excellency at an early hour. 

Tn conformity with your Lordship's instructions | read to him your Lord- 
ship’s despatch No. 32, and communicated to him the drafts of the notes 
inclosed in that despatch, leaving in his Excellency’s hands copies of those 
documents to be immediately submitted to the King. 

His Excellency expressed his concurrence with the arrangement which 
those documents seek to uttain, and seems to entertain great hopes that they will 
meet the end so ardently desired by Europe. 

I likewise communicated to his Excellency the copy of your Lordship’s 
despatch No. 235 to Lord Stratford de Redcliffe, empowering him to admit of 
such modifications as may appear reasonable to his Excellency or his colleagues, 
and which should not be of a character to preclude the acceptance of the note 
by the Emperor of Russia. 

Baron Manteuffel seemed to consider that the tone and nature of these 
documents gave evidence of the conciliatory disposition evinced towards the 
Emperor of Russia, whilst they contain every security and regard for the 
Sovereign rights and dignity of the Sultan 

His Excelleney made but two remarks. First, that the term “le principe 
consacré dans le préambule du Traité de 1841,"' was perhaps rather more than 
was strictly the sense of that Treaty, which in effect merely declared the closing 
of the Dardanelles to ships-of-war in time of peace. Tle thought that the term 
*énoncé? would have been the more correct expression. Secondly, his Excel- 
lency remarked that there were many Greeks in the Ottoman Empire who were 
not subjects of the Sultan, but who, as members of the Orthodox Greek Church, 
would not be included in privileges or immunities which might he accorded to 
members of other churches not subjects of the Sultan. 

I replied to his Excellency that in religious matters they would come under 
the terms of the Greek Church, which enjoyed full religious liberty in the 
exercise of their creed, In temporal affairs, however, they would partake of the 
same civil immunities which were granted to other foreign residents. 

His Excellency, however, did not put forward these remarks in the light of 
objections; on the contrary, he assured me that 1 might safely inform your Lord- 
ship of the entire concurrence of the Prussian Government, and that instructions 
will be sent to Baron Wildenbruch to sign the note, and to support Lord 
Stratford de Redelitle in urging the Porte to aceept the urrangement proposed. 

Of course his Excellency could not inform me until he had taken the 
King’s commands officially of the adhesion of the Prussian Government, but 
he expressed his certain conviction that His Majesty would unhesitatingly accede 
to the invitation which your Lordship has addressed to the Prussian Government. 

I hope by to-morrow evening to receive from Baron Manteuffel His 
Majesty's decision, and shall not fail to transmit it, in obedience with your Lord- 
ship's instructions, by telegraph to the Karl of Westmorland. 

l haye, &e 


(Signed) AUGUSTUS LOFTUS.

My Lord, Foreign Office, Octaber 31, 1853, 
HER Majesty's Government entirely approve the language held by you to 
Baron Manteuffel, and the reasons which you gave to his Excellency against 
the proposal of the Austrian Government to submit a report upon the Eastern 
Question to the Diet of the Germanic Confederation, as reported by your Lord- 
ship in your despatch No, 61 of the 22nd instant. Such a step might improve 
the present position of Austria in the Diet, and aid her future policy in the 
event of war, but it would impair the independent attitude assumed by Prussia, 
and fetter her action both now and hereafter. 
Lam, &c. 
(Signed) CLARENDON.

COUNT BUOL has received a report from the Austrian Chargé d’Affaires 
in Athens, of the irruption of armed bands of Greek subjects from the northern 
provinees of Greece, upon the adjacent territory, and that one of these bands, 
about 500 strong, after having possessed itself of Arta hud marched towards 
Prevesa, of which it was feared it would take possession, and that another party 
were in march upon Samia. Tt was also stated in this despatch that great fears 
were entertained lest an attempt should be made to produce an insurreetion in 
‘Thessaly, where considerable excitement was said to prevail, 

The Greek Government is stated to have deprecated these measures, and 
to have endeavoured to prevent them as far as they have been able, and Count 
Buol (who had already written upon reports he had previously received, directing 
the Chargé d’Affhires to make the strongest representations to the Government 
of King Otho against these proceedings), has repeated these injunctions, and he 
stated that he was aware the Freneh Minister at Athens had acted ina similar 
tnanner, and that he was convinced your Lordship would do the same,

My Lord, Vienna, October 2, 185d. 
THE latest intelligence which Count Buol has reecived from the Inter- 

nuncio is of the 10th instant, from Constantinople. He reports the general 

disposition of the Turkish Government for the prosecution of the war which 

has been declared, and which he supposes will be commenced by hostilities of 

the part of the Turkish army under the orders of Omer Postia, ..... 

Baron Bruck expressts his regret that the assurane®” contained in Count 
Buol's note from Olmiitz did not arrive before the declaration of war, 25 he 
thinks they might have made a favourable iMpression j but he states, that the 
remarks of Count Nesselrode upon the Turkish modifications had fortified 
Reshid Pasha in his conviction, that these modifications ought to have been 
adopted. 

I communicated to Count Buol Lord Stratford's telegraphic despatch of the 
15th instant. He remarked upon it, that he was alneatly aware of the 
disposition which vad been taken with respect to the passage of the combined 
fleets through the Dardanelles: but what he regretted to learn from the despateh 
wag the disinclination which it seemed to imply on the part of the General 
Council in Constantinople, to the acceptation of terms of arrangement with 
Ttussia, towards which it appeared that Reshid Pasha might have been favorably

addressed by Count Nesselrode on the 17th instant vo Baron Meyendorff, and

copy of this deapatch to your Lordship, and you will perceive that it wus 
written in answer to one from M. de Fonton, dated the Gth instant, announcing 
the declaration of war by the Porte, and an expedient proposed by Count Bul 
upon the receipt of that intelligence. 

In placing the copy of Count Nesselrode’s despateh in our hands, Count 
Buol observed, that although it addressed to him alone the authorization to 
anen fresh communications, Upon the plan he had su gested, with the Govern- 
ment of the Sultan, he felt that it was more conformable to that unity of councils 
whieh had existed between the Four Powers throughout the negotiations, to lay 
his expedient before their Representatives in conference, in order that they 
might take the deliberate opinions of their respective Governments upon it; andl 
he stated, that he should await the replies of the three Cabinets before he should 
take any step whatever upon the subject. 

The plan which Count Buol suggests for the approval of Her Majesty's 
Government, and those of our allies, is, that collective note should be addressed 
by the Four Powers to the Porte, founded upon the principle that the 
Government of the Sultan is ready to adhere to the engagements which they have 
epontancously taken in the course of the negotiations, and to re-establish their 
former relations with Russia upon conditions conformable to the dignity and 
sovereign rights of the Sultan, and inviting them to agtee to-an armistice, and 
to the appointment of a Plenipotentiary to treat with o Russian Plenipotentiary, 
the two to meet at some place to be fixed upon by mutual consent of the two

Governments. The proposed note would contain the renewed declaration of 
the Four Powers, of the assurances given by the Emperor of Russia, and their 
adherence to the conditions which the Porte had agreed to accept in the 
modified Vienna note, omitting all reference to any concession, by the Sultan to 
the Greek Church, of the rights and immunities which he might in future accord 
to any other Christian community. As in consequence of the declaration of 
war, a Treaty or Diplomatic Convention becomes necessary, the Ottoman 
Government will be invited by the note to inform the Four Powers, through the 
Turkish Ambassador at Vienna, of the stipulations on which such Convention 
might be agreed to, and these stipulations would be immediately forwarded by 
the Representatives from Vienna to St, Petersburgh, and the Cabinet requested 
to send an answer through the Russian Minister at this place, so that the 
negotiation would not be exposed to, the delays which might arise from direct 
discussions between the Government of Russia and the Porte. The Plenipo-

and the Four Powers would retain a control over the whole of the transaction

No, 164. 
Lord Stratford de Redeliffe to the Earl of Clarention.—(Received October 31.) 


(No. 294.) 
My Lord, Therapia, October 15, 1853. 

" THEE Sultan has invited the squadrons to enter the Dardanelles, 1 have 
the honour to inclose herewith a copy of Reshid- Pasha's official note communt- 
cating Ilis Majesty's request. Your Lordship will observe that the appheation 


127 


is grounded on the Porte’s resolution to make war, and on its declared appre- 
hension that Russia may commence hostilities even before the expiration of the 
fifteen days assigned to Prince Gortchakoff for his evacuation of the Principalities. 
Though war has been hitherto declared only with that reservation, | have 
thought it my duty, under your Lordship's instructions, to comply with the 
Sultan's invitation. 1 have, nevertheless, withheld my consent for a few days, 
and arranged with M. de la Cour that the ships shall not arrive here till after 
the middle of next week. In doing so I have been actuated by a wish to keep 
open the chances of peace for any acceptable result of the meeting at Olmiitz, 
and to guard against the possibility of furnishing a shadow of pretence for the 
continued occupation of the Provinces by Russia, The hope of any available 
proposition from Olmiitz has vanished with the communication made by Baron 
Bruck to Reshid Pasha after the arrival of the last post from Vienna; and 
when the portions of the squadrons destined for Constantinople shall arrive 
here, it will be impossible that any effect should be thereby produced at the 
Russian head-quarters in Wallachia. 

Inclosed herewith is my intended answer to Reshid Paslia’s note, The 
French Ambassador will address His Highness in the same sense. 

I have also the honour to inclose a memorandum of the course which | 
propose to follow, in concert with M. de la Cour and the ‘Turkish Government, 
respecting the entrance of the squadrons. [T have reason to believe that it is in 
uccordance with Admiral Dundas’s opinions. 

Your Lordship will not fail to understand, that in taking a decision on 
this subject I have been guided by a reference to my original instructions. The 
juncture for which the last ones were framed, has long since ceased to have 
any existence in fact, and whatever peril miy in future arise from unforeseen 
cireumstances, | see no reason at present to apprehend its revival. I might 
have preferred an additional delay of a few days, in order to afford a complete 
coincidence between the passage of the Dardanelles by the squadrons, and the 
actual or formal commencement of war. But the instructions of my French 
colleague are, according to his assurance, so peremptory, that, by longer post- 
poning my decision, | should have incurred the risk of separating from him to 
a degree which would not only have proved embarrassing to your Lordship, but 
prejudicial to the interests of our common cause, an! also to the separate 
influence of Her Majesty's Embassy, 

[ have laboured to provide for all the considerations attached to this 
intended movement of the squadrons, and hope that the difficulty of doing so 
will atone for any oversight, and obtain for me, nevertheless, your Lordship’s 
indulgent approval. 

I have, &c. 


(Signed) STRATFORD DE REDCLIFFE.

My Lord, ; Therapia, October 17, 1853, 

I HAD a private audience of the Sultan this morning, and delivered in 
the usual manner the Queen’s reply to His Majesty's letter announcing the 
birth of a Prinee in the Imperial family.

of the ships exposed without necessity to the violent winds which often prevail

We are therefore of opinion that you will best provide for the requirements 
of the case by bringing the whole of your squadron within the Dardanelles as 
soon as you are informed officially that tue necessary firmans for your passage 
have been received by the Turkish officers commanding there, We further pro- 
pose that you should detach two ships-of-the-line with four steam-frigates to

Marmora.

lency the French Ambassador, who dispatches a steamer this evening with our 
joint communication to the squadrons. 

We conceive that your professional experience, united to that of Vice- 
Admiral Hamelin, will best determine the most suitable anchorage for ships 
within the above-mentioned limits. It is proposed, in compliance with the 
wishes of the Porte, that the vessels detached to Constantinople shall anchor on 
their arrival in the Bosphorus opposite to Therapia. 

Orders will be sent from the Porte to facilitate the purchase of provisions 
in those districts which are near to the selected places of anchorage as soon as

nelles in three days from the present date.

of ships destined for the capital, T shall gladly avail myself of the opportunity to 
communicate with you more completely than by correspondence, and I cannot 
but think that the interests of the public service would be promoted by our 
interview. .

WE learn from the communication now made to us that there is an idea of

postpone hostilities during the term in question, and orders have been sent to 
the Commanders in Roumelin and Anatolia by special steamers this day. 

But the war may have begun in some laces before the arrival of these 
orders, and as in that case it will be iavpneaitls to desist, the Sublime Porte 


hopes that no blame will be attributed to her in this respect. 
With reference to the other points, the Porte cannot consent to the intro- 
duetion into the note to be given to Russia of the passage concerning the ancient

solicitude of the Emperors of Russia for the maintenance of the religious privi- 
leges in the Ottoman Empire, as set forth in the corrections made in the Vienna 
draft of note, as well as in the note which accompanied the amended draft ; 
nor that those privileges should be considered as deriving from the natural eon- 
struction of the Treaty of Kainardji. Neither can she consent to the expression 
of “ treaty or special disposition” concerning the participation by the professors 
of the Greek religion in the spiritual advantages granted to other Christian 
communities. The Porte, moreover, cannot consent to the passage in the note 
implying that the participation in question is sranted at the demand of Russia. 

‘As the assurances, stating that it is not the intention of the Russian 
Government to touch the independence of the Sublime Porte, or to meddle with 
the internal affairs, affect the qeat of the Imperial Government of Turkey, the 
securities and guarantee sought for must be limited only to the assurance that 
Russia will not make the note which is to be addressed to her a pretext for 
intermeddling in religious matters. 
___ The acceptance nf the new draft of note in question will depend upon the 
issue of His Imperial Majesty the Sultan’s orders consequent upon the exami- 
nation [of that draft] by the General Council, and the Ministers of the Porte 
cannot hold out any promises in that respect, neither ean the Ministers of the 
Porte, in the event of the draft in question being rejected, again prolong the 
term [for the commencement, of hostilities) already put off. 

Tmake this communication to your Excellency as the Imperial Govern- 
ment considers it important that the Representatives of England and France, 
the sincere allies of Turkey, should be apprized beforehand of the subject of it. 


No. 170. 


Lord Stratford de Redcliffe to the Karl of Clarendon,—(Received October 31.) 


(No, 308.) 


My Lord, Therapia, Oclober 22, 1853. 

IT requires but little sagacity to perceive that the war which has all but 
commenced is likely to prove a contest of no ordinary importance, and perhaps 
of no ordinary duration. The Porte is bringing forward all the remains of its 
strength, and, together with the nation, feels that the issue of the struggle must 
determine its future destiny, It is evident, on the other side, that Russia, 
weary of a precarious and disputed influence in the Levant, will exert its colossal 
force to secure a complete and recognised supremacy, The truce to be imposed 
by winter may offer opportunites for negotiation; but the motives to persist- 
ance are on both sides so powerful, that a pacific arrangement, unpreeeded by 
an exchange of blows, may be considered ‘al but hopeless, and hardly even then 
to be obtained on fair terms without the interference of other Powers. 

Such being the prospect, it is essential that the Turkish Government, and 
those in alliance with it, should fix their attention principally on the means of 
prosecuting an active and extensive war with success. The real independence of 
this Empire, or, at least, the free exercise of legitimate power by its Sovercign, 
being the main object in view, with reference to political, social, and commercial 
interests of the highest order, it is requisite not only that Turkey should come 
out of the contest with honour, bul that her success should be obtained with 
the least possible drain on her resources. This can hardly be accomplished 
under any circumstances, unless all available means of defence or attack be 
prepared and directed with a comprehensive judgment, and effectual measures be 
udopted in time for covering weak points and guarding against dangers which, 
whether from within or from without, may operate as diversions in favour of an 
invading encmy. 

_ Although the Turkish authorities have carried on their defensive prepari- 
tions with remarkable energy and order, deficiencies of no small importance 
remain ta be supplied. Commissariat establishments and field officers are 
wanting ; the regular cavalry is defuctive, especially in numbers. On the other 
hand, an application for otficers has been made to the French Government, and 
assistance of that kind may be obtained from other quarters too, Tam assured 
that provisions are stored in considerable quantities by order of the Porte ; and 

2D 


140 


bodies of undisciplined cavalry may be expected to come in aid of the regulars, 
with less disadvantage than elsewhere, Orders have also been given to collect 
an army in Bosnia; another to defend the mountain pass near Sophia; anda 
third to act in reserve between Adrianople and the capital. ‘To these may be 
added the forces collected on the Asiatic. frontier from Batoom inwards, ‘They 
cannot by this time be far from offering a total of 5,000 men. But Her 
Majesty's Consul at Erzeroom, measuring them against the Russian armies on 
that side, holds out but little prospect of their success in the field. Yet if 
suspect that the Porte + inclined to rely principally upon them, hoping to 
acquire by their means, with the assistance of Mahomedan tribes subject to 
Russia, a footing so firm and extensive in the adjacent Russian provinces, as to 
afford an equivalent for the Danubian Principalities. 

Your Lordship is aware that the Porte has not been able to concentrate 
large bodies of men on special points without leaving a large proportion of the 
Empire with very im erfect. means of protection, and affording a strong 
temptation to its neig bours and tributary subjects to look after their own 
nterests at the instigation of Russian agents. The measures which I have 
suggested, as your Lordship knows, to provide for the maintenance of order, 
have heen generally accepted by the Porte, and partially adopted for practical 
execution. It may be added, that hitherto in Bulgaria, Thessaly, and Albania, 
where the Christian population is held to he sufficiently ill-affected, no symptoms 
of active discontent or dangerous combination have been discovered to any 
alarming amount. But such forbearance can hardly be expected to withstand 
the excitement of war, especially if the Sultan’s armies were to sustain aly 
signal defeat. The Bulgarians would probably, even in that case, be restrained 
by their experience of Russian military rule, and the fear of a return visit from 
the Turks. Servia gives promise of attachment to the Porte, in so far as an 
exemption from Russian occupation is concerned, In the Asiatic provinces of 
the Empire disorder is more likely to break out among the ‘Turks, at the 
expense of the Rayah population. Something of this kind has already occurred 
st Adalia, and also in Kurdistan, In the former case an officer and two 
battalions were immediately sent down, ab nly request, to restore order and to 

unish the offenders. In the latter, repeated orders have been sent to the 
‘Turkish frontier authorities for the same purpose. T may take this opportunity 
to mention, that at Smyrna, where brigandage, not wholly divested of a political 
tendency, has long prevailed in alarming proportions, @ chief of great notoriety 
has been recently compelled to surrender, by the zealous and well-directed 
efforts of the Pasha and his police. 

The exhortations which I have repeatedly addressed to the Porte with 
respect to Greece and Persia, are always received with attention and expressions 
of readiness to comply; but hitherto, nothing effective has been done to deprive 
them of pretexts for doing the Porte an ill turn when her armies are engaged 
with Russia. It would seem, that the professions of both Governments continue 
to be friendly; but there would be less to apprehend, if they were given to 
understand that the Sultan's maritime allies scald not permit them to take any 
unfair advantage of his eventual difficulties. The intimation of a military visit 
from India would operate powerfully on the Persian Cabinet; and 9 small 
detachment of the British and French Mediterranean squadrons would sutlice to 
cool the enthusiasm of Athens. 

[t is far from my intention to outrun the natural course of events; but, 
locking forward to no very (listant period, it may perhaps be worth while to 
consider the expediency of having some addition to our garrison force at Malta 
and Corfu, and enough of naval force to admit of operations in the Adriatic, 
should the bordering tribes of Turkey break into aggression on this Empire, 
under the influence of foreign sympathy with Russia. : 

Officers, urms, and money are points of weakness, tor which the Porte may 
eventually have to cast an imploring look upon her allies, 1 stated in a former 
despatch that the Sultan had given his consent for a loan. L have now to add 
that Namik Pasha is going to Paris and London with the crane eae to contract 
one, if it ean be obtained on moderate terms, to the amount, in the first instance, 


of two millions sterling. It is not unlikely that the Sultan's Commissioner will 
have authority to enter upon other questions of common interest with the 
British and French Governments. Meanwhile, hear very little of those liberal 
measures which seemed at one time to have been all but definitively adopted, 


141 


particularly the equalization of evidence in criminal procedure, and the opening 
of Turkish ports for a free exportation of grain. The delay is attributed to the 
pressure of still more urgent usiness ; but it may be presumed, without unfair- 
ness, that financial considerations and fear of po mular tumult in case of scarcity, 
as on the coast of Africa, may have a share in retarding the one, while the 
remains of Mussulman fanaticism may cause hesitation as to the other, 

With respect to operations in the Black Sea, there is doubtless considerable 
root for those of an aggressive as well as for those of a defensive character. 
We have not as yet sufficient information as to the practicability of attempting 
Sevastopol and Nicolayef with success, But it is obvious that in blockading 
those places, interrupting the conyeyance by sea of supplies for the Russian 
army, encouraging the inhabitants of Circassia, and laying under contribution 
such unprotected coast establishments as Odessa and others, the activity 
of a strong efficient squadron might be a cause of much vexation and injury 
to the Porte’s enemy. 

On these points, however, I beg to reserve any further suggestions until | 
have had an opportunity of conferring with Admiral Dundas. My only object 
at present im addressing your Lordship at all on the question of Turkey's 
prospects in a War with Russia is to draw a seasonable attention to the weak 
points, and also in general to the more obvious means of counteracting the 
dangers attached to them.

(Signed) STRATFORD DE REDCLIFFE.

My Lord, St, Petersburgh, October 20, 1853. 


| THINK it right to offer your Lordship the details of u private conver- 
sation which I held yesterday with the Chancellor, who, in the company of the 
Neapolitan Minister and of Count Kisseleff, passed the evening at m house. 

Count Nesselrode’s manner was more than usually cordial, and on taking 
my hand as he entered the room, he said, “ Eh bien! nous sommes toujours en 
vAIX. 

“Yes,” I replied; “and | hope means will be found for enabling us to 
remain at peace.” | 

"JT hope so,” the Chancellor said; ‘“‘and I believe so. You know that 
Talleyrand used to say, that he only asked for six weeks; lam better off, for I 
have six months before me,” 

Count Nesselrode proceeded to remark, that he felt sure that he knew the 
reason why the English messenger had not arrived; that he was aware that your 
Lordship had been occupied in devising some fresh propositions (systeme was 
the word employed), and that these, when completed, would be sent to Vienna, 
and probably communicated to me, 

The conversation proceeded in the same easy strain, and in the course of it 

Lobtained a confirmation of some of the views which I had before taken of the 
state of things in Turkey. Thus | learnt, that the Emperor had been relieved 
from much anxiety by the accounts received of the safe landing of the reinforee- 
ments sent from Sevastopol to the point at which a ‘Turkish attack was the most 
apprehended ; and that, like myself, the Government conjecture that Omer 
Pasha may, for want of supplies, be unable to remain long in his present 
positon. 
This idea had been suggested to me some days ago by one of the most 
distinguished officers of the Russian army, who knows the ground well, having 
taken an active part in the campaign of 1829. ‘This officer has told me that 
unless constant supplies could be veceived from seaward, it was totally in pos- 
ble that Omer Pasha should long oceupy his present position, Bulgaria being 
so completely barren and without resources, as not even to offerany kind of 
fornge for the cavalry when the summer is over. 

Count Nesselrode appears to share this opinion, and to think that Omer 
Pasha is not unlikely to break up his camp, and crossing the Danube at Widdin 
to throw himself inte Little Wallachia, where he would find plentiful supplies, 


and where he would still have a rapid And difficult river (the Olta) between him 


and the Russian army. 

The important part, however, of Count Nesselrode's conversation was a5 
follaws :— 

will tell you,” he abserved very frankly, * what I conceive to be the 
great danger of the present situation. fit is prolonged, we are exposed to the 
risk of a general rising of the Sultan’s Christian subjects, and that may plunge 
us into almost inextricable difficulties.” He proceeded to explain his apprehen- 
sion by saying that a fabric 80 tottering as the ‘Turkish Empire may by prudence 
be kept from falling, but once fallen its reconstruction ig an event which, evea if 
desired, would be found impracticable. 

T did not wish (particularly in my own hovse) to reply with any usperity to 
the very amicable remarks which had been made to me by the Chancellor, and I 
consequently refrained from observing, as | might have done with great truth, 
that the consideration upon which he laid so much stress was precisely that 
which [ had so often insisted on sith him, and which upon more than one 
occasion | had ventured to press upon the Emperor at the beginning of this 
unhappy quarrel. 

n case this private conversation should be brought to more general know- 

ledge than was ‘ntended, 1 think it right to state to your Lordship that the 
Neapolitan Minister was 80 placed as to hear every word of it, and that he left

my house telling me fairly that it was long since he had possessed the means of 
offering his Court as interesting a report as he was now able to make.

Menchikoff the blame which he so improperly imputed to Lord ‘Stratford de

infer that Baron Brunnow’s correspondence with your Lordship respecting the

Were the allied fleets to enter the Black Sea, the Russians’ remonstrances 
would no doubt be renewed ina louder strain. This effect may indeed be pro-

‘The trespass committed by Russia involved consequences to which the 
aggrieved party had manifestly a right to resort at pleasure. The trespass did 
not lose that objectionable character because it had been persisted in, or because 
its first occurrence was not met by prosecution. 

Among the members of the Corps Diplomatique, there are several who are 
always disposed to consider that the right 1s on the side of Russia. 

These persons, as | understand, argue that there is no analogy between the 
passage of the Pruth and that of the Dardanelles; that the one is a question 
which regards Russia ard the Porte, and that the other is one in which Austria 
and Prussia have a violation of treaty to complain of, or rather which might be 
complained of, | 

This view of the case has been only once noticed to me, and was met by 
me in a manner which caused the subject to be droppedl. j 

You make, T said, a convenient position for Russia, if you allow her to 
come in for hostile purposes from the north, and exclude those who may come 
to the Porte’s assistance from the south.

1 WAITED upon Count Nesselrode yesterday at the Foreign Department, 
and held a conversation with him, which, if not satisfactory in other respects, 
was so at least as regards the calm and even friendliness of his tone and 
manner. 

His Excelleney inquired if 1 had received a travail, which he understood 
Her Majesty's Government to huve been occupied in preparing, and which he

prove acceptable to the Emperor's Government, your Lordship would he ready

as should guard against all ambiguities requiring explanations, and as should 

‘ve to Russia all she professes to claim, and yet not expose ‘Turkey to such an 
interference (ingérence) in her internal affairs as the Emperor declares he does 
not aim at. 

Count Nesselrode replied that he could only repeat to me that the posture 
(position) of Russia was this: that she had no intention of resorting to aggressive 
measures, but should, during the winter, await the overtures for peace which 
might be made to her by Turkey. 

‘To this [ answered that [ considered his Excellency’s observation in the 
light of an acceptance of the offer on the part of your Lordship, that it mattered 
little whether overtures were made by Turkey or on the part of Turkey, and 
that here was a direct proposition to an instrument which might be the means 
of restoring peace to the two countries, and of averting evils the amount of 
which no one could calculate, 

Count Nesselrode assented to this, observing, however, that it was hardly 
necessary to remark that the consideration of the projet de note to be proposed 
by your Lordship did not pledge the Russian Government to its acceptance ; 
that the Emperor's interests and dignity could not be overlooked ; and that it 
must be remembered that all the interference of the English Government had 
hitherto been employed in supporting the views of Turkey.

But, said Count Nesselrode, you must not forget that we are at war with 
Turkey. She has declared war against us, and a state of war can only be put 
an end to by a Treaty ; to obtain a ‘Treaty, Plenipotentiaries must be named on 
both sides, negotiations entered upon, and engagements taken directly by the 
two parties. 

This, I rejoined, does not appear to me to alter the case; preliminaries 
precede the signature of a Treaty, if that be requisite. Well, the Marl of 
Clarendon's note would be a preliminary, and might be followed by a final 
arrangement, ) 

Count Nesselrade expressed his assent, saying, that if your Lordship's note 
should be such as the Emperor would feel at liberty to accept, it might serve as 
a basis of negotiation. 

1 then spoke of the extreme moderation of the measures which had accom- 
panied the Porte’s declaration of war, as indicative of the Sultan’s wish to renew 
‘nicable relations with Russia, ‘To these observations lis Excellency did not 
make much reply, 

During the whole of my visit [ was prepared for some inquiry as to the 
Black Sea, but no such allusion was made, and I judged it expedient not to 
originate the subject. Tam indeed almost inclined to doubt—only that Count 
Nesselrode is possessed of an imperturbable calm in the midst even of disagree- 
able affaire—whether he is aware of the orders which have been transmitted to 
Admiral Dundas. He inquired with some interest whether the fleet had left 
Besika Bay, and appeared to be under the impression of its being still in its old 
place of anchorage. In reply, I stated that I had no information as to the 
arrival of the Aeets, but that I thought it might be safely assumed that they 
were all in the Bosphorus. 

Count Nesselrode adverted to the inconvenience of so large an assemblage 
of ships being anchored in @ very narrow channel; and it is possible (although I

ug @ reason thrown out intentionally for the Bay of Buyukdéré being the station

I will only add, that Count Nesselrode alluded in the course of our conver-

having casually remarked upon the possible chances of misunderstandings which

From all that precedes your Lordship will, I think, infer that there is no

not aware how difficult it is to reconcile professions with acts, and if experience

My Lord, St. Petersburgh, October 22, 1853. 

A SENSE of duty urges me to take the liberty of offering your Lordship 
an observation with regard to the orders transmitted to Lord Stratford de 
Redcliffe in your Lordship’s despatch No. rpAae 

I have every reason for believing, that there is no question of the Sevastopol 
feet being employed for the landing of troops upon the Turkish territory; and 
that, as has been stated to me by the Russian Governor, their wish is to confine 
themselves during the winter to defensive operations, 

If this plan be departed trom, moreover, it will be, [ conceive, upon the 
eastern and not upon the western eoust of the Black Sea, as it is possible that 
the movement upou the populations of Georgia and the Caucasus may lead to 
some attacks being made upon the province of Krzeroom. 

I would then venture to submit to your Lordship whether, if the orders 
transmitted to Admiral Dundas shall not have been acted on immediately, that 
their execution should be suspended. 

It is very far from my wish to deprecate recourse being taken to energetic 
measures, should they be requisite; but I feel certain that your Lordship will 
desire that no unnecessary offence should be given to Russia. 

This consideration it is which induces me to remark, that much less offence 
would, I apprehend, be offered to the Emperor by the eventual orders riven to 
Her Majesty’s fleet being made known confidentially by myself to Count 
Nesselrode, than if a knowledge of them should be brought here in consequence 
of the communieation made by Admiral Dundas to the Russian Admiral in 
command of the Sevastopol fleet. 

According to one method of communication the Emperor, without being 
supposed to have received a summons, might take measures for the security of 
his fleet: while, according to the other, he would learn from one of his own 
naval officers the affront (as His Majesty would be sure to consider it) offered 
to the Russian flag. 

I have, &c. 
(Signed) G. H. SEYMOUR.

My Lord, St. Petersburgh, October 22, 1853. 

| REGRET that it is not in my power to offer your Lordship a copy of a 
despatch which General Castelbajac has just addressed to his Government, and 
which, after having read to me, will be forwarded by to-day’s messenger to 
Count Walewski for transmission to Paris. 

It would haye been agreeable to me if my colleague had laid less stress 
upon the moderation of the Emperor’s views, and upon the strong motives which 
exist for the assistance afforded by France to the Porte being doled out with a 
Sparing hand; but the military details which he gives, and the opinions as to 
the operations of the Russian and Turkish armies which, as a military man he 
expresses, are of considerable interest. 

General Castelbajac states that up to the present time there have been 
56,000 Russian troops in the Principality, which have now been increased by the 
arrival of a corps d'armée under General Lachen, 45,000 strong. 

He imagines that without any very extraordinary effort these forces might 
be brought up to 300,000. 

According to General Castelbajac's anticipation, active operations, when 
undertaken by the Russians, will be directed chiefly against the Pashalic of 
Erzeroom, where they will be less under the observation of the European Powers 
and more removed from the chance of all interference.

No. 188, 
Sir G. H. Seymour to the Earl of Clarendon,—(Received November 2.) 


(No. 560. Confidential.) 
My Lord, St. Petersburgh, October 24, 1853, 

NO intimation has ever been made to me of the Emperor's intention of 
calling upon the Porte for an indemnity for his armaments, in the event of the 
final rejection of the Vienna note; but, as | before stated, the existence of such 
an intention has reached me. 

In the event then, in the happy event of an arrangement of difficulties 
between Russia and Turkey becoming within view, | would (however unneces- 
sary the suggestion may be) take the liberty of submitting to your Lordship 
that this pretension is to be carefully guarded against. 

It might appear incredible that a notion should be entertained of claimin 
dam from an independent Sovereign tor the flagrant trespass camntnitied 
upon bis dominions, but that improbability could not with safety be admitted. 

I say not with safety, because, apart from the enormous injustice of the 
demand, the claim, if once entertained, would defeat the object which the rest of 


150 


Europe must haye in view, namely, that of seeing Moldavia and Wallachia 
delivered from Russian holding. 

It may very safely be assumed that the Turkish exchequer would be totally 
unable to liquidate such an account 2s might be presented for the immense 
military preparations which Russia has been making for the last twelvermonth ; 
and equally certain it is, that the claim being once recognized, and the bill sent 
in, the next step would be an attachment upon the Principalities or some other 
Turkish possessions as a security for payment, 

I have, &c. 
(Signed) G. H. SEYMOUR.

My Lord, St. Petersburgh, October 24, 1853. 

A CONVERSATION which I have held with a person who is upon the 
most intimate terms with the Chancellor and Count Orloff, confirms opinions 
which 1 have already ventured to express to your Lordship, as to the great 
disinelination felt by the Emperor to plunge into a war which might be disastrous 
to himself, and could hardly fail of being se eventually to his closest allies. 

The person in question prepared me for much excited feeling on the part 
of the Emperor, who appears to resent an ‘nterference with what he considers 
his unquestionable rights, but he does not anticipate that these feclings will lead 
His Majesty to push matters to extremities. 

He cautioned meas to the expediency of Her Majesty's Government not 
pressing too heavily upon the Emperor's powers of endurance, but ended by 
saying; “Tout cela ira mieux quien ne croit généralement, Vous en sortires 
pee mais tres lentement; difficilement l'affaire sera terminée avant 
PAques.”” 

I questioned my acquaintance closely as to the existence of some secret 
engagement entered into lately between the Emperors of Russia and Austria; 
the more closely as the idea has for some time possessed My own mind. 

I was assured in the most positive manner the apprehensions might be 
safely dismissed, and at this conclusion, as | may take the opportunity of adding, 
my French colleague had previously arrived. 

The person to whom I before alluded, remarked, and certainly in this 
respect his opinions Agree closely with my own, that an arrangement between 
Russia and Austria for the spoliation of Turkey would give rige to difficulties 
which it would be hardly possible to get over; since besides that Austria, inde- 
pendently of exposing herself to the certainty of a war with Western Europe, an 
of revolutions in Italy and Hungary, could as little expect that she would be 
allowed by her co-partner to become mistress of the Principalities, as she could 
admit, either in the interests of Austria or of those of the whole of Germany, 
that they should become Russian possessions. 

Meanwhile, eaten up a8 these fine provinces are by an immense occupy 
army, and exposed as they will be during the winter to the forays of both 
Cossacks and Turks, mueh of their value will be lost for many years to come,

(No. 392.) 


My Lord, Vienne, October 30, 1853. 

| WALTED upon Count Buol yesterday immediately after the receipt of 
your Lordship’s instructions of the 2th imstant, and informed him that I had 
to lay before him a proposal, which your Lordship considered to be the last 
affort that could be made, with any chance of success, to effect an arrangement 
between Russia and the Porte before the calamities of war should actually com- 
mence, and of which you most anxiously desired the approval of Count Buol; 
and L also stated that the greatest anxicty was felt by Her Majesty's Government 
for the cooperation of Austria and the success of the present proposal. Count 
Buol replied, that he could not fail to be favourably impressed towards any 
proposition so recommended, and he awaited its communication. Tread to hin 
first your Lordship's despatch No. 346, with the tenor of which he was entirely 
satisfied: and I then placed in his hands the copies of the two projected notes, 
the one for the signature of the four Representatives, and the other for the 
acceptance of the Porte. Count Buol said: he looked upon these documents as 
ofso much importance that he should desire to consider them with attention ; 
and he thought as the French Government was already a party to them, and us 
Prussia was invited as well as Austria to become so, that they should be taken 
into consideration by the four in conimon. He therefore proposed that I should 
meet my colleagues with him-at an carly hour on this the following day ; and in 
the meantime he requested that the two notes might be left with him. 1 
consented to this request; and I pointed out to Count Buol that | considered 
these notes to be in every way calculated to meet with his upprobation : first, 
because they fulfilled the great object the Four Powers had always had in view, 
that of guarding against any act or declaration which might be derogatory to 
the honour and independence of the Sultan, or which might leave unsatisfied 
any of those rights and pretensions which were secured to the Emperor of Russia 
by Treaty, or which His Majesty declared that he required, 

L remarked also that, taking into consideration the statement which Count 
Buol had lately made of his own views as to the propositions to be made to the 
Porte, I conceived that the notes now proposed fulfilled his intentions; and I 
particularly called his attention to the adoption of the modified Vienna note in 
all its essential points, and the omission of any claim to the future grant of 
rights to the Greek population of such privileges as the Sultan might at any 
time in future accord to religious communities not subjects of the Turkish 
Empire. 

| left the documents in Count Buol’s hands, and this morning | returned 
to his house, and met there Baron Bourquency and Count Arnim, Count Buol 
read to us two projects of note, and then stated what | have already shortly 
reported to your Lordship in my telegraphic despatch of this day. He felt con- 
vinced that since the declaration of war had been made, and particularly since 
the unfortunate commencement of hostilities which had taken place at Isakteha, 
it would be impossible to hope that the former relations existing between the 
two Governments could be restored by a note of the nature of that now pro- 
posed, He felt at a loss to understand in what way that note was to be com- 
municated from the Porte to the Russian Government. It had formally been 
proposed to send an Ambassador, but this seems to him to be no longer eontem- 
plated: no other form of transmission had been pointed out, The note did not 
call upon the Kmperor for the evacuation of the Provinces, which was most 
essential for the restoration of peace, nor did it make any mention of the mode 
in which this restoration was to be effected, [He therefore thought that the 
purpert of the note proposed for the signature of Reshid Pasha, should rather 
xc addressed to the Representatives of the Four Powers, who might present it to 
the Cabinet of St. Petersburgh as a basis upon which the preliminaries of peace 
might be established. 

| replied that the intense interest which was felt by my Government for 


ea 


154 


the adoption of the present sroject by the Four Powers imposed upon me the duty 
of urging to the utmost its immediate adoption, and I repeated that 1b was con- 
sidered by Her Majesty's Government a the last chance of averting the commence- 
ment of hostilities, the cessation of which it was Impossible to foresee. I added 
that the project had, with the assent of the French Government, been already 
transmitted to Constantinople, where it would, even without the support of the 
other Powers, be submitted, and urged upon the Porte in the strongest manner ; 
and if it should not be accepted, the want of success might be attributed to the 
absence of such support. The note contained nothing which the ‘Turkish 
Government ought to object to, and it granted to Russia all that Government 
professed to claim. It was proposed first to the Turkish Government, in order 
that the reasonable desire of the Emperor Nicholas should be fulfilled, that no 
proposal should be submitted to him, as the former one had been, with the risk 
of being after his acceptance refused by the Porte. In the instruction sent to 
Lord Stratford, although he had been aathorized within certain limits to consent 
to some modifications which the Government of the Sultan might propose, they 
were to be confined to such as the Representatives of the Four Powers would

might suspend hostilities and give achance of peace ; and | stated that Her 
Majesty’s Government could not give a greater proof of their deep anxiety upon 
this matiaek than by the effort they now made for the attainment of success. 
also remarked, that I had every reason to believe that the Cabinet of St. Peters-

aspire to, | hoped | might not plead in wain for the cooperation in this honour- 
ae effort of the Government which had hitherto acted in such cordial alliance 
with us. 

Count Buol assured me that he fully participated in the anxiety which I 
felt for the continued and cordial union of the Four Powers, and he felt all the 
advantage of the adoption at the present moment of any course which might 
hold out a chance of averting the continuance of that state of hostilities which, 
from the recent mecounts of the events at leaktcha, we now know to have 
commenced. lt was not, therefore, from any want of the most cordial adhesion 
to the feelings and intentions expressed by Her Majesty's Government that he 
felt obliged to demur to the immediate adoption of the present proposals, but 
from the sincere belief that they are not applicable, without some alteration, to 
the actual posture of affairs, which had assumed a new aspect with which your 
Lordship was unacquainted when you drew up the notes, He felt convinced, 
from the tenor of Count Nesselrode’s despatch of the 17th instant, that the 
state of war declared by the Porte eould not be put an end to without the 
intervention of Plenipotentiaries or some diplomatic act, and therefore it would 
be risking loss of time and of that weight with the Cabinet of St. Petersburgh 
which we possessed, if we proposed a simple note from Reshid Pasha to Count 
Nesselrode as a sufficient engagement upon which the Emperor of Russia would 
he satisfied to rest the re-establishment of peace. He carnestly appealed to me, 
and to the Representatives, to bring before our Governments the remarks he had 
made, and he should await the answers of our respective Cabinets. Count 
Arnim stated, that he had been instructed by his Government to support the 
proposition of your Lordship, and to forward orders to the Prussian Minister at 
Constantinople to give his best assistance towards carrying it into effect, 
provided it. was agreed to by the other Powers: but such condition not being 
actually fulfilled, he should refer the statement of Count Buol for the considera- 
tion of his Government. 

M. de Bourquency, after supporting with energy the appeal T had made 
for the immediate assent of the four Governments to the proposal of Her 
Majesty's Government, consented also to refer the statement of Count Buol, as 
well as his reasons for the delay which he desired and the modifications he

Sir G. H. Seymour to the Earl of Clarendon.—{ Received November 7.) 
(No, 565.) 


My Lord, St. Petersburgh, October 27, 1853, 

1 KAD the honour of stating to your Lordship, as 1 thought upon good 
authority, that the corps of General Osten Sacken had entered the Principalities. 

This is not so; at least up to yesterday the Government had no knowledge 
of such a movement having taken place. } 

The disposition of the Russian forces, according to an account which your 

Lordship may rely upon, is as follows— 
‘The 4th corps, composed of four divisions under the orders of Prince 
Gortchakoff and General Dannenberg, are quartered at and about Bucharest. 
‘This force hardly exceeds 60,000, comprising detached bodies of troops engaged 
in guarding the line of the Danube some 200 leagues in extent, from Widdin to

Sir G. H. Seymour to the Earl of Clarendon,—(Received November 7.) 
(No, 570.) 


My Lord, St. Petersburgh, October 28, 1859. 

IN one of my last despatches, No. 550, I stated Count Nesselrode to have 
expressed his apprehension of a rising of the Christian subjects of the Porte. 

With reference to this communication I hold it to be of importance that 
Her Majesty's Government should be able to show: first, that the danger had 
not escaped the attention of their agents abroad; and, secondly, that there was 
no remissness in giving due notice of its approach. For this reason, as a paper 
may well be overlooked among the mass of correspondence to which the affairs 
of ‘Turkey have given rise, I think it right to call to your Lordship’s recollection 
a memorandum dated the 8th of January, which, after having read it to Count 
Nesselrode, I forwarded to Her Majesty's Government in my despatch No. 10 of 
that year. 


our Lordship will observe that the evil which Count Nesselrode now 


anticipates was pene that to which | invited his attention at the opening of 
the year; and t 


1at.as | represented it as likely to result from*the gathering of a 
large Russian force on the Turkish frontiers, much more should I now be 
justitied in ascribing it to the violation by that force of an important portion of 
the Turkish territory. 


[ have, &c. 
(Signed) G, H. SEYMOUR.

Sir G. H, Seymour to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received November 7.) 
(No. 571.) 
My Lord, 


St. Petersburgh, October 28, 1853. 
THERE can be, I think, no doubt that a fresh Russian manifesto has been 
for some time in preparation, and according to general belief it may be held to 
contain fresh appeals to the religious feelings of the army and nation. However 
this may be I have been assured, by a person in general well informed as to the 
events of the day, that for the present at least this paper has been withdrawn 
from publication, IT trust that it may never see the light—an appeal to religious 
passions being under actual circumstances both unnecessary and danwerdae: 

_ The “ Journal de St. Pétershourg " of the 25th instant, contains a notice of 
Prince Buriatinsky’s as Chef d’Etat Major of the forces in the Caucasus, where 
he has long served, and where he has obtained the reputation of being one of the 
most rising officers in the Emperor's armies, 

An Imperial reseript, not as yet bani has been issued, in which Prince . 
2 


160 


Menchikoff is thanked for the skilful manner in which the troops were conveyed 
from Sevastopol to the eastern coast of the Black Sea. No notice, as 1 under- 
stand, has been taken in this paper of the Prince's diplomatic services, and upon 
this score very slight thanks are ‘adeed his due. He signally failed, as I betore 
observed, at once in effecting a favourable arrangement, or 1 establishing @ 
reasonable ground of quarrel with Turkey, and he has involved his country in 
difficulties of which, at his ages he may very possibly never witness the 
conclusion. Poh eee 

Justice has not been backward in the case of this intriguing old man; the 
blame which he was so eager to ascribe to Viscount Stratford being now, as | 
observe, very generally imputed to himself. 

There is a great outward appearance of calm here, and the | language held 
about Eastern affairs is in general moderate ; still the indications of warlike 
preparation are not wanting. Wery great activity prevails-at the War Office; a 
captain, lieutenant, and ensign, from each of the regiments of the Guards have 
received orders to join the army in the field, and it has been intimated to the 
remainder of the officers of the same corps that they must hold themselves i 
readiness to march. | 

Ttis now stated to me that should they leave St, Petersburgh the Guards 
wili proceed cither to Moscow or Kieff. | 

As the information respecting the Baltic fleet has continued to be mort 
contradictory, while no reports upon the subject were sent here from the Vice- 
Consul, M. de Michele went him ‘Hf to Cronstadt on the 25th metant. He 
found there nine ships-of-war apparently and nominally all ready for service. 

According, however, to & local opinion expressed by Mr. Consul De Michele, 
twelve or fifteen hours must elapse before these ships, upon receiving their 
sailing orders, could put to sea. a 

The weather at St. Petersburgh continues to be unusually mild, so that the 
navigation may possibly yet remain for some weeks open.

No, 202. 
Sir G. H. Seymour to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Recewed November 7.) 


(No. 577. Confidential.) 
My Lord, St, Petersburgh, October 29, 1853, 

AFTER some days of reflection I made up my mind to apprise the 
Chancellor, on the 27th instant, of the orders which have been issued to Her 
Majesty’s Ambassador at Constantinople, and to the Admiral of Her Bey ¢ 
fleet in the Bosphorus, respecting the opposition to be made to the landing of 
Russian troops upon the Turkish territory, , 

I did so for various reasons ; amongat which the strongest were the desire 
of preventing the possibility of a collision which might he avoided, and of 

arding against the chance of these orders being first learned at St. Petersburgh 
through the Russian Admiralty. A 

In preparing Count Nesselrode for the communication, I began by remark~ 
ing, that 1 was not charged to speak to him officially, but that Sir Hamilton 
Sevmour desired to make a statement to Count Nesselrode which it was 
‘nteresting to him to learn, and which might guard against unnecessary 
complications. 

Count Nesselrode listened with the appearance of some surprise to my 
statement; and then observed that he had one question to make: He would 
ask whether Russia and England were at peace or war? ‘To this | replied, that 
[ could only say that his Excellency had put to me a question of the nature of 
that which had perplexed so many persons during the summer—that there were 
few persons who, when the Principalities were occupied, had not asked themselves 
or been asked by others whether Russia and the Porte were at war or at peace. 

We then spoke of the matter im @ subdued tone ; and I explained to his 
Excellency the cases in which no molestation would be offered to Russian ships 3 
und again, those in which an attempt to violate the Turkish territory would be 


161 


forcibly repelled (la force sera repoussée par la force), Count Nesselrode 
admitted that he had knowledge, through the Russian Mission in London, of the 
resolution of which I spoke, but was not aware of the resolution having already 
given rise to orders being sent to Her Majesty’s diplomatic and naval servants. 

The communication, I can safely say, was made on my part in a friendly 
spirit, and upon the whole it was better taken than I had anticipated. 

I ought to have mentioned, that Count Nesselrode having inquired of me 
what would be the line taken by Her Majesty's naval commanders in the event 
of a collision with the Russian forces being sought by the Turks, Iwas obliged 
to admit that I had no knowledge of the conduct which would be observed. 
I could only hope that the chances of confliet would be avoided by both parties. 

L have, &c. 
(Signed: G. H. SEYMOUR, 


P.S.—Upon reading over my despatch I find that I have omitted to state 
that Count Nesselrode having adverted to the inconsistency of Her Majesty's 
Government in acting as it is now doing, after having admitted that the Porte 
had no casus belli against Russia, 1 replied that neither Her Majesty's Govern- 
ment nor I believed any other had made such an admission; that what was true 
was that, from conciliatory motives and in the interest both of Turkey and 
Europe, Her Majesty’s Government had recommended that the casus belli 


a 5 


should not be acted upon—should not give rise to war; but that as to the real 
nature of the Russian act, no difference of opinion could possibly exist. .
