No. 203. 
Sir G. H. Seymour to the Earl of Clarendon,—(Reeeived November 7.) 


(No. 578. Confidential.) 
My Lord, St. Petersburgh, October 29, 1859. 

THE conversation which I held with the Chancellor on the 27th instant, 
was at one moment so animated that it was highly agreeable to me to find it 
concluding in an amicable manner; that it did so is no doubt to be ascribed to 
that amenity both of manner and character for which Count Nesselrode is so 
remarkable. 

I should find it difficult to state, from the number of subjects touched upon, 
what it was which gave rise to a somewhat violent attack on the part of Count 
Nesselrode wpon the feelings of Her Majesty's Government, 

On a sudden however, he remarked that all the difficulties which at present 
existed had arisen from the conduct of the English Cabinet; that af England 
had had the grievances of which Russia had to complain, redress would have 
been sought in a very different manner from that pursued by the Imperial 
Government in its demands upon Turkey; that after the admission by England 
of a reparation being due to Russia, it appeared as if that admission were Now 
withdrawn ; that if England had insisted as she ought to have done at Constan- 
tinople, the Porte would long ago have given way, and the Vienna note would 
have been signed; that England, in fact, was solely to blame for the complications 
of the moment, and for those disastrous consequences to which they were likely 
to lead; and that the conduct now pursued was an unworthy return for the 
proofs of friendship which had been given to England by His Imperial Majesty. 

‘To this 1 replied that 1 must be allowed to remark that far from this state- 
ment being admissible, it was to the Russian Government, and to them alone, 
that all the difficulties which beset us were to be ascribed ; that I had about me 
a paper to which I had hesitated to allude, but which I desired ta use as a 
weapon of defence, and which showed that on the 8th of January last I had 
distinctly warned him of what would be the consequences of a gathering together 
of troops on the Turkish frontier ; that naturally those consequences, 50 easily 
to be foreseen, had been aggravated by the Russian forces being poured into the 
Principalities ; that as for Her Majesty's Government, all that could be 
reproached to them was an enduring patience, and an absolute confidence in the 
assurances given by Russia, which had laid them open to much suspicion und 


162 


reproach in England, and to which the worst return had been made, first, by 
the event proving that the confidence had beer, misplaced, and secondly, by the 
reproaches now cast upon them. 

With regard to the reparation acknowledged to be the due of Russia, I 
begged once again to repeat that all that was known by Her Majesty’s Govern- 
ment or myself as to the views of Russia in her dispute with ‘Turkey related to 
the holy places; that consequently, all that had been admitted by Her Majesty's 
Government spp to that sole subject; that Russia had no more right to 
make war upon Turkey for withholding a political privilege, than England would 
have if she went to war upon being refused any commercial advantage for which 
she might apply to a foreign Government. . 

I concluded by alluding to your Lordship, and by stating that after what 
had passed, 1 must be permitted to remark that you had been wounded, and 
very deeply wounded, at finding, after the assurances which upon the faith of 
reports received from myself you had made in Parliament, that these statements 
were so little borne out by subsequent facts. 

i spoke warmly, and 1 fear with anger. After a pause of some duration 
the conversation was resumed in its ordinary tone, and I begged to be allowed 
to recapitulate late events. 

The Vienna note, I said, after being withdrawn, appears to be buried 
(enterré). Meanwhile the dispute between Russia and ‘Turkey continues, and is 

vated by an unfortunate declaration of war ; Her Majesty’s Government, 
still bent upon peaceable mensures, offer to draw up a fresh note, and if I 
understand your Excellency aright, this note you are ready to take mto con- 
sideration, 

In this plain statement of facts Count Nesselrode concurred, only 
cautioning me not to expect that anything approaching to assent could be given 
toa note the terms of which were unknown to him, and again remarking upon 
the necessity of providing that no expression, and, as I believe he said, no 
omission, should indicate a wish to lower (amoindrir) the Emperor's position. 
He would, he added, be humiliation to Russia to place her on the same line with 

‘urkey. 

| Having either by word or gest signified that I did not quite comprehend 
this concluding phrase, Count Nesselrode repeated—"' Is it possible that you 
should entertain any idea of placing Russia and Turkey on the same line 2” 

M, le Comte, I replied, I must admit freely that 1 hardly know how to 
answer your query. If you ask me, do T compare the civilization or the power 
of Russia to that of Turkey ? certainly I do not. Tf, on the contrary, the question 
ave to the independence of the two countries, you must allow me to say 
that 1 consider one State to have the same independent rights as the other, 

The conversation after this became more ‘amiliar and amicable, but some 
further allusion being made to the wish entertained by England of defeating 
Russian influence in Turkey, I observed that a man could hardly be more 
English in his feelings than myself; that I Lopes I was a faithful servant of the 
Government; but did not hesitate to say that far from wishing that Russia 
should meet with any defeat or humiliation, all my desire was that an adjust- 
ment honourable to both parties might be arrived at, and might pave the way 
for the resumption of those amicable relations which | considered indispensable 
for the welfure of Turkey and for the tranquillity of Europe. 

) I have, &c. 
(Signed) G. H. SEYMOUR.

Sir G. H, Seymour to the Earl of Clarendon,—(Received November 7.) 


(No. 579, Confidential.) 
My Lord, St. Petersburgh, October 29, 1853. 

A TELEGRAPHIC message, which reached St. Petersburgh on the night 
of the 27th instant, brings intelligence of the Turks having crossed the arm of 
the Danube which separates Widdin from the lange island in the middle of the 
stream. It hus been currently reported here, that they have erossed over the 


163 


river itself to Kalifat; but I am assured, positively, that this statement 1s 
incorrect. " 

The town is full of rumours of military preparation, and it is stated, and | 
1 believe with truth, that the Gth Corps d’Armée, stationed in and about 
Moscow, and the Ist Corps, stationed in the Baltic Provinees and in Poland, 
have received orders to call in their reserves, and to hold themselves int 
readiness. 

In general, the position of the Government appears to be one of consider- 
able embarrassment. Prince Gortchakoff is loudly blamed by some of the first 
military authorities for having exposed himself to great risks by the extension 
wiven to his lines, and it should appear that some not very definite apprehensions 
exist here as to dangers which may manifest themselves nearer to the seat 
of authority. Upon what these apprehensions are founded Lam unable to say, 
but | hear of a conversation which tock place among some of the superior 
officers of St. Petersburgh, in the presence of the young Grand Dukes, in which 
was discussed the expediency of adopting some fresh military precautions in 
Finland, and even in the neighbourhood of the capital. 

This anxicty, even if unfounded—these apprehensions—are suggestive of 
much serious reflection when they suddenty beset the Government of a Monarch 
who, a few months ago, held almost the proudest position ever occupied by a 
continental Sovereign, and who has, up to the present time, considered himeel! 
so perfectly the master of the destinies of Turkey that, to use the expression 
employed hy Count Nesselrode just before his departure for Olmntitz: “ Une 
chiquenaude donnée par VEmpereur, et Empire Ottoman s'éeroule.” 

Gencral de Rochow, a sensible man, and one who knows the country well, 
observed to me the other day, that whereas it is. commonly held that Russian 
policy is the most farseeing of all, he considered it, on the contrary, &% the least 
guided by calculation. 

In Russia,” he said, “whether as regards diplomatic or military affairs, 
the Government is too apt to ‘vivre au jour le jour.’ What is now happening 
‘ustrates this; events are taking them by surprise, and their position is unecr- 
tuin and exposed,” 

[repeat the observation in strict confidence, General de Rochow having 
See his wish that it should not he repeated. 

| have, &c. 
(Signed) G, H. SEYMOUR.

No. 207, 
Lord Cowley to the Earl of Clarendon.—{ Received 2 fovember 7.) 


(No. 819.) 

My Lord, Paris, November 6, 1855, 
M. DROUYN DE LHUYS has received despatches from Constantinople 

up to the 20th ultimo. Nothing was changed in the situation of affairs. 

Reshid Pasha appeared certain that the counter-orders sent to the commanders: 

in Asia would not reach them in time to prevent the commencement ol 


165 


hostilities. He seemed sanguine of suceess attending the Sultan’s arms, and he 
appeared to indulge in hopes that this success would so change the aspect of 
affairs as to superinduce # modification of the nature of the Porte’s obligations 
towards Russia in the Principalities. ‘The idea of the Turkish Minister seemed 
to be that greater independence might be conceded to Wallachia, Moldavia, and 
Servia, which would place them less under the control of Russia, while the 
nominal sovereignty of the Porte would be maintained ; and to this scheme he 
adds another, for the independence of Cirenssia and Daghistan, under the 
guarantee of the Western Powers. 

As M. de la Cour mentions that Reshid Pasha had imparted this idea to 
Lord Stratford, and as his own despatch on the subject is exceedingly vague, 
I confine myself to saymg that such a scheme exists, and that M. Drouyn 
de Lhuys’ first impressions are favourable to it; though when T asked him what 
hope there would be of obtaining the consent of Russia to it, unless she was 
utterly vanquished, he did not, any more than myself, think such a result 
possible. 

The only other point of interest mentioned by M, de la Cour is, that he 
had had the assurance of Reshid Pasha, that he had no knowledge of Lord 
Stratford’s proposition before it was transmitted to Vienna; but his Lordship 
had subsequently informed M. de la Cour that he had since shown it to Reshid 
Pasha, who did not appear dissutistied with it, though he would in no way 
answer for the suceess which it might obtain when submitted for the consideration 
of the Grand Council. 

I have, &e. 
(Signed) COWLEY.

My Lord, Berlin, November 4, 1853. 

* THAD an interview with Baron Manteuffel this evening, and expressed to 
him the satisfaction with which Her Majesty's Government had learnt that the 
project of note to which by your Lordship’s instructions 1 had invited the 
adhesion of the Prussian Government, had been approved by His Prussian 
Tajesty. Soh 
EON this occasion I commmnicated to Baron Manteuffel, in the spint of 
your Lordship’s despatch to me No. 42, the draft of the project whieh had been 
framed by Lord Stratford de Redelitfe, and of which copies are forwarded to 
your Lordship from the Earl of Westmorland by thes messenger. <i setae 
* Linformed his Excellency that the substance andl terms of Lord Stratford's 
project were almost identical with that proposed by your Lordship, and that on 
submitting them to His Majesty it would be advisable to propose that instruc- 
tions should be sent to Baron Wildenbruch, at Constantinople, to support Lord 
Stratford in urging on the Porte the adoption of either of the two projects. As 
the instructions referred to in my despatch No, 64 ol the 90th ultimo, which 
mad been forwarded to Vienna for transmission to Baron Wildenbruch, have been 
retained by Count Arnim, in consequence of the non-adhesion of the Austrian 
Cabinet to the proposal to which they relate, 1 may he desirable that Baron 
Manteuffel should still transmit such instructions to the Prussian Minister at 
Constantinople as may tend to support Her Majesty's Ambassador; and in this 
sensi, therefore, | shall endeavour to urge Baron Manteulfel to authorize Baron 
Wildenbruch to support either of these projects, should Lord Stratford still be 
of opinion that it may lead to a beneficial result, By; 

[ communicated to his Excellency the opinion expressed by Count Buol, as 
reported in the Earl of Westmorlund's despatch No, 805, that © he regarded the 
assurances given in these documents is nearly identical with those contained in 
your Lordship’s project. and would adopt them generally a5 t basis for # 
preliminary arringement for the re-establishment of peace 5 and it wos there- 
fore the form which prevented him from adhering to the project. 

I inquired of his Excellency, what oer he entertained as to any 
successful results to a pacifie arrangement. His Excellency scemed to fear that 
at present the complication of difficulties had increased, and he was but little 


169 


sanguine that Turkey would, under present circumstances, be disposed to accept 
any such arrangement as would be palatable to Russia. He seemed to consider 
that all the pacifie endeavours resorted to are in arrear of events, which advance so 
rapidly that what is proposed to-day is no longer applicable for the morrow. 
He appeared still to revert to his former idea, that nothing efficacious or durable 
can be effected but by a thorough revision of all the Treaties now existing 
between Russia and Turkey, in a conference at which the two contending parties 
shall assist. 

His Excellency believes that the Emperor of Russia is desirous of an 
honourable retreat, and stated, as if from information he had received, that His 
Imperial Majesty would be inclined to make suitable concessions to Turkey, but 
that he would not yield anything to England and France. 

T stated to his Excellency that the recent events had materially changed the 

ossibility of an arrangement by means of a note; that an actual state of war 
1a commenced, and that it per now that a Treaty or Convention could 
alone realize peace between the contending parties. For this purpose it wus 
most important that the union of the Four Powers should be preserved, and 
that they should concert previously together the basis on which a Treaty of 
Peace should be negotiated. 

I remarked to his Excellency that all eventualities must be taken into 
consideration; that the Four Powers might at the present moment arrange 
among themselves not only as to the terms of a future Treaty, to be submitted 
to both parties, but that they should be prepared beforehand, in the event of any 
serious collision, to step in and to impose an armistice of such duration as to 
afford time for negotiation and hopes of a satisfactory result. For my own 
part, | could not believe that if the voice of Europe was raised in the interest of 
peace, and to prevent the useless effusion of blood, it would be disregarded, or 
that the attempt would be made in yain.

No. 215. 
Cireulur to Her Majesty's Missions abroad, 


Sir, Foreign Ojfice, November 7, 1850. 

IN my circular despatch of the 13th of June last L informed you of the 
views of Her Majesty's Government with respect to the rupture of diplomatic 
relations between Russia and the Ottoman Porte, which had then recently 
occurred, i 

You were informed, that although Her Majesty's Government could not 
conceal from themselves the gravity of this occurrence, and had thought it 
necessity in consequence to order the British fleet to approach the Dardanelles, 
they still hoped that an amicable solution might be found of the existing 
differences between Russia-and the Porte. That hope, I regret to say, has not 
vet been realized, On the contrary, affairs have assumed a still graver character 
hy the declaration of war by the Porte, and the actual commencement of 
hostilities. 

| shall proceed, therefore, briefly to notiee the events which have led to this 
lumentable result; and to acquaint : with the views of Her Majesty's 
Government there pon. 

‘The demands made by Prince Menchikoff, and upon the rejection of which 
he retired from Constantinople, were repeated by Count Nesselrode in a letter 
addressed by him to the Ottoman Minister, with the threat that if, within a 
specified period of eight days, they should not be accepted sans variante by the 
Porte, the Russian troops would aceupy the Turkish provinces of Moldavia and 
Wallachia, 

This renewed demand was met by the Porte with the same temperate but 
firm refusal us before; and, accordingly, the Russian troops crossed the Pruth 


Wl 


and oceupied the Principalities. At the same time a manifesto appeared in the 
“St, Petersburgh Journal,” in which the Emperor of Russia isclaimed the 
‘ntention of making war, or of extending his territory; and declared, that he 
ghould hold the Principalities simply as 4 guarantee for the recovery of the 
rights withheld from him by the Porte. | 

Thus the Court of St. Petersburgh proposed, under the name of peace, to 
obtain all the advantages of war. But it is scarcely necessary to point out to 
‘on, that from the moment that the first Russian soldier crossed the Pruth, as 
dir as Russia was concerned, a state of war had virtually commenced. Nor is this 
the less true because actual hostilities were deferred and the chances of an’ amicable 
arrangement prolonged, by the Porte, with the advice of her allies, abstaining at 
that time from issuing, as she had a perfect right to do, a formal declaration of 
war. 

Meantime, with a view to take advantage of the opportunity thus afforded 
for preserving peace, a Conference of the Representatives of the f our Powers 
was established at Vienna, and a note was drawn up by them, which was 
unanimously recommended by the Four Powers to the Sultan for his adoption, 
in the belick that, whilst it would prove he to the Emperor of Russia, tt 
fully guarded the honour and independence of the Sultan. 

These expectations were, however, frustrated. The Emperor of Russia, 
indeed, declared his willingness to accept the note, and engaged upon its 
transmission, without alterations, to St. Petersburgh by the Porte, to withdraw 
his troops from the Turkish territory. But the Porte insisted upon certain 
modifications of it as essential, in its opinion, to the maintenance of the mghts 
and authority of the Sultan, These modifications could not be considered by 
Her Majesty’s Government as in themselves objectionable, but they appeared to 
them unnecessary, as they seemed merely to interpret the note in the sense 
intended by the Four Powers; and they accordingly joined in recommending the 
Cabinet of St. Petersburgh to adopt the modifications. ‘The Emperor of Russia, 
however, declined to accept the note thus modified; and Count Nesselrode 
entered at length into an analysis of the modificntions ina despatch to Baron 
Mevendorff, dated September 7, copy of which is herewith annexed, together 
with a copy of a despatch addressed by me, in consequence, to oir Hamilton 
Seymour.* C 

The Four Powers, in recommending the note framed at Vienna to the 
adoption of the Porte, acted upon the assurances repeatedly given by the 
Emperor of Russia, that he sought no new concessions OF rights m furkey, but 
only the maintenance of existing ‘Treaties and of the status quo Mm relinious 
matters, and the true meaning of that note, the only meaning, a5 they believed. 
whieh could be attached to it, was in conformity with this principle; but the 
reasons put forward by Count Nesselrode in his despatch to Baron Meyendortl 
for rejecting the Turkish modifications, showed that he placed a different 
interpretation upon the original note, and thus, to a great extent, justitied the 
fears of the Porte as to the pretensions which Russia would hereafter found 
upon it; and Her Majesty's Government therefore felt that, under these 
ciroumstances, it would not be just or honourable to continue to urge upon the 

Sultan the acceptance of the note. we | 

‘The presence soon afterwards of the Emperor of Russia at Olmiitz afforded 
Her Majesty’s Government a fresh opportunity of ascertaining, through Her 
Majesty’s Minister at the Court of Vienna, whether the Emperor was still willing 
to aecede to an arrangement, if such could be found, by which the differences af 
Russia with the Porte might be amicably terminated; and they received, through 
the Earl of Westmorland, the most positive and formal assurances that the 
Emperor sought no new right—no further extension of power in ‘Turkey ; and 
that he looked for nothing but the maintenance of Treaties, and the status quo 
in religious matters. 

In the meanwhile, however, the successive events which had taken place ; 
the invasion of the Principalities ; the orders issued by the Russian authorities 
to the Hospodars to break off their official intercourse with the Porte, and to 
withhold the tribute due from them to their Sovereign ; the consequent recall 
of the Hospodars by the Porte; the extensive preparations of war carried on by 
the Ottoman Government, and the passing of large bodies of troops towards the 


* See Part I], No. 341; and Port Hl, No. 11. 
2M 


—— 


172 


Danube, had roused the minds of the population of Constantinople to such a 
pitch of excitement, that the French and English Ambassadors thought it 
advisable to call up from the fleets at Besika Bay four war-steamers to protect 
the utiece of their respective States, and, if necessary, to afford protection to 
the Sultan. 

The conduct of Lord Stratford de Redeliffe in taking this step was, under 
the circumstances, entirely approved by Her Majesty’s Government ; and 
although these apprehensions have now ceased, the whole of the fleets have 
subsequently, at the request of the Porte, entered the Dardanelles to support, by 
their presence, the Ottoman Government, 

t is scarcely necessary to add, that although no formal declaration of war 
had been made by the Porte when the four steamers entered the Dardanelles, 
their entry constituted no infraction of the Treaty of 1841; for, as I have 
already pointed out, the Porte had ceased to be in a state of peace, and the 
Treaty had been virtually suspended from the moment that the Russian troops 
invaded the Principalities. . 

The rejection by the Emperor of Russia of the Turkish modifications of 
the Vienna note rendered it necessary in the opinion of the Porte to put an end 
to the system of forbearance which she had. hitherto pursued, and to have 
recourse to more decisive measures; and after a solemn deliberation it was 
unanimously resolved in the Grand Council of the Sultan that war should be 
declared against Russia. The advice was adopted by the Sultan and his 
Government ; and Omer Pasha, the General commanding the Tu rkish forces on 
the Danube, was directed to summon Prince Gortchakoff to evacuate the Princi- 
palities within fifteen days. 

Although Her Majesty's Government made every allowance for the great 

difficulties by which the Sultan was surrounded, and it was fully admitted that 
a declaration of war was amply justified by the Russian invasion of the Princi- 
palities, yet Her Majesty’s Government could not but regret that this step had 
been taken by the Porte whilst attempts at negotiation were not yet wholly aban- 
doned, but her allies were still endeavouring to bring her differences with Russia to 
a peaceful and honourable termination ; and Fler Majesty's Ambassador at 
Constantinople was instructed to use every effort to induce the Porte to suspend 
hostilities, in order to give time for a further effort for the re-establishment of 
ACE, 
The result of these efforts, made in concert with the Representatives of 
the other three Powers, was successful, and the Porte was induced to suspend the 
commencement of hostilities for a short time in order to allow a fresh proposal 
for an arrangement with Russia to be submitted to her by her allies; but from 
some unexplained cause, either that the orders of the Porte were disregarded, or 
that Omer Pasha, not having received these orders, regarded the negative answer 
of Prince Gortchakoff as the signal for hostilities, by the latest accounts hos- 
lilities appear to have actually commenced. 

Such is a brief sketch of the present state of affairs, and of the events 
which have led to it. 

Throughout these arduous negotiations there has happily existed between 
the British and French Governments the most complete concert and agreement 
both of opinion and action. ‘They look upon the maintenance of the Ottoman 
Empire as a great feature of European policy; and whilst they have left and 
will leave no means untried which may hold out the prospect of saving the Porte 
by a pacific arrangement from the dangers by which she is menaced, and Europe 
from the calamities of war—and they do not even now despair of such an 
arrangement being found—they are at the same time resolutely determined to 
uphold the independence of the Sultan and the inte of 0 Empire.

My Lord, Foreign Office, November 8, 1650. 

THE. drafts of note and declaration inclosed in your Excellency’s despatch 
No. 306, of the 22nd ultimo, as well as the reasons which induced your 
Excellency to frame them, have been entirely approved by Her Majesty's 
Government. 

We learnt by telegraph from Belgrade that that note and declaration were 
on their way to Vienna, We felt sure that in spirit they must be the same, 
and that in form they could not be essentially different from those which were 
inclosed to your Excellency in my despatch No. 254 of the 84th ultimo; and 


Her Majesty's Government therefore, in order to avoid delay, did not hesitate. 


to recommend ta the Governments of Austria and Prussia that your Excellency's 
should be adopted in preference to those transmitted from hance and which 
were then under consideration at Vienna and Berlin, 

Infortunately, however, hostilities had in the meanwhile commenced, and 
the Austrian Government considered that the time for notes was passed, and 
that the difference between Russia and the Porte could only be settled by a 
Treaty. 

Her Majesty's Government have concurred in this opinion, and haye now 
under their consideration the form of Treaty that has become necessary. When 
agreed upon by the Four Powers it shall be forwarded to your Excellency for 
the concurrence of the Porte, who should then have no difficulty im sending 
a Plenipotentiary to sign it at such place as may be agreed upon, that shall be 
neither in the territory of Russia or of Turkey, 

Her Majesty’s Government have received assurances that Russia hes no 
resent intention to cross the Danube; and bya despateh of the Gth instant from 

ord Westmorland, of which your Excellency will find a copy in my despateh 
No. 261 of the 8th instant, you will see that Russia is still prepared to negotiate. 

But although a Treaty is indispensuble for the re-establishment of peace 
between the two countries, Her Majesty’s Government are still of opinion that 

2N 


-~r™ ees Pee ge es aS OS eC 


ly4 


a note will be the most effectual mode of terminating the discussions that have 
arisen upon religious points. 

To Her Majesty's Government it ts indifferent whether the declaration and 
note framed by themselves or by your Excellency be adopted. Both contain all 
that the Emperor of Russia professes or is entitled to ask; both exclude all that 
it would be contrary to the dignity of the Sultan to concede. It will be for the 
Porte, on the recommendation of your Excelleney, to select between them; and 
Her Majesty's Government ould propose that it should be signed by the 
Turkish Plenipotentiary at the same time as the Treaty. 

By this mode of proceeding the Porte will obtain, through the friendly 
mediation of her allies, all that she could expect to achieve by meurring the 
risks of war. The assent of the Sultan and his Ministers to such an arrange- 
ment can hardly admit of reasonable doubt, and in that ease Her Majesty’s 
Government trust that ‘the Sultan and his Ministers will be guided solely by 
sed own views of whatis best. for the dignity and welfare of the Ottoman 

mpire. nd 

It will be obviously expedient that when this negotiation commences it 
should be accompanied by an armistice.

chief.

Consul Brant to Lord Stratford de Redcliffe. 


( Extract.) Erzeroom, October 14, 1853. 


ON the Ith the Mushir left before daylight in the morning, and all the 
troops followed about midday, commanded by Ahmet Reis Sasha, The unex- 
pected and sudden departure of the Mushir, who went post, gave rise to the 
report that the Russians had actually passed the frontier, but this was soon dis- 
covered to be unfounded. 

Three battalions of infantry are left here under the command of Shukri 
Pasha. They are, | hear, the most inefficient of the army, as the commander is 
among the military Pashas. 

The Valee Pasha will command the Bashee Boyoob collecting, with whom 


~ a es * - 


176 


he will join the army. His departure is not fixed, nor can | state the number 
of this irregular force. Hussein Pasha, formerly of Moosb, will be left as 
Governor, 

The report I mentioned of the Armenians haying volunteered to raise a 
reziment is untrue; it was & joke of much one at the Medjlip, which was 
misunderstood by a military Pasha who happened to be present, and was reported 
by him as a serious affair. 

T trust that Reshid Pasha is a competent judge of what an army should be; 
in such case his inspection may do much good, and he may perhaps be in time 
to remedy some, at least, of the existing defects, and to raise the spirits of the 
soldiery, At one time the talk of the soldiers was only of destroying the 
Moscow Giaours without any assistance; but of late they have quite changed 
their tone, and now say, that unless assisted by French or English troops, they 
must be defeated. 

I have no reliable information regarding the Russian forces, but it is said a 
considerable army is assembled at Gumri, and that there is a force of 30,000 
available to act against the Turks, while there are sufficient troops to face the 
Lesghoe and the Circassians. 

The emissaries of Shamil passed through Georgia in the character of 
pilgrims on their way to Mecca. They came to assure the Turks that, a5 soon 
as they attacked the Russians, Shamil would fall upon them on his side. 

There is at present no reserve here for the army, if defeated, to fall back 
upon; and I fear a defeat would be a complete rout, and that the army would 
at once disband, 

It is said, however, that three complete regiments, about 8,000 or 9,000 
men, are shortly expected here, besides twenty-four pieces of artillery, which 
had already been landed at Trebizond.

Lord Stratford de Redeliffe to the Ear! of Clarendon —{ Received November 9.) 


(No. 316.) 


My Lord, ! Therapia, October 29, 1843. 

TN a conversation which I had with Reshid Pasha privately this morning, 
I ascertained, or rather received confirmation of, the following points ; firstly. 
that he cannot take upon himself to propose any further suspension of hosti- 
lities; secondly, that if any satisfactory proposal, involving a pacific arrange- 
ment, were to come from the Four Powers with a proper degree of authority, he 
would not refuse to submit it to the General Council; thirdly, that the 
declaration and note, which I have already forwarded to London and Vienna, 
and which I have since read over in strict personal confidence to him, would 
meet with his own individual acceptance, but that he could take no decision 
without his colleagues, nor would he undertake to pronounce in what light it 
would be viewed by the General Council, to which it must necessarily be 
submitted. 

Judging from the time which has elapsed since your Lordship’s acceptance 
of my SURE oe was made known at Vienna, without my receiving any intima- 
tion on the subject from that capital, and taking also into consideration the 
order received from Vienna for the immediate departure of the Russian officials, 
and Baron Bruck’s declaration of the actual existence of war, I can no longer 
entertain the slightest hope of a pacilie adjustment. 

Reshid Pasha takes credit to himself for having obtained the short suspen- 
sion of hostilities already announced to your Lordship, as having been carried 
in the face of much opposition and difficulty, The truth is, the measure offers 
more prospect of inconvenience and risk than chances of advantage to the Porte's 
interests. 

I have, &e. 
(Signed) STRATFORD DE REDCLIFFE.

The Earl of Westmorland to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received November 9.) 


(No, 400.) 
My Lord, ; Fienna, November 3, 1853, 

UPON receiving last evening your Lordship’s telegraphic despatch of 
yesterday morning, stating ” the earnest desire of Her Majesty's Government that 
the project coming from Constantinople may be accepted in preference to any 
other,'? 1 sent a copy of it to Count Buol, and | requested him to allow me to 
wait upon him this morning, in order to bring again before him your Lordship’s 
wishes; and I also proposed that my colleagues, Baron Bourqueney and Count 
Arnim, should be present at our interview. 

Count Buol replied by stating that he should be happy to receive me at 
any hour which should be convenient to me, and that he begged I would invite 
the other Ministers to meet me, 

In consequence of this appointment Count Arnim, Baron Bourqueney, and 
myself, assembled at Count Buol’s, when I communicated your Lordship’s 
telegraphic despatch, and the proposal from Lord Stratford which I had pre- 
viously brought before them, and I again pressed upon them its acceptance, as 
being a means by which the Porte might give evidence of its desire of 
re-establishing friendly relations with Russia, upon such terms as the Emperor 
had stated himsel to require, and as the Government of the Sultan had already 
declared themselves prepared to concede, I stated that although the term of 
the suspension of hostilities, under which the project of Lord Stratford had been 
proposed, had expired; and although hostilities between the parties had to 


a certain extent taken place, yet, 1 could not but believe that the acceptation of 
the note by the Porte would not be affected by these changes; and | also 
20 


= : 
ee 


178 


declared my conviction that the recommendation of such a document by the Four 
Powers, and its signature by Reshid Pasha, if not received at once by the 
Emperor of Russia as putting an end to the war, would be a great step towards 
facilitating any future negotiation which might take place. I remarked that 
notwithstanding the reasons which had already been stated against the adoption 
of this project in its present form, and against the probability of its being 
accepted as a means of reconciliation, under present circumstances, either by the 
Porte or by Russia, yet 1 had again invited a further consideration of it, in con- 
sequence of the great anxiety which was felt by my Government that it should 
have the recommendation of the Four Powers, and of the importance which they 
attached to the assurances it contained of the desire of the Porte to take the 
initiative towards the re-establishment of friendly relations. 

Count Buol stated that it was on account of the reasons | had given that 
he had at once agreed to reconsider the decision which had been come to upon 
this project, and if he could-see any grounds for changing that opinion, he 
should be most anxious to adopt them; but it was of essential importance lor 
the allies of the Governments now in hostility to each other, to be careful not to 
propose a project which would risk being refused by either party. The first 
object was to ascertain whether the Porte was willing to treat ; for it was impos- 
sible to suppose that a state of war, such as now existed, could be put an end to 
by a note. If the Porte should be willing to treat, an intention which had 
already heen declared on the part of Russia, then a declaration of the nature of 
the present project, addressed to the Four Powers, might be transmitted to 
St, Petersburgh, us the ground upon which the negotiation might be established, 
and the intervention of the Four Powers to recommend and support it, might 
secure itsacceptance. But for the re-establishment of peace there are other points 
to be insisted upon, such as the evacuation of the Principalities, of which there 
‘sno mention in the note; and the regulation of the different interests which 
have been disturbed by the state of war, which by some authentic Act must be 
put anend to. All these interests may be regulated by a transaction between 
the parties, under the friendly control of the Alhed Governments The reat 
object therefore, at present, was to obtain the assurance of both the bellizerents 
that they are willing to enter on a negotiation ; ‘to establish an armistice during 
which the negotiation can be carried on; and to fix upon such a mode of com- 
municating the proposals of each party, as may avoid delay and give protection 
to the interests of Europe, as well as to those of the parties directly concerned, 

Count Buol stated that in considering the project submitted to him, together 
with the documents which accompanied it, he could perceive no assurance that 
it would even be accepted by the Porte, The term of ten days fixed for the 
suspension of hostilities, with the view of facilitating the adoption of a mew 
project of arrangement, is already passed, and hostilities have taken place. The 
passage to which Reshid Pasha objected, concerning the participation by the 
professors of the Greek religion in the spiritual advantages granted to other 
Christian communities,” is placed in the note; and Reshid Pasha has distinctly 
stated that its acceptance by the Sultan must depend upon its examination by 
the General Council and that the Ministers of the Porte cannot hold out any 
promise in this respect. 

Count Buol conceived that your Lordship was probably not aware of these 
details when you transmitted your last telegraphic despatch, as he believes the 
despatch containing Lord Stratford’s note in detail, and Reshid Pasha’s letter, 
which were sent by the “ Caradoc” from Constantinople, could not have reached 
London on the morning of the 2nd. 

Under these circumstances of total uncertainty whether this project of note 
would he accepted by either party; under the conviction that the state of war 
at present existing could not be putan end to by such a document; with the 
persuasion that in its Reoeane form, as addressed ta Count Nesselrode, tt would 
nat be accepted at St. Petersburgh, and that a great loss of time would be the 
consequence, Count Buol, with the expression of his regret, declined to agree to 
it a8 it stood, while he adopted its saletaias if addressed to the Four Powers, 
and proposed as the expression of a desire on the part of the Porte to re-establish 
its friendly relations with Russia, He consequently desired to adjourn the 
consideration of the project till he was informed if the alterations he suggested 
would be adopted by Her Majesty's Government; and he appealed to me to 
report this decision, and to my colleagues to support it by their sanction. 


179 


M. de Bourqueney and Count Arnim both concurred in the decision of 
Count Buol: and I consented to submit the determination which had been 
come to, and to invite the opinion of my Government with regard to 1t 

Count Arnim mentioned that one of the grounds upon which he had been 
directed by his Government to suspend the transmission of the instructions to 
M. de Wildenbruch to support your Lordship's project was, that a proposal of 
the same nature had been made by France, which had been favourably received ; 
he therefore inquired if any such project had been sent to Baron Bourqueney, 
who stated that a project of note had been forwarded to him in his last despatches 
from Paris, and he proposed to communicate it, as it had already been trans-

M. de Hiibner that his own project of arrangement of the 25th ultimo had been

My Lord, Foreign Office, November 4, 1853. 


COUNT COLLOREDO has read to me a despatch from Count Buol, 
reporting the language held by him at the Conference which was held at Vienna 
on the 20th ultimo, and setting forth the motives which have induced the 
Austrian Government to suspend all opinion and action with reapect to the 
propositions of Her Majesty's Government on the Eastern question. ‘The 
‘Austrian Government has been informed that the Cabinet of St, Petersburgh, 
after the declaration of war by the Porte, and which has unfortunately been 
followed by hostilities, insists upon the form of a Treaty to bring back the 
relations of Russia with the Porte to their former state; nor are the Austrian 
Government surprised that Russia should now insist upon a formal Treaty 
which will expressly confirm those Treaties which have preceded it, and which 
the declaration of war has suspended. ; 

Such being the case, the Austrian Government have stronger reasons for 
doubting whether it would be possible to obtain the assent of Russia to the 
mode of arrangement proposed by Her Majesty's Government: nor do they 
think it would be easier to persuade the Sultan to agree to these propositions, a& 
he seurcely would, or indeed could, in the tace of the present state of excitement, 
cause a note to be addressed to the Court of St. Petersburgh, which explicitly 
aflirms his desire “to bind more and more the ties of friendship which unite him 
to the Emperor of Russia,’ until the re-establishment of peace by a formal 
‘Treaty has placed facts and words in harmony. 

Tho mutual relations which subsist at this moment between Russia and the 
Porte can scarcely be otherwise defined than as a state of war; aad, in the 
opinion of the Austrian Government, the Cabinet of St. Petersburgh, in asserting 
that a state of war cannot cease except by a ‘Treaty of Peace, enunciates & 
principle the application of which the Sublime Porte has an equal interest in 
maintaining, inasmuch as she hopes to establish her future relations with her 
powerful neighbour on a sure and solid basis. 

The Austrian Government, in pointing out their reasons for doubting the 
success of the plan proposed by Her Majesty’s Government, consider that their 
endeavours contain materials which may be usefully employed in the interests of 


180 


peace, if the Porte will draw from them the substance of the answer which she 
will make to the Four Powers, in the sense of the plan proposed in Count Buol’s 
despatch of the 27th ultimo, namely, to indicate to the Four Powers the basis 
on which the Porte will be willing to enter into negotiations for peace with 
Russia and to regulate the religious question. 

In consequence of the recent overtures of the Cabinet of St. Petersburgh, 
the Austrian Government {eels called upon, either alone or in concert with the 
other Three Powers, to inform the Porte that the Cabinet of St. Petersburgh is 
ready to enter at once into negotiations for peace. 

The propositions of Her Majesty’s Government have been agreed to in 
Conference by the Representatives of France and Prussia; but as Count Buol 
was not authorised to accede to them, he states that Count Arnim has not 
forwarded the telegraphic despatch to M. de Wildenbruch, empowering him to 
sien the note proposed by Her Majesty's Government, in case his three 
colleagues at Constantinople shall have done so, Count Buol does not know 
whether Lord Stratford will decide to proceed alone, or in concert with his 
French colleague, in the present state of the question.

Sir G. H. Seymour to the Earl of Clarendon.—( Received November 9.) 


(No. 580, Confidential.) 
My Lord, St, Petersburgh, October 31, 1892. 

ALL that I learn disposes me to believe that the want of forethought and 
yrudence which has marked the diplomatic proceedings of Russia during the 

tter months has even characterized their military operations in the Princi- 
palitics. 

In the reports commonly current upon this subject there is probably much 
exageeration, If would still appear that great carelessness has been shown by 
te Russians in obtaining due information as to Omer Pasha’s forees and their 
positions. 

It was probably not considered necessary to take much precaution with 
regard to an army of whom so contemptible an opinion has upon slight grounds 
hewn formed. 

[ would observe that the many statements repeatedly made by the Russians 
of its being intended that the winter should be allowed to pass by without 
hostilities, 1s sufficient to prove that they have been ill informed as to Omer 
Pasha’s resources. ‘They did not desire to begin active hostilities for some 
time, and they therefore thought fit to assume that it would not be in the power 
of the ‘Turks to do so. 


183 


The reports which reach us from the Principalities lead to the belief that 
they are the scene of much suffering on the part of the Russian troops from the 
diseases prevalent among them and from which, as is asserted, a tenth part of 
the army is attacked); on the part of the inhabitants, from the changes of all 
eorts which the disastrous occupation has again brought upon them. 

One thing, and one thing only, ts wanting to disprove the statements of the 
Russians with regard to: the detested rule and the sinking power of the Turks, 
and it may possibly be that this remaining contradiction may be afforded—I 
allude to the rising of a Christian population, not against their infidel masters 
but against their orthodox invaders. 

A report, respecting the correetness of which I am as yet unable to express 
an opinion, prevails here, according to which the Emperor is meditating a visit 
to his army in the south.

(No. 581.) 
My Lord, St. Petersburgh, October 31, 1853; 

AN ineffectual attempt has been made here, as your Lordship will have 
seen by my despatch No. 578, to prove that Her Majesty's Government have 
heen inconsistent with regard to their declarations as to the reparation due by 
the Porte to Russia; if it be desired to oint out a striking instance in which it 
‘s the Russian Government who have laid themselves open to this imputation, it 
will only be necessary to revert to a fact recorded in your Lordship's despatch 
No. 149 of the 22nd July last. 

Your Lordship informed me in that despatch, that in speaking of the 
arrangement to be entered into by Russia and Turkey, Baron Brunnow stated

(No. 585, Confidential.) 


My Lord, St. Petersburgh, November 1, 1853. 

HARDLY a day passes without my seeing General Castelbajac, and 
yesterday I held a great deal of conversation with him. Asa colleague | cannot 
desire that he should be other than he is,—as French Minister | should be glad 
that he took a somewhat different view of the Emperor's policy. 

The following extract from our yesterday's conversation will serve to 
exemplify ny meaning. 

Our Governments,” said General Castelbajac, “‘do not seem to me to 
understand the Emperor's views; they think him warlike, and J, who know him 
well, am convinced that he desires peace, and is, perhaps, apprehensive of war.” 

“My dear General,” I replied, “that is not the question, Certainly, 
he desires peace if he can attain his object without war, but what it is our 
business to find out is this—will he, to avoid the chances of war, forego a 
pretension which your Government and mine have declared to be inadmissible? 
Will he drop his demand for a Protectorate ? that is the question reduced to the 
smallest possible compass,” 

Again, we talked about the Black Sea, and about the difficulty of sustaining 
any argument as to our intended attitude there—a difficulty which | would not, 
indeed could not, admit. 

“The best thing,” 1 said, ‘is to avoid any discussion of the subject, or if 
possible any allusion to it; thus, if it is forced upon you, say, a4 | have done, 
and shall continue to do—‘ Our position in the Black Sea, if hostilities are made 
compulsory, may be very extraordinary, anomalous, whatever you Russians 
may please to call it; only the singularity, the anomaly has been created by 
yourselves: your own occupation of the Principulities has established a state of 
things which is neither peace nor war; we are sorry fo find ourselves in an 
ambiguous situation, but only bear in mind that it is yourselves who have 
involved us in these perplexities.’” 

So again with the ‘Turkish declaration of war: my French colleague deplores 
it, and so do 1; but I request him not to give utterance unnecessarily to the 
feeling, and ubove all to take especial care not to admit (according to the 
Russian version) that the Sultan is now the aggressor. 

This feeling | explain in a few words; I deplore extreme acts, but after all 
if a rnin enters anothers house with violence, Py must not be offended if the 
aggrieved party attempts un ejectment before entering upon discussion. 

General Castelbajac listens to all this with the greatest good-humour, but 
fails, | think, in observing that the chances of the continuance of that peace 


185 


which he is so eager to preserve, would be improved by more energy, more 
oceasional asperity, than he employs in his intercourse with the Russians. 
I will entreat of your Lordship to consider this despatch as strictly con- 
fidential. 
I have, &c. 
(Signed) G, H. SEYMOUR.

Sir G. H. Seymour to the Karl of Clarendon.—(Received November 9.) 


(No. 586. Confidential.) 
My Lord, St. Petersburgh, November 1, 1859. 

AS is well known, the two great motives by which the Emperor's policy 
towards ‘Turkey is represented as being actuated, are the lively interest taken 
by His Majesty in the welfare of his coreligionists under the Sultan’s authority, 
and the barbarous treatment to which it 1s to be understood these and other 
Christian sects are constantly experiencing at the hands of their lawful but 
barbarous Governors. 

It does not often happen that an opportunity is offered for instituting a 
direct comparison between, not the professions, but the acts of the two Sove- 
reigns towards large bodies of this Christian population; but as such an occasion 
presents itself, with reference to the occupation of the Principulities, 1 am 
desirous of turning it to account. 

In the year 1848, the occupation of Wallachia and Moldavia was considered 
to be essential by Russia ; the Porte taking a very different view of the case and 
regarding the measure as unnecessary and even hurtful, 

As it was to be expected, the opinion of the Protecting Power prevailed, 
and large bodies of Russian troops aving crossed the Pruth, the Porte, to 
prevent her provinces being committed to the exclusive keeping of the Emperor's 
armies, was compelled to take part in the oceuy ation. 

Here the contrast between the conduct of the two Powers becomes ut once 
very striking. 

The Russian Commissioner instantly instituted prosecutions and persecu- 
tions upon a very extensive scale, and expressed his surprise at the Turkish 
Commissioner declining to take part in them. 

Fuad Effendi explained that his master was animated by totally different 
views; that his object was not vengeance, but improvement ; that he looked to 
the future, not to the past, and was the enemy of a reactionary course. 

‘The Turkish authorities further stated that it was the Sultan's wish that 
the presence of his troops should be an advantage to the provinces; everything 
that was required for their maintenance was to be paid with the greatest punctu- 
ality, and no precaution was omitted which could prevent an extraordinary 
occasion being made use of for raising prices in & manner calculated to distress 
the inhabitants. 

The character of the Russian proceedings was of another order. 

They paid for nothing, and they devoured the country, Their course was 
to be traced by devastation, Consul-General Cunningham describes their pro- 
gress in a few graphic words. The effect of their presence is, he wrote, like that 
“produced by a flight of locusts.’ | 

It was, however, to be understood that this extensive consumption was not 
to be gratuitous, The charge was to be defrayed by the local Governments, 

To make these payments, nevertheless, the local Governments required 
funds, and not possessing any, they were were compelled to borrow money of 
their invaders. 

This loan the impoverished state of the land disqualified the inhabitants 
from repaying, and before it was possible that prosperity should return to their 
locust-devoured plains, a fresh Kussian occupation, that of the current year, 
took ose f 

t was, however, announced that the Emperor intended to pay for every- 
thing required for his army, and Count Neacatas as your Lordship will have

in 

| 
} 

i 


‘amount of which ig to be deducted from t

read in my reports, stated to me that the occupation might in fact be considered 
as a benetit, as a kind of godsend for the inhabitants. 

The advantage is one which the unfortunate Wallachians and Moldavians 
are little likely to appreciate, for although I believe everything that is con- 
sumed by the Russians is paid for, the nlite are effected in bills (bons), the 

ie sum owing to Russia by the Prin- 
cipalities for the occupation of 1848, owing, that is, to the necessity of having 
had previously to support a large Russian army, whose presence was us unwel- 
come to the inhabitants as to their legitimate Sovereign. 

When this picture and this are looked upon, it should certainly appear that 
Count Neaselrode was borne out in saying that Russia and Turkey are not to 
be placed on the same line. ‘lhe impoverished, the barbarous, the infidel Power 
. seen to hold a conduct which shows in proud relief against that of its mag- 
nanimous, mighty, and believing antagonist.

My Lord, Berlin, November 7, 1853, 

1 HAD an interview this evening with Baron Manteulfel. His Exeellency 
informed me that Baron Budberg, the Russian Minister at this Court, had 


communicated to him this morning, and left in his hands, copy of a circular 
despatch, dated October 19, addressed by Count Nesselrode ta the Russian 


187 


Missions at foreign Courts, inclosing 4 manifesto of the Russian Government 
as a reply to the declaration of war by Turkey. 

His Excellency read to me these documents, and seemed to consider that 
they were written in a moderate and pacific spirit. 

I remarked to his Excellency, that however “pious” the language, the 
arguments the contained, and the statements on which these arguments were 
based, were ait false and unfounded; that at the outset. Russia had stated 
that the mission of Prince Menchikoff solely related to the question of the holy 
places ; but when that question had been satisfactorily arranged (in the solution 
of which the able services rendered by Lord Stratford. de Redcliffe had been 
gratefully, acknowledged by Prince Menchikoff), fresh demands of a distinct 
nature to those previously announced by the Russian Government, and totally 
incompatible with the sovereign rights of the Sultan, were presented to the Porte. 

I observed further to his Excellency, that, for such a cause, and under such 
pretext, Russia had no more right to make war on Turkey, than any Power 
would have to violate the territory of its neighbour for a refusal to sign @ Treaty 
of commerce; and I added, that as to the question of war Russia could alone be 
held responsible to Europe, a8 she herself had first broken the peace of Europe 
by a lawless and illegal occupation of the Sultan’s territory. 

Baron Manteuffel acquiesced in the justice of my remarks, and L trust I 
have succeeded in counteracting an false impression with which Baron Budberg 
may have sought to imbue his mind on the occasion of placing these documents 
in his Excellency’s hands. 

Although your Lordship will probably be already in possession of these 
papers, I have the honour to inclose copies of them herewith, 

I have, &c. 


(Signed) AUGUSTUS LOFTUS.

ship's project or the one he had transmitted from Constantinople, which latter, 
though identical with your Lordship’s project, had the advantage of having

therefore most desirable that Baron Wildenbruch should be instructed by his 
ixcellency to support Lord Stratford in any endeayours he might make to ae

tussia, 

His Excellency assented to this view, and said that he had already written

Prussia: in that letter he referred to the instructions he had previously given to

that circumstances having changed, those instructions were no longer in force. 

His Excellency informed me that he would again instruct Barou Wilden- 
bruch to support Lord Stratford in his endeavours to bring about a pacification, 
His Excellency further added that it was his sincere wish to cooperate with

occur; and 2ndly, To forestall any other engagement which might be addressed

hitherto taken place, 1 think I may safely assure your Lordship that Baron 
Manteuffel is anxious to preserve a thorough independence of action for Prussia; 
and Lam firmly persuaded that it is his wish to act in cooperation with England 
towards the attainment of peace,

No, 241. 
Lord Cowley to the Earl of Clarendon.— (Received November 9.) 


(No. 831. Confidential.) 
My Lord, Paris, November 8, 1858. 

| HAVE seen M. Drouyn de Lhuys this afternoon, who informed me that 
he had received yesterday a pressing telegraphic message from M. de Bour- 
queney, asking to be empowered to sign a note which Count Buol had just 
proposed that the Representatives of the Four Powers at Vienna should address 
to the Porte, requesting the Turkish Government to consent to an armistice, 10 
order that negotiations might be resumed with a view of terminating the Oriental 

uestion in a manner consistent with the honour and independence of the Sultan. 
M. de Bourqueney begged for an immediate answer, which, however, M. Drouyn 
de Lhuys has not yet given, as he wishes to be informed previously of the light 
in which this proposition is viewed by Her Majesty's Government. 

M. de Lhuys’ own impression +; not favourable to this plan. He remarks 
that the Turks will probably refuse the proposition if made to them, unless it 1s 
accompanied by some proof or direct assurance that in ceasing hostilities they 
will obtain that for which they took up arms: and he thinks that it is hardly fair 
by the Turks to put them in a position to refuse a request of the Four Powers. 

e conceives that the wiser course is to abstain from all interference until such 
interference can be interposed with the hope of a successful result. At the same 
tine he feels the odium which may attach to a Government refusing its coopera- 
tion in any measure haying for its object to stop the effusion of human blood ; 
and if he receives no intelligence before this evening from Count Walewski of 
your Lordship’s opinion, he 18 ‘nelined to tell M. de Bourqueney that if Count 
Buol's proposition to the Porte is accompanied by something more tangible, m 
the way of reassuring the Turkish Government, he has no objection to the 
course proposed ; otherwise: he thinks that it had as well be let alone. 1 
remarked that perhaps the better plan would be to leave the matter very much 
in M. de Bourqueney’s hands; to give to that Minister a general idea of what 
the French Government thought should be done if an armistice was proposed ; 
hut to authorize him, since he was so much nearer the scene of action, and 
and moments were sometimes precious where armies were in presence, to join 
his colleagues in proposing an armistice whenever he judged the moment favour- 
able. It seemed to me, moreover, but fair that the proposal for an armistice 
should be made to each of the belligerent Parties; for proposing it to the Turks 
only was more or less indicating an opinion that they were in the wrong; and 
since it appeared that the Russians had attacked the Turkish army which had 
crossed the Danube, the former could hardly continue to plead that they were 
acting on the defensive alone, 

¥hen 1 left him, M. Drouyn de Lhuys continued uncertain what to do; 
he was expecting an answer from the Emperor, to whom he had submitted 
M. de Bourqueney's despatch, as also one from your Lordship. 
I have, &c. 
(Signed) COWLEY.

My Lord, Copenhagen, November §, 1853. 
IN the course of a conversation which I had yesterday the honour of 

holding with the King, His Majesty referred to the continued uncertainty which 


prevails as to the issue of the riental en and expressed serious uneasi- 
2 


190 


ness as to the position in which Denmark would be placed in the event of a war 
between Great Britain and Russia. 

His Majesty said that his own wishes, and the interests of his country, 
would mduce him, on such a contingency, to maintain a strictly neutral policy ; 
but he feared that if the prospect of hostilities should lead either belligerent to 
establish a squadron in a Danish port, and to draw its supplies from Denmark, 
the advantages which it would thus derive might become a canse of complaint 
on the part of the other, and that he might be eventually drawn into a war 
without intending it; and he expressed at the same time the hope that England 
would not again think it necessary to take measures of @ precautionary character 
to prevent such maritime resources as Denmark might still possess from falling 
into the power of her enemies. 

To the latter part of His Majesty's observations I replied that | was sure 
His Majesty would do England the justice to acknowledge, that if in 1807 she 
had adopted a harsh course towards Denmark she had been driven to it by the 
circumstances of the time; and with regard to the question generally, | said 
that though | could not offer His Majesty any official assurances of the policy of 
Her Majesty’s Government respecting contingencies which might never arise, | 
felt convinced that whatever measures they might eventually be obliged to adopt, 
and whatever events might take place in the Baltic, every possible deference and 
consideration would be shown to the wishes of His Majesty, and that there was 
at all events no immediate ground for anxiety on his part, a8 the naval forces of 
Russia would soon be prevented from moving \y the winter; and that if in the 
apring it should be deemed necessary by Her Majesty's Government to send @& 
squadron to the Baltic, which I believe there was every reason to consider an 
improbable eventuality, such a squadron was not likely to remain long in the 
waters of Denmark, and if it proceeded towards the Gulf of Finland it would, 1 
trusted, relieve His Majesty from all apprehension of his neutrality being com- 
promised by the acts of Russia. . 

His Majesty concluded by be ging me to convey to the Queen the expres- 
sion of his earnest desire to cu vate the most friendly relations with Her 
Majesty, saying that his feelings towards “the Queen his sister’? were really 
those of a brother, and that he wished me to express to Her Majesty his anxious 
hope that the policy of Her Majesty’s Government would never be inconsistent 
with the sisterly regard which he helieved Her Majesty to entertain towards 
himself, 

I have, &e. 
Signed) ANDREW BUCHANAN.

Sir, Foreign Office, November 12, 1843. 

BARON REHAUSEN read to me a few days ago a despatch from Baron 
Stierneld, stating that the Eastern question was @ source of great uneasiness to 
the Swedish Government, who wished Her Majesty’s Government to be assured 
that, in the event of war occurring between Great Britain and Russia, Sweden 
would oceupy a position of strict neutrality. nan 

Baron Stierneld added, that the policy of Denmark being similar to that of 
Sweden, he was in communication with the Danish Government upon the 
subject, for the purpose of securing complete concert between the two countries 
+, the event of war, and that he should make known the result to Baron 
Rehausen. 

L thanked Baron Rehausen for this communication, and said, that as taking 
part with Russia would probably be injurious to Sweden, and would certainly be 
unpopular in the country, t was satisfactory to learn that a neutral position 
been determined upon; and that if Her Majesty's Government respected that 
position, they were entitled to expect that the neutrality of Sweden should be 
strictly and faithfully maintained. tay 

Vou will communicate this despatch to Baron Stierneld, and ascertain from 
his Excellency what arrangements have been made wis the Houaai Government.

My dear Count Nesselrode, November 2, 1854, 


ALTHOUGH we are to meet, T am happy to say, at dinner to-day, I must 
write | few lines to say that our messenger is arrived, and that all that ihe brings 
is good, 

Our Government, and not less that of France, although prepared for the 
worst, is working honourably and indefatigahly in the cause of peace. 

___ A fresh projet de note has been prepared and, according to your very 
judicious suggestion, it will be ascertained whether the Porte can be induced to 
accept it before it is submitted to you. 

Meanwhile, a8 pniononaey Lotd Stratford de Redcliffe was unable to 
prevent the declaration of war, he has been labouring to arrest the progress of 
war: and according to news of the 2lst October, from Constantinople, has 
actually determined the Porte to an armistice until news should be received from 
England as to the probability of an arrangement, 

All this looks well; and, as I will take the liberty of adding, peaceful 
prospects will be further improved if Lam enabled to report that the Russian 
Government persevere in their present wise course of abstaining from the 
publication of any declaration or manifesto calculated to increase those suspicions 
and misgivings—those apprehensions as to the danger impending their religion 
and their political existence, which have hurried the Turks into measures which 
all have witnessed with regret.

THE messenger Robbins, who arrived here on the 2nd instant, has

I called yesterday upon the Chancellor, chiefly for the purpose of making 
inquiry respecting a report which had Ac te as to the intended nomination 
of General Budberg as Governor of the Prineipalities. | 

The sum Of the ‘formation which | received is, that General Budberg ts to 


be named Commissioner, the title of Governor being one which was calculated 
to give rise to misapprehensions as fo the Emperor's intentions, which remained 


195 


those of not incorporating the two Provinces (de ne point incorporer les 
Provinces). 

The Government, Count Nesselrode further stated, would have been glad 
to have retained the Hospodars, but since the declaration of war their position 
had become so painful that they were unwilling to continue the exercise of their 
functions; it became therefore necessary to provide some present system of 
government for Wallachia and Moldavia. 

It may be of interest to your Lordship to know that General Budberg was 
aide-de-camp to Marshal Diebitsch in 1829, and was the officer who having been 
sent forward to the Porte to say that the Marshal was upon the point of 
marching upon Constantinople, placed himself in communication with the 
English Ambassador, and by out-staying the time assigned to him by twenty-four 
hours, was able to take back intelligence of Turkish Plenipotentiaries having 
been empowered to treat. 

~~ Before I left him, Count Nesselrode spoke, with a feeling which was mani- 
festly most sincere, of the pain with which he viewed the chances of a rupture 
with England. Although that this event should really occur was a misfortune 
whieh he could not yet. bring himself to contemplate, [ might, he observed, 
readily picture to myself what his feelings must be, if I reflected that the great 
object of his life had been to build up an alliance, which now, at the end of his 
eareer, he saw in such jeopardy. 

Before closing my despatch I may state to your Lordship that I hear upon 
good authority that Admiral Lutke, one of the best officers in the Russian fleet, 
and formerly only the naval instructor of the Grand Duke Constantine, 1s to 
have the command.

My Lord, St. Petersburgh, November 5, 1853. 

I HAVE had the honour to receive (forwarded by Lord Augustus Loftus) 
your Lordship’s telegraphic despatch of the 28th ultimo. 

After some reflection | made up my mind not to notice to the Chancellor, 
or indeed to any one, either the note which you announced as having been pro- 
posed at Constantinople, or that of which the draft was inclosed in your Lord- 
ship's despatch to Viscount Stratford de Redcliffe marked No. 251. 

My resolution was taken upon the ground of endeavouring to guard against 
any confusion which might arise from two notes being brought forward about 
the same time; and, as regards the projet de note prepared (fi your Lordship, 
because it struck me that the chances of its acceptance here would be much 
improved by its arriving through Vienna, more especially if it should have met 
with the full approbation of the Austrian Cabinet. 

Count Nesselrode has twice expressed to me a wish of being put in 
possession of your Lordship’s note, but to this indirect application | returned an 
evasive answer. 

I have, &c. 


(Signed) G. H. SEYMOUR, 


P.S.—Since writing this despatch I have been assured that the note 
prepared at Constantinople has not been approved of at Vienna.

My Lord, Paris, November 13, 1853. 


A ‘TELEGRAPHIC despatch dated the Sth instant, has been received 
from the French Consul at Bucharest, giving some further details of what may 
be called the battle of Oltenizza. 

The ation took place in the village of that name, which consists of a few 
houses and @ ruined fort, and in the delta on which it 18 situated. 

The Turks, to the amount of 9,000 only, not 12,000 as originally reported, 
crossed from Tourtoukai, bringing with them everything necessary to entrench 
themselves in Oltenizza. They were attacked by General Danenberg, with 
what foree is not stated, and @ most obstinate combat partly at the point of the 
bayonet ensued, The ‘Turkish fortress on the opposite side of the river at 
Tourtoukai fired with such precision that the shots fell just beyond the feet of 
the Turkish defenders, doing much execution among the Russiane. 

The latter had 1200 men put hors de combat. Almost all the colonels 
and chefs de bataillon were killed or wounded; @ proof of apathy on the part 
of the Russian oy obliging their officers to expose themselves, as of very 
accurate fring on the part of the Turks. ‘The ‘Turkish bullets were chiefly 


conical. 
Prince Gortchakoff was to make a forced march on the 9th, with the main 
body of his army, to meet the Turks, and it was caleulated that a serious battle 
would be fought on the 10th or 11th. 

Some disaffection seems to have shown itself among the Polish troops, and 
four soldiers who had demurred to fighting in defence of a faith which was not 


their own, had been summarily shot. | have, &c.

Se A. Muelet to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received November 14.) 


(So, bls.) 
My Lord, Frankfort, November 10, 1893, 


IT will not probably strike your Lordship as anything extraordinary that 
the Fastern question affords a new subject ol difference of opinion between 
Austria and Prussia as to the question whether their participation in the nego- 
tiations which have taken place, und their attitude in the present posture of 
affairs, should or should not be communicated to the Diet, and the concurrence 
and adhesion of that body invited. : Tens . 

Your Lordship is no doubt informed of the nature of M. de Prokeschs 
overtures on his passage through Berlin on his rcturn to his post here; and 
that in view of the prospect entertained at the moment of his presence in Berlin 
of effective negotiations being reopened, his Excellency appeared to adit that 
the motives put forward by the Prussian Cabinet for considering the present 
moiuent inopportune for making a communication on the posture of these affairs 
to the Dict, ouglit to prevail. : 

With this understanding the sitting of the Diet on Thursday last passed 
without any reference to the subject; but 1 have learnt from an undoubted 
source that Baron Prokesch received a telegraphic despatch from Vienna yester. 
day, instructing him,to make to the Diet in their sitting of this day a com- 
munication of the neutral attitude assumed by Austrin ; and, us Pam led 
to understand, with an invitation to the Diet to udhere to this declaration of 
neutrality. hice src 

There exists, it would seem, more than one reason for the Austrian Goyern- 
ment taking a course which to a certain extent places her de novo m decided 
opposition to Prussia, ; a . 

In the first plice there is ground to believe that this was one of the mea- 
sures, the adoption of which was stipulated, in conjunction with the recent 
reduction of her forces, in the negotiation not yet fully terminated for her pro- 
jected loan. ive 

Inthe next place, her old policy of showing deference for the Dict, in 


199 


opposition to the course recently taken by Prussia, and thus strengthening her 
German interests, will probably not have been left out of siht. 

By omitting, or even by delaying any notice of the subject in the Diet, the 
two great German States would have thus shown their intention of acting 
independently as European Powers, which would seem to be the purpose of 
Prussia. When one of these States takes the course of making a communication 
fram which the other abstains, and especially when the one communicating is 
Austria, and the one abstaining Prussia, ina matter which incaleulably more 
concerns the former than the latter, the divergence of views becomes the more 
salient and remarkable, 

I have learnt that, since Baron Prokesch left Berlin, Count Thun was 
suddenly summoned to Vienna, and the decision now taken, by which Baron 
Prokeseh is ordered to act ina mode so much at variance with the views of the 
Prussian Government, would appear to have been taken after Count Thun’s 
arrival in that capital. 

Up to yesterday evening the instructions of the Prussian Plenipotentiary 
to the Diet did not admit of his following the example of Austria in the proposed 
communication; but neither, as far as I can learn, would he make any oppo- 
sition to a vote of adhesion, if such a vote was invited by the President. 

I have, &e. 
(Signed) A. MALET,

No. 257. 
Sir A. Malet to the Earl of Clarenidon.—(Received November 14.) 
(No. 120.) 
My Lord, Frankfort, November 11, 1853. 

I LEARN that the repbrt contained in my No. 118, of what would be the 
nature of the communication made by Austria to the Dict in the sitting of 
Thursday the 10th, was substantially correct; but that an invitation to adhere 
to the declaration of neutrality did not form part of Baron Prokesch's communi- 
Calon. 

M. de Prokesch spoke in general terms of its having been the object of 
Austria, in conjunction with Prussia, France, and Great Britain, and with a full 
reliance on the declarations of the Emperor of Russia, to have maintained peace. 
These hopes had, however, in some degree been frustrated by recent events. 
Still Ausiria did not abandon the expectation of preventing the hostilities which 
had commenced from becoming serious; and no greater proof of her sincerely 
entertaining this opinion, and of having no fear of the warfare spreading, could 
have been given than by the reduction decided on, and already effected, in her 
army. 

Austria hoped that the members of the Confederation would approve of 
and concur in her policy. 

‘The Prussian Plenipotentiary, Count Bismark, in remarking on the com- 
munications of the President of the Diet, is reported to me to have spoken to the 
eifect that Prussia, as well as Austria, had, in conjunction with her allies, used 
similar efforts to preserve peace, and entertained similar hopes of negotiation being 
still successful in checking the spread of' hostilities, Count Bismark, in the course 
of his remarks, used the remarkable expression that Prussia, in these matters, 
desired to preserve her freedom of action, and, with some conciliatory plirase of 
his linpe that in so doing she would meet with approval from the members of the 
Confederation, gave them very elearly to comprehend that his Government 
intended acting in this question as an European Power, and not to consider 
herself fettered by uny federal obligations. 

_, Nothing thot passed indicates that Austria and Prussia will not co-operate 
with cual sincerity to settle the Eastern question, in accordance with the views 
of France and England; but the different attitude of the two Powers in respect 
of the Confederation, is, as your Lordship will see, deserving of attention, as 
bemg 80 distinctly marked,
