No. 258. 


Lord A. Loftus to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received November 14.) 


(No. 81.) 
My Lard, Berlin, November “1, 1853. 


| WAITED to-day on Baron Manteutfel, and referred to the circular and 
manifesto which had been submitted to him by the Russian Minister. I stated to 
his Excellency that since my last ‘aterview with him I had read over those 
documents with calmness and attention, and that I thought it necessary to make 
the following remarks to his Excellency on the nature of those documents. 

| first stated that I was not aware that Russia had made any efforts for an 

amicable arrangement with Turkey, unless a-violent attack upon her territory 
could be viewed in a yacific sense ; that she had obviated any settlement by her 
refusal of the Turkish modifications, even though they had been counselled for 
her aceeptance by the Powers of Europe; that consequently if matters had been 
brought to a serious ebb, the shame could only be laid at her door, that the 
possibility of an arrangement had not only been impeded, but absolutely cut off 
by Count Nesselrode’s memorandum, notifying the prounds on which the 
Russian Government had declined to accept the modifications of the Vienna 
note; that during four months the Porte had exbibited (in conformity with the 
advice of the European Powers) the greatest moderation in not declaring war 
against Russia—a right which could not be contested to her, and which, her 
patience exhausted, she wis legally entitled to. exercise 5 that thus her conduct 
could not be stigmatised as governed by warlike propensity or by fanuticiem—an 
accusation indeed which might with more just reason be addressed to Russia. 

With respect to the pacific disposition of the Emperor of Russia referred 
to in the Russian circular, | stated to Baron Manteuffel that we could alone 
judge of their value by the acts of His Imperial Majesty ; he had commenced 
war against Turkey in June last ; it is true that his words are words af peace, 
but his acts were acts of open hostility. 

| referred then to the resolutions published in the Russian circular of j=", 

cited in the circular, and which, though I acknowledge to have been satistactory 
in their theory, had been unfortunately quite the reverse in their practice. ‘The 
Governor of the Provinces had been completely laid hold of by the Russians ; 
the inhabitants had been foreibly compelled to provide provisions, horses. anich 
money ; the tribute due by the Hospodars had been authoritatively confiscated by 
Russia: inshort they had been treated as conquered provinces reduced to the 
yoke of Russia. 

| further remarked, with respect to the satisfaction demanded by Russia, 
that it must be borne in mind that the mission of Prince Menchikofl had been 
solemnly asserted to relate merely to the question of the holy places, which by 
the offices of Lord Stratford de Redcliffe had been satisfactorily arranged ; but 
that subsequently secret demands, incompatible with the dignity and sovercign 
rights of the Sultan, had heen addressed to the Porte, and categorically refused, 
with the unanimous ap srobation of Europe, 1 stated that ‘Turkey as: an inde- 
pendent country had full right to reject these demands, and that Russia had no 
legal power to enforee them by arms. 

L reminded his Exeelleney that Russia had, in invading the Principalities, 
committed the first breach of the European peace, and could not therefore with 
justice nccuse Turkey of warlike propensities or of hostile acts : and that if 
Russia were really desirous of fulfilling those engagements she had repeatedly 
given in writing and 80 repeatedly refuted by her acts, she ought to withdraw 
hev troops within her territory, and that failing to do so, it was her who must 
be saneidered as the aggressive Power. | represented such an act as one the 
most likely to cireumseribe the circle of hostilities, and to save Europe from ity 
dlisnstrous eventualities of war, 

‘The Russian documents to which Talluded, are drawn up with such specious 
reasoning and seeming plausibility, that 1 deemed it my duty, in the interests 
of truth and justice, to-offer to Baro Manteulfel the foregoing observations.

No. 268. 
Lord Cowley to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Recered November 15.) 


(No. 848. Confidential.) 
My Lord, Paris, November 14, 1884, 


ONE of my colleagues, who is desirous that his name should not be 
mentioned, has hal the goodness to communicate to me in strict contidence the 
substance of a conversation which he held the day before yesterday with 
M. Drouyn de Lhuys. He went to the Foreign Department with the intention 
of inquiring whether the French Government recognized and adopted as its own 
the article in the “ Moniteur,” inclosed in my despateh No. 843, commenting 
on the Russian Manifesto of the 20th of October (o. 4). He observed, that he 
thought the tone of it somewhat keen, inasmuch as the name of the Emperor of 
Russia was so often referred to. M. Drouyn de Lhuys replied that, as a 
Minister, he had no explanations to give respecting an article in the “ Moniteur;” 
but that, as a private individual, he had no objection to state that articles of the 
kind were sometimes necessary ; that although there was no longer a Chamber 
of Deputies in France, there existed a publie opinion of which account must be 
taken, and which it was necessary to enlighten. In the present critical state of 
affairs it was impossible to know how soon France might be called upon to make 
sacrifices in defence of the public rights of Europe; and the Government consi- 
dered it therefore necessary from time to time to pronounce an opinion respecting 
the state of public affairs, in order that France might not be taken by surprise, 
and might know if she was called upon to make ‘sacrifices, for what those sacri- 
fices were required. As to the frequent reference to the Emperor of Russia, to 
which my informant had alluded, M. Drouyn de Lhuys could only say that as it 
was in the Emperor's name that the Russian Manifesto was published, His 
Majesty became responsible for the contents of it; and if he chose to assert that 
which was not true, the contradiction must be made to apply to him. 

The conversation then turned on the present state of the Eastern question, 
when M. Drouyn Lhuys declared that he saw but one chance of terminating it, 
namely, that the Four Powers should meet in Conference, and summon the 
belligerent Powers to retire, the one behind the Pruth, and the other behind the 
Danube, and to send Plenipotentiaries to treat for peace. That if either party 
refused their assent to this proposition, the Four Powers should declare that they 
would abstain from all further interference; that they should at the same time 
bind themselves by a solemn engagement, whichever way the war might termi- 
nate, whether to the advantage of Rawk or of Turkey, not to permit the present 
territorial arrangement of Europe to be disturbed ; and that they should 
themselves to employ, if necessary, their united forces to prevent it. If this is 


207 


done, said M. Drouyn de Lhuys, it may be hoped that the belligerent parties, 
seeing that no real advantage can be gathered on either side from the continuance 
of the war, will put a stop to a useless effusion of blood; and, either by 
direct negotiation, or through the mediation of the Four Powers, arrive at an 
arrangement of their quarrel. 

My informant observed to M. Drouyn de Lhuys, that the language of the 
French Government had changed within the last few days: that when M. Drouyn 
de Lhuys had last spoken to him he seemed inclined to favour the continuance 
of the Conference at Vienna, and the measures which Count Buol had proposed. 

_ M. Drouyn de Lhuys rejoined that events had marched with great rapidity 
since; that the action of Austria was less decided than ever: that what was 
possible a short time back was impracticable now. ‘‘ In short,’ he added, * you 
may consider me as having made the proposition for a Conference on the terms 
mentioned above, and report it to your Government.” 

My informant then addressed M. Drouyn de Lhuys as follows ; “I do not 
ask you as French Minister for Foreign Affairs, but as M, Drouyn de Lhuys, 
whether you have really any hope of an early reconciliation between Russia and 
Turkey.” M. Drouyn de Lhuys replied, ‘* I will answer as a private individual 
in language which it would not be right in me to employ asa Minister. I have 
no such hope. My conviction is that Russia has no intention of terminating 
this quarrel but in a manner advantageous to herself, unless indeed Austria or 
Prussia will take a decided tone, which would materially alter the whole question. 
As it is, what has Russia to fear? Whatever may be the present purtial 
successes of the Turks, they cannot continne. England and France cannot by 
their fleets prevent a Russian occupation of the Principalities: but a word from 
Austria, or even decisive language on the part of Prussia, would force the 
Emperor of Russia to retire. He could not brave all Europe, But he knows 
that neither Austria nor Prussia will speak that word; there ore, I repeat it, my 
conviction is the Emperor of Russia is not sincere in his protestations in favour 
of peace ; his object is to gain time and to keep the Principalities.” 


have, &e. 

(Signed) COWLEY.

No. 272. 
The Earl of Clarendon to the Earl of Westmorland. 
(No. 378.) 
My Lord, Foreign Office, November 16, 1853. 


I HAVE received your Lordship's despatch No. 402, inclosing the draft of 
instructions which Count Buol proposes io send to the Internuncio for the 
direction of his conduct in recommending to the Government of the Sultan the 
course they might pursue in the negotiation with Russia, which will have been 
proposed to them by the collective note of the four Representatives, 

Your Lordship states that Count Buol is aware that in the mediating 
position of Austria more management of terms is required towards Russia than 
from England and France, but the objects to be obtained by the Four Powers 
being the same, a general concordance in the way of putting them forward may 
be of the greatest utility. 

Your Lordship will renew to Count Buol the assurances of the satisfaction 
that Her Majesty's Government will experience in cooperating with the Austrian 
Government towards the re-establishment of friendly relations between Russia 
and the Porte; but it seems necessary in the first instance to agree upon the 
collective note that is to be presented to the Porte, before the instructions with 
reference to the answer that is to be returned to it are taken into con- 
sideration, 

The note should in the opinion of Her Majesty's Government simply state 
the desire of the Four Powers to mediate between the belligerent parties, and to 
stop the further effusion of blood; that they have received assurances of the 
readiness of Russia to treat, and not doubting thatthe Porte is animated by the 
sume spirit, they request to know upon what conditions the Turkish Government 
is willing to negotiate a Treaty of Peace, 

On the assumption that this form of collective note is adopted by the Four 
Powers, | will now proceed to state the views of Her Majesty's Government 
upon Count Buol’s draft of instructions. 

Her Majesty's Government donot consider that the object which the Four 
Powers have in view would be advanced by an argument founded on the con- 
ciliatory dispositions displayed by Russia, The recent manifesto of the Emperor, 
the appointment of a Hussian Governor in the Principalities, and the announce- 
ment of Prince Gortchakoif that the subjects of the Sultan in Wallachia and 
Moldavia who spoke disrespectfully of Russian should be hanged without trial, 


* No; 2732. { No. 255 


20% 


render the allusion suggested by Count Buol impossible; but Her Majesty's 
Government entirely concur with his Excellency that no project of answer should 
be submitted to the Turkish Minister, and they should be left free to reply in 
the manner they may think fitting. 

In the probable events of the four Representatives being consulted with 
respect to the answer, Her Majesty's Government, taking the different heads 
in the order proposed by Count Buol, would be prepared to recommend— 

lst. That the Porte should declare that it always has manifested its desire 
to pe an end to the difference, and is still ready to come to an understanding 
with Russia. 

2nd. That the Porte having received formal assurances through the Four 
Powers that Russia seeks no rights nor any new concessions from the Sultan, 
and upon the condition that the Principalities are evacuated with the least 
possible delay, 1s prepared on her part to renew her former offers, 

3rd. That the form in which peace shall be re-established and the religious 
question settled shall be matter for negotiation, upon the understanding that 
the Porte is not required to accede to any demands to which she has already 
objected. 

4th. That the Porte should appoint a negotiator and furnish him with full 
powers to treat with a Russian negotiator, 

Sth. Her Majesty's Government, without any desire to fetter the decision 
of the Porte, will certainly recommend that the Russian and Turkish Plenipo- 
tentiaries should not meet together alone, and that the place of meeting should 
not be in any portion of the Sultan’s territory now oceupied by Russian troops. 
Her Majesty’s Government consider that the intervention of the Four Powers 
in the settlement of a question which vitally affects the present and future peace 
of Europe is indispensable, and they think that the neutral place in which the 
negotiations for this object are to be conducted, should be left to the selection 
of the Porte, subject, of course, to the assent of Hussia, 

ith. The cessation of hostilities would at this moment manifestly be to the 
disadvantage of the Porte: if she were now to consent to an armistice for six 
weeks, at the end of which the negotiators found themselves unable to agree 
upon the terms of peace, but during which Russian reinforcements would have 
arrived in the Principalities, the position of Russia would be greatly improved, 
while that of Turkey would be proportionably deteriorated. But if the Porte 
received assurances from the Four Powers that the terms on which she was 
willing to treat would, without any essential modification, be accepted by Russia, 
then Her Majeaty’s Government would be prepared to recommend that an 
armistice should fe forthwith concluded between the belligerent parties, who 
should fix the line of demarcation that would separate the two armies, 

Your Lordship will give a copy of this despatch to Count Buol. If his 
Excellency agrees in the advice which Her Majesty's Government is prepared to 
offer to the Porte, instructions to that effect will be sent tg Her Majesty's 
Ambassador at Constantinople, provided that they meet with the concurrence 
of the French Government. This despatch shall be communicated by Lord 
Cowley to M, Drouyn de Lhuys, who will doubtless send instructions by tele- 
graph to the Baron de Bourqueney.

No, 274. 


The Earl of Clarendon to Sir G. H. Seymour. 


(No. 296.) 
Sir, Foreign Office, November 16, 1853. 


THE manifesto of the Emperor of Rusaia has been received with astonish- 
ment and regret by Her Majesty's Government, and by all classes of people in 
this country. on oes 

It may be intended only for the Russian people; but a manifesto assigning 
the reasons of the Emperor of Russia for declaring war agaist Turkey 18 a 
document of the highest importance, and challenges the criticism of Europe. 

It is difficult to comprehend what can have been the inducement to put 
forward statements that recent events enable every man to contradict. fF acts do 
not bear out the statement that the principal Powers of Europe had in vain 
endeavoured to shake the blind obstinacy of the Porte; it is true that they 
endeavoured to mediate, and the Porte showed itself willing to adopt their udviee 
with certain modifications; those Powera then attermpted to shake the determi- 
nation of Russia, but in vain; they received only proofs of how real were the 
dangers apprehended by the Porte. . 

The manifesto complains of the violation of Treaties, and implies that the 
Greek religion in Turkey stands in need of defence ; but no Treaty has been 
violated by the Porte, and no specific charge of that nature has at any time been 
brought forward; no complaint has been heard from the Greek Patriarch or the 
Greek subjects of the Sultan: on the contrary there have been expressions of 
gratitude to the Sultan for the privileges he has confirmed, and they have not 
invoked the protectorate that Russia was desirous to exercise. 

No ‘Treaty has in fact been violated except that which forbids the passage 
of the Pruth to Russian soldiers ; and Russia has no right to say she has been 
provoked to war when the Sultan, after long forbearance, endeavours to repel 
the invader from the Turkish soil. ‘The Sultan has not appealed to the 
fanaticism of his people, and he has given no offence to Russia beyond refusing 
to grant what Russia had no right to demand, and which it would have been 
fatal to his independence to concede, 

A comparison between the conduct and the good faith of the two Powers 
has thus been forced upon Europe, and the manifesto has therefore rendered 
signal service to Turkey. 

Lam, &e. 
(Signed) CLARENDON.

Inclosure in No. 277. 
Article from the “ Zeit" Newspaper. 


(Translation.) Berlin, November 12, 1853. 


THE Russian manifesto, so long denied yet now produced, has materially 
altered the position of things. The hopes of peace, which it was thought could 
be attached to the silence of Russia, are now that Russia has spoken without 
foundation. Both parties have proclaimed war, and the existing question will 
now hardly be decided any other way than by arms; by the victory of the one 
and the defeat of the other. te al eee E 

It is more difficult to say now than a few months ago, which side will be 
triumphant. A compact and well-disciplined Russian force was then opposed by 
a weak ill-organised army, which, it was to be foreseen, would be overthrown at the 
first onset. To-day, there is a material difference, The Turkish Empire, con- 
sumptive and gradually expiring as everybody believed, has risen with an energy 
which is the more surprising, as it was notin the least expected. We see enormous 
masses gathered from all corners of Asia and Africa; and what they want in 
discipline and military practice, is made up by the religious fanaticism which has 
been awakened in them. 

Nevertheless, the expectations of Turkey are not so favourable as might 
appear. We must not be deceived by momentary successes of the Turkish arms 
on the Danube and in Asia, though it is certain that these successes will have 
great influence on the spirit and the confidence of the Turkish troops. As yet, 
Russia has not unfolded her power; as yet, it is only with inconsiderable portions 
of the Russian army that the Turkish soldiers haye come into collision ; only in 
a great regular action, in an open battle, will it be shown whether the Turkish 
regiments are a match for those of Russia. 

On the other hand, the defensive power of Turkey has been generally 
under-rated; Russia may have been mistaken in this point.* On both sides 
appeals have been made to religion, and wars waged under the banner of religion 
are the bloodiest and most inveterate; both parties have appealed to their 
holy and just cause. The Emperor of Russia declares the defence of the 
orthodox faith in the East the object of his legitimate solicitude, It 1s quite 
apparent that, in the present defined state of things, diplomatic negotiation 18 no 
longer possible. . wagner 

The duty of the Powers who are earnest in maintaining general peace, will 
new be to take care that the war, which has broke out and can no more be 
repressed by mediating intervention, be fou ‘ht out alone by the parties who 
believe themselves to be in a situation to prefer war to peace—that its origina 
local character may not become universal. As yet, there is every reason for 
expecting that this will be the case. Sout Ae 

The war on the Danube and the Black Sea will, therefore, it is to be hoped, 
affect us no further than that we shall follow it with interest and attention, 


a 


* This thwe she will not come so casily by her victories as in 1528; the resistance of the Turks 
will be much more decided and more violent than it was then.

The Earl of Westmorland to the Earl of Clarendon.—( Received November 18.)

My Lord, Vienna, November 14, 1853. 


TREAD to Count Buol your Lordship’s despatch No. 892, which reports 
the communication made to you by Count Colloredo of the despatch addressed 
to him by Count Buol after the Conference of the 30th ultimo, and which also 
states the opinions your Lordship expressed in reply to Count Colloredo. 

Count Buol considers these opinions as agreeing with his own in substance, 
and differing only in details easy of explanation. 

Your Lordship desired that the note proposed by Count Buol to be 
addressed by the four Representatives at Constantinople to the Porte, should be 
transmitted to London for approval. He considered this desire perfectly 
natural, but he would preter having the note emanate from you, to drawing it 
up himself. So much delay had, however, taken place since he received the 
declaration of the readiness of the Russian Government to treat, and serious 
events pressed on so rapidly, that he felt it was obligatory upon him not to 
withhold a day longer than necessary informing the Turkish Government of the 
opening offered for negotiation, He had fulfilled this obligation by his despatch 
to the Internuncio, of which he had placed a copy in the hands of the Repre- 
sentatives at the Conference, but he had little expectation of any successful 
result for this document; and he had therefore forwarded the Russian proposals 
merely as discharging a duty imposed upon him, and had abstained from enter- 
ing into the merits of them, and had confined his opinions upon them to his 
communications with the Conference, and the proposed instructions to the 
Internuncio, which he had confidentially submitted to Baron Bourqueney and 
me. He felt convinced that the only chance that existed of inducing the 
Porte to listen to the recommendations he had proposed to offer, was that they 
should be supported by the combined influence of the Four Powers. He had, 
therefore, abstained from forwarding them, in the hope that your Lordship 
would now draw up a note which he would receive with the anxious desire of 
concurring in it, and should he consider any modification desirable, it might be 
speedily arranged by telegraphic communication. He will greatly prefer that 
the note should originate in London rather than Vienna. 

I then proceeded to read to Count Buol the parts of your Lordship's 
despatch No, 266, addressed to Lord Stratford, in which you state that, 
‘although a Treaty is indispensable for the establishment of peace between the 
two countries, Her Majesty's Government are still of opinion that a note will be 
the most effectual mode of terminating the dissensions that have arisen upon 
religious points ;" and that “it will be obviously expedient that when this nego- 
tution commences, it should be accompanied by an armistice.” Count Buol 
entirely concurs in these proposals, which are in conformity with his own views, 


216 


He conceives them likely to produce the best results; and he hopes, therefore, 
that your Lordship will not delay in transmitting to him, first, the project of 
note to be addressed to the Porte, inviting the Sultan's Government to treat ; 
secondly, the general form and stipulations of the Treaty; and lastly, the draft 
of the note by which you would propose the religious aneations to be arranged.

Sir, Odessa, October 28, 1853. 


THE announcement of your sudden departure from St. Petersburgh in one 
of the Russian newspapers, subsequently contradicted, could not fail, for a time, 
causing me extreme inquietude; and to the present day every circumstance 
around us is of a nature to darken the gloom rather than to inspire confidence. 

I shall probably not be the first to inform you, Sir, that hostilities com- 
menced on the Danube early in the morning of last Sunday, the 23rd instant. 

Fight gun-boats, with six companies on board, had on the preceding day 
been detached from the Russian flotilla stationed at Ismail, to proceed to Galatz 
and Ibraila in tow of two steamers, the “* Prath” of 100, and the ‘ Vodinaretz,” 
of 60 horse-power. On nearing Isaktcha, it became evident that the further 
progress of the boats would be opposed; upon which four guns were hastily 
brought down to the left bank from Satanova, where 6,000 Russians are tat. 
n order to cover tne passage, ana a cannonade immediately ensued from both 
sides across the river. The Turkish fire was soon diverted by the approach of 
the flotilla, upon which it was then directed; the cannonade was returned by 


217 


the boats, and continued until it had ascended beyond the line of the Turkish 
fire. 

The passage was thus effected, and its success is said to have caused 
animation along the Russian lines, 

The loss on this side is reported to be 3 killed and 3 wounded, at the 
Satanova battery; and in the boats, 6 killed and 70 wounded, and among those 
that fell was unfortunately the commanding officer of the expedition. 

[ have seen no account of the extent of damage done to the steamer and 
gun-hoats; but it is asserted that the Turkish battery was dismantled, and that 
the village of Isaktcha was seen in flames in two different places. ; 

Lam told that on the night of that day a Turkish force crossed over into 
Tehetal, one of the islands of the Delta opposite to Ismail, with guns, and 
opened a fire upon the bridge of pontoons at that place. 

The particulars are not yet known to me, but it is certain that many of the 
inhabitants of Ismail have in their alarm fled into the country. 

po ee es are manifested, even here, of some possible hostile demon- 
atrayion y sea, and orders have been given to strengthen the batteries of the two 
moles. 

Yesterday an Austrian steamer arrived from the Bosphorus, having on 
board the remaining members of the late Russian Mission, and after having 
landed her passengers, immediately sailed on its return. 

Our news from Constantinople comes down to the 24th. There were no 
disturhances in that city. 

‘The combined fleets had not arrived, but a part of them was expected on 
the following day. 

| am sorry to say that hostilities are reported to have taken place on the 
Asiatic frontiers likewise, 

Great efforts were still made to bring forward new armaments, exhibiting a 
greater vitality than Turkey was supposed to possess.

No. 286. 
Lord Stratford de Redcliffe to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received November 19.) 
(No, 319.) 
My Lord, Therapia, October 29, 1853. 

HOSTILITIES commenced between Turkey and Russia on Sunday, the 
23rd instant. 

Omer Pasha has written to the Seraskier, to say that about fifty soldiers 
crossed the Danube at Tatrachan in boats, attacked an advanced post of 
Cossacks, killed four of them and took two. He states, moreover, that some of 
the Egyptian troops swam across the river at Carason, and performed a similar 
exploit, 

‘ Whether the Turkish Commander's object was merely to mark the 
beginning of hostilities, to ascertain the practicability of effecting a passage, or 
to encourage his army, I know not. If he had no distinct object in view, the 
sacrifice of human life, though ona small scale, appears to have been very 
wanton, 

I hear, from the best authority, that Omer Pasha thinks seriously of 
crossing the Danube with a much larger force, and that he reckons with 
confidence on a successful operation. I am assured that the Porte has written 
to admonish him of the danger of such an undertaking, and to recommend a 
more prudent course. Much appears to be lett to the General's discretion, and 
his character for boldness warrants some apprehension of his compromising the 
Sultan’s interests by a premature attack. 

The officer who was sent to Shumla with the Porte’s orders for a suspension 


218 


of hostilities arrived there too late. Ihave applied to Reshid Pasha for an 
explanation of this incident, which, however, is practically of little consequence 
in the present state of our information from Vienna, and his Highness has 
replied that Omer Pasha, calculating from the day on which he knew that his 
summons had been received by Prince Gortchakoff, considered the term of 
fifteen days as having expired on Sunday, the 23rd. Lt appears from Colonel 
Neale’s report, that the Porte’s officer disembarked at Varna on the 22nd, and 
proceeded to Shumla without delay. 
T have, Xe. 
(Signed) STRATFORD DE REDCLIFFE.

(No, 321.) 
My Lord, Therapia, October 31, 1853. 

IT is my duty to inform your Lordship that Captain Slade, who holds 
the temporary rank of rear-admiral in the Turkish service, under circum- 
stances known to Her Majesty's Government, is gone into the Black Sea in 
command of a double-bunked ‘Turkish frigate. He called a few days ago to 
inform me of this intention, and [ reminded him of the heavy personal respon- 
sibility which he would incur by placing himself, while a half-pay officer in 
Her Muajesty’s service, in a situation where he might be called upon in the 
performance of his duty towards the Sultan, to take part in attacking the 
forces of a power which is still at peace with his own Sovereign. I warned 
him of my inability, without instructions from your Lordship, to interfere on 
his behalf, if the fortune of war should betray him, as a prisoner, into the 
hands of the Kissians. 

I have explained my view of the matter to Reshid Pasha, and I request 
that your Lordship will inform me whether that view, such as I have described 
it above, is correct. 

Your Lordship will, no doubt, remember that Captam Slade was received 
into the Turkish service, by arrangement between the Porte and myself, for the 
purpose of tendering advice on naval matters to the Captain Pasha. 

I have, Xe. 
(Signed) STRATFORD DE REDCLIFFE, 


P.5.—From information which has réached me since writing the above, | 
have reason to doubt whether Captain Slade has the command of the frigate 
in which he is embarked. 

It is for your Lordship to judge how far that circumstance makes, if it 
be correct, any difference of principle in the considerations attached to his 
position.

to the principal local authority for that purpose. !

Dear Sir, Therapia, October 31, 1853, 

LINCLOSE herewith for your own information a copy of a despatch which 
| have addressed to-day to Her Majesty's Consuls at Bucharest and Jassy. 

Mr. Colquhoun having a political character us ageht, and Mr, Gardner 
residing at the court of a Prince, similarly circumstanced with the Hospodar of 
Wallachia, there could be no hesitation as to the propriety of their retirement 
from the Principalities, The case is different with respect to you; and com- 
mercial and shipping interests placed under your charge have the strongest 
claims to our protection, especially at a moment when the exportation of grain 
to England and Franee is going on to so great an extent, It ts, therefore, my 
wish and intention, that you should hold on as long as possible, applying to the 


220 
local authorities while you are allowed to do so with good effect, and even to the 
Russian intruders, when forced by their arrangements to do so. How long this 
annoyance may be necessary, and how soon it may cease to be possible, T cannot 
yet undertake to say; but my expectation is, that the Russian Commiander-in- 
chief will now exert a direct authority over the Principalities, and it is impossible 
to shut one’s eyes to the contingencies which may raise immediate differences 
and bring on rupture and war between Russia on the one side and England and 
France on the other. 

The combined squadrons are now within the Dardanelles, and detachments 
of them will be in the Bosphorus as soon as the violence of the prevalent north- 
cast winds will allow. 

I am, ke.

Lord Stratford de Redeliffe to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received November 19.) 


(No. 326.) 
My Lord, Therapia, October 31, 1853. 

THE Greeks have followed the example of the Armenians in presenting 
an address to the Porte expressive of their loyalty, ‘gratitude, and devotion to 
the Sultan's Government. A French translation of the address is inclosed 
herewith for your Lordship’s information, ‘The original, in Turkish, was drawn 
up by «a Bulgarian Greek, who owes his fortune to the Porte, in a strain better 
suited to the past than to the present times. It contained passages of such 
exaggerated and ignominious flattery, even in a religious sense, that | made it a 
point of duty to insist upon its being redueed to its present form, even after it 
had received the signatures of the Patriarch and Synod. This was effected by 
the exercise of private influence ; and I am persuaded that a service has been 
thereby rendered both to the Porte and to the Greek nation, whose spiritual 
chiels had laid themselves open to the suspicion of having sacrificed even their 
religious sentiments to some unworthy motive. The present form of address, 
though not a little Oriental in its expressions, may be considered as fairly repre- 
senting, in substance, the improved state of feeling between the Porte and its 
Christian subjects, especially with reference to the existing pretensions of 
Russia. 

I have, &c. 
(Signed) STRATFORD DE REDCLIFFE,

Memoir on the subject of raising a Turkish Party in Wallachia. 


Constantinople, le 1 Octobre, 1853, 

IL y avait un temps ou l'action de la Russie était considérée par les 
habitans des Principautés comme toute favorable aux principes de justice, de 
progrés, ct de civilisation. 

L’exportation des céréales, et le commerce de Yoccident avec la Valachie 
et la Moldavie était encore trés peu de chose, il y a vingt-cing ans, eb une 
occupation Russe était accucillie par les Roumans comme une époque de 
prospérité et de bien-étre; eétait cent ou deux cent mille consommateurs, 
payant d’excellents prix et toujours au comptant. 

Les jeunes Valaques et Moldaves se tenaient préts prendre fait et cause 
pour l’Empereur Chrétien; et les généraux Russes formaient, a chaque guerre, 
d’excellents corps de volontaires qui combattaient vaillamment contre les ‘Turcs. 

iin evacuant les Principautés, les Russes emportaient les regrets de toute la 
population, [Hs semblaient avoir pour but de gagner l'affection des Moldo- 
Valaques et de les rendre favorables. 

nis depuis la guerre de 1828, le Cabinet de St. Pétersbourg a changé de 
conduite: soit Vidée qu'une Puissance aussi formidable que la Russie saurait se 
passer de l'affection d'une population sans organisation; soit limpossibilité de 
pourvoir convenablement aux besoins dune armeée qu'on a augmenté dans les 
derniers temps dans une progression qui ne correspond en aucune fagon au 
développement des ressources de Empire Russe; soit simplement conséquence 
du caractére personnel de /homme qui a pris place & la téte de cet Empire; le 
fait est que depuis 1828, le Gouvernement Russe a pris pour systéme de passer 
sans scrupule et sans conscience par dessus toutes les considerations de justice 
et d’humanité A l'’égard des Principautes. 

A cette époque le Genéral Withenstein franchit le Pruth; une proclamation 
4 la main pleine de bonnes assurances et de belles esperances ; toutes les 
fournitures, disait-il, seront payées en argent comptant ; la guerre ne devait rien 
couter aux habitants des Principautés: il n’est pas moins vrai que plus de deux 
cent mille soldats Russes s’abattaient sur les pays non point en troupes d'une 
grande Puissance, mais en hordes affamees et devastatrices, Pendant deux hivers 
soldats et officiers furent logés, nourris, et chauffés aux frais des famnilles 
Valaques et Moldaves sans la moindre indemnité, soldats voraces, pillarces, et 
brutaux; ils graspillaient trois fois plus quils ne pouvaient consommer; volaicnt 
ce que ne pouvait ¢tre mange pour le vendre au Cabinet, Des demandes 
exorbitantes de provisions et de fournitures en farine, orge, pailles, et viandes, 
farent faites et prises chez les fermiers et propriétaires contre les bons qui 
souvent ne portaient que de 40 4 60 per cent de ce quion delivrait. Les pay- 
sang avec leurs voitures et leurs beeufs furent obliges de transporter ces appro- 
visionnemens jusqu’’ Schoumma et 4 Gabrova. Les meilleurs maisons furent 
transformées eu casernes et hOpitaux. 

Sans tenir aucun compte des vols, des gaspillages, des dégits et des vexa- 
tions, on peut estimer des trois cent & quatre cent millions de piastres ce qu’a 
couté aux Principautés Voceupation de 1828 4 1836. Or, pour tout ecla il a 
&é payé, & grande pompe, environ vingt millions de piastres des bons de 
fournitures. 

Pendant ces six ans d’occupation Russe les habitans furent disputes entre 
la peste, la famine, et le choléra ; pas une famille ne fut épargnée par lun de 
ces fleaux—paa une maison de commerce s’echappa a la fillite, 

De 1848 A 1851 un corps Russe de trente A soixante mille hommes a été 
logé, nourri, et chauffé aux frais et ala charge des habitans des Prineipautés ; 
et, malgré cela, le jour de l'évacuation le Consul de Russie présenta aux

Ce qui se passe cette année depuis le mois de Juillet, donne & penser qu’en

trouvent depuis Tzernetz jusqu'i Calafat; les montagnes des Mébédintz et de 
Gorgi entre les Portes de fer et le Gii sont les plus favorables pour organiser des 
troupes Valaques; ce sont JA les deux districts qui conservent encore des 
traditions guerri¢res, et dont les habitans ont tenu en échec, pendant la guerre 
de 1828 et 1829, sous Solomon et Maghero; c'est dans ces montagnes que ce 
dernier chef avait organisé en quelques sewaines en 1848 quinze mille volon- 
taires, excellentes troupes, qu'il n'a licenci¢es que par les conseils du Consul- 
Général d’ Angleterre. 

Les points les plus favorables pour tomber de Ii sur les Russes se trouvent 
dans les montagnes de Bonzeo et de Rimerico ; ils ne sont qua une dtape de la 
route militaire des Russes. 

Si on tient un corps de troupes Turques dans le Dobrodza, 4 la moindre 
petite bataille perdue par les Russes, les quinze mille hommes de la Valachic 
peuvent comprometire toute larmée Russe du Danube.

Congul-General Yeames to Lord Stratford de Redcliffe. 


My Lord, Odessa, October 29, 1853. 


MEY last letter was dated the iSth instant, and went by the e« Jamaica, 
P. Lewes, master, under cover to the Consulate. 

efore this time your Excellency will probably have been ap rized of the 
hostilities which commenced on the Danube last Sunday, the 23rd instant. 

Right gun-boats, with six companies of infantry on board, had on the 
preceding day been detached from the Russian flotilla stationed at Ismail, to 
proceed up to Galatz and Tbraila, in tow of two steamers, the “ Pruth,” of 100, 
and the “ Vodinaretz,” of 60 horse-power. On nearing Isaktcha it became 
evident that the further progress of the boats would be opposed ; mpon whieh 
four guns were hastily brought down to the left bank from Satanova, where 
6,000 Russians are posted, in order to cover the passage, and a cannonade 
immediately ensued from Hoth: sides across the river. “The Turkish fire was 
soon tiverted by the approach of the flotilla, upon which it was then directed, 
The cannonade was returned by the heavy guns of the boats, and continued tll 
they had ascended beyond the line of the Turkish fire. . 

The poseage was thus effected, and its success 1s caid to have caused 
some animation along the Russian line. 

‘The loss on this side is reported’ to be two men killed and three wounded, 
at the Sutanova battery; and im the boats, six killed and twenty wounded, the 
commanding officer of the expedition, Captain Vichaborsky of the navy, being 
among the former, 

Thave seen no account of the extent of damage done to the boats and 
steamers, but am told that it is not very material; and it is, on the other hand, 
neserted. that the Turkish battery was dismantled, and that the village of 
Isakteha was seen in flames im two places. 

On the night of the same day, namely, the 23rd instant, 4 Turkish foree 
erossed over to 'Tehetul, one of the islands in the Delta, opposite to Ismail, and 
opened a fire upon the pontoons lying in the northern channel, prepared for a 
bridge. ‘The particulars are unknown to me, but 1 am told of one Cossack 
being killed, and that: the enemy retired before the morning. Great, however, 
was the fright of the inhabitants of the lower town of Ismail, who fled in 
numbers inte the country, 

This last exploit was a brilhant affair; and the opposition at Tsakteha has 
given cause to a low estimation of Turkish batteries and of their artillerymen. 

. General Liiders with his etaff is now in Ismail, ancl his particular comman 
extends to [braila. 

I know of no movements, and believe that there are none, to reinforce the 
Ruseians in the Principalities ; and 1 may therefore still refer to the account of 
their numerical strength contained in my letter of the 99nd August. Of the 
sick I am told there are about 5,000 men in hospital. Intermittent fever is said 
to terminate in typhus, after which the convalescent seldom become again fit 
for service, 

Here the cholera is still lingering, most virulent in individual cases, but as 
an epidemic not active. The authorities of the town have hitherto persisted in 
declaring the disease not to be Asiatic cholera, notwithstanding the testimony of 
facts and of the best physicians: 

I have, &e.

No. 294. 


Lord Stratford de Redcliffe to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Recetved November 19.) 
(No, 331.) 


My Lord, Therama, November 5, 1853. 

I HAVE succeeded in dissuading the Porte from sending a detachment of 
line-of-battle ships and sailing-frigates into the Black Sea at this moment, and 
also in obtaining the transmission of orders to Omer Pasha to postpone any 
attempt which he may have in contemplation to pass the Danube at the head of 
his army; and to Selim Pasha, on the Asiatic frontier, to keep as much as 
possible on the defensive for the present. : 

But I cannot answer for the strict execution of these expressive instructions; 
and I am not without apprehension that such interference with the plans of the 
Commanders-in-chief may embarrass their proceedings, and give an unfair 
advantage to their opponents. 

Her Majesty's Consul at Trebizond informs me that the officer sent from 
Constantinople with orders for Selim Pasha to suspend the commencement of 
hostilities for ten days, arrived at the camp some hours before any aggressive 
movement had taken place, but that an attack on the Russians was nevertheless 
made soon after, the bearer of the instruction himself taking part in the attack. 

On applying to Reshid Pasha for an explanation of so strange a contradic- 
tion, he assured me that Mr. Stevens had not been correctly informed ; and that 
the attack had been made from the advanced post where Hassan Pasha held the 
immediate command, 

It is impossible not to view with regret and anxicty this prolonged state of 
vacillation between peace and war. However well meant our efforts may be, it 
is impossible not to deny the embarrassment which they occasion to the Porte 
under its present circumstances; and it is therefore to be hoped that some 
manifestations of reluctance at the Porte to continue in a state of such danger- 
ous indecision may be viewed with friendly indulgence, 

I inclose herewith some extracts of my later and hurried instructions to 
M. Pisani, for the purpose of throwing some additional light upon the character 
of my communications with Reshid Pasha in that respect. 


I have, &e. 
(Signed) STRATFORD DE REDCLIFIE. 


Inclogure 1 in No. 294. 
Lord Stratford de Redcliffe to M. E. Pisani. 


Therapia, November 5, 1853, 

1 HOPE you understand fully the grounds on which | propose to act with 
respect to the squadrons. In the first place it is generally desirable that, being 
e0 far engaged in support of the Turkish Government, we should know before- 
hand what course is to be followed for obtaining the common object of our 
exertions, and have an opportunity of expressing an opinion thereon, In the 
second place, we have a more immediate concern with operations in the Black 


202 


Sea, The presence of the combined squadrons in these waters is the basis of 
any Turkish operations to be undertaken there; and among the consequences of 
those operations may at any Hime be our active participation in measures calcu- 
lated to commit us with Russia. The Porte and her allies stand, therefore, in 
relations of mutual responsibility towards each other; and we must at least be 
careful, on our side, that we are neither drawn into operations contrary to our 
better judgment, nor confounded with those who, against calculation and ex 
rience, incur hazards which are out of proportion with the results in view. We 
do not pretend to lay our commands upon the Porte, or to deprive her in any 
degree of her free liberty of action; but we claim for ourselves the right of not 
partaking in measures which we do not approve, and of keeping 4 oof—and 
marking to the public that we keep aloof—when attempts are made to carry 
them into effect against our declared opinions. 

Thus it is that, in the present instance, we suspend the orders for bringing 
up the remainder of the squadrons until we know the Porte’s final decision with 
respect to the proposed expedition into the Black Sea. 

Read and explain the above to Reshid Pasha. 

Lam, &e. 
(Signed) STRATFORD DE REDCLIFFE.

Lard Stratford de Redcliffe to the Earl of Clarendon.—( Received November 19.) 
(No. 336.) 


My Lord, Therapia, November 6, 1852, 

I WAS informed last night, by a letter from M, Pisani, that despatches to 
the 2nd instant had been received in the afternoon from Omer Pasha, who states 
that he had taken possession of the island opposite Tortoukai, supposed to be 
an important point, and that he was preparing to seize: another position, of 
which he has not mentioned the name, intending subsequently to ben on the 
defensive. 

The partial advantages obtained by the Turkish forees in Europe and Asia 
have given occasion to the revival of an ancient usage, according to which the 
surname of Ghazee, or Victorious, is assigned to the Sultan. This compliment 
was paid to Sultan Abdul-Medjid the day before yesterday; and His Majesty, 
whatever may happen ata later period, will continue to enjoy the honours of 
heraldic victory. 

I have, &e. 
(Signed) STRATFORD DE REDCLIFFE,

My Lord, St. Petersburgh, November 11, 183. 

WHEN I called yesterday Upon Count Nesselrode, he acquainted me that, 
according to intelligence received on the Yth instant, there has been a sharp 
engagement between the Russians and Turks on the Russian territory, not far 
from Batoum. . 

This report stated that the Turks, having suddenly crossed the frontier, 
had driven in an advanced post and captured a small fort, called Fort Nicholas; 
that they were subsequently attacked by a strong detachment under Prince 
Gagann, when an action took place, which cost the Hussians 45 men and the 
Turks 500, the fort remaining, however, in Turkish possession. 

Count Nesselrode regarded as inexplicable an attack on the part of the 
Turks ata moment when a suspension of hostilities was believed to have been 
agreed to. 

The explanation, as L stated, was very plain. Viscount Stratford had 
been extremely desirous first of obtaining o cessation of hostilities, and then of 
cuusing timely orders to be sent off to Batoum; but, from the shortness of the 
time, his Lordship had felt and expressed his anxiety that the counter orders 
which he caused to be dispatched would not arrive in time to prevent bloodshed,

No. 301. 


Sir G. HH. Seymour to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received November 19.) 
(No. G18. Secret and Confidential.) 


My Lord, St. Petersburgh, November 11, 1859. 

ALTHOUGH at a moment like the present I feel some scruple about 
troubling your Lordship with a despatch written near a quarter of a century ago, 

I venture to call your attention to the inclosed copy of a report made to Count 
Bernstorff by the Prussian Envoy Baron Royer, when dispatched to the camp of 
Adrianople, at the close of the campaign of 1829, 

I do so partly because the history of the past is in general the best guide as 
to future events, partly because I have thus an opportunity of remarking, that it 
is in great measure to language and opinions like those of the Prussian diplomatist 
that I conceive it to be owing that Europe finds herself in her present 
difficulties. 

It is well known (and the opinion was held by the late King of Prussia 
himself) that the grounds of complaint given by the Porte to Russia very inade- 
quately justified the Russian invasion of 1825 and 1829. 

It was known, or it ought to have been known to Baron Royer, that at 
Adrianople the conclusion of a peace was at least as much required by Marshal 
Diebitch as by the Sultan, and yet we sce the Prussian Envoy, who had nota 
word of blame to bestow upon an unjust invasion, perplexed how to find expres- 
sions strong enough to give utterance for his admiration of the attack not having 
heen followed up to the utter destruction of the Ottoman Empire. 

Unfortunately Baron Royer's views have been those of too many of the 
public men of Europe, and henee it has happened that the Emperor’s magnani- 
mity has been regarded as a sort of palladium of Turkey, and that Europe has 
been constantly reminded that she was under deep obligations to His Imperial 
Malcety for not having overturned that Monarchy which he had so roughly 
shaken, and which he is now submitting to the same process, 

The evil does not rest there, Baron Royer's report being a fair specimen of 
that language as to the irrevocably ruined state of Turkey which has been of 
such infinite service to those who, under the mask of friendship and sympathy, 
have sought to hasten that ruin, 

I will only request your Lordship to consider the accompanying communi- 
cation as strictly confidential, the paper, of which the inclosed is a copy, belonging 
to the archives of ny Prussian colleague, who would be much compromised were 
it to be known that it had been brought to your Lordship’s knowledge. 

I have, &c. 


(Signed) G. H. SEYMOUR.

most serious embarrassments with Russia, the Imperial Government being as 
completely opposed to any such scheme as the Governments of England and 
Franee can be. 

The desire felt by the secondary Courts of Germany to promote the cause 
of peace is perfectly intelligible, and their views will be best forwarded by the 
expression of their disapprobation of the agressive policy of Russia, and by such

No, 306. 
Sir G, H, Seymour to the Earl of Clarendon.—{ Received November 19.) 

(No. 625.) 
Ay Lor, St. Petersburgh, November 12, 1854, 
T ie task which is imposed upon [ler Majesty's Government of preserving 
Turkey from injury, or it may be absorption, and of averting war from Europe, 
is one of the most honourable and arduous which could be undertaken. 


242 


Of the extent of its difficulty indeed, no one, I think, who is not acquainted 
with this country can fully judge. e, 

The reason is plain: this country sees only with the: e res of its master ; 
and, according to his views, contradiction is not allowable, and interference with 
his intentions upon Turkey an encroachment upon his peculiar rights. 

Upon this point more especially there is a perfect conformity of views 
between the Emperor and his people. ; 

The immense majority 1 believe to be convinced that His Majesty would 
be justified in taking possession of Turkey when he thinks proper; but that his 
right to the possession of an almost exclusive influence at Constantinople should 
be called into question, is an idea which they appear incapable of entertaining. 
This is so perfectly true that, in the course of the late transactions, I have been 
repeatedly asked, and in the simplicity of good faith, why England should inter- 
fere about Turkey ?—why England should intrude in an affair which, being 
purely Russian, inno way regards her? Say SEAN 

independently, too, of this national prejudice, there is that religious feeling 
—as I suppose it is regarded here—which leads a Russian to consider that no 
measure is to be kept with his infidel brethren. Of this your Lordship will have 
observed traces in one of my last conversations with Count Nesse rode, who, 
although of the Anglican Church, is of course compelled by position to be 
politically * orthedox.” 1 Oe 

Far from cndeayouring to check these fanatical prejudices, they have been, 
as your Lordship has seen, encouraged and appealed to by the Government; a 
flagrant violation of the territory of an inoffenswwe neighbour has been spoken of 
in language such as may have been employed by aL crusader chieftain when 
departing for the Holy Land; and the prayers of the Church are a up for the 
success of an ageressive act, which calls rather for repentance and atonement, 

All this proves how difficult it will be for the Emperor to recede from the 
position which he has thought fit to make for himself; and proves, further, how 
necessary it will be for Europe not to receive as a detinitive peace what Russia 
may only regard asa limited truce. woh 

Once again I would venture to remind your Lordship of the words used to 
me in early summer, by Count Nesselrode, who perhaps was not aware how 
carefully I should store them up. ‘Do what you will,” said the Chancellor, 
“but you will not finally avert war; it may be kept off fora time, but this 
respite will be considered by the Turks as a triumph, and their insolence will 
become such that before six months are passed we shall be obliged to go to war 
with them.” 

I have, &e. 
(Signed) G. H, SEYMOUR.

Sir G. H. Seymour to the Earl of Clareniton—(Recetoed November 19.) 


(No. 626, Confidential.) 
My Lord, St, Petersburgh, November 12, 1853. 

A CURIOUS fact, by no means unconnected with passing events, has just 
come to my knowledge. 

A Russian employé—an honest man, but not a wise one—has just returned 
here from an inspection in the provinces, which has lasted during several 
months. 

He describes the religious excitement ngainst the Turks as bemg very 
strong among the lower orders in the villages and small towns of the interior. 

Upon being questioned as to the cause of these excited feelings, the 
person in question (not perceiving the inference to be drawn from his reply) 
answered that the cause was well known; that for the last twenty months or 
two years the whole country had been overrun by monks, who travelled from 
village to village making collections for churches which had been robbed, 
monasteries which had been set fire to or plundered, and families, many of 
whose members had been put to death by the Turks. 

The Russian in question failed to perceive that so extensive an appeal to 


243 


the religious feelings and the credulity of his countrymen can hardly have been 
made, except under the countenance of very influential persons, 
This statement throws some light upon the report of a traveller from Kietf, 
to which Sir A. Malet alludes in his despatch No. 111 of the 26th ultimo. 
l have, &c.

No. 314. 


Lord Cowley to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received November 20.) 
(No, 863.) 


My Lord, Paris, November 18, 1853, 

I WENT early this morning to Fontainebleau, for the purpose of seeing 
M. Drouyn de Lhuys and executing the instructions conveyed to me in your 
Lordship’s despatch No. 457. 

Before stating the nature of them to the French Minister I said, that as 
M. de Hiibner was at Fontainebleau he had probably made his Excellency o 
communication similar to that which your Lordship had received through Lord 
Westmorland, and on which | had your directions to consult the Vrench 
Government, 

M. Drouyn de Lhuys replied, that a courier from Vienna had reached 
M. de Hiibner yesterday ; and that he had last night received a conimunication 
from that Mimster, the substance of which coincided with advices which had 
been received previously by the French Government from M, de Bourqueney. 
As the communication is identic with that made to your Lordship by Lord 
Westmorland in his despatch No. 402, I need not dwell on it further. 

M. Drouyn de Lhuys went on to say, that he had given the proposition of 
the Austrian Government no encouragement; that he had told M. de Hiibner 
that the spirit of it was in contradiction with the policy which France had 
prescribed to herself since the commencement of this question, inasmuch as it 
recommended a direct negotiation between Turkey and Russia, while the efforts 
of France had been directed to bring the Eastern question within the pale of 
general European jurisdiction; that France, moreover, could not participate in 
making demands upon the Porte which she knew beforehand would be refused ; 
that ‘Vurkey could not agree to an armistice on the terms proposed by Austria ; 
and finally, that there was some peril in asking the Porte to state on what 
conditions she would consent to make peace, for she might put forward pretensions 
in Which her friends even would not be able to support her. ' You see," said 
M. Drouyn de Lhuys, “that my remarks to M. de Hubner were not very 
encouraging; but I have not, since 1 made them, had an opportunity of speaking 
with the Emperor.” I rejoined, that from what I had heard, I could not doubt 
that his Excellency would approve the answer which your Lordship had made 
ta the Austrian Gavetngaece. and 1 proceeded to read to him your despatch 
No. 378 to Lord Westmorland. After reading it, I said, that if it met with his 
concurrence, I trusted that he would instruct M. de Bourqueney to hold a 
similar language. 

The French Minister replied that, since Her Majesty's Government wished 
it. he would not refuse to direct M. de Bourqueney to regulate his language by 

a1 


JESS 


246 


the instructions sent to Lord Westmorland; but he must add, that he did it 
unwillingly (& contre cotur), because he felt convinced that it would lead to no 
good result; nor could he shut his eyes to the inconvenience which must arise 
were the Porte, as was too probable, to put forward pretensions which could not 
be realized. I observed to M. Drouyn de Lhuys, that so long as the two 
Governments were bent on endeavouring to preserve peace, they should make 
the best of any proposition which was submitted with that view to their 
consideration, The instructions which I had read to him were, he must 
recollect, addressed to Vienna and not to Constantinople, and it was only in the 
event of Count Buol concurring in your Lordship’s suggestions, that you 
proposed addressing instructions founded on them to Her Majesty's Ambassador 
at Constantinople. Should Count Buol refuse, the language of Her Majesty's 
Government would, 1 presumed, not differ from that which he (M. Drouyn de 
Lhuys) had deseribed himself as having held to M. Hiibner. On the other 
hand, should Count Buol acquiesce, the two Governments would have succeeded 
in obtaining of the Austrian Government a more impartial view of the relative 
interests of Russia and Turkey. With regard to the pretensions which the 
Porte might put forward I remarked, that a firm language on the part of the 
English and French Ambassadors at Constantinople would soon convince the 
Porte that the support of England and France was not to be reckoned upon, 
except for the attainment of that which was due in strict justice to: Purkey, 
and was consequently pertaining to the general interests of Kurope, After some 
further conversation of a similar nature, during which I referred to several 
passages in your Lordship’s despatch to Lord Westmorland, M. Drouyn de 
Bias seemed to take a more fuyourable view of it. He asked me, finally, to 
leave it with him, promising to draw up adespatch in the same terms for 
M. de Bourqueney's guidance ; and at my suggestion, he agreed to instruct that 
Minister in the meantime, by telegraph, to put himself in communication with 
Lord Westmorland, who would no doubt impart to him your Lordship’s views on 
which M, de Bourqueney might act.

My Lord, Paris, November 20, 185:4. 

YOUR Lordship's attention may not have been called to an advertisement 
which appears to have been inserted in the “ Journal de Constantinople” of the

M. de Kisseleff. He replied in the negative, and did not seem to attach so 
much importance to the advertisement as, I confess, | was myself inclined to 
give to it. Hesaid that he suggested that it had been inserted in the “ Journal 
de Constantinople” by order of the Turkish Government, in order to mark the 
intention of the combined fleets to cooperate with the Turkish squadron in the 
Black Sea; but he either could not or would not inform me, whether the form

up by order of the Admiral commanding the French fleet in the Bosphorus.

No. 316. 
Lord Cowley to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Recetved November 21.) 


(No. 869. Confidential.) 

My Lord, Poris, November 20, 1853. 

AT the close of the conversation which I had with M. Drouyn de Lhuys at 
Fontainebleau, on the [8th instant, recounted in No. 863, his Excellency observed! 
that he could not help entertaining the idea that, with a little more pressure, 
the position of Austria in the Eastern question might be brought more in unison 
with the policy of France and England. There was not time at the moment to 
pursue this subject with him, but hearing that he was in town for a few hours, | 
called upon him this morning, and reverting to what had fallen from him on 
Friday, | asked him on what he founded his hopes. He replied that M. de 
Hiibner had read to him on the previous day a despatch written by Count Buol, 
in answer to the observations which M, de Bourqueney had been instructed to 
make on Count Buol’s proposition, that the Four Powers should engage the 
Porte to enter into direct negotiation with Russia. I beg to refer your Lordship 
to my confidential despatch No. 816, should the instructions to M. de Bour- 
queney have escaped your memory. Now, Count Buol, M. Drouyn de Lhuys 
remarked, had in his answer, transmitted through M. de Hiibner, raised no 
objection either to his (M. Drouyn de Lhuys) arguments, or to the policy which 
he advocated as that to be pursued by the Great Powers; he had merely 
remarked on tlie difficulty of obtaining the consent of the Emperor of Russia. 
M. Drouyn de Lhuys was therefore of opinion that it might be possible to obtain 
from Austria a aslanion in conformity with that which she admitted to be the 
policy which ought to guide the Cabinets of Europe in all questions concerning 
the East. 

I ingitired whether he had any proposition to offer, in order to attain an 
object which was certainly most desirable. 

He replied that he had no distinct proposal to make, but that he thought 
that Austria might be invited by France and England to declare, in a Protocol, 
that the integrity and independence of the Ottoman Empire was part and parcel 
of the international arrangement of Europe, and the contmuation of them neces- 
sary to the balance of power. That consequently all questions relating to the 
welfare of Turkey had been treated as European questions; that in virtue of 
this principle, the present misunderstanding between Russia and Turkey was 
matter for European interference; and that the Four Powers would not admit of 
any permanent change in the territorial possessions of Russia and Turkey as 
settled by Treaty. 

I remarked that such a declaration on the part of Austria would no doubt 
be of great value, but it might not have much real effect. Russia would con- 
tinue to give assurances that she intended no permanent occupation of the 
Principalities, which would probably satisfy Austria. What did M, Drouyn de 
Lhuys propose to do in that case ? 

M. Drowyn de Lhuys thought that a declaration on the part of Austria 
such as he had indicated, could not fail of carrying great weight with it, and 
must produce an impression on the Councils of Nussia, A conference might 
then be proposed at some place to be decided on, and Russia and ‘Turkey invited 
to send Plenipotentiaries to assist at it. Should either refuse to appear, it 
would place itself so completely in the wrong, that the united action of the 
conference ought to be brought to bear on the recusant party. 

_. “Letus comprehend each other,” I rejoined, “1 understand your propo- 
sition as applied to Russia; but suppose Turkey to refuse, do you mean to 
aba her in that case, and to leave the aggressor in quiet possession of his 
spoils 2” 

M. Drouyn de Lhuys answered that the fleets would still cover Constanti- 
nople, because it was a European and not a Turkish interest they were pro- 
tecting ; but he begged me to recollect that he was only stating his own ideas, 


and that any official communication upon the subject we had been discussing 


must depend upon the orders he might receive from the Emperor.

No. 333. 
Lord A, Loftus to the Earl of Clarendon,—(Received November 22.) 


(No. 97, Confidential.) 


My Lord, Berlin, November 19, 1853. 

I HAD an interview this day with Baron Manteuffel. 

His Excellency was anxious to learn what view your Lordship had taken 
of the proposals submitted by Count Buol tothe English and French Cabinets ; 
and inquired of me what was the nature of this note which Count Buol was 
s0 anxious to have transmitted to Constantinople. 

I thought it so important that the Prussian Cabinet should be fully informed 
of the views of Her Majesty’s Government in order that Baron Manteuffel might 
report to the King in the same spirit, and give a similar direction to the Prussian 

olicy, that I communicated to his Excellency your Lordship’s despatch 
o. 378 of the 16th instant, addressed to the Earl of Westmorland, which | 
trust will meet with your Lordship’s approval. 

His Excellency wholly concurred with the views and opinions expressed in 
that instruction, and his Excellency requested me to leave a copy of that des- 
patch in his hands for communication to the King. 

[ replied that T had no permission or instruction to that effect, and that I 
could not give hima copy of the entire despatch; but that I would take upon 
myself to give him an extract which would place him in possession of the views 
af Her Majesty's Government, so clearly and ably laid down by your Lordship. 

I have, therefore, confidentially given to his Excellency an extract of that 
despatch commencing from “ It seems necessury in the first instance,” down to 
the paragraph, “ That would separate the two armies.” 

His Excellency is in great perplexity on the present state of affairs, He is 
doubtful and suspicious of Austria. He feels that there can be no result to the 
proposals with which the Austrian Cabinet have been lately engrossed. He 
views the negotiations as brought to a stand-still; the peacemakers reduced to 
despair and inaction, while the combatants are progressing in a sanguinary con- 
test. In short, his Excellency could see nothing but darkness and gloom in this 
question, without a ray of light or of hope. 

T rephed to his Excellency that unless the Emperor Nicholas was prepared, 
even at the eleventh hour, to recognise the injustice of his demands on Turkey, 
and to take into consideration the fearful responsibilities which he would incur 
in suffering his ambitious projects to expose Europe to the calamities of war, | 
feared that all the moderation which has hitherto been displayed, and the 
unceasing efforts of Europe to maintain peace, would prove unavailing and of no 
effect. 

; I have, &e. 
(Signed) AUGUSTUS LOFTUS,

Lord A. Loftus to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received November 22.) 


(No. 98. Confidential.) 


My Lord, Berlin, November 19, 1853. 
SINCE the communication received from Count Arnim, as reported in my 
despatch No, 94 of the 15th instant, Baron Manteuffel informs me that further 
reports have been addressed by that Minister, confirming the desire of Count 
Buol that some collective note should be presented to the Porte on which might 
be tounded future means of arranging a Treaty between Russia and Turkey. 
Count Arnim states that Count Buol, in the event of any such note being 
framed and secepted, proposed that a Russian and Turkish Plenipotentiary 
should be invited to take part in the conference for the arrangement of a Treaty, 
He further stated that there had been some question of establishing a Conference 
3 L 


204 


elsewhere, but this idea had been very distasteful to Austria, on the grounds of 
the central geographical position of Vienna. Count Buol referred likewise to 
the question of the medium of communicatmg any note signed by Turkey to 
Russia, and was of opinion that it might be collectively transmitted by the 
Conference, combining at the same time an invitation to Russia to appoint a 
tiator. ‘ 
ve Finally, Count Arnim stated that Count Buol had expressed his satisfaction 
at the identity of views between Austria and Prussia on the Oriental question. 

Baron Manteuffel expressed to me his opinion that the plan proposed by 
Count Buol was, under present circumstances, useless and impracticable, and 
has avowed both to the French Minister and to myself, that he considers this 
attempt at mediation on the part of the Austrian Cabinet, as being undertaken 
more with the view of adducing evidence to Russia that the Austrian Cabinet 
have exerted their best endeavours to promote an arrangement agreeable to the 
Emperor Nicholas than with any possible hopes of eventual success. . 

Baron Manteuffel here particularly called my attention to that part of 
Count Buol’s instructions to Baron de Bruck, which reproduces the very 
objectionable sense of the projected Olmiitz note; viz., the non-omission ol the 
term “subjects of the Porte," in connection with the concluding phrase“ a 
d'autres rits Chréetiens.” ke 

Baron Manteuffel is totally at a loss to comprehend the views and aim of 
the Austrian Cabinet. In order that L might not have been mistaken in the 
substance of what [ reported to your Lordship, I read over to Baron Manteuttel 
my despatch No, 94 (omitting that paragraph relating to his alarm at the aspect 
of affairs), when his Excellency conhirmed the correctness of that report. 

He stated to me that he had replied to Count Arnim that he could not 
instruct Baron Wildenbruch to support the terms of the instructions to Baron 
de Bruck, as he considered that there was no prospect of the Porte accepting the 
advice tendered in that instruction, and that Baron Wildenbruch had already 
received instructions of such latitude, that in the event of any proposal being 
submitted to the Porte that offered any chance of success, he would be enabled 
to give it his support. ; a oatl 

I was happy on this occasion to inform Baron Manteuffel that his views on 
the subject of Count Buol’s instruction were perfectly in harmony with those of 
Her Majesty’s Government, and I took it upon myself to read to his Excellency 
your Lordship's despatch No. 379 to the Earl of Westmorland, which I trust 
your Lordship will approve of. a (fried 

Baron Manteuffel entirely concurred in the justice of your Lordship’s views, 
and told me that he had also stated to Count Arnim that he viewed the proposal 
which Baron de Bruck is instructed to make as not only being certain of being 
rejected by the Porte, but that it was ealeulated to awaken suspicions and 
distrust in the mind of the Turkish Government, and was likely to indispose 
Turkey to listen hereafter to European counsels.

No. 335. 
Lord A, Loftus to the Earl of Clarendon.—( Received November 28.) 


(No. 99. Seeret and Confidential.) 
My Lord, Berlin, November 19, 1853. 

1 HAVE been informed that great bitterness has been expressed at Vienna 
against the Prussian Government for having refused to jom in the Austnan 
declaration to the Diet on the Oriental question ; and I have further learnt that 
Count Buol has insinuated that Prugsia was secretly in the interests of Hussia, 
stating openly that Baron Manteuffel had expressed to Baron Budberg that the 
refusal of Prussia to join Austria in a declaration of neutrality at the Diet had 
been actuated by feelings favourable to Russia. . 

I have further reason to believe that this language has been repeated at 
Paris, and that it is likely to produce a very false and unfavourable opinion of 
the Prussian Government. 


200 


I, therefore, deemed it to be my duty at once frankly to state to Baron 
Manteuffel the tenour of this language, and the motives which had been 
attributed to the Prussian Government in refusing to accede to the Austrian 
proposal, 

I most emphatically assured his Excellency that [ personally treated these 
reports with the contempt they deserved; but that I thought it very material 
that they should be positively denied in other quarters, as unfortunately false 
statements were always prone to influence and prejudice the public mind. 

I was the better able to bring this subject to his Excellency’s knowledge, as 
at the time I had expressed to him my opinion on the importance to Prussia of 
not acceding to the Austrian proposal, and his Excellency had unreservedly and 
most confidentially communicated with me on the subject. 

His Excellency thanked me for this information, and requested me to 
convey to your Lordship, in case any such reports should reach you, the most 
formal denial of the truth, or even of the foundation for the truth, of any such 
statement, 

In discharging this duty, I feel that I should not be rendering justice to 
Baron Manteuftel were I not to add the high opinion, respect, and admiration 
which I ‘entertain of his Excellency’s honourable, straightforward, and noble 
character. 


I have, &c. 


(Signed) AUGUSTUS LOFTUS.

Berlin, November 19, 1853. 

_ _ WITH reference to a statement which has been put forth by Austria that 
the Prussian Government had at first agreed to the Austrian proposal for a joint 
declaration of neutrality to the Diet on the Oriental question, and had afterwards 
on Baron Prokesch’'s arrival at Berlin withdrawn from its fulfilment, Baron 
Manteuffel explained to me in the following manner the grounds on which that 
statement rested, 

One evening in his salon the Austrian Chargé d'Affaires took him aside, 
and stated that his Government proposed in the interests of peace to invite 
Prussia to make a joint declaration of neutrality to the Diet, and sought his 
Excellency’s opinion on this measure. On the spur of the moment Baron 
Manteuffel replied that he was happy to learn that the Austrian Cabinet were 
ready to take so decisive a step, ‘an signified in general terms an approval of 
the proposition, 

One or two days after Count Crivelli called upon Baron Manteuffel, and 
stated that Baron Prokesch would arrive that evening to treat on the subject which 
he had previously mentioned. His Excellency was rather surprised at this precipi- 
tation, and stated that he had not even submitted the question to the King, but 
that he would be happy to see Baron Prokesch. It was on the same day that 
his Excellency first mentioned the subject to me, and which I reported to your 
Lordship in my despatch No. 51 of the 22nd ultimo. f

by she Austrian Cabinet to their Missions at the German Courts on this

Inclosure ] in No. 436. 
Circular addressed to the Austrian Missions in Germany. 


(Translation.) Vienna, October 30, 1853. 


THE Imperial Cabinet, in the present position of the Russio-Turkish 
differences, believe themselves to be able to entertain the certain hope that the 
duty of the Courts of Austria and Prussia in this important question of the 
day, will be confined to preventing by their conduct the quarrel between Russia 
and ‘Turkey from extending and leading to a conflict between the former Empire 
and the two Western Powers. 

Both the Courts of Vienna and Berlin have in their point of view felt the 
necessity not only of being neutral with regard to that difference, but also to 
express on all sides and as openly as possible the position taken by them in 
-ommon. With this intention we have proposed to the Cabinet of Prussia to 
make a common declaration to our German allies regarding the neutrality of 
the two Powers, and for this purpose to profit of the opportunity of the 
approaching opening of the session of the Diet. The Cabinet of Berlin has 
approved of this proposition, and | have taken occasion of inviting the President 
of the Diet to return to Frankfort vid the capital of Prussia, for the purpose of 
there concerting the details for the said purpose. : 

We flatter ourselves that the intended joint declaration of Austria and 
Prussia will considerably strengthen the hopes of maintaining general peace, 
and that in any case it will meet with the most decided concurrence on the part 
of the Sovereigns of the Germanic Confederation. 

[t will be agreeable to us if you communicate this despatch confidentially 
to the Government of —— if you find a feeling in favour of this 
measure, and if you will cause similar instructions to be sent to Irankfort. 

I have, &e. 
(Signed) BUOL,

Inclosure 2 in No. 336. 
Circular addressed to the Austrian Missions in Germany. 


(Translation.) Vienna, November 6, 1853. 

IN Circular No. 2 of the 30th October, we informed our allies that we 
had proposed in Berlin, in common with Prussia, to make a communication 
to the Germanic Diet respecting the position of the two Courts in the Russio- 
Turkish question, and that this proposal had been approved by the Prussian 
Cabinet. 

Nevertheless we are now only able to make a declaration of this sort in 
Frankfort, not as we hoped in common with Prussia, but in our own name. 
Explanations are therefore due to the Governments who received that information 
through us. 

[t will not certainly be necessary for us to affirm that we were perfectly 
justified in calculating on the concurrence of the Prussian Government in the 
present proposition, When at the end of last month we inquired in Berlin 
whether the Prussian Cabinet deemed it advisable, as that of Vienna, that after 
the formal declaration of war by the Porte against Russia, @ tranquilizing com- 
tnunication should be addressed to the Diet by the two Germanic Powers to 
demonstrate their neutral position, this proposal was not only willingly accepted 
by the Prussian Government, but met even with that full concurrence which 
we believed its evident motives entitled us to expect. We were informed that 
the Prussian Government entered into our proposition, and that they only 
entertained the wish to agree on the expressions of the communication to be 
delivered in common in Frankfort, 

As we were very ready for such an agreement, and wanted to leave the 
particulars of form and language to the Prussian Government, and as time 
sressed if it was to be laid before the Diet the first session fixed on the drd 
instant, we believed we could not forward the object in view by any better
