LATE yesterday evening M, de Hibner gave me the gratifying intelligence, 
that the Austrian Government adopted the whole of the conditions which your 
Lordship had instrueted Lord Westmorland to represent to Count Buol, as 
those on which Her Majesty's Government would be prepared to address a 
further communication to the Porte, with a view of inducing the Ottoman 
Government to enter into fresh negotiations with Russia for the settlement ot 
the Eastern question. M. de Hiibner was further informed, that M. de Buol 
left it to France and England to decide whether the note to be addressed to the 
Porte ghould be the work of the two Cabinets, or whether they would intrust 
the Conference of Vienna with the task of drawing it up. He left it equally to 
those two Cabinets to decide whether the note should be collective, or whether 
each Representative of the Four Powers at Constantinople should present a 
separate one to the Porte; observing, howe thas Austria would prefer the 
former mode, as likely to carry greater weight wilh it, 

There was 0 aaaueenh i the end of M, de Hitbner’s despateh which had 
not been clearly deciphered when I saw him, but the spirit of whieh appeared to 
be, that the Four Powers should give the Porte to understand clearly that they 
expected that their proposal would be accepted. Tee TP 

This morning M. Drouyn de Lhuys called on me, on his way from 
Fontainebleau. He said that the Emperor was much preoccupied with the 
present state of the Eastern question, and was anxious to place it ina clearer 
light (dans une position plus nette) than it was at present, Phat he (M. 
Drouyn de Lhuys) had consequently, by His Majesty's orders, drawn up a 
project of Protocol of Conference, which he was about to send to London for 
your Lordship's approval, when the intelligence from Vienna which I have 
related above reached him. He read me the project.in question. It was to the 
effect that the Four Powers, convinced that the present state of the relations 
hetween Eussia and Turkey were dangerous to the peace of Europe and eould 
not he permitted to continue, and having failed in all thetr elforts to mediate 
between the contending parties, invited them to send Plenipotentirics to meet 
their Representatives in Conference; that, as the Emperor of Russia had 
constantly declared that he sought no new right, &c. (the declaration of Russia 
was here reproduced), andas the Porte hud stated its readimess to give Satistactory 
assurances, it might be hoped that, with the aid of the Four | owers, this 
misunderstanding would thus be put an end to; but should the Four Powers be 
unfortunately mistaken, they declared that they would continue to watch closely 
the progress of the war in the East, reserving to themselves the nght to inter- 


209 


fere whenever they judged it necessary for the preservation of the integrity of 
the Ottoman Empire or the independence of its Sovereign and Government. _ 

This project, M. Drouyn de Lhuys continued, must now be modified to suit 
the circumstances aa they now stood, As it was now decided to ascertain in the 
first place the Porte’s intentions, he wishes that your Lordship should undertake

Pfordten on the Turkish dispute, which I presume to be regulated by the

ment, and with the Minister for Foreign Affairs in particular, remarked to me a 
short time since that Prussia was still the Prussia of 1848 and 1849.

Protocol to be signed by the Conference at Vienna, of which the note and 
‘nstructions were to be annexes, and which was to replace the declaration he had

which guided them in the Eastern question. ‘These papers, he added, he hitch 
sent for your Lordship's consideration ; but i you adopted them, he said that 
the form of the instructions must be somewhat changed, as they had been 
drawn up under the supposition that they were to be issued by the Conference 
at Vienna, while it was obvious that they must emanate from the Governments 
who were represented there, 

During the conversation which ensued, M. de Lhuys insisted very strongly 
on the value which his proposed Protocol would acquire were Austria and 
Prussia to agree to sign it; but he added, that he attached so much value to the 
declaration which it contained, that he had proposed to your Lordship that the 
French and English Representatives should sign it, even if their colleagues 
refused to do so, leaving it open for the eventual acceptance of the latter. 

He was equally desirous, he continued, that the note to be addressed to 
the Porte, inviting the Turkish Government to renew negotiations with Kussin, 
should be signed by the Representatives in Conference, He attached great 
importance to this document having a collective form, as it would carry more 
weight with it when presented to the Porte, and would be a proof to Russia that 
the Four Powers were acting in coneert. On the other hand, Austria had 
expressed n preference for this form of proceeding, to which it might be prudent 
to-attend. Finally, he must say that he thought every fact, however slight, 
which bound Austria to the policy of France and England, was of importance, 
An alliance commenced in the most simple manner, might, with perseverance 
and caution. be extended to measures of far greater activity and more positive 
worth. 

It will be for your Lordship to consider the value of these observations. 
For myself, I could not gainsay stem, though | was most careful to reserve full 
latitude of opinion for Her Majesty's Government,

My Lord, Berlin, November 24, 1853. 

_ BARON MANTEUFFEL has received intelligence from Vienna that 
differences of a serious nature were likely to arise between the Bosnians and 
Servians, which might lead to a collision between those two provinces ; and 
that the Austrian Government had directed a corps of observation to be stationed 
on the Servian frontier in the direction of Temesvar. 

_ His Excellency is fearful that any conflict between these two races may 
increase the complications of affairs in the East, and views with some alarm any 
demonstration on the part of Austria which, whilst it might seriously com- 
promise the neutrality she had so overtly made at Frankfort, might also cause 
umbrage to France, and give rise to counter-demonstrations by that Power on 
the borders of Italy. ; 

His Excellency had accordingly instructed Count Arnim to recommend to 
the Austrian Cabinet the greatest caution and prudence, and to take no steps 
which might be interpreted in an adverse or even in 8 doubtful sense by the 
western Powers.

very much excited and extremely incensed against the Turks; but | could not 
learn what. ultimate course was likely to be pursued, either in a military sense or 
in the way of negotiation. . 

Baron Manteuffel seems to be of opinion that Count Nesselrode is at 
present allied with the old Russian party, and that Count Orloff represents the 
more moderate counsellors of the Emperor. If such be the case (which does 
not appear to be borne out by the valuable opinion of Sir G. H. Seymour) I can 
only draw this conclusion, viz., either that the far-seeing politician may look to 
gain through diplomacy a triamph for Russia which the distinguished General 
ean searcely hope to achieve by arms, or that the wily veteran of diplomacy may 
seek by apparent concessions to dominate a party in the Russian Empire which 
he could no longer risk openly to oppose. a 

Baron Manteuffel has given me to understand, that he has been bitterly 
reproached by the Cabinet of St. Petersburgh for the line of policy which Prussia 
has pursued in the Oriental question.

Lord A. Loftus to the Earl of Clarendon,—(Received November 27.) 


(No, 108.) 
My Lord, Berlin, November 25, 1853. 
BARON MANTEUFFEL called upon me this evening, on his return from 
Potsdam, anticipating the hour at which he had appointed to meet me at his 
own house, | | : 
His Excellency told me that he had received a despatch from the Chevalier 
Bunsen, informing him of the projet de note which post Lordship had drawn up 
for presentation to the Porte collectively by the Representatives of the Four 


267 


Powers, and stating that the text of this note would be forwarded by your 
Lordship to Berlin and Vienna on Saturday the 26th instant. 

I informed his Excellency that the terms of this note, and of the instruc- 
tions to accompany it, were in exact conformity with the opinions conveyed in 
your Lordship’s despatch No. 378 to the Earl of Westmorland, of which 1 had 
already given his Excellency a copy ; and I likewise stated that they had been 
most favourably received by the Austrian Cabinet. 

I then inquired ‘specifically what opinions the King had expressed with 
respect to the views of Her Majesty’s Government as set forth in that despatch. 

His Excellency replied, that the King had entirely approved of them, and 
had further authorized him to give his adhesion to any note conceived and drawn 
up in the sense and spirit of the views expressed by your Lordship, 

His Exeellency remarked that, although perfectly willing to cooperate with 
the other Powers in the sense conveyed in your Lordship’s despatch, he should 
not, however, wish to embroil himself with the Emperor Nicholas by submitting 
to His Imperial Majesty proposals as emanating from Prussia alone. 

Baron Manteuffel stated that, from intelligence he had received from 
St. Petersburgh yesterday (which confirms the report of Sir H, Seymour), he 
much feared that the Emperor would never consent to a Conference at which a 
Russian and a ‘Turkish negotiator should take part; and he is likewise convinced 
that the Emperor will never consent to evacuate the Provinces until some final 
arrangement has been concluded.

(Signed) AUGUSTUS LOFTUS.

200 


doubt that Batoum is one of those places for acquiring and retaining which great 
efforts will be made. 

The best proof, however, that can be afforded that the Sultan has been 
ill advised in choosing Asia as the battle-tield on which his differences with the 
Russians is to be settled, will be, if that theatre of operations is found to suit 
the Emperor’s views, and this, I am inclined to believe, will be seen to he 
the case. 

Although I speak with great diflidence of matters of which | am so wholly 

ignorant as of all that relates to war, | imagine the Emperor to be, for the 
present, quite contented to carry on nothing but a defensive war in the Danubian 
Provinces, and to have, or to believe that he has, a sufficient force to effect this 
purpose. 
At the same time he is known to have been much incensed at the initiative 
of operations having been taken by an enemy of whose power he had long 
spoken so contemptuousty,.and the fecling is believed to have been increased by 
the recent events at St. Nicholas. 

This affair is indeed spoken of by the Russians as a victory, although not of 
a decisive kind ; but its real character is of course as well known to themselves 
as to the rest of the world, 

The result, as I fully expect, will be that the appeals of Prince Worontzow 
(who has been more clear-sighted than his master) will be attended to ; that large 
reinforcements will be sent to him, and that he will be encouraged to wipe out 
i partial surprise and failure by some signal successes. 

This will suit Prince Worontzow, who is known to be anxious about 
obtaining the only honour which it remains for the Emperor to bestow upon 
nim—the staff of a marshal; and it will suit his Imperial master, who must be 
supposed to be not otherwise than well satisfied at having an excuse for not 
heing fettered by such obligations as are imposed by voluntary assurances, 

If, in the place of positive information, | submit to your Lordship conjee- 
tures and hypotheses, | will beg of you to remember that the former T have not 
to offer. 

The Emperor's real intentions are known to himself and to two or three of 
his confidants,—probably not even to the most trusty and experienced of his 
ministers; and in this well-trained society not only is any information as to 
passing events sought for in vain, but allusion to them is as much as possible 
avaided, 

I will venture upon one concluding observation, | am well aware that, if 
the necessity of any expansion on the part of Russia is admitted, Austria, 
Germany, France herself, would infinitely prefer her frontiers being enlarged 
at the expense of Asia, 

England, on the contrary, has interests which make it extremely desirable 
that even the easternmost limits of Russia should not be extended, since every 
step taken by a Russian army in an eastern direction brings it nearer to the 
Indus. f 

In the midst of the anxieties caused by the numerous contingencies to 
which the ageressive policy of Russia gives rise, one ground of confidence and 

comfort appears to be atforded, 

I do not allude to declarations and promises, the value of which I consider 
as infinitesimal, but to those financial embarrassments of which the commence- 
ment is already to be perceived,—embarrassments which have been prepared by 
the practice of collecting large armies when they were assembled only for 
amusement, and which will render it difficult to increase, maintain, and move 
them about when they are required for mischievous purposes. 

I have, &c. 
(Signed) G, H. SEYMOUR,

Sir G. H. Seymour to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received November 27.) 


My Lord, Bt. Petersburgh, Navember 18, 1653. 4 

IN a late despatch [ had the honour of making known to your Lordship 
a wish conveyed to me in the shape of an inquiry on the part of the Emperor 
by Count Nesselrode. 

Upon reflecting upon that wish, I am more and more convinced that it 
cannot safely be com lied with. . 

The railway to Warsaw will be used either for military or for commercial 
purposes ; in either case the interests of England and Russia lie m opposite 
directions, the interests of humanity, T will likewise observe, agreeing with those 
of England, since both require that a war should be brought to the quickest 
possible conclusion, and since every er given to commence would render it 
more easy for Russia to prolong the struggle: 

As the disposal of its agricultural produce is the great resource upon which 
this country has to depend, every art will of course be tried, in the occurrence 
of war, to carry on trade by indirect means. The great facility indeed which 
Russia possesses for indirect ex ortation would make any attempt to injure her 
ne this manner difficult, unless Prussia could be induced to join heartily in the 
effort. 


ports of Memel and Dantzic would be the resort of hundreds of vessels which 
now never enter them. 

It may be expected indeed that Russia will bid high for the amity or the 
continued neutralization of Germany, The newspapers have lately stated that 
in case of a rupture with England the Russian tarifl will be modified in favour 
of the Zollverei, and an acquaintance of mine asserte not only that this plan 
really exists, but that some intimation of it has been already made to the 
Cabinet of Berlin, 

I have some reason for believing that the Emperor and his military advisers 
have a very inadequate idea of the importance af trade to this country, yet 
even His Majesty was struck with the scarcity of vessels at Cronstadt, and 
learned with surprise that vague rumours of war had been sufficient to cause 
this unusual blank. 

This perception it was which led to the communication lately made to the 
British merchants of St. Petersburgh; and the customs’ returns of the season 
must make it a matter of regret that the notification bad not been made at an 
earlier period. 

Various circumstances combine to make me infer that the Government is 
already suffering from financial difficulty. Thus, smell payments which are 
usually made without hesitation are now deferred, the Government finding it 
niore convenient to pay interest thereupon ; thus the works of the Warsaw Rail- 
way have been suspended, and the building of all public edifices, except those 
under construction by contract, is given up. 

One of the persons here, whose opinion is of the most value in all that 
relates to financial matters, has not hesitated to express to me his conviction 
that these symptoms are only the forerunners of more serious ones; and consi- 
ders it almost certain that the Government will be unable to proceed beyond 
the month of February, without cither having recourse to 4 loan or to a 
depreciation of the currency. 

Truly it may be said that supposed diplomatic superiority is producing 
results in this country which must render it a matter of regret to its inhabitants 
that their foreign relations are not conducted by more sober and hetter-established 
mediocrity, 

I have, &c. 
(Signed) G, H, SEYMOUR,

275 


It was highly improbable, Count Nesselrode stated, that before the spring 
any operations would be taken by the fleet at Sevastopol: still, what a position 
had been taken by the English and French Governments towards that of Russia | 
The Turks, it was evident, were at liberty to attack any part of the Russian 
territory, whilst, as it had been made known, any attempt on the part of the 
Russian ships to land troops on the coasts of Turkey would be met by the 
armed resistance of the allied fleets. 

All this was said in a tone of deep regret and feeling, but without the 
slightest indication of anger, so much so as to render it unnecessary for me 
again to point out by whose fault an anomalous state of affairs, as well as a 
very deplorable one, has been brought about. 

In the course of our conversation, Count Nesselrode enumerated the various 
concessions which had been made by Russia, since her first demands for satis- 
faction signified through Prince Menchikoff. 

He concluded the conversation by saying, that for the moment there was 
nothing to be done; that the affairs between the two armies had been unim- 
portant; but that it was possible that a few days might change the features of 
the case, and that a decided success obtained by Prince Gortchakoff might open 
the way to a speedy and satisfactory Treaty of Peace.

No. 366. 
The Earl of Clarendon to the Earl of Westmorland, 
(No, 396.) 
My Lord, Foreign Office, November 29, 1853. 


HER Majesty’s Government have learned with much satisfaction, that the 
form ofa collective note, suggested in my despatch No. 378 to your Lordship, 
together with the amendments to Count Buol’s proposed draft of instructions to 
the Representatives of the Four Powers at Constantinople, have met with the 
concurrence of the Austrian Government, And as Count Buol conveyed to me 
through your Lordship and Count Colloredo, his wish that the draft of note and 


277 


of instructions should be prepared in London, I lost no time in communicating 
upon the subject with the French Government, to whom it appears that Count 
Buol had addressed a similar request. No difference of opinion existed between 
the two Governments, and by both my despatch No. 878 has been strictly 
adhered to, The French Government preferred our form of note, and we adopted 
their draft of instructions with some amendments which were approved of by 
the French Government. Copies of the two documents are herewith inclosed,* 
Your Lordship is instructed to sign the note on the part of Her Majesty's 
Goverment, in conjunction with Count Buol, M, de Bourqueney, and Count 
Arnim; and you will then transmit a copy of it so signed to Her Majesty's 
Ambassador at Constantinople, who will receive from me the instructions as to 
the advice which his Excellency will tender to the Porte, 

I inclose also a Protocol of Conference, to which the concurrence of 
Austria is earnestly invited by Her Majesty's Government and that of the 
Emperor of the French, who desire to place on record a principle which at the 
present moment may be conducive to the restoration of peace between Russia 
and the Porte, and which will be vitally important to the existing balance of 
power and to the future tranquillity of Burope. 

Her Majesty's Government ure convinced that this principle must be in 
accordance with the policy and the true interests of Austria, and they will 
deeply regret that she should decline to join England and France in a declaration 
of which the moral effect cannot fail to be advantageous. 

If, as Her Majesty's Government confidently expect, the Protocol is agreed 
to by the Austrian Government, your Lordship will sign it with Count Buol and 
Baron de Bourquenev, and with Count Arnim, whowill probably receive instruc- 
tions to that etiect; but if for any reason which Her Majesty's Government 
cannot anticipate, Count Buol should decline to do so, your Lordship will not 
sign the Protocol until you have made known to Her Majesty’s Government the 
reason of Count Buol’s objections. Lam, &e. 

(Signed) CLARENDON,

No. 368. 
The Earl of Clarendon to Lord Stratford de Redcliffe. 


(No, 292.) 
My Lord, Foreign Office, November 49, LBGd. 

LINCLOSE the copy of # note which Her Majesty's Minister at Vienna 
has been instructed to sign, together with the Representatives of Austria, France, 

and Prussia, as a fresh proof of the identity of views that exists between the 
Four Powers, and of their earnest desire to contribute by their union to the 
re-establishment of peace between the Porte and Russia. 

The remarkable moderation which has characterised the various documents 
emanated from the Porte induces the Four Powers to hope that the proposition 
they now make will be regarded by the Turkish Government as alike consistent 
with the dignity and the intentions of the Ottoman Empire. The Four Powers 
frankly address an inquiry to the Porte to which it will doubtless reply i @ cor- 
responding spirit, without extending its differences Ww ith Russia beyond their true 
limits, or introducing elements of discord beyond those which already exist. 

With this expectation the Four Powers feel that the answer fo their inquiry 
should he left entirely to the wisdom and experience of the Turkish Government, 
but in the event of your Excellency and of your colleagues being consulted upon 
the subject, it would be desirable to advise the Porte to declare that the Four 
Powers have done justice to its conciliatory ‘ntentions by assuming that it is 
still desirous, upon honourable conditions, to terminate its difference with Russia, 

and to come to an understanding with that Power: and that with reference to 
the assurances that Russia has on various occasions given that she asks for no 
new concessions, nor for any right derogatory to the sovereignty of the Sultan, 
the Porte is prepared to renew ‘ts offers and to discuss the form in which peace 
shall be re-established and the religious question settled, upon the condition of 
not being asked to accede to any demand that it has already refused, and of an 
arrangement being concluded for the evacuation of the Principalities. 

That discussion must naturally tuke place between @ Turkish and a Russian 
negotiator furnished with full powers to treat; but in order to facilitate agree- 
ment between them the two Plenipotentianes should not meet alone—they should 
assist at conferences where ‘Austria, France, Great Britain, and Prussia would be 
equally represented 

It is presumed that the Porte would not negotiate with Russia in any 

rtion of its own territory occupied by the troops of that Power, while Russia, 
on the other hand, might object to any other place belonging to Turkey ; and the 
two parties ought, therefore, to agree together upon @ neutral town in which the 
conferences should be held. 

‘The object of the Four Powers would not be fully attained if the prelimi- 
nary negotiations for peace were not at the same time a signal for the cessation 
of hostilities, and they conceive that the Porte would not object to an armistice, 
the conditions of which should be arranged between the belligerent parties, if it 
received from the Four Powers an assurance that the terms on which the Porte 
was disposed to treat would be accepted also by Russia. 

But even if the terms propose by the Turkish Government were not such 
as Russia would be likely assent to at the commencement of negotiations, the 
Four Powers would still counsel the appointment of i ‘Turkish Plenipotentiary 
and the choice of a neutral place where the Plenipotentiaries of T urkey and 
Russia might meet the Representatives of the Four Powers. 

It is the earnest hope of those Powers that the Turkish Government will 
carefully weigh against the riska and eventunlities of war the proposal which 
they now submit for the consideration of the Porte.

. Lord A. Loftus to the Earl of Clarendon— (Received November a0).) 
(No. 113.) 


My Lord, Berlin, November 28, 1853. 

IN reply to my inquiry, Baron Manteuffel informed me that he has 
received no telegraphic intelligence from the Princinalities for some davs, 

He has, however, received a letter from Bucharest by post, stating 
that the Russian authority is daily consolidating itself in those Provinces, 
and that the chiefs of the Wallachian Administration are divided among 
themselves, 

There is a report here (on which I cannot wholly rely) that the 
Emperor has ordered another corps d’armée to Bessarabia.” In such an 


event it would probably be the second corps d’armée, now stationed in 
Poland, which would probably be relieved by a corps of grenadiers from 
St. Petersburgh. 


L have, &e. 
(Signed) AUGUSTUS LOFTUS.

Sir G. H. Seymour to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received November 30.) 
(No. 643.) 


My Lord, St. Petersburgh, November 21, 1853. 

THE messenger had hardly taken his departure on the 19th instant, 
when I was informed (and, as I believe, upon good authority) that Prince 
Woronzow has written to the Emperor, droposing that he should be 
directed to attack Erzeroum, with a corps dare composed of excellent 
troops, such as he is now able to select from 


| those under his command. 
The Prince's forees haye now been strengthened by a corps of some 
10,000 or 12,000 men, commanded by Prinee Dolgorouky, who, after 


repelling Schamyl, has made a most remarkable march from the north to 
the south of the Caucasus, leading his men across the highest ridges of 
that mountainous district by paths which were never before trodden by a 
Russian soldier, and it is possible, as it has been explained to me, that 
this movement ny have a very decisive eflect upon the operations now in 
progress in Asia Minor, 

[t appears, accordingly, that Prince Woronzow has represented that 
it would be useless to attempt an aggressive war with a numerous army, 
which the miserable resources of the country he desires to attack would 
be unable to maintain; but that, with some 25.000 of picked troops, he 
shall be able to overcome any resistance which may be made to him. | 

Up to this point my informant does not doubt of the correctness of 
his intelligence. 

Beyond this he can only express his belief in the 
the proposal of his lieutenant having been given, 

He helieves the Emperor to have hesitated during several days as to 
the expediency of resorting at present to offensive operations; but at 
length, under the influence of excitement eansed by the late reverses on 
the Danube, and by the representations of some of the more ardent of his 
advisers, to have adopted the views of Prince Woronzow.

Sir G. H. Seymour to the Earl af Clarendon.—(Received November 30.) 


(No. 647. Confidential.) 
My Lord, St, Petersburgh, November 23, 1853. 


A VERY good effect appears to have been produced by the conver- 
sution which your Lordship has held with the British merchants concerned 
in the Baltic trade, as to the probabilities and contingencies of war. ‘The 
effect has been that the British merchants of St. Petersburgh have declined 
entering into any contracts for goods to be delivered to them next year, 
and thus that a salutary foretaste has been given to the Russians of the 
losses to which a rupture with England will expose them, 

One of the leading merchants of the town is reported to have said, 
“In the event of war breaking out, it will depend upon the English 
Government whether hostilities shall last five years or five months ; it will 
be the shorter period if the Government should find means for stopping 
every outlet of Russian commerce,”

My Lord, St. Petersburgh, November 23, 1853. 

IF the Emperor has brought himself into severe difficulties, he is at 
least paying a hea penalty for his imprudence; accounts upon which | 
can entirely rely proving to me that His Majesty is in a very unenviable 
state of mind, 

His depression is such as to be very painful to himself, and his irri- 
tation of a nature to be occasionally very trying to those about him. 

I know from the most certain source of the Chancellor having saul 
that his position became very disagreeable to him, that he was hardly able 
now to transact business with his master, 

The same thing has been more obscurely expressed by the Grant 
Duke Constantine, who until very lately has been his father’s constant 
companion, 

Mr. Baird, who is the owner of some very extensive iron-works at 
St. Petersburgh, is as enger to dispose of them as the Grand Duke is 
desirous that they should be secured with a view to the manufactory of 
machinery for the steam navy. Knowing this, one of the Grand Duke's 
attendants asked him the other day, “* Why, if your Imperial Highness 1s 
so cager about the purchase, do you not speak upon the subject to the 
Emperor?” “Itis precisely because | am anxious about it,” replied the 
Grand Duke, * that | do not speak to him.” 

His Majesty’s manner, as [ hear, is more generally expressive of 
dejection than of anger; and as T understand, this observation was made 
the other day by several persons when the Emperor, with an English 
newspaper in his hand, entered the great room at Gatchina, in which the 
whole Court are in the habit of assembling. Throwing the paper upon 
the table, the Emperor said slowly, “ Vola done les Anglais qui me 
brulent en effigie, Quelle démence!" 

No reply was made, no observation offered, and the Emperor after 
walking up and down the room several times with his arms folded, 
withdrew. 

The Emperor possesses several very devoted servants, but unfortu- 
nately devotion in this country never takes the turn of making known 
unpalatable truths to its object, the result being that errors as to plain 


285 


facts have been allowed to prevail in the mind of the Sovereign which have 
led to his own misery, and to those prospects of war and confusion by 
which all Europe is troubled, 
I have, &e. 
(Signed) G. H. SEYMOUR.

Russian army.

was in Asia that this advantage was to be realized; and he states that 
Prince Woronzow, who was to take the command of the Russian Asiatic 
army, had coneeived a plan for advancing on and taking Erzeroum, 
M. Drouyn de Lhuys, however, said that the General had, in a letter of 
subsequent date, modified this opinion, and given it to be understood that 
the expedition was abandoned in consequence of the illness of Prince 
Woronzow and the difficulties of provisioning an army on its march to 
Kirzeroum,

15th instant, and had his first audience of the Sultan to-day, has sent me 
word that an express steamer will start for Marseilles with his despatches 
in the course of the afternoon; and | therefore avail myself of the oppor- 
tunity to inform your Lordship that, although no official answer has been 

et given by the Porte to the new proposition sent in to Reshid Pasha by 
M. de la Cour and myself, with the view of ascertaining the Council's 
disposition respecting it, I conclude, from the language of Reshid Pasha, 
and roth other indications, that there is now even less chance than in the 
outset of obtaining its acceptance, even ina modified shape, * 

As the language of M. de In Cour’s successor, in so Har as it has been 
addressed to me, is eminently pacilic, there is still a possibility of a 
change in the counsels of the Porte, consequent upon a joint representa- 
tion, by both of us, in the sense already expressed and urged by me. For 
this chance, | have been anxious to keep the door open, especially as the 
Prussian Minister has received, within the last few days, authority to act 
in-eoncert with me; and as the Austrian Internuncio appears to expect 
some instruction of a similar tendency by the next courier from Vienna, 

I have hitherto exerted my almost solitary efforts in favour of peace 
under every conceivable disadvantage, including even that which results, 
in Turkish estimation, from the presence of the allied squadrons in these 
waters. ’ : 

The unexpected change which has taken place in the k renely Embassy, 
by the substitution of General Baraguay d’Hilliers for M. de la Cour, has 
naturally increased the embarrassment and delay to which T was previously 
exposed. es ) Ades | ead 

I abstain from going into further particulars at present. The day 
after to-morrow a safe and expeditious opportunity of forwarding 
despatches to your Lordship will probably be at my disposal, Should | 
be disappointed in this expectation, | have no doubt that Vice-Admiral 
Dundas will readily afford me the means of transmitting my correspond- 
ence to your Lordship with the least practicable delay.

Lord Cowley to the Karl of Clarendan.—(Reeeived December 5.) 
(No. 911, Confidential.) 


My Lord, Paris, December 4, 1853. 

M. DROUYN DE LAUYS stated to me this afternoon, that he had 
received this morning from M. de Hubner o communication of consider- 
able interest It appears, as the sequel of this despatch will show, to have 
been caused by conversations which M. de Hiibner had held lately with 
the Emperor and with M. Drowyn de Lhoys, the eeneral tenor of which 
may he gathered from the details of one held with the latter 
confidential despateh No, 886, 

The summary recounted to me by M. Drouyn de Lhuys of the 
communication made to him this morning, is taken partly from an open,

My Lord, Berlin, December 2, 1853. 

BARON MANTEUFFEL informed me to-day that the King, on 
authorising him to accede to the proposals which had been submitted to 
Prussia for the collective action of the Four Powers at Vienna, had also 
desired him to address to the Cabinets of the Four Powers a wish that 
some steps should be ultimately taken in order to provide for the security 
and welfare of the Christian Church in the East, with due regard to the 
sovereign rights of the Sultan, . 

His Excellency was not very clear or explicit as to the exact favour 
or rights which His Majesty seemed to desire. But he stated that it was 
a subject which interested His Majesty most intimately, and which he had 
deeply at heart. 

His Majesty also desired Baron Manteuffel to instruct his Ministers at 
the Courts of London and Paris to inquire what steps the English and 
French Governments were prepared to tuke should Turkey refuse to 
accede to the collective invitation that will now be addressed to the Porte 
by the Representatives of the Four Powers at Vienna.

My Lord, St. Petersburgh, November 26, 1855. 

| WAS sitting on the evening of the 23rd instant with the Prussian 
Minister, who is confined by illness to his room, when the Chancellor, 
who is a daily visitor, entered the room, 

His Excellency read us a despatch which he had just received from 
Baron Mevendorff, giving an account of the Turks having withdrawn 

recipitately from the Principalities, leaving only a small corps at 
Culafat, 

The intelligence appeared to have given great satisfaction to the 
Chancellor, from whose observation 1am disposed to infer the intention 
on the part of Prince Gortchakoff of occupying Little Wallachia. 

What struck me the most forcibly in M. de Meyendorf’s report was 
the assurance which he has given his Government of the general sympathy 
which the cause of Russia, os he learned, meets with from all classes, 

My mental reflection upon the phrase was—either this is true, and 
then the Court of Austria is wanting in that impartiality which should 
characterize a mediating Power; or it is not true, and we have here a 
fresh illustration ol the disposition of Russian diplomatic agents to mis- 
lead their Government by representing: matters not as they are, but as 
they are desired to be, 

The substance of M. de Meyendori?'s despatch will be found in the 
bulletin published in the © St, Petersburgh Journal” of this date, a copy 
of which is inelosed in another despatch. 

I have, &e,

Sir G. H. Seymoar to the Earl of Clarendon.—( Received December 5.) 


(No. 662, Confidential.) 
My Lord, St. Petersburgh, November 26, 1893. 


WITH reference to Lord Cowley’s despatch No, 548, a copy of which 
was inclosed in your Lordship’s confidential despatch No, 293 of the 16th 
instant, | would venture to observe that it appears to me that M. Drouyn 
de Lhuys’ plan, if adopted by the Four Governments, would be the best 
which could be devised, either for putting an end to the war between 
Russia and Turkey, or for guarding against those consequences by which 
a war might very possibly be attended. | 

It is indeed to be feared that the Courts of Austria and Prussia 
would be reluctant to give their assert to a measure, which although con- 
formable to their best interests, might be repugnant to the personal feel- 
‘nes of the two Sovereigns towards the Emperor Nicholas. But on the 
other hand, there appears to be little reason why they should not avail 
themselyes of a precedent which His Imperial Majesty provided 

When after the revolutionary movements of 1545 the relations of 
Austria and Prussia became of so unfriendly a nature that the attack of 
one of these Powers upon the other was consilered imminent, the Emperor 
of Russia, looking to the welfare of Germany, did not hesitate to declare 
that whichever country took the initiative of war would find his battalions 
on the side of the party attacked. 

His Imperial Majesty then will have no right to complain if a system 
(and that devised by himself} be resorted to in the interests of Europe 
which was found very eflicacious when the interests of Germany were at 
stake: and Austria and Prussia need have no scruples in following an 
example set them by their illustrious friend and ally, A resolution whi¢h 
was excusable for guarding against war, becomes much more so when it is 
for the purpose of putting an end to war. 

As regards M. Drouyn de Lhuys’ altered opinion as to the Vienna 
Conference, the change appears to me to be reasonable after the over- 
tures for peace which Count Buol persisted in making single-handed to the 
Porte. 

It is impossible that the Austrian Minister should nat have foreseen 
the result of this isolated attempt; and the suspicion which it suggests 1s, 
that in making it he was acting with partiality, with the object of further 
establishing the pacific intentions of Russia and the intractable dispo- 
sition of the Turkish Government, 

M. Drouyn de Lhuys—as Lord Cowley reports—is of opinion that 
the Emperor Nicholas intends, if possible, to keep possession of the Prin- 
cipalities, I grieve to learn that such are his expectations, for he has 
taken throughout these deplorable transact ions so correct a view of the 
course which would be followed by Russia, that his past judgments give 
reat weight to those which he now makes known, 

Some months ago a distinct declaration of the Emperor's wold in my 
mind have outweighed opinions however sagacious, anid appearances 


however suspicious. As it is, | must fairly state to your Lordship, that as: 


regards myself confidence in Russian promises is wholly destroyed, 

| have witnessed the violation of a series of distinct engagements, 
and whether any addition is to be made to the number must, I infer, 
depend more upon the profit or loss to be expected than upon impossibility 
that His Imperial Majesty should be wanting to his word, 

Lregret to be obliged to write in such a style of an exalted per- 
sonage, but in moments like the present L should feel to be wanting: in 
duty if 1 hesitated to express an honest opinion in pliin language, . 

| have, &e. =

Sir G. H. Seymour to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received December 9.) 


(No. 666. Confidential.) 


My Lord, St. Petersburgh, November 26, 185d, 

I WAS not quite sure, from your Lordship’s despatch No, 292, 
whether it was intended that my protest against the incorporation of the 
Principalities should be verbal or in writing, but I inclined to giving it 
the latter form. | 

___ After anxious consideration, I have revised this partly-formed resolu- 
tion, from reflecting — 

1. That a written protest would give offence to the Russian Govern- 
ment at a moment when the evacuation of Wallachia by the ‘Turkish 
troops may possibly render them more disposed to negotiation than they 
have been of late. : 

2, Because, interested as Austria is im seeing the Principalites freed 
from their present occupants and restored to their legitimate Sovereign, | 
feel tolerably confident that the Russian Government will not expose the 
most valued of her alliances to such a trial as would be incurred by an 
attempt to keep possession of these Provinces, And, 

3. Because, if I do not greatly err, the quarter in which the Sultan 
has to ap eceneng territorial spoliations is rather on the eastern coast of 
the Black Sea than in Europe: an apprehension which, if judged to be 
well-founded, would suggest the expediency of the protest heing extended 
from the Principalities to the whole of the Turkish dominions. — 

_ It will be very satisfactory to me if the conclusion at which I have 
arrived should meet with your Lordship’s approval. 
| U have, &c. 
(Signed) G. Hl. SEYMOUR.

ALTHOUGH Ldid not feel at liberty to read to Count Nesselrode 
your Lordship's despatch No, 206, 1 was convineed that it was written

and according | communicated to him faithfully the feelings with which 
Her Majesty’s Government have taken cognizance of the last Imperial 
manifesto. 

My report was listened to without interruption, but evidently not 
without some impatience; and, when it was concluded, Count Nesselrode 
observed, that it appeared that it was a fixed resolution (parti pris) on the 

vart of Her Majesty's Government to find fault with every act of the 
isin Cabinet. Russia had been assailed in the most virnlent manner 
from every quarter, and when her voice was heard in reply, a shout was 
raised against her. It came really to this: all that was done by Russia 
was wrong; all that was done by the Porte was right. 

This he must consider was a very strange way of showing impartiality, 


and certainly it was not by pursuing such a course that the difficulties 


of which all complained would be solved in a peaceable manner, 


J requested that his Excellency would bear in mind that the fact was, 
that Her Majesty's Government had from the outset considered that 
[tussia was exclusively to blame in this affair; inasmuch as demands had 
been made, and violent measures atopted, for which no grounds had ever 
been adduced; having been wrong too, I added, at the outset, every step 


you have taken in that direction made you more so,

tine when England was alarmed: by rumours of invasion; and ended by

COUNT BUOL begged M. de Bourqueney, Count Arnim, and nye 
to call upon him to-day to prepare the mode of arranging and forwarding 
the communication to Constantinople, the substance of whieh had been 
agreed to (as announced by telegraph) by England and Prussia, but of 
which the documents had only as yet been received by M, de Bour- 

1eneyV. 2 

Se Count Buol stated that these having been communicated to him, he 
had taken the Emperor's opinion upon them, and he had received his 
orders to state his entire agreement with them, F 

Count Ruol added, that with respect to the draft of the instructions 
he thought it would be advisable that each Government should also send 
a confidential communication to its Representative, in which might be 
get forth more forcibly than in the ostensible instructions the anxious 
desire of the Four Governments that the Porte should favourably receive 
and act upon their suggestions, and the deep regret with which fy 
appearance of disinclination on her part to do so would be viewed by 
them. : 

In reply to this invitation, it was remarked, that if such a anaes on 
was proposed to our Governments, they would expect that s M ee be 
aceonpanied by the reciprocity of a similar assurance from t ie Aus sa 
Government, that if, alter the consent of the Porte had heen i nol i 
the proposals of the Four Powers, any reluctance to accept them shoulc 
be manifested on the part of Russia, they would adopt hinguage as press- 
ing and as energetic to the Cabinet of St, Petersburgh, | 

Count Buol consented to take this engagement, and added, that 
ehould the case occur, he would ina like spirit consult with and adopt the 
ciowa of the other Allied Powers as to the most advisable course to be 
pursued, q el cae ar 

Baron Bourqueney, upon this understanding, undertook to recommend 
the sugeestion of Count Buol to the favourable attention of his (iovern- 
ment, aud Lalso stated that L had no doubt the same language of friendly 
interest towards the Porte, which had dictated the instructions contained 
in your Lordship’s despatch to Lord Stratford de Redcliffe, No. 234, 
would be adhered to upon the understanding to which reference Is above 
made, relative to the language to be held, if necessary, at St. Peters- 
burgh. she f 

Count Buol inquired in what manner we proposed to transmit the note 
to Reshid Pasha, He stated that he considered the best line to be adopted 
would be to desire me, as the organ of the Conference and in their name, 
to transmit it to Lord Stratford, and to request him, as the senior Ambas- 


307 


sador, to take upon himself the duty of delivering it; and he thought that 
Lord Stratford might judge that the best mode of doing so would be (after 
consulting with his allesenen to propose an interview of the Four Repre- 
sentatives with Reshid Pasha, at which he would deliver to him the note, 
when each of the Representatives would have an opportunity of commu- 
nicating the substance of the instructions with hich they were charged, 

In stating this view of the manner of proceeding, Count Buol 
remarked that he did so merely as a suggestion, but that if Lord Stratford 
took charge of the note, he considered it due to his high character and 
great experience to leave him to decide upon what he considered as the 
most proper method to be adopted, 

[stated that Twas quite ready to charge myself with this commission, 
and that I would transmit the note to Lord Stratford, accompanied with 
the proposed suggestion, but leaving it to him to decide the manner of 
proceeding, 

Count Buol begged to mention a mere verbal alteration which he 
would propose in the Protocol to be signed by the Four Representatives. 
He thought the word “ plaisir” in the third paragraph, and the words at 
the close of it ‘Ala tranquillité,” would be better altered respectively to 
‘satisfaction’ and “au repos.” M, de Bourqueney and Count Arnim at 
onee concurred in these alterations as being preferable expressions and 
bearing precisely the same import, and I also Sore ently gave my 
consent to them. As we were quilting Count Buol, M. de Bourqueney 
remarked that it would be a step in the progress of the important nego- 
tiation we were entering upon, if the present meeting, although not a 
rerularly constituted conference, should take some step which might have 
the character of attesting our joint consent to the documents submitted 
to us; he therefore proposed that the Note and Protocol should be 
‘paraphéed" by the signature of our respective initials. Count Buol 
agreed to this proposal, and expressed his pleasure at thus taking a step 
which gave evidence of the concurrence of the Four Powers in the line 
of policy which might now be considered as adopted. He then placed his 
initials to the drafts of the Note and Protocol, which was equally done by 
Baron Bourquency, Count Arnim, and myself, 

Count Buol stated that he would charge himself with the preparation 
of the different documents which were to be signed hy the Conference, 
and with their transmission by messenger to Belgrade, and thence by 
Tatar to Constantinople; and aa it was uncertain when the despatches 
from London and from Berlin might arrive, he proposed that we should 
meet in confereuce on Monday for the signature of the documents and 
their immediate transmission. He stated also that he would prepare the 
form of the Protocol of the Conference, which it had been decided should 
be kept and registered, 

Count Buol said that with regard to the communication of the note 
to the Russian Minister and to the Turkish Ambussador, he thought the 
best manner of proceeding would be that he should undertake to place a 
copy in the hands of Baron Meyendorff, and that (at the request of the 
Conference) Baron Bourqueney and myself should do the same with the 
Ambassador of the Porte, As to the Protocol of the Four Powers, Count 
Buol thought it should be considered as a confidential document, of which 
no copy should be given, but that the contents of it might (after the 
departure of the messenger for Constantinople) be communicated con- 
fidentially to Baron Meyendort¥ and to Arif? Effendi, in the same mode as 
had been adopted with regard to the note. 

I have, &e,

I could have but little hope that anything which I could say would 
make much impression on the Pasha; still I thought it advisable not to 
allow his observations to pass sud stlenfio, the more so as Vely Pasha 
was present during the conversation, and | therefore said that 1 trusted 
that no such wilful determination would prevent the Porte’s accepting the 
advice of the Four Powers, and nominating a Plenipotentiary to treat ; 
that demanding the previous evacuation of the Principalities was tanta- 
mount to a refusal to treat, since the point which it was hoped to obtain 
by negotiation was that which the Pasha insisted on as preliminary to 
naming a Plenipotentiary, and it was impossible to suppose that Russia, 
however much in the wrong, would be more amenable now than she had 
been during the whole progress of the quarrel; that the honour of Turkey 
was completely guaranteed, for a Turkish army had not only passed the 
Danube and entered Wallachia, retiring at the will and pleasure of 
the General whe commanded it, but that the Turkish troops still held a 
most important point in Wallachia, that of Kalafat, which put them more 
on equality with their enemy now than when negotiations were broken 
off; that the cause of Turkey was so just that she had twice succeeded in 
obtaining a record of the Four Powers in her favour: that she had lost 
this advantage the first time by not accepting the Vienna note: let her 
beware of placing it in jeopardy a second time by refusing to treat, except 
on terms that, it was obvious beforehand, could not be accepted. 

Namik Pasha replied that he considered the request of the Conference 
could not be complied with. Public opinion at Constantinople could not 
permit the nomination of a Plenipotentiary while the Russians were on 
Turkish territory; nor, when the composition of Omer Pashi’s army was 
taken into consideration, and the sumber of irrezular troops which it 
contained, would it be possible to keep them in idleness during the winter, 
This was a vital question to Turkey ; the Sultan's authority was at stake; 
no terms that could be acceptable to the Porte would be agreed to b 
Russia; an armed struggle was inevitable. He hoped that the Porte 
would have the material assistance of England and France, and he should 
have no fear of the result. 

It appears to be so much the habit of the Turks to suppose that it is 
the individual cause of Turkey which we are defending, rather than the 
general principles of international law violated in their persons, that I 
was not sorry to have an opportunity of protesting in a friendly manner 
against such an imprudent assumption, | said, therefore, to Namik Pasha 
that the presence of the English and French fleets in the Bosphorus was 
an carnest of the solicitude of those two Governments for the maintenance 
of the integrity of the Ottoman Empire, or to speak more correctly for the 
maintenance of the present territorial distribution of Kurope; for that the 
territorial limits of a country was a question distinct from its dynasty or 
its possessors; that the one could not be altered without influencing the 
balance of power, while a change in the other did not necessarily disturb 
that equilibrium: still Turkey having certain possessions in Hurope we 
were (desirous that she should retain those possessions, but that if an 
pase of her territory was threatened there were two ways of defending: it, 
sy negotiation or by the force of arms—and that it was the duty of every 
Government to exhaust the former before it had recourse to the latter ; 
that if Turkey claimed to be considered as a member of the European 
family of States, she must recollect that she could not consider her own 
interests alone, but must make them in a measure subservient to the 
ecneral interests of Murope ; and that the Porte would best prove its sense 
of its own superior position in this lamentable quarrel, and of its desire to 
consult the general good of Europe, by aceepting the advice of the Four 
Powers, and naming a Plenipotentiary to treat for pence. 

Namik Pasha still held to the opinion that negotiation was impossible 
unless the Russians quitted the Danubian provinces. 

I then asked him whether he really ‘aren that Turkey was in a 
condition to support with success a prolonged struggle with Russia. 
Namik Pasha replied that he was under no illusion on this point; that he 
had been all his life a soldier, and knew well of what the Turkish army 
was capable; that he had been also three or four times in Russia, and 


310 


had some knowledge of the Russian troops, and was aware that Turkey 
single-handed was no match for Russia. He hoped, therefore, for the 
assistance of France and England; Austria, he was convinced, would 
never dare take up arms against the Czar—she would verify the trath of 
the fable of the wolf and the lamb; but notwithstanding these Os 
tages, so strongly was the Porte impressed with the conviction that 
Russia was at Jength come to claim what she called the key of her house, 
that the Ottoman nation would resist to the last, and if they were destined 
nerish, would do so with honour. 
5 PT entioned to M. Drouyn de Lhuys my having had this conversation 
with Namik Pasha, and he said that he was glad of it, for that he himself 
had held similar language to him, and. that he had more particularly 
reminded him that Europe had a double interest to attend to, the preser- 
vation of peace as well as the integrity of the Ottoman Empire ; and that 
‘f the Porte persisted in hostilities contrary to the advice of the Four 
Powers, a question would arise, which of the two interests was of para- 
mount importance. The Porte, he had told the Pasha, would also do 
well to recollect that it had not always been in her power to foree Lurope 
to take her part, and that every war in which she had been engaged w ith 
Russia had ended disastrously for her, and in the acquirement by Russia 
of some new right, and some further portion of the Ottoman territory.

their advice, 1 had hoped to make head, if possible, against the prevailing 
tendencies, It appears, however, that the leading: Ministers have taken

arrangement, by means of a note addressed to the Russian Cabinet, and 
other tneidents or other suggestions are necessary to overcome the existing 
obstacles to a pacific settlement, ;

M. E. Pisani to Lord Stratford de Redcliffe. 


My Lord, Pera, November 20, 1853. 


HAVING thoroughly and without reserve explained to Reshid Pasha 
your Excelleney’s instruction of this day’s date, his Highness re Hie pos 
the speech pronounced by the Sultan, in answer to the Wrene ant aS- 
sador, was drawn up NY himself (Reshid Pasha), and by intraducing 
“that at present every kind of arrangement 18 inadmissible, without a 
total abandonment of the pretensions put forward by Russia,” he ex: 
sressed the resolution of his principal colleagues, and his: Sovereign's. 
Vhat he means by the pretensions of Russia, is “ the demand the 
Emperor to interfere in the religious matters of the Greek Church and tts 
clergy.” : 

With respect to the memorandum, Reshid Pasha repeated again sunt 
it would be a mere paper of remarks, without any formality or officia 
r cter. . 

Se echid Pasha appears to be most certain that the note will not be 
accepted, even with alterations: and he cannot induce his Sovereign to 
accept it without acting against his conscience, and without endangering 
the independence of his country. ‘The Porte wishes for peace, ndded he, 
on ohaltien that Russia will abandon all her former demands, and 
evacuate immediately the Principalities. Should your Iexcellency think 
that he (Reshid Pasha) is an obstacle to the success of the new proposi- 
tion, vou have but to express the wish, and you will find him most wi lin 
to tender his resignation at once. Perhaps, added he, his suceessor wl 
take another view of the matter, 

With reference to the want of consideration manifested towards Her 
Majesty’s Government and your Lordship on this occasion, Reshid avi 
protests against such a charge, and begs to observe that none of the 
Turkish Ministers ever evinced so much respect, deference, and considera- 
tion, both towards your Government and yourself in particular, 

This is word for word what Reshid Pasha told me to be reported to 
your Lordship. irasaten 

(Signed) E. PISANI.

Inclosure | in No. 426. 


Speeck addressed to the Sullan by Lord Stratford de Redeliffe. 


IN presenting to your Imperial Majesty the admiral and captains of the 
squadron which my gracious Sovereign has sent at your Majesty’s request, 
and in concert with the Emperor of the French, Her Majesty's powerful 
ally, to protect the rights and independence of this friendly Empire, | perform 
a duty honourable and gratifying alike to them and to me. 

Their presence here at so extraordinary a juncture shows how wisely 
your Majesty, and your Majesty's Government, have appreciated the driend- 
ship, and relied upon the sympathies of the British nation. 

Such binding and generous sentiments derive no small accession from 
the just and enlightened benevolence displayed in your Majesty's administra- 
tive poliev. Tt is not only to the successful maintenance of a great European 
principle, that the British Government look for the reward of any sacrifice 
which they may have to make in contributing to the protection of Turkey 


from unprovoked aggression, They look with equal steadiness to the 
prosperity and strength which your Majesty could not fail to realize through- 
out your extensive dominions by carrying into effect a system of improve- 


ment, complete though gradual, towards all classes and interests of your 
Majesty's subjects. 


Sull, their unrelinguished hope, and the more immediate aim of their 
effective concurrence, is peace ; 


hot, indeed, an illusive or precarious peace, 
but one which, by simple means, would fix on safe and honourable grounds, 
Without injustice to any other Power, the rights of your Majesty's sovereignty 
and the independence of your Majesty's Enipire. 
To obtain such a peace at the earliest practicable moment is always, | 
Must presume, the anxious desire of your Majesty, as it is the point most 
earnestly recommended by your Majesty’s allies. [should be happy to learn 
that it is also an object duly appreciated, 


at and strenuously promoted, in a 
spirit of continued moderation by your Majesty's Ministers,

Aprés tout ce que se passe, la sécurité que le Gouvernement Ottoman

sur le méme pied que celle de Empire Russe, et l'un et autre étant

a cet égard renfermeraient le sens que le Gouvernement Russe pourrait 
se méler des affaires de la Turquie, mais que par générosité il ne le 
fera pas. 

Auparavant, les assurances qu'on demandait de la Russie se bornaient 
A ceci, savoir: que les Russes ne se méleraient point des affaires religicuses 
Grecques; mais comme les assurances en contestation ont été mises de 
edté, ce point n'a plus d’objet. 

Quoiqu'il en seit, ce que la Sublime Porte désire principalement c'est 
la conclusion, entre elle et les grands Puissances, d'un nouveau Traité 
qui compléte celui de an 1841, relativement aux Détroiis, C’est JA une 
mesure que la Sublime Porte demande et sollicite de ses alliés, parceque le 
nouveau Traité mettrale comble a la parfaite sécurité qui sera commune a 
toutes les Parties par rapport aux T'raités généraux existants avee les 
Puissances; seul moyen de garantie pour la Sublime Porte a I'égard de la 
Valachie et de Moldavie, soit 4 d'autres ézards. 

L‘opinion que le Gouvernement Ottoman pense A entrainer l'Angleterre 
et la France dans la guerre, est inadmissible. Personne n'a le pouvoir de 
faire tenir 4 ces deux Grandes Puissances une conduite contraire A leur 
maniére de voir et a leur volonté; voili ce qu'il yade bien certain, Seule- 
ment, comme ces deux Hautes Puissances ont vu dés le début de la ques- 
tion que la Porte a raison et la Russie tort, et que, euidée par les sentiments 
de cette justice qui les caractérise, elles se sont mises dans l'attitude de 
donner des secours 4 la Sublime Porte, moralement et matéricllement, et 
cela dans le double but de la préserver de tout préjudice, et de maintenir 
la balance politique, la Sublime Porte espére avee raison que cette position 
bienveillante se maintiendra jusqu’d Ja conclusion de la question, et que 
ees deux Puissances, les plus fortes du monde, et ces deux nations géné. 
reuses, continueront toujours de secourir la partic injustement traitée, 

La Sublime Porte se voit dans Vobligation de déclarer de nouveau a la 
fin de ce mémoire, ce qui suits aprés tant de faits qui ont eu lieu, non pas 
donner a la Russie, dans quelque forme que ce soit, des assurances relatives 
dla question des priviléges reigicux, mais méme faire mention de cette 
question, en passant, c'est lui donner du relief, et, en quelque facon, servir 
ses intéréts, et, au contraire, sacrifier la dignité de la Sublime Porte. 

Comme il sera de toute impossibilité dla Sublime Porte d’écrire un 
seul mot concernant les priviléges religieux des Grees, ni dans la note, ni 
dans le ‘Traité, ni enfin dans un papier queleonque, et que ses bonnes 
dispositions & conclure la paix sont tout-A-fait subordonnées A la suppres- 
sion compléte du mot ‘privilége,” quelques propositions qu'on puisse lui 
faire ayant trait i des priviléges, seront rejetées. Et comme aussi de

any proposition invested with the badge of their old inferionty towards 


Russia, and calculated to disappoint the hopes of the nation, and with the 
averthrow of their popularity, to expose diem to most serious embarrass- 
ments, 

It may be alleged with truth, and I have striven to impress the truth in 
every form of language on their minds, that however natural such sentiments 
may be, their indulgence on the present occasion is neither just, nor wise, nor 
humane, seeing that the original difference can now be settled on safe and 
honourable grounds with every moral and political advantage on the Sultan's 
side, while an unnecessary continuance of hostilities would involve the most 
perilous hazards, the most exhausting sacrifices, a vast effusion of blood, and, 
more than possibly, the horrors of a general war. 

Unfortunately, the motives to forbearance are thrown into the shade by 
the dazzling illusions of hope, and passion is in league with occasion to merge 
all fears of danger and all considerations of prudence in a wild, though 
attractive speculation, difficult, at best, ta realize, and of which even the 
accomplishment would not be unattended with formidable drawbacks. 

L question whether at all times Reshid himself is entirely free from these 
delusive influences, though, todo justice both to him and to his colleagues, 
they still profess a willingness to seek no further advantaye from war than a 
Pee Aa of Russia's religious pretensions, and of the notes prepared 
toembody them, In their hearts they may aspire to arrangements calculated 

to secure them from future disturbance, and they would gladly put forward 
claims to a new disposition in the Provinces, to the recognition of Cireassian 
independence, and to the reimbursement of their military expenses. But 
deference to the advice of their-allies would prevail with them to forego such 
notions, and their cooler aspirations would, I think, be satisfied witha renewal 
in clear and comprehensive terms of the formal declarations and Treaties 
already existing in favour of the Porte, What they never cease to insist 
upon isaclear and unquestionable deliverance from Russian interference 
applied to spiritual matters. They are persuaded that silence would be the 
best and safest form of accomplishing that purpose, and they are now bent 
upon excluding every kind of note, however carefully expressed, as liable to 
offend their own people, and to afford a dangerous opening for what they 
presume to be the real designs of Russia, 

This apprehension ts, | fear, but too well justified by the late proceed- 
ings of the Russian Cabinet, and after so many sacrifices forced upon Turkey 
by that Power, it is but fuir that the Porte should be secured from further 
molestation on the same score, not only virtually, but ina form and manner 
calculated to leave no room for mistake upon the subject either here or 
elsewhere. . 

Should the Emperor of Russia, acting in the spirit of his new manifesto, 
aller giving the lie publicly to his neighbour, and supporting by force of arms 
his usurpation in the Principalities, decline a form of arrangement accepted 
by the Porte, and recommended by her allies, your Lordship would probably 
agree with the Ottoman Ministers in thinking that.a wider range would then 
be opened for diplomatic views, as well as for military operations. 

Most sincerely do I deprecate the occurrence of any such case, and no 
exertion will be wanting on my part, under the guidance of your Lordship's 
instructions, to dissuade the Porte from wantonly bringing on a necessity of 
the kind. But should itso happen that Russia herself continues to be the 
obstacle to a pacific arrangement, the interests of international security, no 
less than those of Turkish independence, will probably be found to require 
exertions and remedies little short of those which the more sanguine Maho- 
medaus already contemplate, 

I have, &e,

Lord Stratford de Redcliffe to Vice-Admiral Dundas, 
Sir, Constantinople, November 11, 1853. 
THE French Ambassador agrees with me in thinking it desirable, the 
squadrons being now united here, that measures should be forthwith taken 
for visiting Bourgas, Varna, and other places on the European coast of the 
Black Sea between the mouths of the Danube and the entrance of the 
Bosphorus. 

In requesting that you will communicate with the French Admiral 
in order to direct the performance of this service in concert with him, I have 
to inform you that according to official advices received from Sulina under 
date of the Sth instant, “four large Russian Government steamers” had 
arrived there and were “lying at anchor in the roads outside the bar.” It 
is added in Mr. Lloyd’s report that “a large Russian steamer” had also 
arrived there, and left again after discharging a cargo of cannon and ammu- 
nition, and that a small steamer and a viin-boat were still there. 

l infer from the same report that British commercial shipping is exposed 
to much embarrassment, danger, and loss, fram the want of water at the bar 
of the Sulina passage, and you will be the best judge whether any vessels 
sent in that direction can be instructed, as I hope, to assist them, without 
prejudice to the more urgent necessities of Her Majesty's service. 

Despatches from Varna of the Gth instant state that on that day a large 
steamer, supposed to be Russian, had looked into the harbour, and that two 
others had been seen in the offing. 

I mention these circumstances in order to assist your judgment as to the 
rank and force of the vessels, English and French, which it may be advisable 
to send out on this occasion, 

You are aware that Her Majesty's Government are anxious to renvain at 
peace with Russia, and that the employment of foree, except for the pro- 
tection of any Turkish territory attacked, or threatened with a direct attack, 
by Russia, would involve the commanding officer in a most serious respon- 
sibility. 

In conelusion, IT have to request that you will give directions for the 
conveyance hither of Her Majesty's Consuls at Bucharest and Jassy on board 
any vessel that you may select to receive them at Varna, together with their 
respective families and attendants, 

They were to proceed to Varna under instructious from me. 

I have, &e. 
(Signed) STRATFORD DE KEDCLIFFE,

Inclosure | in No. 433. 
The Earl of Westmorland to Lord Stratford de Redcliffe. 


My Lord, Vienna, December 5, 1890, 

MY colleagues, the Members of the Conference assembled here, under 
the instructions of our respective Governments, having, together with myself, 
afixed our simnatures to the note which we have been directed to address 
to his Excellency Reshid Pasha, have requested me to be their organ in 
placing in your Lordships hands, as the senior Ambassador at the Court of 

is Imperial Majesty the Sultan, the original ducuments. 

My colleagues, Count Buol, Count Arnim, and Baron Bourqueney, 
desire that the mode in which this note should be submitted to his Execel- 
lency Reshid Pasha should be left to be decided by you, in concurrence with 
your Lordship’s colleagues. They would, however, suggest for your consi- 
deration, whether, with the view of giving all the importance to this docu- 
ment which, as emanating from the Governments af the Four Powers it is 
calculated to command, it might not be advisable to ask, in conjunction with 
your colleagues, an audience of his Excellency, when your Lordship might 
place the note in his hands, and when they might, together with you, explain 
the abjects of the identical instructions, with reference to this note, which 
each Representative will have received from his Government, 

It is the intention cf the Conference, that your Lordship’s expecience 
and the high consideration you command should be resorted to in the delibe- 
ration which will take place between your Lordship and your colleagues as 
to the most advisable method to be adopted in carrying this commission 
Into execulion. 

[have ouly to add, that T feel great satisfaction in being the channel 
though which this communication is made to your Lordship, and in forward. 
ing to you this important document. 

I have, &e. 
(Signed) WESTMORLAND.

My Lord, St. Petersburgh, December 1, 1852. 

MY Freneh colleague informs me that at his last interview with the 
Chancellor, it appeared to be his Excellency’s object to make out that there 
was some difterence of opinion between the Enylish and French Govern- 
ments, the latter not showing the same disapprobation of Russian acts as 
Her Majesty's Goverment had done. 

The Marquis de Castelbajac represents himself to have stated that there 
were no grounds for such a suspicion, that owing to the circumstance of a 
weekly messenger being sent to the Englisli Mission, Her Majesty’s Minister 
was occasionally a few days inadvanee of him, but that the accordance of 
views between the two countrics was such, that he was quite ready to con- 
sider an English instruction as addressed to himself. E 

The Chancellor had observed to General de Castelbajac as he did to me, 
“ Qu'il fallait pesernn peu moins sur la Russie, et un peu plus sur la Turquie, 
si l'on cherche une solution amicable.” 

On two points the General was of opinion that the suggestion might be 
adopted with advantage. De thought it would be for the Sultan’s interests 
to discountenance active hostilities in Asia Minor: he thought that the 
evacuation of the ‘rincipalities by the Russians should not be made a pre- 
liminary condition of peace with Russia, however much desired, Should 
the point be insisted upon, he was convinced that it would be tantamount to 
a declaration of war on the part of England and France. 

In this respect my own opinion, as | would state to your Lordship, 

agrees with that of my French colleague: should ler Majesty's Govern. 
ment, however, nol insist upon such an evacuation as a preliminary con- 
dition, | would venture to submit that merit might be taken for the con- 
sideration thus shown for the difficulties of the Emperor's position, and that 
this very consideration might be made the ground of increased insistance 
upon Eis Majesty's acceptance of thase terms which the two Allied Cabinets 
are disposed to grant lim, 
_ talluded ina former despatch to a private letter received by General 
Castelbajac from the Freneh Minister of War, in which (as I did not state) 
there was an incidental phrase complimentary to the high character of the 
Emperor Nicholas. 

The Chancellor requested General Castelbajac to permit him to read 
this letter to His Majesty, observing that as he had been much hurt at the 
mistrust shown of his word, the letter would prove very acceptable, and 
adding, as though he were a party lo the appeal to be made to his own 
master, “Cela nous viendra peut-ttre en aide dans nos tentatives de ramener 
Sa Majeste 4 des dispositions plus favorables.”

Owing to no fault of Russia these parties have now become belligerent; 
and whilst the vight of the Emperor to endeavour to conduet the war toa 
conclusion conformable to lis. interest cannot be questioned, any act of 
hostility on the part of the Western Powers against Russia would throw 
upon them the onus of aggression, anid would leave the Emperor at liberty to 
consider himself freed from the obligation which he took upon himself by the 
declaration which preceded the war, é eae 

This, reduced toa few simple words, appears to be the meaning of the 
involved phrases, in which the momentous eventualities. now impending ar 
spoken of at St. Petersburgh." Leave us, the Russian said, six months 
avo, “in a situation in which, ifa little anormal, will enable us to negotiate a 
peace in the interests of Europe.” ‘Leave us,” they now have the appear- 
tuce of saying, “ina position which you yourselves have recomnized, and in 
which we ean negotiate with reference to our own dicnity and mlerests, 
which latter are always those of Europe,” | 

It las been observed to me lutely by several persons, that im the post 
which | oceupy | may render good service to the cause of peace by expressing 
to Her Majesty s Government full confidence in the intentions of the Russian 
Government, My answer ts always to the same effect: I shall do so very 
readily upon the first suitable oceasion; as a preliminary step, however, 
must mysell acquire that confidence which I desire to be able to express. 

Your Lordship may believe that, at a erisis like the present, It ts painful 
tome to employ the language of mistrust; but it would be In neat more 
painful to express feelings which are not mine, and to encourage expectauions 
which | consider as very likely to end in disappomtment,
