(No. 601. Confidential.) 
My Lord, St. Petershurgh, December 5, 1853. 


WHEN [| entered Count Nesselrode’s room on the Ind instant, he 
observed at once that he understood that Her Majesty's Government were 
engaged in drawing up a Treaty between Russia and Turkey. 3 

* Heine aware that this belief prevailed here, and that it had eaused con- 
siderable irritation, | replied that his Excellency lind been misinformed ; that 
as far as | was aware, twas in devising the preliminaries and basis of a 
Treaty that Her Majesty's Governinent was engaged, , 

The poimt is of the greater importance, as T cannot doubt that very 
momentous results may turn pon the pature of these preliminaries, and the 
manner in which they are brought to the Emperors knowledge. 

His Majesty can hardly fail of being aware of the imereasing difficulty 
of his position; the perception has certainly nat escaped Count Nesselrocde 8 
experienced eyes, and | have some reason for helieving that Wan opportunity 
for extricating his Government henourably frony its embarrassments should 
present itself, his Exectleney will not be backward in recommending that 
it should be turned to cecount, 

After licaring vhat Thad to say respecting the note about to he pre 
sented ta the Parte in consequence, L observed incidentally, of a suggestion 


which had been made by the Austrian Cubinet, Count esseirode questioned 
me as to the accounts received by your Lordship respecting the state of 
public fecling in ‘Turkey. re ; ; 

L did not conceal from him that great exasperation existed among the 
Turks, aud that all the influence which was pussessed by Lord Stratford de 
Redcliffe and his three colleagues would be required to induce the Porte to 
listen to peaceful counsels, 

1 added that I learned from the correspondence sent to me by your 
Lordship, tat Lord Stratford de Redcliffe pursued uninterruptedly the same 
wise and conciliatory course which he had followed throughout the negotia. 


343 


tions, and that I would take the SpROretnEY of remarking, if I might do so 

without giving offence, that if the Turks had been restrained from following 
the example set by Russia in giving a religious character to the war, it might 
be inferred that it was to the prudence of Lord Stratford's advice that this 
result was attributable. 

At the conclusion of a desultory conversation, the details of which are 
unworthy of your Lordship’s attention, the Chancellor spoke of the threaten- 
ing aspect of affairs, and made the following observation - 
{lest stir que les affaires sont trés embrouillées: néanmoins nous avons 
Uhiver devant nous pour les négociations, Selon moi done il en sortira au 
printemps, soit une paix, soit une guerre ¢pouvantable,” 

“In my opinion,” I replied, * the decision upon this point will be taken 
long before the arrival of spring.” 

Count Nesselrode desired to know upon what circumstances my opinion 
was formed. 

_ * Beeause,” [ rejoimed, “ negotiations have been carried on so long and 
so ineffectually, that they are now regarded with mistrust, and because the 
uncertainty which continues to hang over affairs is so injurious to interests of 
every kind, that all classes unite in desiring a prompt solution by whatever 
means it is to be obtained.” | 

I would venture to remark to your Lordship, that in my opinion there 
are many considerations which render it desirable that the idea of Russia 
being allowed to gain time by protracted negotiation should be discoun- 
tenanced by every possible means, 

Among these not the least important is the necessity which exists fur not 
permitting that Russia should have the means of having a powerful force at 
ae 8 ne noun when a large portion of Her Majesty’s ships are engaged in 

In the event of war becoming unavoidable, it is to be hoped that an 
operations which may become necessary in the Black Sea wiil be concluded 
before the breaking up of the ice in the Gulf of Finland, so that by the time 
the Northern fleet will be able to quit Sveaborg and Cronstadt, they may 
find the whole of Her Majesty's disposable naval forces in their close heigh- 
bourhood. 

I have, &c.

Sir G. H. Seymour to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received December 12.) 


(No. 698. Confidential.) 


My Lord, St. Petersburgh, December 5, 1853. 

WHEN I saw Count Nesselrode on the 2nd instant, he was very eager 
to learn from me what would be the position of neutrals in the event of war 
breaking out. 

I begged to assure his Excellency that I had received no communication 
from your Lordship with regard to the eventualities to which he alluded. 

ven if I had not, Count Nesselrode concluded that I had formed some 
opinion upon the subject, and he should be glad to hear what my unofficial 
opinion was as to the facilities which neutrals trading here would enjoy 
during a war between Russia and England. 

I begged to state my belief that there would be no trading and no 
neutrals, 

Count Nesselrode did not quite apprehend my meaning; Lord Clarendon 
had expressed an opinion unfavourable to the old practice of embargoes; it 
was therefore to be inferred that Her Majesty's Government were of opinion 
that the evils of war ought not be increased by the further evils of an inter- 
ference with general commerce. 

The case, L replied, M. le Comte, appears to me to stand thus :—motives 
of humanity render the English Government desirous that war should fall as 
little heavily as possible upon individuals, but those same motives will make 
the Government anxious to brine any war which they may undertake to the 
speediest possible conclusion. We learned this from the Duke of Wellington. 
He taught us to avoid all wars as long as possible, but when we engage in 
them to push them with all possible activity, Russia is a very large country, 
great parts of which are wholly inaccessible. As regards the coast it is not 
quite the same thing; and, as you ask my private opinion, I will not conceal 
from you that a declaration of war is likely to be speedily followed by the 
disappearance of trade, neutrals, and commercial movements of all sorts from 
your ports: blockades offer great facilities for weakening the resources of a 
country, and I think it may be assumed that, in the event of hostilities break- 
ing out, very effectual blockades would be established. 

Count Nesselrode said that it could hardly escape the attention of Her 
Majesty's Government, that the destruction of trade was a weapon which had 
two edges. 

I did not, I replied, doubt that Her Majesty's Government would make 
that reflection, but that it would be probably considered that it would not be 
the sharpest of the edges whieh would be turned towards England, 

I will request your Lordship to take note that these statements were not 
volunteered on my part; explanations were pressingly asked of me by the 
Chancellor, and i are his inquiries without reserve and without 
excitement. 

The whole conversation, indeed, although upon a very trying subject, 
passed in so perfectly amicable a manner, that when his Excellency apologized 
to me for having spoken upon such painful contingencies, I requested that he 
would offer no excuses, observing to him at the same time that the arrange- 
ment of testamentary dispositions could not have the effect of hastening 
dissolution. 

I have, &c. 


(Signed) G, H. SEYMOUR.

My Lord, Berlin, December 7, 1853. 

_ BARON MANTEUFFEL informed me confidentially this day, that he 
had instructed Count Arnim to propose to Count Buol some action in concert 
with Austria, to move the Emperor of Russia to adopt the pacificatory views 
of the Four Powers in their present endeavours to bring abouta reconciliation 
with Turkey, . 

His Excellency conceives that some movement on the part of the great 
German Powers may have some effect in disposing the Emperor Nicholas to 
form a due appreciation of his position, and to lend his efforts to the attempts 
of united Europe in the cause of peace, 

His Excellency was not prepared to say What nature of communication 
would be most judicious; whether a collective step on the part of Austria 
and Prussia, ora separate instruction to their respective Ministers at St. 
Petersburgh. Bit his Excellency was anxious to concert-and unite with 
auaitts in any way which she might deem advisable to attain the desired 
end, 

His Excellency also considers that he shall be 
answer which he may receive to his proposal, as to the real intentions of the 
Austrian Cabinet, and their ultimate views on the Eastern question. 

His Excellency is of opinion that, at the present moment, some good 
might be effected by the two great German Powers exercising their moral 
power and influence at St. Petersburgh, 

Being informed that his Excellency had taken this step, and feeling that, 
if acted up to in the sense reported to me by Baron Manteuffel, it could not 
have any other than a beneficial effect, 1 did not feel myself authorized to 
discourage the attempt; but I shall take every precaution in my power to 
prevent any engagement being entered into between the two Cabinets which 
may tend to fetter the free action and independence of Prussia, or which may 


enabled to judge, by the 


bind her hereafter to any course prejudicial to that pursued by the Western 
Powers, |

Lord A. Loftus to the Earl of Clarendon.—( Received December 12.) 


(No. 132, Confidential.) | 
My Lord Berlin, December 10, 1853. 

1 SAW Baron Manteuffel this evening, and in conversation I referred to 
the intentions which he had previously intimated to me (as reported in my 
despatch No, 128 of the 7th instant) of advising the King of Prugsia to 
address a letter to the Emperor of Russia, 
ie 1 stated to his Exeellency that 1 was very advisable at this moment to 

repare a salutary rece ition for the work of peace which has been lately 
Agreed to at Vienna, and to dispose the at mind to receive it in the 
- oe Jaudable spirit in which it had been framed. J 
ee eyccilency informed me that he had this very day submitted the 


o49 


project of a letter to His Majesty, and also a memoir which he had drawn up 
for General Rochow to read to Count Nesselrode. 

In both a conciliatory spirit was counselled, and the attention of the 
Emperor Nicholas specially drawn to the dangerous course he was 
pursuing. 

In the memorandum Baron Manteuffel stated that if war was to ensue, 
Austria and Prussia were both exposed to its dangerous elements, and that in 
such an eventuality Prussia would be found opposed to Russia. 

The memorandum warns the Emperor against the risks he is incurring, 
and gives him to understand that isolation will be the result of the policy he 
has adopted. 

Baron Manteuffel told me that the King had evinced some hesitation to 
adopt this letter to the Emperor, but that he hoped to overcome it. 

_ He told His Majesty that the Emperor of Austria had written to the 
Emperor Nicholas two letters in the same spirit, and that it did not become 
him to hold back. 

[ strengthened Baron Manteuffel in this opinion, stating that His Majesty 
might hereafter reproach himself with not having exhausted all his influence 
to avert the calamities of war. 

Baron Manteuffel seems to think that there isa somewhat more con- 
ciliatory disposition at St. Petersburgh, and is evidently of opinion that the 
Emperor will appoint a Plenipotentiary to the Conference, if Turkey will do 
the same, 

Baron Budberg, in conversation with him this evening, said in rather 
an unguarded moment, that of all places he hoped that Vienna would not he 
selected as the seat of the Conference; to which Baron Manteuffel replied 
that this was a point of minor importance, and cited Hermanstadt as being 
nearer the seat of war. 

[ have, &e. 
(Signed) AUGUSTUS LOFTUS.

My Lord, Vienna, December 6b, 185d. 

THE Conference assembled yesterday at Count Buol'r, according to

No, 436. 

Count Buol anounced that the documents which we were to sign had 
heen prepared, and that he had directed legitimatized copies of them to be 
made, which would be delivered to each of the Representatives. 

He then proceeded to read the note which was to be addressed by the 
Conference to Reshid Pasha, as also the Protocol which was to be signed by 
the Members of the Conference. 

These documents having been found to be in accordance with the copies 
which bad been transmitted to us by our respective Governments, were signed 
by Count Buol, Baron Bourqueney, Count Arnim, and myself, and the note 
sAdiessed to Reshid Pasha was placed in my hands for transmission to Lord 
Stratford de Redeliffe, according to the arrangement which | have already 
announced to your Lordship in my despatch above referred to, It was settled 
that the Protocol should be placed in the keeping of Count Buol as presiding 
over the Conference, and that it should for the present be considered as 
confidential, 

Count Buol then read the instructions which he had drawn up for the 
vuidance of the Internuneio, and which were found to be identical in substance 
with those which had been addressed by our Governments to M,. de Bour- 
queney and to myself. 

Count Arnim also read the instructions he was charged by his Govern- 
ment to forward to M. de Wildenbruch, which although somewhat different 
in language, were considered as identical in meaning.

of the Sultan, by their adherence to the measure now proposed, to give effect

If any one else than Count Hatzfeldt lad told me that M. Drouyn de 
Lhuy’s language had abounded in this sense, I should have conceived, con- 
sidering what has since taken place, that there must have been some misunder- 
standing of the French Minister's words ; but s0 over scrupulous is Count 
Hatzfeldt, if such an expression can be used in regard to truth, when he has 
a statement to make, that I am sure he reports correctly when he pays that 
M. Drouyn de Lhuys admitted the prudence and justice of his remarks, and 
promised to pay attention to them. 

Nevertheless the result has been the article in the “ Moniteur’” alluded 
to above, and a circular to all French diplomatic agents couched in the same 
language. 

It was natural that Count Hatzfeldt, after reading the former, should 
reproach M, Drouyn de Lhuys with this infirmity of purpose; for he could 
not suppose, he said, that there could be in so short a time any change in 
his opinion, and he must, therefore, attribute the article in the ** Moniteur” 
to some other pen than that of the foreign department. 

M. Drouyn de Lhuys appears to have defended himself but feebly, and 
to have said that, seeing that there was a strong wish elsewhere that an article 
of the kind should be written, he had not thought it his duty to oppose it; 
and that there was nothing ta the article that was not perfectly true. 

T should add that Count Hatzfeldt ‘nformed me that he had acted in this 
matter without instructions from his Government, and that he had been 
careful to state as much to M. Drouyn de Lhuys. 

I have myself expressed to M. Drouyn de Lhuys regret at the publi- 
cation of the article, as 1 feared that it might indispose Austria to continue 
in the course into which we had with so much trouble induced her to engage. 
He did not enter into the subject at much length, but confined himself to 
remarking. that while all the public papers of Europe were commenting upon 
the proceedings of the Vienna Conference, it was impooriD's for the French 
Government to remain silent. I observed that it would have been better to 
have stated the case in-a few lines, and to have avoided referring in such clear 
lancuage to the isolated position in which the united action of the Four 
Powers had placed Russia. He did not gainsay this opinion. 

T have, &e. 
(Signed) COWLEY.

Lord Cowley to the Earl of Clarendon. —( Received December 13.) 


(No, 946.) 
My Lord, Pavis, December 12, 1853. 

| SAW M. Drouyn de Lhuys for a few moments this afternoon, when 
he informed me he had spoken with the Emperor this morning, on the subject 
of the disastrous intelligence received esterday from Constantinople. He 
need not add, be said, that he had foun His Majesty preoccupied with this 
untoward news. 

Both the Emperor and his Minister are of opinion that the instructions 
sent to the Ambassadors and Admirals would have justified them in giving 
material support to the Turkish squadron, had any French or English vessels 
been near cnough to do so, At this distance from the seene of action they 
do not see what fresh instructions can be sent, and they opine that, at all 
events, nothing can be done until accounts are received from Constantinople, 
giving more ample details of the affair than those which we now possess, 

I have, &c. 
(Signed) COWLEY.

No, 472. 
Lord Cowley to the Earl of Clarendon,—( Received December 16.) 


(No. 953.) 
My Lord, Paris, December 15, 1853. 


M. DROUYN DE LHUYS read to me yesterday the draft of a despatch 
which he proposed to address to General Baraguay d'Hilliers, with reference to 
the late event in the Black Sea. The despatch, he added, would not be sent to 
Constantinople until it had received the approval of Her Majesty's Government, 
for which purpose a copy had been transmitted to Count Walewski. It is not 
necessary, therefore, for me to go into its contents. 

M. Drouyn de Lhuys read to me at the same time a des atch which he 
had received from Count Walewski, recounting a conversation held with your 
Lordship in consequence of the desire expressed by the French Government to 
bind Austria in some formal act to a repetition of the promise which Count Buol 
had made, both to M. de Bourqueney and to Lord Westmorland, to use the 
same pressing language at St. Petersburgh in order to obtain the consent of the 
Russian Government to treat with the Porte under the mediation of the Four 
Powers, as he was desirous to see employed at the Porte, to ensure the consent 
ot the latter to treat with Russia. Count Walewski represents your Lordship to 
have told him that you had desired Lord Westmorland to tuke note (prendre 
acte) of Count Buol’s words, but that you objected to the signature of a Protocol 
binding the Four Powers to make use of comminatory language towards either 
of the belligerent Powers which might resist their late peoposal; that such 
language ought not to be held until it was to be followed, if necessary, by acts, 
and that although it might with justice be addressed to Russia, it could not be 
employed towards the Ottoman Government, who were only resisting an act of 
aggression. Count Walewski recounts further the arguments of which he made 
use to induce your Lordship to change your opinion, and he adds that you 
expressed your willingness to enter upon the subject with him on a future ocea- 
sion, should the French Government after hearing your objections persist in the 
proposal which he had been directed to make, 

M. Drouyn de Lhuys informed me this afternoon that notwithstanding the 
objections which your Lordship had stated to Count Walewski, lie was desirous 
that Count Buol’s words should, if possible, be consigned toa Protocol ; that 
he thought that the sense of the yard “eomminatoire ' was not clearly under- 
stood. that it could not well be translated by the English word “ threatening.” 
and that the French Government intended to admonish rather than to threaten. 
Vasked him whether some other word or phrase could not be substituted for 
 comminatoire,” such as * frank and energetic,” and he did not seem to object. 
although he gave me no positive answer,

No. 479. 
Lord Cowley to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Recetved December 18.) 


(No, 957.) 
My Lord, Paris, December 16, 189d. 

LATE yesterday afternoon M. Drouyn de Lhuys made me acquainted with 
the outline of a proposition, to be laid before your Lordship this morning by 
Count Walewski in the name of the Imperial Government, which has for its 
object to prevent the repetition of such sanguinary seenes as that lately enueted 
at Sinope, and to make the Iussian Government understand that Franee and 
England are determined to hold possession of the Black Sea as an equivalent for 
the Russian occupation of the Danubian Provinces. This afternoon his Excel- 
leney read to me the despatch on this subject, addressed to Count Walewsli for 
communication to your Lordship, Whatever Her Majesty's Government may 
think of the proposition itself, they will do justice to the clearness and precision 
with which M. Broun de Lhuys has placed it before them. 

Supposing, then, your Lordship to be in possession of this document, ! 
abstain from offering any analysis of its contents, and propose confining myself 
to a statement of the arguments put forward by M. Drouyn de Lhuys m a 
lengthened conversation in support of the plan of action which he reeommends. 

He first examined the abstract right of France and England to interfere in 
the summary manner which he proposed. He argued that, it being both their 
interest and their duty to protect the Turkish territory from all aggressive 
attacks on the part of Russia, motives of humanity should impel them to 
prevent the repetition of such # carnage as must haye accompanied the destruc- 
tion of the Turkish flotilla at Sinope. They had not, unfortunately, the means 
(he observed) of enforcing a suspension of hostilities, cither upon the Danube or 
in Asia Minor; but they could enforce it in the Black Sea, and the interests of 

eace and humanity not only gaye them the right, but enjoined them so to do, 
f the two Governments had not sent their fleets into the Black Sea at an carher 
period, it was because they confided in the voluntary assurances of Russia not to 
prosecute the war by offensive operations, and they were unwilling to meet so 
laudable » declaration by any act of theirs which could imply distrust, or which 
might give the Russian Government an excuse for taking a less conciliatory 
course. Now, however, that Russia had thrown off the mask, he saw ne certain 
means of controlling her action in the Black Sea, but by sweeping that sea of 
the Russian flag. 

That the two Powers were strong enough to enforce their will in this 
respect, M. de Lhuys would he ashamed to doubt, The Russian fleet must 
either remain shut up in Sebostupol, or expose itself to certain destruction if 1 
attempted to resist, 

But there were other considerations of hardly less importance which 
M. Drouyn de Lhuys said must be taken into account in the consideration of his 
proposition, He alluded to the material, moral, and commercial consequences 
by which it must be followed, should the short-sightedness of Russia give nny 
permanence to its execution, 

lst. As to the material effect which would be produced, Besides the forced 
suspension of hostilities between Turkey and Russia within the limits of the 
Black Sea, the latter would find it very difficult, if not impossible, to ndvance 
from the Principalities on Constantinople, unless. slie had her sea COMMmMUnicE= 
tions with Odessa and Sebastopol assured; she would be equally unable to 
transport reinforcements, arms, ummiunition, or provisions for the use of the 


4h 


305 


troops engaged on the Asiatic coast. On the other hand, the various resources 
af water communication would remain open to the Turks. 

Snd. As to the moral effect. At this moment the Russian flag of war was 
paramount inthe Black Sea. In fact, that sea was little better than a Russian 
lake. ‘The races which inhabited its shores believed probably that there was no 
navy which could compete with that of Russia, or dispute her maritime pre- 
ponderance, They would now be taught that there were other nations with 
superior naval means at their disposal, ready to exert them for the protection of 
the oppressed. ‘They would be encouraged to nse against thew hereditary 
enemies, and thus render the position of the latter far more perilous, 

rd. With respect to commercial effects. Vessels from the combined 
fleets would visit every nook and corner of the Black Sea; would sound its 
coasts and examine its harbours and roadsteads, A more intimate knowledge 
would thus be gained of the races which people its shores; of their wants ; of 
their means? and of the productions of the countries which they inhabit. 
Foundations might thus be laid for commercial intercourse of great future 
value. 

It was perhaps natural that in addressing the agent of a Government whose 
approbation of his plan M. Drouyn de Lhuys was auxious to secure, he should 
endeavour to show that the individual and general interests of that Government 
equally invited them to adhere to it, He necordingly took great credit for the 
disinterestedness of the French Government in proposing a scheme of action 
which must be-of such immense advantage to British interests in Asia, by 
crippling the means of Russia; imposing on the vacillating policy of Persia; 
and thus giving greater security to Her Majesty's pessessions in India ; and he 
added that he could not conecive that Her Majesty's Government would refuse 
their consent toa plan which would be productive of such benefit to them, 

I wis not enetined, with a question of such pressing necessity under my 
eyes, to enter into a discussion foreign to the purpose. I allowed, therefore, 
M. Drouyn de Lhuys’ observations to pass unnoticed, reserving to myself to 
recur to this exaugerated view of bis whenever a fit opportunity occurs, 

Passing from the superior claims which M. Drouyn de Lhuys supposed his 
proposition must have to the sympathy of the Lritish Government and nation, 
he dwelt with some emphasis on the consequences which it must produce on the 
volicy of Austria, Tussia, he argued, excluded from the Black Sea, and humi- 

iated in the eves of those wild tribes who had thought her invulnerable, would 
seck compensation elsewhere, and would try te eounterbalanee her maritime 
inferiority in the Black Sea by extending her conquests on land, ‘The European 
provinces of Turkey would become the object of her ambition: Servi, Bosnia, 
ind Montenegro would be menaced, and it would be impossible that Austria 
should not then attach herself’ body and soul to the cause for which France and 
England were striving, 

T have left to the lust, though it is almost the first in importance, the novel 
but ingenious iden of holding exclusive possession of the Black. Sea by the 
combined flects as an equivalent for the continued ageressive occupation of the 
Principilities by Russia; in other words, of making the reappearance of the 
Russian divin those waters depend on the Russian army recrassing the Pruth. 
This idea is but faintly indicated in M. Drouyn de Lhuys’ despatch to ‘Count 
Walewsaki, but it is in fact the essence of his proposition. Itis in the opinion 
of the French Government the vindieation of the honour of the French and 
Boglish flags, somewhat compromised by the unremitting eforts of their Govern- 
ments to solve the Eastern question without eompromising the peace of Europe. 
Ji is the tardy but merited punishment of Russiin presumption. It will be a 
heavier blow to the pride and prestige of the Caar than an extension of his 
present iniquitous nggression cat counterbalanee, 

On this latter point, [have thought it my duty to caution M. Drouyn de 
Lliuys against plucing the occupation of the Danubian Provinces by Russia, and 
the presence of the combined tleets in the Black Sea, on the same footing of 
jeregularity. ‘lo do so would be to allow that the Euxine was a “ mare 
clausum,” and would be a dangerous admission to make, True, our late 
Treutics with the Porte eflectually shut the Black Sea to our ships of war in 
time of peace; but the exclusion was the effect and not the stipulation of o 
Vreaty; and it behoved us, in any negotiation on this matter, to keep this 
distinction in view,

2nd. Whether they proposed making any communications on the subject to 
the Austrian and Prussian Governments. 

M. Drouyn de Lhuys will answer Count Walewski, that for the present 
it would be perhaps advisable to interdict all maritime operations on the part of 
the Turks against the Russian territory ; that this would be more in accordance 
with the humane intentions of the two Governments put forward in lis proposi- 
tion; and would perhaps give them greater authority in urging the adoption of 
analogous measures by land on Austria and Prussia; but he is of opinion that no 
engazement should be taken on the matter, and that while a summary declara- 
tion should be made to Russia that the Black Sea is shut to her, the action of 
the Turkish fleet shoul! be regulated by a friendly understanding between the 
Ainbassadors and the Porte, 

With regard to making a communication to the Austrian and Prussian 
Governments, M, Drouyn de Lhuys conceives that it will be impolitic to consult 
those Governments respecting the operations of the fleets, but that whenever 
France and Kngland have agread on the measures which are to be taken, it will 
be proper to make Austria and Prussia acquainted with their intentions.

(No. 140. Confidential.) 


My Lord, Berlin, December 15, 1853, 

THE Chevalier Bunsen has written to Baron Manteuffel saying that your 
Lordship had mentioned having heard from an undoubted source that the King 
of Prussia had lately written a private letter to the Emperor of Rnssia explana- 
tory of the political position which Prussia had assumed on the Oriental 
question. 

Baron Manteutfel told me that on addressing to the King an inquiry on 
this subject, His Majesty said that he had written to the Emperor, and that he 
had quite forgotten to show him a copy of the letter which His Majesty then 
placed in his hands. . 

Baron Manteutfel expressed lis regret that His Majesty had written this 
letter; but he assured me that it did not contain anything of that positive nature 
which apparently had been reported to your Lordship. 

Baron Manteulfel, on my referring to the conversation I had with his 
Excellency as reported in my despatch No, 128 of the 7th instant, stated that at 
that time he had no cognisance of His Majesty having addressed any private 
communication to the Emperor. 

I inquired of his Excellency whether the King was still steady in the 
opinions he had represented to me at different periods as being entertained by 
His Majesty. 

Baron Manteuffel replied in the affirmative, saying that, that very evening 
His Majesty had impressed upon him the necessity of acting upon France 
through England, “comme c'est notre allié naturel; to which | added, ® et le 
plus sir,”

further measures whi 
} it ymirticularly adverted to by Count Buol is the manner in which 


374 


the communication is to be made to St. Petersburgh, on the receipt, which he 
searcely doubts, ofa satisfactory answer from the Porte; whether the communi- 
cations should proceed from the Ministers of the Four Powers, or from 
the Austrian Minister alone, but-supported by a subsequent communication on 
the part of his colleagues. But Count Buol also wishes to know how an unsatis- 
factory answer from the Porte is to be dealt with. 

T have to state to your Lordship in reply, that the subject has received the 
careful consideration of Her Majesty's Government, who agree with Count Buol 
that the Conference shonld, as far as is practicable, be furnished with instruc- 
tions, in order to avoid delay upon the arrival at Vienna of the answer of the 
Porte to the collective note. That answer, 45 Count Buol justly observes, is the 
property of the Conference, and can only be dealt with in the manner that may 
be unanimously agreed upon by the Four Powers. 

It is difficult to provide for the various contingencies that may arise, and 
for circumstances that cunnot be forescen ; and Her Majesty's Government, 
while endeavouring to guard against delay, are anxious that no course should 
hastily be adopted which might prove a cause for regret hereafter. 

it is only upon the following cases that Her Majesty’s Government consider 
that precise instructions can with safety be given to your Lordship : 

Should the terms proposed by the Porte be in conformity with the instruc- 
tions given to the Four Representatives at Constantinople, and such consequently 
as in the unanimous opinion of the Conference ought to be accepted by the 
Emperor ef Russia, your Lordship is instructed to agree to their being sent 
forthwith to St. Petersburgh. Should those terms, liowever, be of a character 
to render them unacceptable to Russia, your Lordehip is not authorised to agree 
to any change or modification of them. The answer of the Porte must then be 
transmitted to London for the consideration of Her Majesty's Government. 

Your Lordship will inform Count Buol that Her Majesty's Government 
would think it neither proper nor expedient to he party to any communication 
to Russia in a form different to that which was observed towards the Porte. A 
collective note was sent to Constantinople, and asiinilar document should there- 
fore be transmitted to St. Petersburgh. But as the basis of the recent comma- 
nication to the Porte was an assurance given by the Cabinet of St. P ‘tersburgh, 
‘answer to an inquiry from the Austrian Government. that the Emperor was 
ready to treat, notwithstanding the commencement of hostilities, and as Count 
Buol has suggested that he might be wuthorised lo communicate the answer of 
the Porte to the Russian Government, your Lordship is authorised to agree to a 
collective note to Count Nesselrode, stating the terms (L assume that those terms 
are unanimously adopted by the Conference) on which the Turkish Government 
is prepared to nerotiate a Treaty of Peace, and earnestly recommending, in the 
name of the Four Powers, that they should be adopted by Russia, in order to 

mit-an end to the deplorable effusion of blood and, to a state of things in the 
saat which, if further prolonged, must involve Europe ina general war, This 
note might then be placed in the hands of Count Buol by your Lordship and 
your Irench and Prussian colleagues, in the same maaner that the collective 
note to Reshid Pasha was confided to your Lordship for transmission to Her 
Majesty's Ambassador at Constantinople, upon the condition, however, that 
Count Buol shall cause it to be presented at St Petersbugh, when it will be 
supported by the Ministers of the Four Powers at that Court, in the event of any 
proceedings not bemg successful which in the meanwhile Count Buol may think 
proper to adopt for the purpose of securing the assent of the Emperor of 
UaSlit. 

Qn the other hand, should these proceedings lead to the result desived, and 
Count Buol be charged to express the willingness of the Emperor of Russia to 
agree to the terns proposed, and to send u Plenipotentiary to treat with a 
‘Turkish Plenipotentiary under the mediation of the Four Powers, no further 
demand on the part of the Conference would be necessary. Your Lordship will, 
however, clearly expliin to Count Buol that in this matter Her Mujesty’s 
Government can make no distinction betwean Wussia ant the Porte, and. that 
they can be no party to communication with the former Power except in 
conjunction with Austria, France, aid Prossia.

My Lord, Constantinople, December 5, 1853. 

COPIES of three despatches, which 1 have recently received from Her 
Majesty's Vice-Consul at Samyoon, are inclosed herewith for your Lordship’s 
information. ‘They relate, in general, to the naval operations in progress along 
the Asiatic sea-board of ‘Turkey ; and show how greatly a confirmed ascendancy 
on the part of Russia is likely to prove injurious to the interests of commerce, 
and to the Porte’s maritime establishments on that line of coast. ‘The scarcit 
of grain in Western Europe presents an additional consideration of no small 
importance, 

Your Lordship will perceive from Mr. Uiuarracino’s reports, that the danger 
to which the Turkish flotilla at Sinope was exposed had not escaped observation 
before the catastrophe. Unfortunately, our knowledge of the position was not 
obtained in time to prevent the disaster which has occurred, | have proposed 
to my French colleague a joint expression to the Porte of our opinion that an 
inquiry inta the causes of that occurrence ought to be instituted, It is probable 
that the step will be taken a5 soon as complete information arrives from the 
scene of action, Meanwhile, it is whispered that the Captain Pasha will find it 
difficult to retain his office. In case of his dismissal, a professional man will 
probably be appointed in his place.

Tidjaret.” I now beg to acquaint your Lordship that a merchant-vessel, which 
arrived here the day before yesterday with a Jerusalem flag, met the Russian 
squadron which T mentioned as eruizing in the neizhbourhood of Sinope and 
was boarded by several hoats from one of the Russian ships, and examined to see 
if there were any ammunition or Government stores on board for the Turks 
The captain of the merchant-vessel, who isa Greek, was then ordered to Zo close 
to a Russian frigate, the captain of which interrogated him about the news from 
Constantinople, the number of English and French men-of-war at anchor in 
the Bosphorus, and asked exultingly ifthe capture of two Turkish steamers by 
the Russians had been heard of at the capital. The Greek captain tells me that 
this Russian squadron is composed of seven sail of frigates and corvettes, and 
one large steamer; that the vessels appeared to form a line across the Black 
Sea, or from north to south, and commencing about fifteen miles from this coast 
so that it would be almost impossible for any ship to pass to and fro, between 
this and Constantinople, without being observed by ‘te Russians: There are 
two or three Turkish craft at Sinope laden with corn from this, the captains of 
which are afraid to proceed with their cargoes lest they should fall into the hands 
af the Russians. 

The Greek captain before mentioned told me that he was also accosted by 
a Russian corvette about 100 miles on this side of the Bosphorus, and that this 
corvette ran foul of his vessel in approaching her, and carried away her jib-boom 
and fore-topmast; the vessel in port is now minus this part of her rigging. 
These Russian cruizers will prove very prejudicial to the trade of this coast, and 
to many Constantinople merchants who have Turkish vessels laden with corn 
because the masters of these are kept in port now from fear of the Russians, 
and in two or three weeks hence they will be afraid to venture out to sea on 
aceount of the weather, so that the carzoes of corn will most probably remain on 
their way until spring. ; 

Yesterday nearly 100 horses, for the use of the Turkish army, left this for 
Trebizond and Batoorm under an escort provided by the Pasha. The horses

Lord Stratford de Redeliffe to the Earl of Clarendon,—(Received December 20.) 


(No. 372.) 
My Lord, Constantinople, December 5, 1953. 

THE despatches from Persia, which | forward to-day by the messenger 
Purdie, will inform your Lordship that Her Majesty's Chargé d’Affaires at the 
Shah's Court had found it necessary to suspend his diplomatic relations with the 
Persian Government. Your Lordship will observe that Mr. Thompson attributes 
in part to Russian influence that sell of the Government which prevailed 
against his carnest and repeated demands of reparation for the offence of which 
he had to complain. 

A day or two before Mr. ‘Thompson's correspondence reached me, L received 
from the Persian Chargé d'Affaires at this Court two communications, putting 
me in possession of notes which he had just addressed to Reshid Pasha on the 
questions of Kotoor and the Kerbela indemnity, On both subjects his language 
is sufficiently peremptory, and, unhappily, on both the claims of his Government 
ure more or less well-founded. 

On visiting Reshid Pasha immediately after my arrival in town, 1 drew his 
attention to the above-mentioned circumstances; and, expressing an appre- 
hension of some hostility on the part of Persia, made no concealment of iny 
regret at the indifference with which my repeated admonitions on the subject 
had been heretofore received, 

Qn the same alternoon an express arrived at the Porte with despatches, 
later by seven days than the date of Me, Thompson's, from the Ottoman 
Ambassador at Tehran. Copies, or rather translutions, of these despatches are 
inclosed herewith for the information of Her Majesty’s Government, | received 
the originals hefore they had been sent tothe Sultan, Your Lordship will learn 
from their contents that Russia has bribed high with promise and menace to 
obtain the concurrence of Persia in her present war against Turkey. Unfortu. 
nately it is to be feared, indeed it is all but certain, that the Russian offer has 
been accepted ; and it would seem that the Turkish Ambassador, despairing of 
any successful resistance, intended to leave his post, after going through the 
formality of ascertaining by diplomatic application the correctness of the con- 
viction which he had already uequired, that nothing could be done against the 
preponderance of Russia. 

The Porte is waiting for the Jast conclusive information from her Ambas- 
sador. I heed not point out to your Lordship the extreme gravity of the cir- 
cumstances related above, not only as affecting the Porte’s immediate interests, 
but also as bearing on those of our trade. 

It is not improbable that the courier charged with the Russian proposals to

Inclosure 2 in No. 490. 
The Persian Chargé d’ Affaires to Reshid Pasha. 


(Translation. ) 18 Sefer, 1270. (November 16, 1853.) 
YOUR Excellency is aware that it was. stipulated in Article III of the 
Treaty of Erzeroom that the Contracting Parties engaged themselves, by virtue 
of that very ‘Treaty, to abandon respectively all claims upon the territory af the 
other, and, as a corollary to that engagement, to apport officers and engineers 
from each Power for the delimitation of the frontiers, ‘The two Mussulinan 
States accordingly dispatched their respective Commissioners to the frontier, 
with the concurrence of the Commissioners of the ‘Iwo Mediating, Powers ; 
which latter Powers, moreover, decided at the same time that the duties of the 
Commissioners should be limited to tracing the frontier upon the map, and 
forwarding it to their respective Governments, and that they should act strictly 
upon the principle of the stafus quo, abstaining altogether from any interference 
or occupation, whether open or steret, as regarded respectively the tribes, 
subjects, and territories at that period actually in the possession of the other 
party. In spite of these conditions, however, Dervish Pasha, who had been 
appointed frontier Commissioner by the Ottoman Governinent, ueshcn 
upon his arrival at the frontier, without waiting for the presence of the other 
Commissioners, and before commencing the survey of the boundary, has pro- 
cosded to violate the principle of status quo by setzing and forcibly occupying the 
territory of Kotoor, a dependency of the province of Kho, and iw positive, clear, 
and indisputable possession of the Kingdom of Persia. He has there erected & 
stone slab, upon which he lias caused the following inscription to be carved t 
“The boundary of the Imperial Ottoman Empire the district of Kotoor, 
year 1265" (a.p. 1848). ae rae 
* He has also committed numerous acts of aggression and violent interference 
in the aforesaid territory, such as forming military posts with artillery, appomting 
4 Kaimakam, numbering the fumilies and heads, levying the military conserip- 
tion, raising the revenue, building numerous and strongly fortified castles, 
cuurdhouses, barracks, i ulso hospitals, mosques, storehouses, mills, and many 
other buildings of the like description. Such are among the manifold aggres- 
gions, territorial and) others, committed by the agents of the Ottoman Govern- 
ment upon the Kingdom of Persia, on its frontier. Sinec, in necordance with 
the instructions and plan of action which I received from my Government for 


Bisp: 


my guidance, the most important part of the duties of my mission consist i" 
demanding the cessation of the aggressive occupation of Kotoor, and since, on 
my first arrival upon this mission in Constantinople, | communicated in writing 
with and informed their Excellencies the Representatives of the two Courts 
residing there, in virtue of their character as mediators, to that effect; I have 
now accordingly procceded to address this official note to the Sublime Porte, 
and to demand of right and officially the discontinuance of the aggressive 
occupation of Kotoor, a positive, clear, and indisputable portion of Persian 
territory. This aggression has been committed by the agents of the Ottoman 
Government, in violation of the stalus que, of the explicit declaration of the 
Treaty, and of the rights of the tribes, before the Commissioners of the Four 
Powers had commenced the frontier survey; and if now, after the investigations 
of the Commissioners, a stop is not put to this forcible occupation, what occa- 
sion is there for any further settlement of the frontier henceforth? But, please 
God, considering the unanimity existing between the two States, | trust that 
the Porte will come to the decision of terminating its forcible occupation of the 
above district, and that your Excellency will speedily acquaint me with its 
decision to that effect. . 


Inclosure 3 in No. 490. 


The Ottoman Ambassador in Persia to Reshid Pasha. 


(Translation.) 1] Sefer, 1270, (November 12, 1853.) 

J HAVE the honour to represent, that in my report to your Excellency of 
the last of Shaval it was clearly stated, that although in all the questions which 
had hitherto arisen between this Embassy and the Persian Government, the 
greatest regurd had been shown on our side for the preservation of friendship 
between the two countries, yet in proportion as they were hard pressed by the 
opposite party, and were unable to make any head against them, the Persians 
would change their language, and accord their friendship to these latter. In 
fact, indeed, for more than a week past they have been studiously endeavouring 
to bring forward proofs of their friendly feclings, and, recognizing the force of 
the considerations relative to the Russian question which | had submitted to 
them in compliance with instructions from your Excellency, they have presented 
every appearance of sympathy with us. 

However, the Russians having held out threats on the one hand of invading 
Azerbijan with Bebman Mirza, who had been living as a refugee at Tiflis, and, 
on the other hand, prowised to march troops into Khiva, and annex Afighanistan 
to Persia, the Persians have changed their minds under these inducements; and, 
though protesting their neutrality and absence of any hostile purpose, they yet 
are again endeavouring to raise an army by recalling the soldiers whom they had 
disbanded upwards of a month ago, and this, though they have no money, no 
military stores, and no provisions; they also talk publicly of taking Kotoor. 

As I know by past experience how improbable it is to expect that the Shah 
can be diverted by advice and reflection from any design which he has once 
tuken into his head and decided upon; in order to understand, at least, of what 
pretext they are likely to avail themselves, the march of the above army towards 
the frontier will naturally cause a great deal of exeitement. In consequence of 
this | have demanded verbally and in writing the abandonment of this project, 
and an explanation of its causes; the execution of such a design without 
previous communication being unprecedented. 

_Lreceived in reply a stiff letter, in which they not only utterly deny all 
their former promises, but even omit the ordinary meaningless assurances, 

This senseless document, sent me under the name of an answer, l have the 
honour to inclose for your information, together with copies of my memorandum 
to the Grand Vizier, and of his answer. 

As Porsia is at this moment completely destitute of preparations, and would

Inclosure 6 in No. 490, 
The Ottoman Ambassador in Persia to Reshid Pasha, 


(Translation. ) November 12, 1853. 

1 HAD the honour to represent in my eleven preceding despatches that it 
had been the intention of the Shah, ever since the 2lst of Mouharem, 1269 
(November 9, 1852), to assemble troops at Sultanich; that as His Majesty 
had concerted this measure with the Representatives of the mediating Powers 
alone, without making any official communication whatever to this Embassy, I 
had made the most urgent and strong representations to the Mimsters of Russia 
and England, who had been obliged to oppose the intention of the Shah; that 
the Persian Government had then appealed to this Embassy; and that when His 
Majesty the Sultan’s permission had been obtained for proceeding to Sultanich 
the Shah, without listening to the official representations of the English and 
Russian Representatives, proceeded thither with a body of about 30,000 troops 
and followers, ‘with the intention of not remaining more than fifteen days; 
that the position and policy of the Russian Minister had changed, and that all 
his efforts for keeping the army in summer quarters had failed; that this mission 
had even gone before that of Russia; that [the Persian Government] had agreed 
to disband their troops, which were at Tehran, and to retain only 2,500 troops 
already armed at Tehran, and 20 battalions for the rest of Persia ; that the 
Imperial instructions, concerning the Russian question, had been duly commu- 
nicated to the Persian Ministers, and that | had, on each occasion, received from 
them renewed assurances of friendship. My detailed communications were 
forwarded not only by the monthly messenger of this Mission, but also by every 
intervening one sent fram the English Mission. 

After a month’s contention on the subject of a Kandahar merchant, whom 
the British Mission claimed the right to protect, and which the Perstan Govern- 
ment refused to acknowledge, a quarrel ensued between some people of the 
Mission and the police, and the Mission has broken off its relations altogether. 
As the question was protracted for several days afterwards, the Enelish 
messenger was kept two weeks after his time; but although | received your 
Highness’ four despatches of the 22nd September and of the beginning and 
10th October ten days ago, it was impossible to reply to them as early as usual, 
Other occurrences having now arisen, there is neither time nor need for replying 
to each of your Highness’ instructions. 

Since the return of the Shah from Sultanieh, His Majesty has been most 
friendly in his professions towards this Embassy. Indeed, the military Governor 
of Azerbijan, the Veziri-Nizam, a creature of Russia, having at their instigation 
prohibited the sale of provisions to Turkey, he was immediately dismissed by 
the Government. Some of the dignitaries sent once a-week on the part of the 
Shah with a civil message of inquiry to the Embassy, even broached the subject 
of renewing the permission to proceed on the pilgrimage to Kerbela, prohibited 
during the last three years, in order to remove any coldness on the part of the 
public, I have been myself active in endeavouring to promote the relations of 
concord, and on the occurrence of the question with the English Mission the 
Shah sent for me twice, and spoke to me in the greatest confidence and sincerity 


tothe purport that he intended to request of the Sublime Porte, through me, 


to settle tlie question between His Majesty and the British Mission, alter my 
friendly interposition lad been inefeetual, In short, our relations were on the 
beat possible footing.

expresses opinions almost entirely identical with those of his colleagues who looked

endangered, not only by the declared pretensions, but also by the real, yet

power, to overcome this tendency of his mind; and in order to increase my 
chances of success I have admitted fairly all the truths of the question between 
Turkey and Russia, and laboured not the less strenuously to open his eyes to the 
dangers of a war pursued on a fresh basis without the full assent and concur- 
rence of the Porte’s efficient allies. .

equal frankness on what principle, and in what modes, such proposals for peace 
might be arranged between him and me as would afford a reasonable prospect of 
acceptance as well by the General Council as by the Porte’s allies.

only chanee of success is now to be found in setting aside all the preceding

No, 496. 
Sir G. H. Seymour to the Earl of Clarendon,.—(Received December 20.) 


(No, 703. Secret and Confidential.) 


My Lord, St. Petersburgh, December 10, 1853. 

GREAT as my reluctance is to write in a manner which can hardly fail of 
inducing Her Majesty’s Government to mistrust the declarations which are made 
on behalf of the Emperor, as to the moderation and pacific nature of his 
intentions, I have no option as to conveying to vour ecdabin some intelligence 
which is singularly in opposition with those protestations. 

I hear from a person of the highest respectability, and who has peculiar 
facilities for obtaining correct intelligence, that the Government have made a 
contract for provisions, of the value of seven millions of silver roubles, which 
are to be delivered in the Principalities alter the month of May; and, secondly, 
that nine millions of roubles, of which eight millions in gold and one million in 
silver have been sent from hence to Prince Menchikoff. 

The heavy expense of even conveying this amount of silver was urged, 
but the objection was overruled, as is stated, by the Emperor himself. Prince 
Menchikotl, His Majesty said, had desired to receive money of a particular 
deseription; it should be delivered in a manner perfectly conformable to his 
suggestion. . 

The fact of these large remittances being made, acquires additional 
importance from the circumstance that Prince Menchikoff has been or ts 
to be named commander of the military and naval forces at Odessa, and in the 
Crimea. 

I have, however, no doubt that considerable portions of this money will 
be applied neither to naval or military purposes; the arts of corruption are 
at least as well understood by the Russians as those of war ; and from his long 
intercourse with Bastern people, Prince Menchikoff is skilled in the ways of 
dealing with them, 

I may take this opportunity of stating to your Lordship that I have the 
authority of a naval officer of high rank, that a large portion of the Baltic 
fleet is in a very unseaworthy state, and that the fact being known to the 
Emperor and the Grand Duke Constantine increases their wish to substitute 
screw ships of the first class for the ordinary ships-of-the-line. 

I have reason for believing that no less than twenty-five of these first-class 
screw ships are wanted for the northern and southern fleets, and that the 
machinery of six of them is already contracted for. 

I will only add, my Lord, that when I am told, as 1 am upon every 
occasion, by various of my diplomatic colleagues, that the English Government 
commits an error in not placing entire confidence in the Emperor's moderate 
intentions, | reflect that after all, that error, supposing it to be one, is shared 
by His Majesty's own officers, who generally appear to believe that a serious 
war is at hand. I reflect further, that mistrust hardly requires an excuse when 
entertained towards a Government whose late acts have been almost invariably 
in direct contradiction of their foregoing declarations. 

The history of Prince Gortchakofl’s proceedings in the Principalities, as 
contrasted with the assurances which were given upon the passage of the 
Pruth, is of itself sufficient to warrant any amount of mistrust and incredulity in 
Russian protestations, 

[have thought it right, upon the terms on which Lam with the French 
Mission, to communicate the intelligence contained in this despatch to General 
Castelbajac. 

It was not difficult to see that he attached no credit to it, and that he 
is disposed to think that the Emperor's pacific intentions may be safely counted 
upon, 

I said to General Castelbajac, “ Ayons les yeux ouverts, et gardons nous 
de faire le metier de dupes.” 

I have, &c. 
(Signed) G. H. SEYMOUR,

No. 498. 


Sir G. AH. Seymour to the Marl of Clarendon.—( Received December 20.) 
(No. 706. Confidential.) 


My Lord, St. Petersburgh, December 12, 1863. 

IT will be my endeavour to return brief but explicit answers to the queries 
which your Lordship has done me the honour of addressing to me in your 
despatch No. 800 of the 21st ultimo. 

I will begin by statmg that the Roman Catholic Church has, I think, the 
right of considering itself oppressed by the Russian Government; amongst other 
reasons, upon the main ground of the full intercourse of the priesthood with the 
mother church being interdicted, . 

For a religion the chief principle of which is unity, it follows that direct 
communication with its chief authority is a mutter of first-rate importance ; this 
description of freedom, like every other, being wanting in Russia, 

The state of the Roman Catholic Chureh in this country is that of complete 
subjection or dependence, it may be cbserved incidentally, which is shared with 
the Orthodex Greek Chureh, of which the religion of the State is an offset, 

Everything relating to the Latin Church is directed by the head of a 
department of the Ministry of the Interior, who, besides being of the Greek 
persuasion, 15 represented as being a fanatic, 

It seldom happens, as the Roman Catholie priests themselves admit, that 
Government influence, or | should rather say, Government pressure, is resorted 
to for the purpose of inducing a man to change his religion. 

The Greek Church is not proselyting by its nature, and would never inter- 
ere with the creed of any one but for political reasons, 

[ts toleration, however, is far from being extended to persons who abandon 
the Greek fnith for any other. Ifsuch a person should happen to be the father 
or mother of a family, the management of their estate is taken fram them, and, 
practically, every public career would be closed against the children, 

‘There appears, indeed, to be an occult but unceasing working ogainst 
Roman Catholicism, which is carried on principally in the following manner : 

The children born of mixed marriages, when one of the parties is Russian 
and a Greek, must belong to the Greek Church, a measure which, rigorously 
carried out, destroys Roman Catholicism in numerous families, 

Russian employes are sent into Poland; Polish employés are transplanted 
to Russia; and the children of such of these persons as contract marriages are 
brought up invariably in the Greek faith, 3 


472 


a92 


The Court of Rome asserts that, as regards itself; the Concordat. entered 
‘ato with the Russian Government in 1846 is faithfully observed, while it main- 
tains equally that its provisions are eluded unceasingly by the Imperial Govern- 
ment; much care and dextenty, however, being exhibited in keeping the 
infractions from public knowledge. 

Thus, for srutenee! the Bishop of Cherson, formerly a monk at Riga, 

although consecrated several years since, has never been able to take pees 
of his diseese. No very open opposition is made to him, but a series of fut 2 
reasons are found for preventing iis entering upon the discharge of his episcop 
duties. 
» So again with various of the bishoprics in Poland, which remain vacant 
without its being known, even to those the most concerned, whether is sae 
of things has been produced by the want of necessary presentations Dy the 
Russian Government, or by the objections entertained by the See of ome to the 
‘dividuals who have been presented by the Imperial authorities. 

Further, the churches of the Roman Catholics in the distant provinces, and 
more especially in the villages of ancient Poland, are left Oe He most 
necessary repairs, whilst those of the Greeks are kept in the dest ore er; it re 
even asserted that, if a small Greck community 15 formed 1n i village, the ehurel 
is made over to their use, the Roman Catholies being lett to perform: their

My Lord, St. Petersburgh, December 12, 1853. 

I CALLED upon Count Nesselrode on the Sth. instant, and was mainly 
intent upon learning his opinion upon the Protocol drawn up in London and 
Paris, which I knew to have been communicated to him by the Prussian Mission. 

Upon his Excellency asking me what intelligence | had received from 
London, I replied by an allusion to the collective Note and Protocol, respecting 
which, in reply to an inquiry, I gave full particulars, 

Count Nesselrode, who had evidently made up his mind not to proceed with 
the conversation, remarked cvasively that no doubt the two papers would be 
soon sent to him from Vienna. 

I remarked that the Protocol was a paper to which | was disposed to attach 
great importance; that it laid down very decided opinions as to the political 
existence of Turkey, and the maintenance of present territorial circumscription ; 
and tliat these opinions being entirely conformable to the well known views of 
the Emperor, while they were expressed in language the most respectful to His 
Majesty, | was willing to believe that no possible objection could be raised against 
the acceptance and the signature of so valuable an Act. ; 

_ Count Nesselrode changed the conversation, and in the course of that 
which ensued, the difficulties of the winter navigation of the Black Sea having 
been casually alluded to, L observed that in one respect | was lad to learn that 
this navigation was attended with danger, that this circumstance would, [was 
willing to believe, prevent any Russian troops being moved by sea, a good pre- 
caution against the chances of collision with English and Mreneh ships; 4 point 
of great importance to all who are intent upon a peaceful solution of very 
delicate questions. 

Count Nesselrode was convinced that no collisions of the kind adverted to

Sir G. H. Seymour to the arl of Clarendon.—(Received December 20.) 


(No, 714.) 


My Lord, St. Petersburgh, December 12, 1853. 

THE Russians have the merit, and it isa very great one, of possessing 
strong national feelings. These have been exhibited by the excessive satisfaction 
with which the accounts of the late successes have been received by all classes. 

On the side of the Court nothing has been omitted which could excite 
public feeling. 

A-Te Dewn in honour of the vietory over the Seraskier was performed 
yesterday at the metropolitan church; the only captured flag yet received from 
Achalzikh was carried triumphantly through the streets; a circle was held at 
the Winter Palace, at which their Imperial Majesties received the congratulations 
(on this occasion very sincerely offered) of their subjects, and at night the town 
was illuminated. 

In this latter demonstration I found to my considerable annoyance that | 
was taking part, my house having been illuminated in the coarse manner 
employed here, by the care of the Russian servants belonging to my landlord, 
to whom the custody of the house is entrusted. ; 

It is understood that Prince Menchikoff has written to the Emperor to 
congratulate His Majesty upon the state of his flect, and to say that. supposing 
the numbers to be equal, he should be perfectly ready to meet the English and 
French ships. | 

That Prince Menchikoff is a fearless soldier is well known, but whether the 
encounter Which he appears desirous of seeking would lead to another Te Deum 
may well be doubted. 

I have, &c. 
(Signed) G. H, SEYMOUR,

No. 505. 
The Earl of Clarendon to Lord Cowley. 


(No, 513.) 
My Lord, Foreign Office, December 24, 1853. 


COUNT WALEWSEI has communicated to me the important despatch of 
M. Drouyn de Uhuys which forms the subject of your Lordship’s despatch 
No. 957 of the 16th instant, 

That despatch has received the attentive consideration of Her Majesty's 
Government, whose views, as it must be superfluous for me to inform your 
Excellency, are in entire accordance with those of the French Government upon 
the unjustifiable course that Russia has throughout pursued on the Eastern 
question, and the absolute necessity of preventing the recurrence of no disaster 
anch as that which has lately taken place at Sinope. 

That necessity is in fact so evident that Her Majesty's Government did not 
doubt that the combined fleets had at once been sent into the Black Sea, and as 
your Excellency has already been made aware by my despatch No. $14 of the 
17th instant, to Viscount Stratford de Redcliffe, Her Majesty's Government did 
not consider that any fresh instructions were called for on the occasion, because 
special instructions having already been given to protect the territory of the 
Sultan from attack, they must be faithfully and effectually carried out, 

Despatches have since been received from Lord Stratford de Redcliffe by 
which it appears that on the 4th the fleets were about to be sent into the Black 
Sea, either to clear Sinope of the Russians or to protect the coasts of Turkey 
generally, and that the Russian Adiniral at Sevastopol was to be apprised of 
the service on which they would be employed ; and, thereupon, I have conveyed 
to his Excellency the approval of Her Majesty's Government: 

In my despatch No, 318 to Lord Stratford, of the 20th December, 1 have 
also stated that it was! only by obtaining a complete command of the Black Sea 
that the policy of the English and French Governments could be effectually 
curried out, and the recurrence of disasters such as that at Sinope could be 
prevented, 

These instructions are in accordance with the instructions that Count 
Walewski told me would be addressed to the F rench Ambassador at Constanti- 
nople; but the French Government now propote to us in addition that the 
Ottoman flag, as well as the Ottoman territory, should be protected by the com- 
bined fleets, and that all Russian vessels, other than merchantmen, met in the 
Black Sea, should be required to return to Sevastopol. 

Her Majesty's Government having clearly announced that the recurrence 


of a disaster such as that at Sinope must be prevented, and that the commund of 


the Black Sea must be secured, would have been content to have left the manner 
of executing those instructions to the discretion of the Admirals, but they attach 


ooo 


so much importance not alone to the united action of the two Governments, but 
ta the instructions addressed to their respective agents being precisely the same, 
that they are prepared to adopt the specilic mode of action now proposed by the 
Government of the Emperor. : 

Instructions to that effect will accordingly be addressed to Lord Stratford. 

fven if the Governments of England and France were not in honour bound 
to protect the Sultan, they could not, in the interests of humanity, tolerate that 
such scenes of horrible carnage, as that of which Sinope has been the theatre 
should be renewed, and for both these objects they must exercise complete com- 
mand in the Black Sea; but they will at the came render a signal service to the 
Porte ; and Her Majesty's Government consider it indispensable that no naval 
operation should be undertaken by the ‘Turkish fleet without the previous know- 
ledge and sanction of the British and French Admirals, who cannot be made 
responsible for operations of which they may be kept inignoranee, or of which 
they may disapprove, Nor can Her Majesty’s Government think it just, so long 
as England and France are not actually at war with Russia, that the combined 
fleets should aid and protect the Turkish forces in acts of aggression upon the 
Russian territory, while the Russian fleet is prevented from repelling such attacks 
or conveying the means necessary for the defence of that territory. 

Her Majesty's Government have not hesitated to adopt the course which 
the honour and dignity of this country preseribe, but at the same time they do 
not disguise from themselves that it may at no distant period involve England 
and France in war with Russia, and they consider if equally for the honour and 
dignity of the two Powers not to allow the peace of Europe to be dependent 
upon that national spirit in Turkey, which, however admirable in itself, and 
however useful amninst the aggressor, is now evidently beyond the control of 
the Turkish Government. Her Majesty’s Government would theretore propose 
to the Government of the Emperor that, im making known to the Porte the 
course which the two Governments are about to pursue, the English and French 
Ambassadors should at the same time be instructed to demand, in the event of 
the answer to the proposal recently sent trom Vienn# having heen unsatislietory 
that the terms on which a Treaty of Peace between Russia and ‘Turkey shall he 
negotiated may be left to the decision of England and France, on the distinct 
understanding that nothing shall be proposed on her part to which she has 
already officially objected. — | 

I communicated this proposal on the 9nd to Count Walewski, who engaged 
to refer it to his Government, and his Excellency has this day informed me that 
it has been entirely approved of by M, Dronyn de Lhuys. 

Lam, &e. 
(Signed) CLARENDON.

The Earl of Clarendon to Lord Stratford de Redcliffe. 
(No, 329.) 


My Lord, Foreign Office, December 27, iR5l. 
_ YOUR Excelleney will have learned by my despatch No. 318 of the 20th 
instant, that the entry of the whole of the combined fleets into the Black Sex, 
and the communication with the Russian Admiral, which were announced as 
probable on the 4th instant by your Excellency, in your despatch No. d08 met 
with the approbation of Her Majesty's Government, who considered that no 
instructions were necessary in addition to those already in the posseasion of your 
Excellency, for defending the European and Asiutic territory of the Sultan from 
attack. ; 
The French Government wrote in the same sense to General Baraguay 
d'Hilliers. mynehey 
The details which have subsequently arrived, respecting the disastrous affair 
ut Sinope, have given rise to further communications between Her Majesty's 
Government and that of the Emperor of the French, and the necessity of more 
stringent instructions have been recognized, ; 
la my despatch No, 318 J stated that it was only by obtaining the come 


He F 


400 


plete command of the Black Sea that the policy of the English and French 
Governments could be effectually carried out, and the recurrence of disasters 
such as that at Sinope, be prevented. But in order to exercise that command 
to the fullest and most beneficial extent, we have agreed with the French Govern- 
ment thatthe Russian naval commander should in appropriate, but unmistakeable 
terms, be informed that the Governments of England and France are resolved 
to prevent the recurrence of another such event a8 that at Sinope; that every 
Russian ship of war will henceforth be required to return to Sevastopol, or the 
most neighbouring port 5 and that allaggression against the Ottoman territory or 
flag would impose upon the Admirals the painful necessity of repelling force by 
force. 

Your Excellency is accordingly ‘astructed to communicate this to Vice- 
Admiral Dundas for his guidance in conjunction with Admiral Hamelin, whose 
instructions from the French Ambassador will be in all respects similar. 

In adopting this course, and in giving this substantial aid to Turkey, 
England and Franee are far from intending to abandon {he position in which 
they are now placed with respect to Austria and Prussia, They think, on the 
contrary, that it is their duty and their right to demand the acceptance by the 
Porte of the proposals recently made by the Four Powers, and which have for 
their object to secure the dignity and independence of the Sultan. 

Were England and France to act otherwise, they would impart, if not 
destroy, the union which now exists between the Four Powers, and which on 
every account it 16 50 important to maintatn, and they would endanger the peace 
of the world by encouraging the prolongation of a war which they would then 
regard as unnecessary’. 

In short, if the Governments of England and France are prepared to act 
with all the energy that the efficient protection of Turkey may render necessary, 
and if they are prepared to meet all the consequences it may entail, they are not 
the less anxious to act cordially with Austria and Prussia for the restoration of 
peace npon the bases established by the Conference at Vienna. ‘The measures 
they are about to adopt will afford to Europe a guarantee that. the Ottoman 
Empire will be maintained inviolate; and they expect im return that whenever 
negotiations commence, the Porte will honourably contribute to their success, 
and will abstain from putting forward demands which might be impracticable, 
and which the great Powers of Europe could have no interest In sustaining at 
the cost of a general war.

(Signed) CLARENDON.

The Earl of Clarendon to Sir G. FH, Seymour. 


(No. 044.) 
Sir, Foreign Office, December 27, 1854. 

AUTHENTIC information, dated the 9th instant, from Constantinople, has 
reached Her Majesty's Government, that on the 30th ultimo a Turkish squadron 
at anchor in the harbour of Sinope was completely destroyed by an over- 
whelming Russian force; that 4,000 Turks perished ; and that the survivors, 
not exceeding in number more than 400, who have been brought away by 
English and French vessels, were all more or less wounded. 

The feelings of horror which this dreadful carnage could not fail to ereate, 
have been general throughout all ranks and classes of Her Majesty’s subjects in 
this country. 

The circumstances which have attended this disastrous affair are of the 
greatest Importance, and with respect to them it is necessary that there should be 
no misunderstanding between Her Majesty's Government and the Cabinet of 
St. Petersburgh. 

The object with which the combined fleets were sent to Constantinople, was 
not to attack Russia, but to defend Turkey; and the English and French 
Ambassadors and Admirals were ‘formed that the fleets were not to assume an

Ihe events of the last six months, and the proceedings of the English and 

French Governments, afford abundant proof of their desire to maintain. friendly 
relations with Russia, and to effect an honourable settlement of the difference 
between that Power and the Porte; but the Cabinet of St. Petersburgh has 
greatly erred if it has mistaken forbearance for indifference, or has calculated 
upon any want of firmness in carrying out a policy which those Governments 
have adopted with a due regard to their own and to Furopean interests. 

Her Majesty's Government have not abandoned the hope that peace may 
be re-established, for they are unwilling to believe that any insurmountable 
obstacle can exist to carrying out the declared objects of Russia in a manner 
compatible with the dignity and the independence of the Porte; and it would 
therefore have been a matter of sincere satisfaction to Her Majesty's Govern- 
ment that the combined fleets should have remained at anchor in the Bosphorus 
while negotiations were pending, But this has been rendered impossible by the 
attack on the Furkish squadron at Sinope, ‘The intentions of the English and 
French Governments, which were long since announced to the Porte, must be 
firmly and faithfully executed. For this purpose, although with no hostile 
design against Russia, it is essential that the combined fleets should have the 
command of the Black Sea; and the necessary instructions have accordingly 
been addressed to the Ambussadors and Admirals of England and France, 

In making known to Count Nesselrode that such instructions have been 
sent, you will govern yourself by the language of this despatch, and you will 
inform his Excellency that in order to prevent the recurrence of disasters such 
as that at Sinope, ithe combined fleets will require, and, if necessary, compel 
Russian ships of war to return to Sebastopol, or the nearest port ; and it is 
considered that the ‘Turkish fleet should undertake no aggressive operations by 
seu so long as matters remain in their present state. |
