My Lord, St. Petersburgh, December 14, L853, 


GENERAL CASTELBAJAC has had the kindness to give me some 
interesting particulars of a conversation of one hour's duration which he held 


with the Emperor on the 1th instant, 


The interview is represented by the Russians as‘having been sought hy 


General Castelbajac, and by him as having been proposed by the Finperer. 


The trath is, that the General had written a note to Count Nesselrode. itt 
terms which appear to me inprudent, styings that as ‘a Christian, a soldier, 
and an European,” he rejoiced in the Russian victories, and should be still 
happier should they conduce to peace, and that this letter led to a summons to 


the palace. 


403 


In the conversation which took place, the Emperor began by expressing 
his gratitude for the manner in which M. de Kisseleff had been received at 
Fontainebleau, his displeasure at the language of the French press, and his 
astonishment that such a piece as the “ Cosaques” should have been tolerated 
at Paris. 

He spoke of the Black Sea, and of the various motives which might induce 
the allied fleet to appear there. If it should be to protect commerce, he him- 
self had taken every precaution for commercial security ; if it were to prevent 
the Turks from undertaking rash enterprises, he could only feel obligation to the 
allies, but at the same time believed that his own forces were sufficient for the 
safety of the Russian coast; if again the allied fleets interfered to take part 
with the Turkish ships against his fleet, that would evidently constitute a cause 
of war. 

This was one of the points upon which the Emperor manifested the greatest 
interest. He was very evidently anxious to learn to what measures on the part 
of the allied fleets the late ‘Turkish naval disaster was likely to give rise. 

His Majesty justified the attack by stating that it was truly a defensive 
measure: that the Turkish ships were laden with military stores for the Cir- 
eassian mountaineers; the fact was proved by their decks being crowded with 
barrels of powder: that circumstance indeed was the cause of their being blown 
up. As regarded the disembarkation of troops on the coast of European Turkey, 
this Majesty contemplated no operation of the kind. 

General Castel bajic found the Emperor discursive and excited in his 
conversation; His Majesty passed rapidly from one subject to another, and upon 
some spoke with considerable animation. He appeured particularly annoyed 
at the assurance given him by the French Minister of the note and protocol 
having been signed at Vienna, spoke of the ingratitnde of the Emperor at 
Austria in thus requiting his erituitous services, and hinted at the possibility of 
all Europe being arrayed against him. Here a little more than excitement was 
betrayed; excitenient became exultation. fven if this combination should be 
formed, he would not give in. Russia had already passed through great 
straights. His cause was just. He could not abandon his faith and the cause 
of his co-religionists. God would judge his actions and support his cause, &c. &c. 
As for his position it would remain what it had been and still was, defensive and 
expectant. He should be ready to receive propositions of peace, and to accept 
terms if they should prove consistent with his richts and dignity. 

These were the principal points of this remarkable conversation which were 
reported to me by the Marquis de Castelbajue, 

At the close of our conference I related n former transaction with a French 
colleague Mahe to in No. 722), in which 1 had some reason to complain of 
his want of frankness, General Castelbajue asked why | made this allusion ? 
what was the conclusion which I sought to draw? It is simply this, | said, that 
I had very little confidence in the person I advert to, and that I have a great 
deal in you. ‘This was not an empty phrase. My colleague gave me ample 
assurances of his sincerity, and | attach much confidence to his words, Before 
dropping the subject, however, I said, Now, in my turn, you shall let me tell you 
two things the Emperor said to you. 

He professed to have great, reliance on France and very little on England. 
“Eh bien, non,” General Castelbajac replied, “il s'est asses bien conduit & ce 
sujet. Je lui avais fait observer que notre union était des plus loyales, des plus 
complétes; et je vous assure que vous Naves j!as été trop mal traités. I n'a 
dit que tres peu de chose contre |’ Angleterre.” 

The other point, I rejoined, is this: Tam convinced that His Majesty told 
you that he had the greatest confidence in your Emperor, and not the slightest 
in his Minister for Foreign Affairs, “ Cette fois ci,” rejoined General Castel 
bajac, “ vous avez parlaitement raison. ll m’a dit avoir une compléte confiance 
dans la sagesse de I'Empereur Napoleon, mais qui nen était pas de méme de

Sir G. H. Seymour to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received December 27.) 


(No. 734. Confidential.) 
My Lord, St. Petersburgh, December 19, 1853, 

[ LEARN from Lord Cowley’s despatch No. 911, of which a copy was 
inclosed to me in your Lordship’s despatch No. 327 of the 7th instant, that 
Austria has received from Russia assurances 50 often reiterated and so positive 
that the Russian Government seeks neither an increase of territory, nor an 
extension of power, that Count Buol cannot but believe in them. 

Upon this declaration of opinion I can only remark that it may be that 
Russia has no intentions (that is, present intentions) of increasing her ternitory 
at the expense of the Sultan's dominions: the hypothesis is indeed the more 

robable as the attitude of all Europe is discouraging for such an attempt. 

With regard to an extension of power the case is widely different, and it 
appears to me hardly possible that Count Buol should hold the opinions which 
he expresses, | 

Power inthe sense employed by the Austrian Minister means the result of 
power—influence; and so little has any attempt been made by the Russian Govern- 
ment to conceal that an increased influence was sought through the concessions 
demanded of the Porte that, as your Lordship will have seen by various passages 
in my correspondence, the common excuse put forward by the Russians for these 
demands having been made, is the necessity for restoring that influence which 
by a convenient fiction is supposed to have been neutralized at Constantinople. 

Respecting the increase of actual power ot influence ‘whichever the term 
employed may be), no doubt is admissible only that the wish of obtaining a fresh 
hold woon ‘Turkey is caused by the pretence of seeking only that which is 
assumed to have been lost.

YESTERDAY another Te Deum was celebrated at the Winter Palace, to 
which, as the newspapers had announced, the persons belonging to the Court, and 
those usually received there, were summoned to take part in a thanksgiving for 
the late victory of Prince Béboutoff, obtained over the Turks. 

This notice is deserving of attention, as it proves that the persons assembled 


were called together upon an extraordinary occasion, and not upon that of the 


Féte of St. Nicholas. i ietoicr 
The ceremony was attended by the Austrian Chargé d’Affaires, the Prussian 


Secretary of Legation, and by the Ministers of Holland, Naples, Bavaria, and 
Belgium, the last of these accompanied by hig son and his Secretary of 
Legation. VEC t oe 
The Austrian and Prussian diplomatists had received special invitations 5 

the reat attended in consequence of the Chancellor (in reply to an inquiry ma 
of him by Count Bray, the Bavarian Minister) having stated that the Corps 
Diplomatique would not be invited, but that, if they thought fit, they were at 
liberty to present themselves. | : 
The oppertunities of visiting the Winter Palace being extremely rare, My 
colleagues availed themselves of the occasion unexpectedly offered. | . 
As regards the greater number of these gentlemen, it is probably very 

‘ nmaterial whether they were or were not present at the ceremony ; as regar 
the diplomatic servants of Austria and Prussia the case 1s different, and I would 
submit to your Lordship, that they neither ought to have been invited, or, beme 

o, ought to have attended. . ; ; 
- orcas and Prussia, 95 I would submit to your Lordship, besides having 
loudly proclaimed the neutral position which they have assumed, are acting as 

mediators in the unhappy quarrel between Russia and ‘Turkey. ae 
It appears to me, therefore, to be perfectly unsuitable that their Represen- 
tatives, of whatever degree, ghould take part in any court or religious ceremony 
intended to celebrate the Victorics obtained by one of these Powers over the 

the other. ) ; = 
The Turkish Government is probably too sensible to regard any trifling 
cireumstance of the kind, but if their attention should happen to be attracted to 
what has passed, some surprise may well be felt at the servants of two countries 
which are professing their feclings of friendship and impartiality, having been 


q a ‘ ¥ arty ul 
among the number of persons assembled on several occasions at St. Petersburg 


to return thanks to God for the destruction of a great number of the Sultan's 
subjects, Who have fallen victims to 4 most unholy Ware 

‘To guard against the possibility of misconstruction, I think it right to state 
to your Lordship that neither of the Te Deums celebrated at Court have been 


attended by any member of the French Mission.

I have mentioned privately to two or three persons belonging to our English

Russians are ‘ndebted in the second as in the first instance to their own autho- 
rities, an opinion which appears to have foundits way (as it had been my purpose

The same paralysis of commerce is observable here as when I last addressed 
your Lordship upon the subject, and confidence in the duration of neutral trade 
during a war being shaken, little more is doing by foreign than by English 
10uses. 

The only large prospective operations of which T have an knowledge is the 
a by a foreign firm of 75,000 quarters of rve for delivery next year in 

lolland, and the sale of 500 poods of copper by Baron Stieglitz to a German

the Russians definitively of their English customers for tallow and hemp, bristles 
being almost the only article of commerce upon which the English markets are 
dependent upon Russia, and the stream of commerce once directed being with 
difficulty brought back to its former channel. 

All this, however, is so little understood by the Russian wublic that, accord- 
ing to Peers opinion, the results of a war cannot fail of being more disastrous 
to English than to Russian commerce. 
I have, &c. 
(Signed) G. H. SEYMOUR. 


P.S.—Since writing this despatch I have learned some facts which may 
perhaps clear up the step lately faken by the Russian Government in withdrawing 
their funds from the Bank of England. : 

At the time when this arrangement was entered into, the inquiry was made 
as to what would be the consequence in the event of war between the two coun- 
tries, and the Russian Government were informed that the case heing an excep- 
tional one, it would be impossible to say but that in all probability the money 
would be lost. 

[have received this information in a most confidential manner from the 
very person who negotiated this arrangement for the Government, and whose 
mistrust of the pacific assurances lately given by the Finance Minister is not to 
he wondered at, as he was aware when summoned with the other merchants to 
receive them, that a few hours before orders had been sent to England to 
withdraw this money.

No, 527. 
Lord Cowley to the Earl of Clarendon.—( Received December 30.) 
(No. 996.) 
My Lord, Paris, December 29, 1853. 


THE communications which have recently taken place between Paris and 
Vienna had inspired M. Dronyn de Lhuys with the belief that no difference of 
opinion existed among the members of the Conference as to the manner in which 
the answer of the Porte, if considered favourable to peace, should be transmitted 
to St. Petersburgh. M. de Buol had indeed, in the first instance, expressed, as 
vour Lordship knows, a wish to be the main channel of communication between 
the Conference and the Russian Government, but appeared to have yielded to 
the representations of the Representatives of England and France, who had 
abjected to the Conference employing any other mode of communicating with the 
Russian Government than had been udopted towards the Porte, and that mode 
having been, at the desire of the Austrian Cabinet, collective towards Turkey 
they had demanded that it should remain collective towards Russia. 

M. Drouyn de Lhuys was, therefore, somewhat surprised when M. de 
Hiibner yesterday morning again put forward the pretensions of Austria to 
represent the Conferences in its communications with St. Petersburgh. His 
Excellency, however, met the Austrian claim with a decided negative, and told 
M, de Hiibner that he saw in the renewed proposition a vacillation of purpose 
on the purtof Austria whieh gave him: sincere regret. 

It appears now from a telegraphic despatch received yesterday from 
M. de Bourqueney that this difficulty had been arranged to the satisfaction of 
the Conference, when a telegraphic despatch from Lord Stratford of the 19th 
instant, was received by Lord Westmorland and laid before the Conference. 
Your Lordship will have received that despatch before this can reach your 
hands, and you will have learnt the painful impression which the non-presenta- 
tion to the Porte of the collective note of the Sth instant, had made upon the 
Conference, and of the resolution to which the members lad come to ask per- 
mission of their respective Governments to address a duplicate of that note to 
the Turkish Minister at Vienna, and thus to ensure its reaching the hands of 
the Sultan's Ministers. 

Simultaneously with this intelligence M, Drouyn de Lhuys had received 
his mail of the 14th from the Levant, ©The Vieuna note had not then arrived 
at Constantinople ; but the Representatives of the Four Powers had commenced 
negotiations with the Porte on pretty nearly the same basis as those wh ch were 
sugcested from Vienna, and which appear from Lord Stratford's telegraphic 
despatch to have been received subsequently. In ease your Lordship should 
not have a copy of the note addressed to the Porte by the Representatives of the 
Pour Powers [do myself the honour to inclose one, 

Such was the state of inatters when 7 ealled on M. Drouyn de Lhuys this 


ne 


morning. I found him annoyed at the summary way in which the Vienna 
collective note had been laid aside by the Representatives at Constantinople, 
and somewhat embarrassed to know what answer to send respecting the new 
proposition of the Conference, ss , 

L said that, until we were informed of the reasons which had induced the 
Representatives to pursue the negotiations on which they had entered with the 
Porte rather than present the collective note, we could not form a proper 
opinion; that, knowing as I did the soil of Constantinople, | could well 
understand that any alteration in the form of treating a negotiation already 
commenced would lead to delay, if not to a worse issue; and that as the 
suggestions made by Representatives to the Porte comeided or nearly so with 
those which emanated from Wienna, it did not Hypeee to me that the state of 
things was much altered ; a conclusion in which M. Drouyn de Lhuys coincided. 
L observed, moreover, that the mode of proceeding which had been adopted at 
Constantinople might come to our assistance at Vienna, as I did not suppose 
that either Her Majesty's or the Emperor's Government would desire to 
insist on the collective form at St, Petersburgh, if it had not been made use 
of at Constantinople. As to placing « duplicate of the note im the hands of 
Anf Pasha, it might be done if Count Buol pressed it, but on the distinct 
understanding that a collective note would be presented to the Russian 
Government, In short, ong of two ways was open to us: to await the result of 
the negotiations pursuing at Constantinople, and to frame our future proceedings 
in consequence, or to sanction the transmission of a duplicate note to Arif 
Pasha on the condition that a collective note should also be addressed to 
Russia. ; 

On the whole M. Drouyn de Lhuys appeared to lean towards the latter 
course, which led to my telegraphic communication to your Lordship of this 
morning's date. |

(Signed) COWLEY.

The Earl of Clarendon to Lord Cowley, 
(No. 529.) 
My Lord, Foreign Office, December 30, 1853. 


THE messenger having been delayed on the road, I did not receive your 
Excelleney’s No. 996 of Ae 29th instant, this afternoon, until after Count 
Colloredo had called upon me to read a despatch from Count Buol, pre- 
cisely similar to that which M. Hiibner appears to have communicated to 
M. de Lhuys. 

My answer ta Count Colloredo was the same as that which M. Hibner 
received from the French Minister for Foreign Affairs. I expressed my regret 
that Count Buol should be disinclined to adhere to the arrangement that had 
been agreed upon, and I informed him that Her Majesty's Government would be 
no party to any communication to the Cabinet of St. Petersburgh, except in con- 
junction with France, Austria, and Prussia. 

Count Colloredo stated that Count Buol was chiefly moved to made this 
proposal by the fear that a collective note to Russia should, like the one addressed 
to the Porte, find its way into the newspapers before it could even reach the 
Emperor's hands. 

I said that the negligence or bad faith which led to the publication of docu- 
ments that the Conference had determined should be kept secret, was much to be 
lamented, but that the policy of Her Majesty's Government was not to be guided 
by such considerations, and that there was no use in further discussion upon the 
subject. 

I subsequently saw Count Walewski, and held to him nearly the same 
language as your Excellency to M. de Lhuys, upon the proposal of Count [Buol, 
that the collective note should be delivered to the Turkish Ambassador at 
Vienna. 

That proposal, 1 said, appeared to be useless in itself, and unjust towards 
the Four Reenre-entatives at Constantinople. The Turkish Ambassador could 
only transmit the note to his Government, and where would be the advantage of 
inquiring a fortnight henee of the Porte, whether she was cinpees to negotiate 
for peace, when we already knew that she was so disposed, and, in substance, the 
terms to which she was ready to agree? On the other hand, such a mode of 
proceeding would amount to a disavowal of the Representatives, and a rebuke to 
them in the face of Europe forthe course they had pursued, without even waiting 
to know on what grounds, or under what circumstances, they had abstained from 
delivering the collective note to Reshid Pasha. The Four Governments would 
thus appear to be less anxious about the settlement of the differences between 
Russia and the Porte, than about its being effected according to their own pro- 
ject, and that they would run the risk of delay and confusion upon no other data 
than an imperfect telegraphic despatch from Lord Stratford. 

At the ime I was conversing with Count Walewski, I had not seen the 
note which has been addressed to the Porte, but assuming that some reasonable 
propasition had been made before the collective note arrived from Vienna, 
I said that the Four Representatives had probably exercised a sound diseretion 
In suspending it, as the Turkish Ministers might otherwise have been induced 
to depart from what they had already agreed to, and to think that it was open 


Ny thein to propose fresh terms in replying to the collective note of the Four 
oWwers, 


5F 


oe 
* a," 


416 


Count Walewski, on finding that I had not seen the note, was so. good as 
to give me acopy he had with him, and it confirmed my opinion with respect 
to the judicious course pursued by the Representatives, as the terms are such 
as the Porte has thought proper to accept, and which the Emperor of Russia 
will put himself more than ever in the wrong by refusing. : , 

Count Walewski having agreed with me, that upon the whole it would be 
advisable to take no further step until complete information had been recetved,

My Lord, Vienna, December 20, 1853. 

I COMMUNICATED to Count Buol your Lordship’s despatch No, 406, 
in which you direct me to state to him the sincere pleasure with which Her 
Majesty's Government had learnt that he had received the Emperor's commands 
to agree to the Protocol andthe drat of the note to Reshid Pasha, which had 
been submitted to him by Her Majesty’s Government, and the Government of 
France, and by which the concurrence of the Four Powers in the same line of 
poliey on the Eastern question might be considered os established, 

Count Buol reciprocated these expressions of satisfaction at the important 
result which had thus been obtained, and coincided with your Lordship in the 
hope that, by a strict adherence to it, peace might be reestablished between 
Russia and the Porte, and the dangers which now menaced the general 
tranquillity of Europe be averted, 

Count Buol was perfectly satisfied with the assurance given by your 
Lordship, that Her Majesty's Ambassador at Constantinople had been made aware 
of the anxiety felt by Her Majesty’s Government for the suceess of the 
propositions now about to be made to the Porte, and he renewed his assurance 
that he should consider himself bound to act in consultation and in entire unity 
with the other allied Powers towards Russia, in case that Government should 
refuse to accept the proposals of the Four Powers which the Porte might have 
agreed to. 

Count Buol was glad to find that the verbal amendments introduced into 
the Protocol had been agreed to by Her Majesty's Government, and that the 
mode of proceeding recommended to the Representatives at Constantinople 
hy the Conference, had been approved of. 

In closing this despatch 1 beg to express to your Lordship my acknowledg- 
ments for the manner in which you have conveyed to me the approbation by 
Her Majesty's Government of my language and conduet throughout the course 
of these transactions,

(No. 452.) 
My Lord, Vienne, December 20, 18538. 
WITH reference to the desire expressed by your Lordship to learn more 
distinctly than you had done from a communication you had received from 
Count Colloredo, whether Count Buol was decided to maintain the principle of 
a negotiation between the Government of Russia and the Porte, to which the 
Four Powers should be parties, I read to him the despatch | had addressed to 
your Lordship upon that subject No. 444, in which I had detailed the manner 
in which he proposed that the acceptation by the Porte of the proposals, 
transmitted hy the Four Powers, should be submitted by the Conference of 
Vienna to the Cabinet of St. Petersburgh, and the collective form in which he 
desired they should be recommended and supported. Count Buol entirely 


assented to the representation of his intentions and wishes which were contained 
in that despatch, which he conceived would dispel any doubt which your 
Lordship might have felt as to the policy he meant to pursue. 

With respect ta the communication from Count Colloredo to which your 
Lordship referred, Count Buol stated that the instruction he had addressed to 
that Minister was written with the view only of establishing the fact that, if 
the Cabinet of St. Petersburgh should absolutely object to a Conference of the 
Six Powers, in which the Treaty for the re-establishment of peace with Turkey 
should be negotiated, that determination should not be considered as a total bar 
to any negotiation. He said that he approved entirely of the proposal that the 
negotiation should be carried on in presence of the Six Representatives, and that 
this opinion was cntirely in unison with that of the Emperor. He, therefore, 
would neglect no cifort to obtain its adoption by the Russian Government; but 
that if a decided obstuecle as to form was at once opposed to that proposal, he 
had thought it right tocall the attention of the allied Governments to the danger 
which might arise from insisting upon an exclusive form of negotiation, for 
which it was not impossible that an equivalent might be found without 
inipairing our action as mediators. 

In stating this, Count Buol remarked that he meant in no way to admit of 
a negotiation between the two belligerents without the control of the Four 
Powers: he disclaimed entirely any admission of that nature; he insisted upon 
the action of the allied Powers in every stage of the negotiation, upon every 
dificulty which might arise between the negotiators, ant consequently upon 
receiving a constant report or communication of their proceedings; but he 
conceived that if an objection which he should look upon as futile should be 
raised by Russia as to the negotiation being carried on in the presence of 
the Representatives of the Four Powers, they ought not to bind themselves by 
a positive refusal to a course which would prevent all negotiation from taking 
dace. 

Count Buol stated that this alone was the view with which he had put forward 
the opinion he had instructed both Count Colloredo and M, de Hilbner to 
submit for the consideration of the Governments to which these Ministers are 
aceredited. He gave his decided preference to the negotiation in presence of 
the Six Representatives ; he would support it with all the means he could dispose 
of; but he thought the alternative he had suggested might lead to the same 
general result, for it was impossible that the ‘many questions which must be 
brought into the negotiation, and which would partake entirely of an European 
character, should not necessitate the direct intervention of the allied Powers; 
and as to the question of the re-establishment of peace between the belligerents, 
even if it was agreed to and signed by their Representatives alone, it would be 
with the entire approval of all its conditions by the Representatives of their allies. 
Count Buol repeated that the reasoning he had thus put forward was merely 
in support of the views he conceived he was bound to submit to the allied 
Governments, as those which might meet a case of difficulty which it would be 


419 


advantageous to be prepared for, but he in no way desired their adoption ; it was 
a suggestion with regard to which, if unfortunately the case he apprehended 
should arise, he was entirely prepared to attend to the views and opinions of 
the allied Governments, and to adopt the course which, in consultation with 
them, should be decided upon as most advisable.

My Lord, Vienna, December 20, 1853. 

| INCLOSE the report which has appeared in the Vienna “ Presse” of the 
decision which has been taken by the Administrative Council of the Principality 
of Wallachia, which was ordered to assemble by Prince Gortchakoff, by which 
the whole of the militia of that province has been formally incorporated in the 
Russian army. It is also stated that these troops will be considerably increased 
in numbers, and it is supposed they will be placed under the orders of the 
Imperial Russian General Sala, 

I brought these circumstances under the notice of Count Buol, who, 
although not officially informed of them, believed them to be correctly stated, 
and considered them as highly reprehensible. The explanations upon this 
subject which he had received from Baron Meyendorff were, that it was not 
intended these traops should be employed against the arms of the Sultan; but 
he did not look upon this assurance as being in any way to be considered as a 
satisfactory explanation of the measure, and he had so expressed himself in his 
communications on the subject.

Inclosure in No. 534. 


Extract from the ‘‘ Presse" of December 18, 1853. 
(Translation.) 


INTELLIGENCE has been received from Bucharest that in a sitting of the 
Administrative Council of the Principalities, by order of Prince Gortchakoff, the 
Whole Wallachian militia had been formally incorporated in the Russian army. 
This measure was only sanctioned by a majority of four voices to three. The 
President of the Council protested against it on the grounds that the Wallachian 
country was not at war with either Russia or Turkey; on the contrary, it 
belonged to Turkey, and the participation of the militia in a war against the 
Porte was in fact high treason against their legitimate Suzerain. . 

The regiments forming the Wallachian militia are to be inereased from 2,000 
men Ae present complement) to 4,000, and an additional infantry regiment 
raised. 

The intelligence received from Bucharest of the 13th instant states that the 
Imperial Russian General Sala will probably take the command of the 
Moldavian and Wallachian troops, and that they will be augmented according to 
the orders already issued.

My Lord, Vienna, December 23, 1853, 

COUNT BUOL requested Baron Bourqueney and myself to call upon him 
yesterday, to consult with us upon the important question as to the form in 
which the reply from Constantinople should be transmitted to the Cabinet 
of St. Petersburgh, which we may be called upon very shortly to decide upon, 
He feels that the great anxiety of the Four Governments must naturally be 
to adopt the form which will hold out the greatest chance of success in 
obtaining the object of peace which we are striving to re-establish, [tis well 
worth while, therefore, indeed it is incumbent upon us, to weigh and consider 
every mode by which we might best proceed. 

Count Buol had received the despatches of Count Colloredo of the 16th 
instant, and from M. de Hiibner of the 17th from Paris. which reter to the

In conformity with the plan sketched out im the first of these despatches, 
Count Buol entirely adopted the suggestions made by M. Drouyn de Lhuys to 
M. de Hiibner: first, as to the Assembly of the Conference to decide whether 
the answer which should be received from the Porte was of a nature to be 
transmitted to St. Petersburgh; secondly, that the decision being taken in 
favour of transmission, and consigned in a protocol, it should be intrusted to

forwarded to Count Nesselrode; and thirdly, that a collective note, addressed 
to Count Nesselrode, should be signed by the Four Representative: to be 
forwarded in case the communication of which Count Buol will have been 
the organ, should not have had the success which might be expected from it, 

Count Buol, accordingly, gives up, in conformity with the representations

Conference should transmit to their ealleagues at St. Petersburgh the answer of 
the Porte and the result of their deliberations, and in reference to the plan he is 
ready to adopt, he made a remark upon the communication he had received from

ofthe answer from the Porte; but upon the condition that it should not be made 
use of, unless the communication of which Count Buol will have been the bearer 
should have been refused.” aa 

Upon this proposition, Count Buol stated, that the lamentable publicity 
which had been given to the acts of the Conlerence obliged him to put the ques- 
tion, whether it was to be hoped that any other document could in fature Sepp 
a similar fate: for, notwithstanding the engagements which the members of the 
Conference had taken with each other, it was understood that the documents 
signed on the 5th of December had previously been sent to St. Petersburgh, and 
communicated to Count Nesselrode, confidentially, by M. de Rochow. Under 
these circumstances, he thought the collective note, which was only eventually 
to be transmitted, would have the same fate, and his pos to Count Nesselrode 
would be received by him under an impression that it was unfairly brought 
before him,as it only awaited his refusal to be succeeded by another document 
of a stronger character, and which was unfairly concealed from him, 

Count Buol considers that the two gradations that he proposes would offer 
i better chance of the success we all so heartily desire, although he is not san- 
guine in his expectations of it, Should the result pases our hopes, we 
should certainly have lost twelve or fifteen days, but the Conference having in 
the first instance transmitted through a single organ its decision, would at 
once proceed to the production of a collective document of the greatest 
Importance. 7

Lord Cowley to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received December 30.) 


(No. 995. Contidential.) 
My Lord, Paris, December 29, 1853. 

M. DROUYN DE LHUYS has related to me, in strict confidence, the 
substance of a conversation which occurred between himself and M. de Kisseledt 
on the 26th instant. 

He had not seen M. de Kisseleff for some weeks. The latter called 
ostensibly for the purpose of lamenting the present misunderstanding between 
Franee and Russia on the Eastern question, adding that the solution of this 
question was in a great measure in the hands of Franee, that the Emperor 
Napoleon might cover himself with glory, and secure the gratitude of Europe by 
not deviating from that pacifie policy which he had proclaimed, while if he 
permitted himself to be dragged into the wake of England, who was acting solely 
for her own interests, he would find himself engaged in a war from which no 
profit could result to France. The Emperor, his master, would, M. de Kisselef 
continued, be always ready to listen to any suggestions which the Emperor 
Mapolean in whose wisdom His Majesty had the greatest confidence, might 
make. 

M. Drouyn de Lhuys replied that M. de Kisseleff! was quite mistaken in 
supposing that France was dragged, as lie had intimated, in the wake of England. 
France had entered into a double engagement—the one with Great Britain, 
Austria, and Prussia, which had for its object the assertion of a great principle 
of European policy, and which was of a much closer nature than M, de Kisseletf 
seemed to be aware; the other, with Great Britain for the defence of the Turkish 
territory, which he might be assured they would pursue to the end Neither 
could he assume for the French Government the merit which M, de Kisselelf 
seemed willing to attribute to them, of being more peacealily inclined than their 
maritime ally, since, to speak the truth, although the two Governments were 
unanimous in the decisions to which they had come, yet in discussing them it 
was France that had advocated more active and decided measures, while more 
moderate and prudent councils had prevailed in the English Cabinet, If English 
Interests were more directly at stake in the Eastern question, whose fault was it 
but Russia's? Instead of leaving the question as it originally stood, as one 
affecting the holy places alone, on which Russia had obtained an advantage over 


424 


France, she must needs occupy the Principalities, which had obliged not only 
England, but Austria and Prussia to take part against her, and now, by her 
conduct in Persia and other parts of Asia, she had succeeded in uniting the 
entire opinion of the British nation against her. Lf then Great Britam profits 
more than France will by the good understanding which prevails between them, 
the fault will be with Russia, As for the French Government, they are 
convineed that it is with no hope of individual benefit that England is ranged 
side by side with them. 

“You say,” said M. Drouyn de Lhuys to M. de Kisseleff, “that the 
[Emperor Nicholas will listen with attention to any suggestions for the settlement 
of this question which may come from hence. Our suggestions are to be found 
in the resolutions adopted by the Conference at Vienna. I do not know what 
else to advise. The propositions are very simple and such as you cannot 
abject to, You tell the Porte that, notwithstanding her declaration of war, you 
ure still ready to treat for peace; and we advise the Porte to accept the offer and 
to let you kuow the conditions on which she is willing to treat. You cannot 
object to that. We advise the Porte to name a Plenipotentiary, without which 
there can be no negotiation, and to propose a neutral place where he may mect 
1 Plenipotentiary from Russia, You cannot object to that. We advise further, 
that this negotiation shall not take place in the dark, but in the presence of the 
reat Powers of Europe, who are interested in the result of them. Ifyou are 
consistent you cannot object to that, for you have sanctioned the right of Europe 
to interfere in Turkish affairs, by your presence in all the conferences which 
have taken place on the different questions relating to the integrity of the 
Turkish Empire. If you have any more feasible plan, I shall be ready to give 
it the fullest consideration.” 

M. de Kisseleff rejoined that he had no instructions either to discuss or to 
propose any plan, and that in fact his visit was a spontaneous effort to endeavour 
to produce a better understanding between his own Government and that of 
the Emperor Napoleon, 

Lusked M. Drouvn de Lhuys what on the whole was the impression left 
upon his mind by M. de Kisseletf's language, He replied, that it seemed to him 
that the Enyeror of Russia was fully aware of, and regretted, the false 
situation in which le had placed himself; that he felt the isolated position to 
which the establishment of a Conference at Vienna had condemned him, though 
he still hoped that the attitude of Austria and Prussia would be confined to 
remonstrance. He knew, however, the danger he incurred, were hostilities to 
ensue on the part of France and England alone; hence his whole tactics were 
directed to disuniting them, As to what the Czar may be inclined to do 
towards a pacific arrangement at the present moment, M. Drouyn de Lhuys 
said that the language of M. de Kisseleff was as vague as ever. 

In the course of the conversation some allusion was made by M, de Kissele{? 
to the discourtesy shown to the Emperor by the refusal of the French Govern- 
ment to alloy General Guyon, when invited by His Majesty, to attend the 
reviews at Warsaw; as also to the hostility shown towards Kussia by the French 
press, which enabled M, Drouyn de Lhuys to say that, although the Emperor 
af ltussia had refused the title of “ brother" to the Emperor of the French, there 
was no ill-will in the latter’s mind in consequence ; that he hada great admiration 
for the Emperor Nicholas, and would be very glad to take any fit opportunity of 
ahiawing ib. 

M. Drouyn de Lhuys observed to M. de Kisseleff on the latter taking his 
departure, that he reserved to himself to recount to the Emperor what had 
jussed between them, in order that His Majesty might have an opportunity of 
dissenting from or assenting to the language which he had used. 

M. Drouyn de Lhuys has since seen the Emperor, who accorded entire 
approbation to the sentiments expressed by his Minister. 

1 understand that M. de Kosseleff takes every opportunity of stating that 
his interview with M. Drouyn de Lhuys was pertectly sutisfactory. 

I have, &e. 
(Signed) COWLEY.,

(Nc 1002. Most Confidential.) 
My Lord, Paris, December 30, 1853. 
REPORTS have been current in Paris that General Castelbajac had 
addressed a letter of congratulation to the Russian Government in consequence 
of the late s1tcvesses of the Russian troops, I believe that these reports may be 
a 


426 


traced to the Russian Mission; and I have further reason to know, that asser- 
tions of a similar nature have also been prevalent in the Russian capital, 

I determined, therefore, to mention the subject to M. Drouyn de Lhuys, 
at the same time that | avowed my disbelief in the possibility of the French 
Minister at St. Petersburgh having so completely forgotten his character as to 
have complimented the Russian Government on successes which might possibly 
be the immediate cause of war between his own Government and Russia, 

M. Drouyn de Lhuys assured me with so much earnestness that he did 
not believe in the truth of the report, that Tam persuaded he knows nothing of 
this extraordinary proceeding, if it has really occurred; and it seems so 
impossible that a man in General Castelbajac’s position should take a step that 
would place him in contradiction with the policy which it was his duty to 
defend, that I cannot but indulge in the hope, that the rumour is a weak 
invention of the enemy, intended to throw dust in the eyes of the society of 
St. Petersburgh as to the real sentiments of France. 

Having answered my question, M. Drouyn de Lhuys said that he had seen 
M. de Kisseleff again yesterday, when he informed him that he had communi- 
cated to the Emperor the substance of the conversation which had passed between 
them on the 26th instant, and which is recounted in my confidential despatch 
No. 995; and that His Majesty had fully sanctioned all that he (M. Drouyn 
de Lhuys) had said on that occasion, His Excellency added, that in order that 
the fact might not be falsely interpreted at St, Petersburgh, he would inform 
me, in strict confidence, that the Emperor had himself written to General 
Castelbajac, and had told him that were the question for the arrangement of 
which M. de Kisseleff had asked the advice of the French Government one 
which concerned French and Russian interests alone, he should be ready with 
a proposition for its settlement; but that this was a question which concerned 
European interests generally, and on which he had been consulting with the 
other Powers of Europe, that he could not now with honour separate himself 
from those Powers; and that he had no other advice to offer than that which it 
was known had emanated from the Vienna Conference. If, however, the 
Emperor of Russia had any proposition to make, he would give it. every 
consideration; but in that case His Majesty had no time to lose. France, 
who had begun by being a spectator and witness to the contest engaged 
in the East, was now called upon to take a more active part in it, and he (the 
Emperor) could not disguise from himself that matters were on a declivity 
which might lead to a war. 

M. Drouyn de Lhuys added, that he was happy to give me this informa- 
tion, of which I might make a confidential use, as it was possible that the 
Emperor's words might be misrepresented in the mouths of Russians. 

M. Drouyn de Lhuys seemed anxious that | should not understand the 
Emperor's assurance, that he would give his best consideration to any proposal 
which might come from Russia, as indicating an intention to treat separately 
with that Power. [ therefore said to him, that I was perfectly convinced of 
the loyalty both of the Emperor and his Government ; ‘a that | was sure that 
your Lordship and Her Majesty's Government had the same trust and con- 
fidence in their honour, Moreover, | would venture to add, that if, through any 
advice given to the French Government to Russia, the Eastern question could 
he settled without extending hostilities beyond their present sphere, Her 
Majesty's Government, so far from feeling jealousy of French influence, would 
sincerely rejoice to see it exercised in so beneficial a manner. 

1 have, &e. 
(Signed) COWLEY.

Lord A. Loftus to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received January 4, 1854.) 


(No. 163. Confidential.) 
My Lord, Berlin, December 30, 1853. 


BARON MANTEUFFEL expressed to me this evening, with evident 
satisfaction, that he was reassured as to the King's political views and opinions. 
His Majesty had stated to him this day his conviction that Prussia in the present 
aspect of affairs must preserve a neutrality, and was of opinion that no assistance 
could be given to the Emperor of Russia. 

Baron Manteuffel appears to have confidence in His Majesty's present 
present disposition, although he confessed to me that he was constantly obliged 
to combat false impressions which irritated the King's mind, and he further 
confided to me that on this account he held it as indispensable to have daily 
intercourse with His Majesty. sets 

lam happy to report to your Lordship that the Prince of Prussia 1s 
expeted to arrive at Berlin on the 15th proximo. The presence of His Royal 
Highness at Berlin at this critical moment is most desirable, as he exercises 
considerable influence over the King, and will give additional support to Baron 
Manteuffel, and the system which his Excellency is pursuing. 

I have to report to your Lordship the death of General von Radowitz on 
the @4th instant, who has been for some time in a declining state of health. 
He had retired from public affairs since December 1851, but he maintained to 
the last the personal confidence and affection of the King; his death, although 
depriving thé country of a distinguished statesman, will exercise no influence 
on the present state of parties here, or on public affairs in general. 

Thave, &e. 
(Signed) AUGUSTUS LOFTUS.

(No. 164. Confidential.) 
My Lord, Berlin, December 30, 1853. 

BARON MANTEUFFEL informed me this evening that the Prussian 
Consul-General at Warsaw, M. Wagner, who had lately arrived from his post, 
represents Prince Paskewitch as highly disapproving the war with Turkey, and 
extremely grieved (désolé) at the course which the Emperor of Russia is 
pursuing, 

M. Wagner is reported to me from another souree as having stated that 
Prince Paskewitch had blamed the line of conduct pursued towards the Walla- 
chians and Moldavians as being unwise and impolitic, and calculated rather to 
disgust than to gain those populations, and that he had also censured the Russian 
military operations on the Danube as having been badly devised, and still more 
ineficiently carried out, 

Consul Wagner further reports, that from information he had received, it 
appeared to be the intention of Russia to porsess herself during the winter 
season, if possible, still of the smaller forts on the Danube, such as Hersorvia, 
Matschiu, Isaktshi, and Tultscha, and even to invest Silistria, so as to be thus 
fur advaneed for early operations in the spring. ; 

He had been likewise given to understand that some idea was entertained 
on the part of Russia of crossing the Danube and advancing on Constantinople 
by the circuitous line of Sophia, thus working round in lieu of facing the 
Balkan. 

This design, however, may probably have been counteracted by the judicious 
foresight of the Turkish Government in recognising the neutrality of Servia, 
which territory, in such event, she would have been obliged to traverse. 

Consul Wagner reports that the two Russian corps d’armee, the first and 


429 


second corps, stationed in Poland and the Baltic provinces, had not changed 
their position, and that them force had not been diminished. 

1 have thought this information of sufficient interest to report to your 
Lordship, taking the precaution of informing your Lordship of the source from 
which it is derived. 

I have, &e.

My Lord, Berlin, December 31, 1853. 


1 HAVE the honour to inform your Lordship that a telegraphic despatch 
has been received from Count Arnim, stating that by intelligence which has 
reached Vienna from Constantinople, the collective note lately signed at Vienna 
had not been presented by the Four Representatives to the Porte. 

Baron Manteuffel has been informed that a note similar in substance, but 
more explicit, has been agreed upon at Constantinople by the Four Represen- 
tatives, and had been collectively presented to the Divan on the 14th instant. 
It is further reported to his Excellency that the Divan had shown a disposition 
to accept the invitation, and to enter on the arrangement of a basis of 
negotiation. 

His Excellency refrained, until further reports shall have reached him from 
Constantinople, from expressing his opinion on the conduct of Baron Wildenbruch 
in this matter, but he stated that great annoyance had been felt at Vienna on the 
receipt of this intelligence. 

Count Buol had proposed to the Conference, that a copy of the Vienna note 
should be presented collectively hy the Conference to the Turkish Minister at 
Vienna, for transmission to Reshid Pasha, and Count Arnim had applied for 
authorization to associate himself to this step. 

Baron Manteutfel has replied, that if the proposition to which Count Arnim 
alludes is supported by the Representatives of the Four Powers, he is authorized 
to join in it; but that if any difference of opinion should arise, he was to refer to 
Berlin for further orders, 

His Excellency then informed me that he had received a long report from 
Count Amim concerning the mode of transmission of the answer of the Porte to 
St. Petersburgh, 

[ stated to his Excellency, that Count Buol appeared to have proposed 
that the collective note, conveying the answer of the Porte to Count Nesselrode 
should be signed, but kept in reserve, while he (Count Buol) was separately to 
submit any reasons he might think proper to obtain the Emperor's assent to the 
recommendations of the Conference; but that, in case of his failure, the collee- 
tive note should be presented. 

In support of this opinion, Count Buol had represented the possibility of 
Count Nesselrode refusing to recognize the wxistence of the Conference, or to 
recoznize the validity of the Conference to interfere in the affairs relating to the 
differences existing between Russia and the Porte, in which latter opinion Count 
Arnim had coincided with Count Buol, 

With respect to the farmer opinion of Count Buol, I stated to his Excel- 
lency that it appeared to me that Count Buol had materially changed his 
opinion; for he had previously stated that ‘he did not wish to go alone to 
St. Petersburgh, and had further acknowledged the answer of the Porte to be 
the property of the Conference.” 

I further remarked to his Excelleney that, if any other than a collective 
form was adopted towards Russia, it would be recognizing the very argument of 
Russia, namely, that the Powers of Europe had no right to interfere between 
Russia and Turkey. It would also be derogatory to the dignity of the Four 
Powers to sign a collective note which should be only kept in reserve to be used 
as Austria should think fit, 

I represented also to his Excellency that it could not be supposed that 
Russia would refuse to recognize the existence of an European Conference on the

affairs relating to the differences existing between the Government of the 
Emperor and that of Turkey, when Russie had already in public acts referred to 
that Conference, and had even accepted a note which had issued from then 
hands. 

His Excellency appeared wholly to concur in the justice of my remarks, and 
seemed to be of opinion that the dignity of the Conference either required 4 
collective action, or that Austria should be deputed to act in the name of the 
Conference. 

In making the foregoing remarks, | took care to inform his Excellency that 
they must be regarded solely as my own opinions, for his Excellency must be 
aware that I could have received no ‘nstruetions on the points to which they 
refer. 

T venture to hope that they will meet with your Lordship’s approbation.

A PERSON on whose veracity T can fully rely, has informed me in the 
greatest secrecy that an intrigue is carrying on here by the partisans of Russia, 
‘atthe instigation of the Emperor himself, to induce the King of Prussia to 
yeni Prussian officers as military commissaries to the Russian army on the 
Danube. ‘ 

There is a double aim sought to be obtained by this move; first, to 
engage Prussia thus furtively and insidiously in the cause of Russian, or at least 


431 


to give to Europe an appearance of Prussian support; and secondly, to obtain 
the aid and assistance of two officers who possess valuable information on all 
matters relating to Turkey and the Turkish forces. 

The two officers who have been specially applied for, are (as | am informed) 
Colonel Molthe, who has been for many years employed in Turkey in a military 
capacity, and has a thorough knowledge of Turkey; and Captain Oerbzel, who 
is conversant with all matters relating to ‘Turkish fortresses, and has extensive 
geographical and military information, capable of very great assistance to the 
Russian army. : 

_ Baron Manteuffel in great confidence alluded to this subject in conver- 
sation with me this evening, and informed me that he had strongly dissuaded 
His Majesty against any such measure, stating that great embarrassment might 
result from it with no counterbalancing advantage. : 

The King, as Baron Manteuffel informs me, has promised that he will 
decline the proposal and let the matter drop. 
Baron Manteuffel told me that Colonel Thom, an Austrian officer, is now 
serving as Austrian commissary at the head-quarters of Prince Gortchakoff.

Lord Stratford de Redcliffe to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Recetved 
January 4, 1854.) 


(No. 90.) 
My Lord, Constantinople, December 17, 1853. 


IN reporting on the subject of my efforts to overcome the Porte’s 
reluctance to aceept the note and declaration which the late French Ambassador 
and myself were authorized by our respective Governments to present to Reshid 
Pasha, 1 stated in substance that the inducement to recommend that mode of 
restoring peace was not so much my hope of suecess, Which was very faint, as 
an impression that a failure in that respect, if not invested with an official 
character, might smooth the way for some proposition better suited to the 
altered circumstances of the case. 

Acting upon this principle, when | had thoroughly ascertained that even a 
modified note and declaration would not prove acceptable to the 7 urkishi 
Ministry, | entered into private communication with Reshid Pasha on the ground 
of taking a common sense view of the existing circumstances, and endeavouring 
to form a plan of proceeding which in its issue might secure every reasonable 
advantaye to ‘Turkey without injustice or palpable humiliation to Russit. 

1 was encouraged to embark in this course by the corresponding disposition 
which | found in my new French colleague, and by the knowledge which your 
Lordship's correspondence uflorded of the views of the several Powers BAe 
take a leading interest in the settlement of the Eastern question. The principal 
difficulties to be encountered were the illusions of frontier suecess, the national 
enthusiasm in favour of war, the fears of leading statestnen unwilling to oppose 
the eurrent of popular sentiment, and, above all, the necessity of applying to 
the General Council for permission to entertain any plan of pacification with 
Russia. ‘The Sultan, his Ministers, and the Council, all stood in fear of cach 
other, aid though, perbaps, at heart desirous: of peace, were reluctant to forfett 
their share of the popularity enjoyed by the votaries of war, 

The first necessury step towards a negotiation for peice was to wean Reshid 
Pasha from his new-born propensities to war; the second was to obtain his 
sincere cooperation in opening & door for his more moderate colleagues to avow 
their real sentiments with safety. Aided by auxiliary incidents, | succeeded, 
after a time, in aking hima partaker of my own convictions. It was in con- 
sequence agreed between us that the General Council should be assembled, that 
its consent should, if possible, be obtained for negotiating a pacific settlement 
on safe and honourable terms, and that a more distinct proposition, satisfactory 
to hoth of us in the interest of the Porte, should be submitted officially to him 
and his colleagues. 

On my part [ followed out this plan by putting logether in a practicable 
form the several points which it was evidently desirable or necessary to provide 
for in the contemplated negotiation and its preliminary steps. Sufficient ele- 
ments were fortanately at hand in your Lordship’s correspondence with Prris 
and Vienna, ‘They had only to be combined with some indispensable additions, 
and adapted to the present state of things and of parties here. 

The short memorandum inelosed herewith exhibits the project of arrange- 
ment approved in private by Reshid Pasha, aud aubenqusntty we Ce in private 
also, by General Baraguay d'Hilhers, with whose ideas I had made myself 
previously acquainted, 

In concert with him, and after sounding Baron de Bruck, I proposed a 
meeting of the Four Representatives at the Intermuncio’s house. 

The result of our deliberations there on the /2th instant was the adoption 
in substance of the plan which, on a perfect understanding with the French 
Ambassador, | submitted to our colleagues in the terms already made known to 
vour Lordship. A sccond meeting, which took place at his Excellency’s house 
on the Lsth, confirmed, with some verbal alterations, the agreement already 
made; and | joined in signing it, thus completed, with the more confidence as 
iad in the interval ascertained privately that Reshid Pasha saw no objection to 
its amended fort, 


Our principal difficulty in coming to un agreement lay with the Internuncio, 


435 


who wished to avoid a collective mode of proceeding, and the insertion of any 
word which might offend the delicate sensibilities of Russia. With every incli- 
nation to meet his wishes, I found it impossible m some imstances to acquiesce 
in his proposals, whether of omission or of insertion, But I truat that in 
striking ovt expedients for the removal of his scruples, his colleagues at the 
meeting, including myself, have retained whatever was necessary to guard the 
interests of Turkey and of Europe; while his acceptance of our counter-amend- 
ments may warrant a sanguine hope that the plan, as it stands now, will, 
if accepted here, present few points of reasonable objection, even at St. 
Petersburgh. 

The form of an identic communication to the Porte, subsenbed separately 
by each Representative, and presented by their respective interpreters in a body, 
is referable to the same spirit of scrupulousness towards Russia, on the one side, 
and of accommodation, as far as principles admit, on the other. 

In recording these circumstances, 1 must in justice ac uit Baron de Bruck 
of any personal disposition to make difficulties; and nothing could be more 
satisfactory than the support afforded to every just and reasonable view of the 
points in question by General Baraguay d’Hilliers and M, de Wildenbruch. 

Our simultaneous communication of the plan agreed upon was made to 
Reshid Pasha officially on the 15th; and the manner in which his Highness 
received it is best described in the words of M. Pisani, a copy af whose report, 
together with a copy of my instruction to him, is inclosed herewith. 

As soon as possible after the decision to be taken by the General Council 
to-morrow on the broad question of peace or war, our note will be submitted by 
the Ottoman Seeretary of State to his colleagues in the ministry. Appearances 
are at present in favour of a pacific vote, but not with unanimity, nor without 
considerable opposition, 

The proposition in favour of peace will, if adopted, make room for a nego- 
tiation on the two conditions of evacuating the Principalities, and guarding Com- 
pletely the sovereign rights and independence of the Sultan. The hope which | 
entertain, incommon with Reshid Pasha, is that the adoption of such a basis by 
the General Council will enable him to prevail upon his colleagues to accept the 
proposal which he has already received from the Four Representatives. 

I have, &e. 
(Signed) STRATFORD DE REDCLIFFE,

M. E. Pisani to Lord Stratford de Redcliffe. 


My Lord, Pera, December 15, 1855. 


IN obedience to your Excellency’s instructions of yesterday's date, L waited 
upon Reshid Pasha and presented to his Highness, in concert with my colleagues 
of Austria, France, and Prussia, the identical note, dated the 12th instant, and 
signed by each of our respective chiefs. 

After attentively perusing the note, Reshid Pasha told us that he could not 
take upon himself to give any answer previously to communicating it to the 
Ministerial Council. That, as soon as the mecting of the General Council, which 
was to be convened on Saturday next, for the purpose of discussing the principle 
of peace so repeatedly recommended by the Four Powers, had come to some final 
conclusion, he would then submit to the consideration of his colleagues the basis 
proposed in the above-mentioned note.

Lord Stratford de Redcliffe to the Earl af Clarencdon.—( Received

(No. 891.) 


My Lord, Constantinople, December 17, 1893, 

1 RECEIVED yesterday from Lord Westmorland, in pursuance of your 
Lordship’s instructions, a collective note addressed to the Porte by the Repre- 
sentatives of the Four Powers at Vienna, acting together in the authorized 
eapacity of a resuscitated Conference, 

The sealed letter directed to Reshid Pasha, und containing the note in 
question, reached me at the same time, with a request that I would personally 
present itto his Highness, accompanied by my colleagues the French Ambassador, 
the Internuncio, and the Prussian Envoy. 

This note, suggesting the expediency of an early pacification, and inviting 
the Porte to state the terms on which it is disposed to negotiate with Russia, 
would, | conceive, be of questionable advantage under other circumstances ; but 
| do not hesitate to express my clear convietion that it could not be delivered to 
the Porte at this juncture without unsettling our prospects of peace, and rendering 
the acceptance of the projet, received on the 15th by Reshid Pasha from me and 
my colleagues, still more precarious and difficult than it is even now. Such is 
also the opinion of my colleagues. ‘The terms of the note are, doubtless, most 
considerate and flattering to the Turkish Government, but they afford, at the 
same time, so much encouragement to the pretensions ‘of the war party, that the 
communication of them could hardly fail to strengthen that interest, and to 
vender a successful negotiation more remote, At all events, by reserving its 
delivery we retain inour hands an cecasion for reopening the question of negotia- 
tion in the case of our pending proposal being declined. Such is, therefore, the 
course which I have determined to pursue, and [trust that it will meet with your 
Lordship's approval. 

I have, &c. 
(Signed) STRATFORD DE REDCLIFFE,

Lord Stratford de Redcliffe to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received 
January 4, 1854.) 


My Lord, Constuntinople, December 17, 1893. 


MUCH as | regret the necessity, and alive as Lam to the objections of 
more than one kind, I entertain, nevertheless, a decided opinion that reasors 
of a preponderating order require the appearance of the combined squadrons in 
the Black Gea, 1 cannot indeed conceal from myself that the late destruction 
of so many Turkish vessels at Sinope would probebly never have occurred if 
the ships of England and France had been sent thither at an earlier period. 
Not that 1 would throw the blame of that disaster anywhere but on the Porte 
and its officers. They alone, or their professional counsellors, were cognizant of 
the miserable state of the land defences at Sinope. ‘They alone are answerable 
for the obvious imprudence of leaving so long in helpless danger a squadron 
exposed to attack from hostile ships of far superior force. But referring to the 
simple fact, irrespective of its causes, 1 am naturally anxious that the loss of the 
example should not he added to that of the ships. 

We have learnt from an occurrence which cannot be sufficiently deplored, 
that the Russians are willing as well as able to attack: and destroy the Sultan's 
means of defence even in the fancied shelter of a port. ‘They have committed 
not only an act of overt hostility, but of direct aggression, on the Ottoman 
territory. Their commander was indeed most careful not to land, and he 
excused the rigours of his violence by presuming that the Turkish squadron 
had in view an ingurrection in Circassia, and by endeavouring on thiat 
presumption to. put his attack in the light of a defensive operation. But he 
seems to have forgotten that the Porte had been compelled to take up arins by 
the original siggression of Russia, and that a fresh violation of the Sultan’s 
territory was not to be justified by & supposed intention of counter erression, 
in principle defensive, on the part of His Majesty's forees. It is evident that, 
ifa British squedron had been eruizing off Sinope when the Russians advanced 
on their errand of destruction, it would have been the duty of its commander to 
‘aterpose for the protection of Her Majesty's ally, threatened in @ manner 

which involved the violation of his territorial rights ; and had the friendly inter- 
vention failed, ie would have felt. himself ultimately compelled to enforce it 
according to: his means, It is not hagarding too much to say, that in either 
ease the Sultan's successes on the frontier would not have been cancelled at once 
by the blow struck at Sinope. 

lt is true that what has been elected so cruelly there is not likely to he 
attempted again for the present in the same shape. 

Tat the Russians have a general interest in weakening their adversary. 
Since they frown upon his progress in peace, and thwart it as oceasions oOlfer, 
are they likely to neglect the opportunities which war presents of crippling his 
means and curtailing his power? ‘They have already been defeated in an attempt 
to land troops in the rear of the Turkish positions. ‘The attempt may be 
repeated by a disembarkation on ‘Turkish territory ; and on the same territory 
are defenceless: commercial towns and ports at best imperfectly protected, to 
say nothing of coul depots and building yards completely exposed, 

Your Lordship's instructions to me are positive as to the employment of 
Her Majesty's squadron for the protection of the Sultan's territory from direct 
ageression, and they are equally clear as to its passage into the Black Sea in the 
ayent of the Russian fleet coming out of Sevastopol. 

Now, the known facts, with respect to the latter point, are these; six sill 
of.thecline, half of them three deckers, have come out of Sevastopol at once, and 
stoam and sailing frigates from the same quarter are also known to have been 
at sea, partly in company with the liners, 

Surely adivision of such magnitude must be considered as constituting to ail 
iitents and purposes the fleet, ‘As to the aggression itself, it was not indeed 
accompanied with any landing of troops or occupation of the soil, But it was 
«direct attack on thé Sultan's means of defence within his territorial limits, and 
it involved the partial conflagration of a town, and the destruction of at least one 
‘noflensive merchant-vessel under British colours, to say nothing of the batteries.

So much for the facts, as cases in point and as warnings for the future 
But there is more, distinguishable indeed from proved fact, yet worthy of atten-

of British trading vessels have stated that they saw a Russian fleet-—one asserts 
of twelve or more sail-of-the-line—about nine days ago at sea, in the neighbour- 
hood of the Crimea. Another has deposed to haying seen six sail-of-the-line on 
the afternoon of the 9th instant between Samsoon and Sinope, and the dista 
he adds, was such that there might have been more. AM 
_ From all that precedes it appears that the cases for which your Lordship's 
instructions provided have actually occurred, that a severe loss which a timely

aggressive operations by Russia in some shape or other. ae

the late tempestuous weather. oe ea

judgment which later times will pronounce upon our conduet at this unpre-

squadrons into the Black Sea now, I feel that an explanation of the causes 
which restrained them from going sooner, might be more reasonably expected 
The causes in question may be reduced to the following heads ; want of bale 
information as to the movements of the Russian fleet, an unwillingness to 
incur any risk of collision, or to narrow the claims of peace by premature

departure of one French Ambassador and the arrival of another, pe

Lord Stratford de Redeliffe to Vice-Admiral Dundas. 


Sit, British Embassy, December 11, 1853. 
IT’ is my opinion, under the instructions which | have received from the 
Karl of Clarendon, that the appearance of the combined squadrons, or of an 
adequate portion of them, in the Black Sea, can be no longer deferred without 
prejudice to the important interests which their union is intended to protect. 

Having conferred with the French Ambassador on the subject, | have reason 
to believe that his Excellency writes to Viee-Admiral Hamelin in a similar sense. 
We think, morcover, while submitting to your judgment and to that of your 
French colleague whatever concerns the ne performance of this service, that 
supposing the Russian squadron no longer at sea, the object in view would be 
sufficiently attained if the ships of the two Governments were to pass along the 
coasts of Turkey as far as Varna on the European side, and as far as Sinope on 
that of Asia. 

Her Majesty's Government being at peace with Russia, it is obviously 
desirable that, in redeeming the pledge of territorial protection given to the 
Porte, no kind of unnecessary provocation should be offered to the Russian 
authorities. You will doubtless agree with me that, in order to avoid even the 
semblance of any offensive intention while a hope of negotiation remains, tt 
would be advisable for the ships under your command to keep out of sight of the 
Russian coast, and even in crossing the Black Sea, when necessary, to take sucli 
course us would be least likely, in case of bad weather and strong winds, to cause 
any exception to that rule, 

The same principle holds good with respect to any Russian vessels which 
vou may meet at sea, Communication, when not to be avoided, 1s, of course, to 
be conducted as long as possible in the most friendly forms, even should it be 
requisite to interpose for the protection of the Sultan's territory from direct 
aggression and overt hostility, or for that of any Turkish vessel which, to avoid 
an imminent peril of capture, may have taken refuge beneath your guns. 

In these two cases, as in that of being attacked, a resort to force may be 
miata unavoidable, but to justify its employment the necessity must be 
clear, 

__ Thave finally to request that, in concert with Vice-Admiral Hamelin, you 
will take meusures for giving effect the onjest of this despatch. 
I have, &

My Lord, Constantinople, December 18, 1853. 

| HAVE the honour to report that the General Council which met to-day 
for the second time has come to the decision that peace should be concluded 
with Russia on the following bases, namely: immediate evacuation of the 
Principalities by the Russian troops; preservation of the sovereign rights 
unimpaired; and a guarantee from the Four Powers for the future. 

Having asked for explanation as to the nature of the guarantee expected 
by the Council, Reshid Pasha replied, that the note given in lately by the Four 
Representatives provides for that contingency.

My Lord, Constantinople, December 23, 1853. 


DURING. the last three days the Turkish capital has been in a state which 
threatened insurrection. The Softas, or religious students, took umbrage at the 
acific decision adopted by the General Council, and formed themselves into 
assemblies of an illegal character; expressed. loudly their discontent ; and 
threatened to wreak their vengeance on Reshid Pasha and other obnoxious 
Ministers. [tis supposed that they were secretly encouraged by Mehemet Ali 
Pasha, the Seraskier, and perhaps also by the Sheik-ul-Islam ; the former heing 
loader of the war party, the latter ‘nelined to temporize with the fanatics. 

Early the day betore yesterday, information reached me to that effect, and 
‘¢ was soon followed by alarming statements of intended violence, including the 
conflagration of the city and the massacre of its Christian inhabitants. ‘These 
reports, with other indications of terror, came ‘nso thick that, even making 
allowance for much probable exaggeration, it became a duty to lose no time in 
adopting precautionary measare. Such as it was in my power to take, | there- 
fore took, but with as little display or demonstration of alarm as possible. ‘The 
diplomatic body assembled at my house; addressed, with their sanction, 
letter—copy inclosed lerewith—to the Ottoman Secretary of State; and 
steamers from the British and French squadrons were prepared for any service 
which might be required. 

Before long it became evident that the danger was less urgent than had 
hoen at first apprehended ; and on sending to the Porte, I found that, although 
the Ministers were not there, the streets were free from tumult, and the autho- 
rities prepared to maintain order. I could not, however, learn tll late in the 
evening where Reshid Pasha, who had left his house im the morning, was to be 
found. 

At an early hour next morning I went to see that Minister, who had taken 
refuge in his son's house at a distance from the city, and not far from the 
Sultan's palace. While | was listening to his recital of the late occurrences, and 
to his opinion of their cause, @ miessage arrived from the President of the 
Council, to inform tim that the Soltas were etill in a state of agitation and 
disobedience to the Government; that the effects of their example upon the 
more dangerous classes of the populace were to be apprehended; and that 
doubts were entertained of the steadiness of the troops. It was clearly the 
opinion of both Ministers that the factions were encouraged by the intrigues of 
Mohemet Ali, and the favour of the Sheik-ul-Islam. There was reason, more- 
aver, to fear that the Sultan hesitated to take those decisive measures which 
were required hy the continuance of danger, notwithstanding the advice given 
by Reshid Pasha to: His Majesty on the preceding day, and seconded, more or 
less, by his colleagues in office. 

Conce'ving that under such circumstances there was but one course to 
pursue, and that further indecision would endanger the most vital interests, and 
render every immediate chance of peace impossible, { went at once to the 
Soraulio, and requested a private audience of the Sultan, His Majesty having 
received me with his usual affability, [ made no secret of what T understood to 
be the real state of things, and placed before him in strong colours the absolute 

necessity of acting with vigour and determination, 80 48 to leave no time for the 
rebellion to gather strength and to assume more formidable proportions. 

I will not trouble your Lordship with the details of a long conversation, 
whieh showed that His Majesty was by no means insensible to the demands 
upon his resolution, though not perhaps thoroughly aware of those tendencies 
whieh called for an immediate exereise of his authority. ‘The interview ended 
by an assurinee fron His Majesty that he would forthwith order the measures 
which T had recommended to be carried into effect 5 and that he would himself 
pass over into lis elty palace in order to make an additional impression on his 
subjects, He informed me ut the same time that he had decided on giving his

SINCE | addressed your Lordship last week relative to—what I still con- 
ceive to be most desirable—the appearance of the combined squadrons in the 
Black Sea, | have had several communications on that subject, partly in writing, 
and partly by word of mouth, with General Baraguay d’Hilliers. 

Vice-Admiral Hamelin’s reply to the letter, which he addressed to that 
officer at the same time that | wrote to Vice-Admiral Dundas in the terms 
already known to your Lordship, lus had, to all uppearance, the effect of indis- 
posing him completely to the measure which 1 recommended, and which | con- 
ceived at one time that he also was inclined to adopt. All | know of Admiral 
Hamelin’s letter is that it points out the risk of sending line-of-battle ships 
under gail into the Black Sea at his time of year; that the efficiency of the 
squadrons might, in his judgment, be impaired by exposure to that risk; and 


448 


that Admiral Dundas coneurs in opinion with his colleague, although he has 
declared his readiness to go out with his squadron, if required. 

My reasons for wishing the squadrons to cruize, notwithstanding the 
chances to be apprehended in navigating the Black Sea at this season, are fully 
stated to your Lerdship in another part of my correspondence. They are not 
diminished. On the contrary, the complete ascendancy of Russia in the Black 
Sea, and its effect in paralyzing every movement and enterprize of the Turkish 
Government in that quarter, become more palpable and embarrassing with each 
successive day. It is even reported, within the last cight-and-forty hours, that 
three Russian sail-of-the-line have been scen off the entrance of the Bosphorus ; 
hut of this report I cannot speak with any degree of certainty. My reasons for 
not having issued a peremptory instruction are, first, my unwillingness to pro- 
claim either a marked dissent from our allies, or an offensive confidence in our 
naval superiority ; secondly, a reluctance to expose our squadron to the hazard 
of encountering, single-handed, the whole fleet of Sevastopol; and thirdly, 
a natural regard for the joint opinion declared by the two Admirals. 

The result of my latter communications with the French Ambassador is 
still incomplete, Though his Excellency appears to have made up his mind as 
to the inexpediency of sending out the French line-of-battle ships, he is ready to 
join in sending out a combined force of steam-trigates, and he would also send 
out a single vessel under French colours with any ships of ours in order to give 
public evidence of agreement. He propases at the same time that single steam- 
vessels of each nation should be stationed in turn at Sinope on the one side, and 
at Varna or Bourgas on the other. o 

To the latter very limited precaution Tam far from objecting, provided it 
be not meant to supersede a more efficient arrangement of the forces. 

Nor do I object to sending out the steamers alone, if the Admirals declare 
their opinion that a force of that description would suffice to accomplish the 
object of your Lordship’s instructions, | mean, the protection of the Ottoman 
territory against any act of direct ageression or overt hostility on the part of 
Itusaia, ‘The measure, even if it were satisfactory in that respect, would, 
however, be attended with the disadvantage of taking from the Bosphorus 
exactly that part of each squadron which is most likely to-be wanted there, At 
all events | have submitted the question, which ts a purely professional one, to 
Viec- Admiral Dundas, and I wait his reply. 

Whatever resolution may finally be taken here, it will be highly desirable 
forme to learn as soon as possible the views of Her Majesty’s Government 
respecting the several points which I have mentioned as causing a divergence of 
opinion between me and my colleagucs. Circumstances have compelled us to 
moot them, and I greatly doubt the possibility of our arriving at any agreement 
calculated to mect the exigencies of the case, I have reason to believe that 
General Baraguay has already written home for instructions. 

L have, &e. 
(Signed) STRATFORD DE REDCLIFFE.
