(No, 399.) 
My Lord, Constantinople, December 26, 1853. 
AT an carly hour to-day I sent to Reshid Pasha requesting that no further 
delay might iake place, now that order was restored through the capital, in 
coming toa decision on the subject of the proposed a alasene Linvited my 
colleagues to send a message of similar purport to his Highness. The result of 
the several applications addressed to him, is, that to-morrow, if possible, or 
i day or two luter if necessary, the proposals sent in to him by the Four 
Representatives on the 15th instant shall be taken into consideration by the 
Council of Ministers. 
The Pasha exeused his inability to meet our wishes to-day on the ground 
of some remaining apprehension us to the tranquillity of the capital, It appears 


449 


that although 170 of the Softas were shipped off for Candia yesterday, those 
who remain have ventured to express their discontent. It has consequently 
been deemed prudent to keep a part of the troops under arms and to extend the 
number of arrests ‘The Ministers were to assemble forthwith at the Porte, anil 
certain known ringleaders, six in number, were to be placed under arrest anc 
brought before the Council. 

Upon the whole, I see no reason to apprehend any disturbance of a more 
serious kind, and if the Ministers accept our proposals and the Sultan takes 
measures to reform his Ministry, | hope a more steady and cheerful state of 
things will ensue. For the moment there is much to regret in the general 
interruption of business which has attended the disorderly manazuvres of the 
last three days. Not only is the matter of paramount importance retarded, 
but every kind of pending affair has undergone 4 total stoppage. 

The French Ambassador, who saw Reshid Pasha this morning, has sent me 
word that appearances are less favourable to our views than before the late 
disturbance: but M. Pisani, who saw his Highness and other members of the 
Government after the Ambassador's departure, assures me that he entertains 
little or no doubt that our proposals will be accepted. 

I have, &e. 
(Signed) STRATFORD DE REDCLIFFE.

(No. 400.) 
My Lord, Constantinople, December 24, 1853. 

| HAVE received from M. Pisani the report, dated yesterday, of which a 
copy is inclosed herewith. Its object is important, and the interests of peace are 
perhaps involved in its accomplishment. It serves to set im a strong light the 
disadvantages accruing to Turkey from the undisputed ascendancy enjoyed by 
Russia in the Black Sea. 1am extremely anxious to relieve the Porte from ail 
embarrassment which presses so heavily on her means of defence, and exposes 
her to more than one kind of danger. But as at present advised, I eaunot per 
ceive any mode, unless it be that of sending out the squadrons in full foree, by 
which the Porte ean be enabled to transfer her suspected troops to Trebizond 
without an imminent danger of having them taken in the course of their voyage 
by a Russian squadron. If British ships were to convey, or to convey them to 
the place of disembarkation, Her Majesty’s Government would incur the charge 
of taking a hostile part against Russia without 4 declaration of war; and if they 
went out with a force nnequal to meet the flect at Sevastopol, they might be 
obliged to witness the destraction or capture of their friends, without being able 
to make an effort for their escape. -

No, 568, 
Sir G. H. Seymour to the Earl of Clarendon.—( Received January 4, 1854.) 


(No. 754. Confidential.) 
My Lord, St. Petersburgh, December 26, 1854, 

THE French Minister has shown me in strict confidence a very important 
despatch, dated the 15th instant, which he has received from his Government, 
respecting the effect produced in France by the news of the destruction of the 
Turkish ships at Sinope, and the resolution taken in consequence of despatching 
the fleet into the Black Sea. The measure has for its object the security to be 
afforded to the Turkish ships destined to carry supplies (ravitailler) to the 
Turkish fortresses on the const, and its necessity is explained to be the more 
urgent from the disregard of the national feeling of England and France evinced 
by the late attack of the Russians upon a squadron in its own waters, and those 
understood to be placed under the allied protection. 

M. Drouyn de Lhuys’ despatches contained an extract of that addressed by 
him to Count Walewski on the 12th instant, and the copy of another addressed 
to Baron Bourqueney, the last manifesting the warm satisfaction of the Emperor 
Napoleon at the concurrence of the Austrian Cabinet in the policy of France on 
the Mastern question. 

[allude to these despatches chiefly for the purpose of remarking that, far 
from offering any evidence of an intention on the part of the French Cabinet to 
separate their interests from those of Her Majesty's Government, they afford 
satisfactory proof of the unity of purpose which animates the two Governments, 

This circumstance confirms my original notion as to the letter of congratula- 
tion addressed by General Custelbajuc to the Chancellor having been an act of 
personal indiseretion not to be considered as indicative of a change of policy on 
the part of the French Cabinet, 

It was not difficult to perceive that the intention of entering the Black Sea, 
announced to my colleague, and which, | may observe, he is not directed to notice 
to the Russian Government, was very unwelcome intelligence ; this feeling being 
created, first, by an honest belief in the statement of the Russian authorities, 
according to which the attack upon the Turkish ships was a defensive act, 
destined to prevent the conveyance of military stores to the mountaineers of the 
Caucasus; and secondly, by the apprehension that no armed resistance offered 
to Russia by France and England will be supported eventually by the two 
German Governments, 

To these motives may be added another: the eonviction entertained by 
General Castelbajac that the fullest confidence may be placed in the Emperor's 
assurances of seeking neither territorial aggrandizement or extension of 
inthuence. 

This confidence, as 1 have repeatedly explained to my colleague, it is not in 
my power Lo share, 

Extension of influence is the point avowedly aimed at ; extension of territory 
has not uncommonly been obtained by Russia in the face of very positive 
declarations. 

[ will only add that, in speaking as i lave spoken of late of the French 
Envoy, | have, as T beg vour Lordship to believe, done great violence to my 
own techngs. 

1 may safély assert that | should prefer being removed from my post to 


452 


running the risk of injuring @ very worthy man, with whom Tam living upon 
terms of amity and confidence ; but the magnitude of the interests at stake have 
left me no choice of conduct. 

The difficulties of the moment are immense, and all the zeal and hearty 
eooperation which can be given by their servants to the Governments of Her 
Majesty and of France are required for giving a fair chance of their views being 
carried out. | 

I have, &c. 
(Signed) G. H. SEYMOUR.

(No, 755. Secret and Confidential.) 
My Lord, St. Petersburgh, December 26, 1853. 


A PERSON thoroughly attached to English interests sends me word that 
I may take for certain that orders have been sent to General Grimewald to use 
every exertion for the purchase, in the United States, of eighteen screw 
steamers (vaisseaux a hélice), which are required, with the least possible delay, 
for service in the Black Sea. + pee

YOUR Lordship's wishes as to the frankness to be observed towards the

The language which | held to his Exeelleney when [ waited upon him the

Dismiss, I entreat of you, from your mind the unfounded notion of the

My Lord, St. Petersburgh, December 26, 1853, 

1 HAVE just learned upon excellent authority that the Government have 
ardered the construction of cighty gun-boats, which are to be ready for delivery 
at Cronstadt, if the river is open, in the month of April. 

It has been intimated to the contractors that a further number may be 
required, 

Rach boat is to be armed with two pieces of cannon, one forward, the other 
ab the stern. 

Any measures taken for the security of the Russian coasts and harbours of 
Russia may, I think, be viewed with indifference, exeept in so far as that 
invasion is hardly to be apprehended, except under circumstances which may 
justify an attack on the part of foreign Powers; the ease, however, is widely 
different with regard to the large steam foree which it is undoubtedly the 
purpose of Russia to form, and which, as she possesses neither foreign trade or 
colonies, can hardly be destined for other than offensive purposes. 

The creation of an immense steam fleet is the object upon which the Grand 
Duke Constantine is the most intent,and the great influence which he has of late 
established over the Emperor renders it probable, if not certain, that the object 
will be carried out. |

457 


received by the French Government, refers solely to the pending negotiations 
between the Porte and the Four Powers, and to the disturbances which had inter- 
rupted the progress of them. M. Drouyn de Lhiuys, however, was evidently 
ill at ease while conversing’ with me. He read me various passages from his 
own instructions to General Baraguay d’Hilliers, and from those of the Minister 
of Marine to Admiral Hamelin, in order to prove that the intentions of the 
French Government could not be doubtful, and that the French fleet ought to 
have entered the Black Sea. He frankly admitted that the proceedings at Con- 
stantinople were inconsistent with the language of the Government at Paris, and 
he seemed aware of the false construction which might be placed in the East, on 
the conduct of the combined squadrons. In fact, my Lord, I gathered from 
M. Drouyn de Lhuys’ observations, that he was deeply mortified at what had 
oceurred, but that he had neither the Ambassador nor the Admiral under his 
control. 

Your Lordship will naturally inquire how this can be, and | can only answer, 
that it proceeds from the natural defects of the French Government and of the 
French character. There is no unity of action among the members of the Govern- 
ment, no concert, no interchange of opinions; each department acts for itself, 
without reference to others; and cach Minister is as jealous of an interference with 
what he considers his prerogatives, as he is determined to make use of them. 
Hence, when two or more departments are concerned in the same business, all 
is confusion. It is probable that General Baraguay d’Hilliers, besides the 
instructions which he received from M. Drouyn de Lhuys, had orders from the 
Emperor, from the Minister of War, and from the Minister of Marine, each of 
them drawn up with some difference of expression and colouring. Admiral 
Hamelin, without doubt, is in the same position. Then comes into play the 
vanity of the French character, the rivalry of the military and naval professions 
at Constantinople, and the dishke of both to be under the direction ot a civilian. 
In short, if your Lordship saw behind the seenes, as | sometimes do, you would 
be astonished that, in complicated questions with the French Governinent, any 
progress is made at all. 

The report, which I mentioned above as having been received from General 
Baraguay d’Hilliers, agrees, in all essential points, with the report of Lord 
Stratford upon the same subject; but it wakes mention of a change in the 
Ottoman Ministry to which Lord Stratford does not advert, unless, in the 
hurry under which I was necessitated to read the Constantinople despatches, | 
aveclonked a passage concerning it. General Baraguay says that Riza Pasha 
had been made Capitan Pasha, and Halil Pasha admitted into the Sultan’s 
Councils. 

In a postscript the General acknowledges a receipt of a telegraphic despatch 
of M, Drouyn de Lhuys of the 14th ultimo, which was written after the news of 
the disaster of Sinope, and reiterated the order for the French fleet to enter the 
Black Sea. It does not appear, however, to have had any effect, as a 
telegraphic despatch from Constantinople of the 26th announces the seceptance 
by the Porte of the propositions of the Four Powers, but does not mention the 
fleets.

stating the embarrassments under which the Porte labours as to removing 
to Trebizond 10,000 Rediffs and 1,500 irregulars whose presence in the capital 
appears dangerous to the public peace, it is the opinion of Her Majesty's 
Government that if the instructions of which your Excellency is in possession 
are carried out, and the British and French fleets have the command of the 
Black Sea, these troops may safely be conveyed in Turkish vessels; but it must 
be distinctly understood that they are to go to Trebizond, and are not to eornmit 
any act of aggression in the Russian territory. 

If the Turkish Government desire that their vessels while employed on 
this duty should receive further protection than that which I have indicated 
above, your Excellency in conjunction with the French Ambassador and the 
Admirals will make such arrangements for the purpose as the good of the 
service will permit; or if a sufficient British and French force should not be 
available for this special duty, your Excellency will inform the Sultan's 
Ministers of the reasons which prevent your complying eae request.

(No, 25.) 
My Lord, Paris, January 8, 1854. 

| HAD a few days ago some further conversation with M. Drouyn de 
Lhuys, as to the course to be adopted by the Conference at Vienna whenever 
the answer of the Porte to the cotumunication sent from Vienna on the 5th 
ultimo should be received. 

M. Drouyn de Lhuys said that, in his opinion, something must depend 
upon the proceedings of the Four Representatives at Constantinople, According 
to the information which we had received at the present moment, they, having 
commenced a negotiation with the Porte before the reeeipt of the Vienna 
propositions, had judged it advisable to leave those propositions in abeyance ; 
but circumstances might since have oceurred to render, in their opinion, the 
presentation of the collective note necessary. In that case, he continued to 
think that a similar mode of ccmmunicating with the Cabinet of St. Petersburgh 
should be adopted. If, on the other hand, the Representatives at Constan- 
tinople had transmitted to Vienna the result of their negotiations with the Porte, 
as an answer to the propositions of the Conference, without having presented 
the collective note, he was of opinion that the Conference should accept it as an 
answer, consign it to a protocol, in which they should declare that it ought to 
satisfy the Russian Government, and leave Count Buol, if he wished it, to 
be the channel of communicating the opinion of the Conference to Count 
Nesselrode. 

I observed that another course might be taken by the Representatives at 
Constantinople. As they had not acted on behall of the Conference, they might 
make no answer to the overtures of that body, but might address the result of

enable it to make the contemplated communication ta St. Petersburgh. A

Lord Cowley to the Earl of Clarendon,—( Received January !0-) 


(No. 27.) 

My Lord, Paris, January 9, 1854. 
M, DROUYN DE LHUYS has received a despatch from M. de 

Bourqueney, dated the Srd instant, mentioning the extreme susceptibility 

shown by the Emperor of Austria at not having been informed of the intentions 


465 


of England and France to gend their squadrons into the Black Sea, previously to 
the execution of that measure. His Majesty appears to have said that this 
mark of confidence was due to him, considering that since the 5th December 
the Four Powers had been acting in concert. 

In a telegraphic despatch of the Sth instant, M. de Bourqueney announces 
that his own instructions relative to the movement of the fleets had at length 
reached him, and that he had communicated them to Count Buol, and that he 
could assure M. Drouyn de Lhuys that the Austrian Government, although 
not prepared for the lengths to which the two Governments had gone, would not 
separate from them in consequence. 

M. Drouyn de Lhuys purposes answering the Emperor of Austria's 
reproachful observations, by remarking that every deference had been shown to 
to the Austrian Government by communicating to them the instructions sent to 
St. Petersburgh and Constantinople, on the very day on which they were 
expedited ; that there were two sides to the Eastern question, the diplomatic and 
the military ; that France was engaged in the one with Austria, England and 
Prussia—in the other with England alone; that the object of the one was to 
restore peace between Russia and Turkey, the object of the other, the defence 
of the ‘Turkish territory from Russian ageression; and that until Austria 
declared herself ready to aid in the latter, she could not expect to be consulted 
on the measures necessary to insure its success. 

| observed that he might add that the instructions now sent were but a 
complement to those which had been issued long before the establishment of a 
Conference at Vienna, and which, if they had been acted upon, would have 
produced nearly the same state of affairs as existed now ; besides, what was the 
use of consulting other Governments, unless we intended to listen to their 
advice, a course clearly impossible so Tong as the intentions of the Conference 
were pacific only? Moreover, untess the statement had been made too con- 
fidentially to allow of its mention in an official despatch, Count Buol might be 
reminded that both he and M, de Hiibner had insinuated that the inactivity of 
the fleets was serving the war party in Russia. 

I have, &e.

The Earl af Westmorland to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received January 10.) 


(No. 4.) 
My Lord, Vienne, January 4, 1854. 


UPON the receipt of your Lordship’s despatel No, 420, I waited upon 
Count Buol in pursuance of the ‘nstructions contained in it, and 1 read to him 
first the despatch No, 345 addressed to Sir H. Seymour, and next the one 
addressed to Lord Stratford No. 32). 

Count Buol remarked upon the language of the former, particularly the 
expression '*taking command of the Black Sea and requiring, and, if 
necessary compelling, the Russian ships of war to return to Sevastopol, or the 
nearest Russian port.”’ He expressed surprise ut these strong declarations, and 
stated that although he was fully prepared for the entry of the combined fleets 
into the Black Sea, with a view of establishing a state of neutrality between the 
belligerents, he was not prepared to expect that they would be directed to use 
coercion against the Russian ships of war while navigating upon their own coasts 
in the manner deseribed, 

With respect to the despatch addressed to Lord Stratford, Count Buol 
observed that while the same language was adopted as. to the operations of the 
fleets, yet he saw with satisfaction that the Governments of England and France 
adhered to the position in which they were at present placed with respect to 
Austria and Prussia, and that by the words, “ It was the duty of the English and 
French Governments, aud their right, to demand the acceptance by the Porte of 
the proposals recently made by the Four Powers,” they gave undoubted assurances 
that the two Gavernments still looked to the re-establishment of peace, and to 
the maintenance of the union which ney existed between the Four Powers, 

5 ay 


i 


466 


Count Buol stated that he cordially adopted these views. He looked upon the 
continuance of that union a5 most essential to the best interests of the Powers 
engaged in it, and he would use every effort to maintain it and to secure its 
SUCCESS. vet ahh ! 

| stated to Count Buol that in judging of the measures which the Govern- 
ments of England and. France had now adopted, he must bear in mind that 
they considered the attack upon the Turkish squadron in Sinope as an offence 
which they were called upon to resent, and it was because the Austrian and 
Prussian Governments had not the same cause for action, that they had 
ahetained from secking to make them a party to the measures which had now 
heen adopted, but he might rely upon i that both those Governments were as 
little desirous of going to war at present, as they had been at any time since the 
commencement of the unfortunate discussions between the Governments of 
Russia and the Porte. 

Count Buol acknowledged the explanation which I had thus given for 
not calling upon the Austrian and Prussian Governments to be parties to the 
decisions which had been taken; but he thought that it might have been 
considered as an understanding between the Four Powers, that while they were 
engaged in a mediation for peace, which appeared at present. to promise some 
success, time should have been given to ascertain its result, without endangering 
the common action by any act which might be construed by Russia as an 
operation of war. 

Count Buol felt that the more decided and menacing position which the 
Governments of England and France had now taken by their declarations to 
Russia would render it more essential that any pacific offers which might be 
transmitted from Constantinople, should in the first instance be recommended 
by Austria as the channel through which the proposal to treat for peace had 
been transmitted from Russia, He was satisfied, from the reports he had 
received from the Internuncio, that no reply from the Porte would be directed to 
the Conference, but that it would be addressed to the Representatives at 
Constantinople, who would transmit it to their Governments. Tle should 
therefore, upon the receipt of this communication, and as the mode which 
would offer the greatest chance of success. submit it to the Conference, and if it 
was judged of such a nature as to be recommended, he should consult with 
them as to the nature of the announcement he should make to the Russian 
Cabinet, but he should transmit it without delay to 5t. Petersburgh, and he would 
employ every means in his power to obtain its weceptation, 

T had yesterday a second interview with Count Buol at which 1 read o 
him the statements | have thus given to your Lordship of his remarks, and he 
said that so soon as he received the communication of a similar nature which 
he was-expecting from Baron Bourqueney, he would instruct Count Colloredo 
to convey to your Lordship the sane sentiniants. 

Upon the receipt of your Lordship’s despatch on Monday, before I waited 
upon Count Buol, aay Mf. de Bourqueney and informed him of the nature 
of the communications | was directed to make; and immediately after my 
interview with Count Buol, | reported to him the observations which his 
Excellency had made with regard to them, M, de Bourquency had not then 
-eceived hie instructions from Paris. He has been in hourly expectation of them 
ever since, more particularly as their general purport 1s in the newspapers;

My Lord, Berlin, January 8, 1854, 

THE Marquis de Moustier, the French Minister at this Court, has lately 
communicated to Baron Manteuffel, us also to myself, various despatches which 
he has received from his Government relating to the Hastern question. 

Some of these despatches referred to the communication which had taken 
place between the French and Austrian Cabinets with respect to the mode of 
negotiation between Russia and Turkey, aud were explanatory of a divergence 
of opinion which had apparently ated ns to the necessity of those differences 
being regulated in a joint Conference of the Six Powers; or in a negotiation 
between Russia and ‘Turkey at some given place, under the auspices of the 
present Conference now sitting at Vienna. 

it is not necessary that | should refer more minutely to these documents, 
as your Lordship will have had cognizance of them from other quarters. 

Other despatches have been communicated by M. de Moustier to Baron 
Manteuffel pourtraying the cordial union and understanding existing between 
England and France, giving assurances to Prussia that she had no reason to fear 
the policy of France towards herself; stating that France would not abandon 
her; and donlarin if not in the following very precise terms, in language almost 
analogous, “ que la France et l'Angleterre irant ensemble jusqu'an bout, et se 
trouveront alors avec tous ceux qui n'auraient pas arrétés moitié chemin.” 

The Marquis de Moustier has stated to me his satisfaction at the language 
which Baron Manteuffel has on each occasion held to him, He has, likewise, 
communicated to his Excellency copy of the instructions which have been 
forwarded to General Baraguay d'Hilhers, and which he states arc identical with 
those which are transmitted to Viscount Stratford de Redelifle by your 
Lordship.

I take this opportunity of stating to your Lordship that the language held

Sir G, H. Seymour to the Earl of Clarendon,—(Received January 10, 1654.) 


(No. 771.) 
My Lord, St. Petersburgh, December 31, 185d. 

YOUR Lordship’s telegraphic despatch of the 22nd instant desires me to 
« endeavour to find out whether the instructions to the British Admiral, which 
| communicated to Count Nesselrode on the 20th of October, were made known 
to the Russian Admiral in the Black Sea,” 

1 must candidly admit to your Lordship my imability to reply to this 
inquiry. The secrecy observed in the public offices of this country 1s such that 
not only is one department kept in ignorance of what 1s passing in another, to a 
degree Which is constantly injurious to the service, but the employes of the same 
department or office are prohibited from communicating to one another the 
iuusiness in which they are severally engaged. 

My belief is, that it would be contrary to Russian practice that the 
Government should make known to their Admirals the information which they 
receive from foreign Missions with regard to the orders sent to the Commanders 
of foreign fleets; but 1 do not doubt that such information would materially 
‘nfluence the orders dispatched by the Government to these their own servants, 

Your Lordship may have observed that my prepossessions in favour of the 
Russian Government are not strong; that I am not prone to take the defence 
of their acts; but | may take this opportunity for stating my belief that, upon 
the present occasion, more blame has been awarded to them than is their due. 

‘As the Russian Government is very anxious to avoid, more especially for 
the present moment, the chance of a collision with England and France, | can 
hardly believe that the destruction of the Turkish ships at Sinope was intended 
as a bravado, the object of which was to bring the intentions of the allied fleets 
to a test; and | am much more disposed to believe that the Russian Govern- 
ment were intent upon preventing supplies being afforded to a warlike population 
in districts in which, as Russia may find to her cost, she is very assailable, 
Unless I grossly err, the Russian Government are still under the conviction of 
the ‘Turkish squadron having been engaged in the conveyance of such supplies 
to the tribes of the Caueasus ; but even supposing this belief to be erroneous, | 
would submit to your Lordship that the Russians are rather to be regarded as 
having been reckless in their wish to inflict injury upon an enemy, than as 
having sought an occasion for converting doubtiul friends into open opponents, 

I have, &c. 
(Signed) G. H. SEYMOUR.

No. 599. 
Sir G, H. Seymour to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received January 10.) 


(No. 5. Most Confidential.) 


My Lord, St. Petersburgh, January 2, 1854. 

MY French colleague appears to disapprove highly of the measure taken by 
Her Majesty's Government and that of France, and has explained his views to 
me in a very long conversation, of which I feel myself the more called upon to 
give your Lordship an outline as he acquaints me that he has made known his 
opinions to his Cabinet. 

General Castelbajac considers the dispatch of the combined fleets into the 
Black Sea to be unfortunate, because he regards the measure as directed against 
the intentions imputed to the Emperor of despoiling Turkey, intentions which 
he is convinced do not exist. 

But even were it otherwise, General Castelbajac is of opinion that, asa 
ensure either of intimidation or of offence, it will fail in its object. 

The flects might take any Russian ships that were found in the Black Sea ; 
might ravage the coast; might possibly, but not probably, be able to destroy 
Sevastopol; but these reverses would not be felt sensibly by the Russian nation, 
and would not prevent the Emperor from continuing to occupy the Prinei- 
palities. 

To dislodge the Russian forces from these provinces an immense force 
would be required, and France and England cannot send the requisite number 
of troops to such a distant battle. 

Were Austria and Prussia to join England and France in their armed 
exertions, then indeed General Castelbajac admits that the Russian troops would 
be compelled to withdraw within their frontiers, but no such cooperation is to be 
expected. 

The two German Powers may unite with us in signing Notes and Protocols, 
but will never take the resolution of engaging with us in war against the Emperor 
Nicholas. 

A schism then would be made between the West and the North of Europe ; 
a war utterly destructive to Turkey, and jnjurious to the other Powers engaged, 
would then be carried on; and the evils of this war would press less heavily 
upon Russia than upon the other belligerents. 

Russia, too, ig now in a bad position, has lost all the “ prestige” attached 
to the Emperor's reign, and is opposed, in greater or less degree, by the Four 
Great Powers: if war were to be carried on, it might have the result of retrievitig 
a portion of her former character, and it might convert two of the Powers whe 
now oppose her into close allies. 

‘The conclusion at whieh General Castelbajac arrives is this, that Russia 
being in a bad position should be left there, and with this view that every 
exertion should be made for the conclusion of peace. 

To obtain this result, he argues that slight ceremony should be observed 
towards the Turks; that instead of being as he terms it “4 la remorque de la 
Turquie,” the Allied Powers should sienify very authoritatively what conditions 
they are willing to obtain for her, and that the great principle to be kept in view 
should be the fullest territorial guarantees to be given to the Porte, and some 
satisfaction as to the protection to be secured to the Greek subjects of the Porte 
to be given to the Emperor of Russia. 

‘This satisfaction, which constitutes the real difficulty of the whole question, 
the French Envoy disposes of in an off-hand manner, describing it #5 something 
which may satisfy the subjects of His depen Majesty, high-sounding phrases 

i) 


474 


(des expressions rouflantes’’), a something gratifying to Russian vanity, and 
not really injurious to Turkish interests. 

Upon finding that General Castelbajac’s views differed so much from my 
own, and that the arguments which I made use of had little effect in reconciling 
our opinions, I observed at last that, assuming even that he was quite right and 
myself equally in the wrong, he must see that his observations and objections 
were out of date, and that measures had been taken by our Governments which 
could not be receded from with honour. 

To this my colleague replied, that he could only see with his eyes and judge 
according to his judgment , that the views which he had before glanced at and 
now more fully entered into, were those which he conscientiously held, and con- 
sequently that, whether they were to give satisfaction or offence, he could not 
do otherwise than submit them to his Government. 

This he had already done, his despatch must by this time have been 
received at Paris. 

I have, &c. 
(Signed) G. H. SEYMOUR.

My Lord, St. Petersburgh, January 2, L854. 


WHEN I waited upon the Chancellor on the 30th ultimo, he inquired 
with some eagerness whether f had any communication to make te him upon 
the subject of the entry of the allied fleets into the Black Sea. 

| replied that 1 had not, but that, as 1 had before stated, they were to be 
expected there. 

Count Nesselrode inquired with what intent? To which I replied by 
adverting to the feeling which had been produced in England and France by the 
affair of Sinope, and by saying that it might be assumed that it was intende 
to take measures for preventing the recurrence of a similar catastrophe. 

In the course of an amicable conversation which ensued, Count Nesselrode 
expressed his belief that the Russian fleet would in consequence of the advanced 
season be little likely to leave Sevastopol. He spoke likewise of the possible 
operations of the English and French ships, observing that if it were intended 
that their presence in the Black Sea should prevent the ‘Turks from being 
attacked by the Russians, there would be little justice in the proceeding, unless 
+t were likewise proposed that the Turks should be restrained from molesting the 
coast of Russia. 

I replied that upon this and other points of the kind I had no information 
to offer, but that it was not likely that a Power so eager for peace as England, 
a Power which hind recommended the Turks to cone ude an armistice with a 
view to peace, should come forward to promote warlike operations, but certainly 
that the defence of Turkey was an object never lost sight of by Her Majesty's 
Government. 

| proceeded to express my hope that the communications which might 
stiortly be expected from Vienna, after the overtures made to the Porte, would 
he received in a friendly spirit at st. Petersburgh. 

Till the Sultan's answer should be made known here, it was impossible, 
Count Nesselrode said, that he should express any opinion upon the subject. 

He would only say that the diplomatic papers jately made public did not in his 
opinion improve the chances of the Sultan being brought to such conditions as it 
would be in the power of the Emperor to accept. 

Again the Chancellor adverted to the idea of a negotiation at which a 


Turkish negotiator should be admitted, and to the extreme re ugnance of THis 
Imperial Majesty to countenance a plan so much at variance with the established 


visage of Russia in her dealings with the Porte.

Lord Stratford de Redeliffe to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received

(No. 382.) 
My Lord, Constantinople, December 15, 1853. 


SINCE | had last the honour of addressing you, three matters, intimately 
connected with the great question still unhappily pending, have almost entirely 
occupied my thoughts and my time. 

Firat, the acquirement of adequate means for setting on foot 4 winter 
negotiation calculated to restore peace OF fair and durable grounds. 

Secondly, the employment of the combined squadrons i such manner os 
may best redeem the pledges given to Turkey without exposing them unneces- 
sarily either to the hazards of u cruise at this season in the Black Sea, or to 
collision with the naval forces of Russia. 

Thirdly, a just appreciation of the ultimate arran moments which it will be 
desirable to keep in VICWs supposing the war to be unavoidably prolonged, and 
of the means or measures by which @ result proportioned to ‘ts sacrifices might 
in due season be obtained, 

On cach of these subjects ] propose to address your Lordship ina separate 
despatch as clearly and concisely as. their delicate and complicated nature will 

ermit. 

3 For the moment I confine myself to stating, with respect to the first, that, 
im concert with the Austrian, French, and Prussian Tepresentatives, [ have 
framed a plan of proceeding which will be presented to Reshid Pasha collectively 
and officially im the course of the day; that the General Council is to be 
assembled the day after to-morrow under circumstances favourable to hopes of 
peace ; and that the Sultan’s Ministers are at length disposed, as it would seem, 
to take a more sober view of their prospects and difficulties. 

With respect to the united squadrons, Pam decidedly of opinion that moral 
and political considerations of much weight require their appearance In the Black 
Sea; and that, if my opinion continues to prevail, professional objections, 
suggested by the season, will alone prevent the execution of that measure, 

On the wider question of future contingencies which might arise out of a 
protracted and extended war, | lave submitted some notions to your Lordship in 
earlier parts of my correspondence. What remains to be brought under ¢on- 
sideration ney easily be found to re wire more time than the present occasion

No. 613, 


Lord Stratford de Redcliffe to. the Earl of Clarendon.—( Received 
January 14, 1854.) 


(No, 410.) 
My Lord, Constantinople, December 31, 1853. 

I HAVE the honour to inclose herewith, in copy and translation, the 
Porte’s official answer to the identic note of the Four Representatives, dated the 
19th instant, and presented collectively to Reshid Pasha on the 15th, 

Your Lordship will perceive that the Porte's note confirms entirely what I 
have already announced by means of a telegraphic message. It 1s addressed not 
only to me, but to each of my three colleagues respectively. Our proposals are 
formally accepted under the Sultan's sanction, and it now remains with the Four 
Powers to obtain the assent of Russia, and to set on foot the negotiation which 
they have expressed their desire toobtain, and which, if the Court of St. 
Petersburgh be sincere in its professions, ought to terminate at an early period 
in peace. 

[ venture to congratulate your Lordship on the prospect of that consum- 
mation. ‘The hope which it encourages may not, indeed, be realized ; but it will 
always be gratifying to remember, that the mjured and by no means unsuccessful 
marty was the first to give proof of its pacific views, and to accede, with almost 
unlimited confidence, to the suggestion of its European Allies. 

The Porte has intimated an expectation that the answer from Russia shall 
not be more than forty days from the present date in reaching Constantinople. 
It is also her intention that the armistice, proposed to be established on both 
sides during the negotiation, should be of limited, though sufficient extent, 

It appears to me that in both particulars the Porte takes 8 just view of what 
is required alike by her interests and by her duties. Exposed to the attacks of 
Russia even at this season, and obliged, therefore, to continue her defensive 
operations at great cost, It is: very desirable that the present uncertainty should 
not be indefinitely prolonged. An armistice, it is true, would suspend the prose- 
cution of hostilities on either side; but it would also leave undiminished what- 
ever disadvantage results from continued preparations against the contingency of 
their renewal, and it would operate at once as a damp on military ardour, and as 
u motive for popular discontent. 

Whether in substance or in form, the Porte, 1 verily believe, has reached 
the utmost verge of concession with respect to spiritual privileges, Nothing 
short of prostration, the consequence of military reverses, could, to all appear- 
ance, induce her to overstep the line traced out in the plan of negotiation 
proposed by the Four Iepresentatives, and now accepted by her. 

With respect to the last two paragraphs of the Ottoman reply, 1 conceive 
that the Porte does not so much pretend to a positive technical guarantee against 
future encroachments, as a formal admission into the circle of Europe’s inter- 
national law and system of mutual respect for each other’s rights, established 
among its independent States. 1 am further of opinion, that with a view to the 
condition of the non-Mussulman communities in this Empire, and the develop- 
ment of those resources on which the Porte’s independence must ever mainly rest, 
it would not be safe to hedge round the Ottoman Limpire with European 
guarantees, unless the Porte engaged at the same time to realize and extend 
her system of improved administration in good earnest. 

it was under this conviction that I urged the adoption of the paragraph 
which concludes the identic note of the Four Representatives. 

I have, &c. 
(Signed) STRATFORD DE REDCLIFFE.

Inclosure 10 in No. 615. 
Vice-Admiral Dundas to Lord Stratford de Redcliffe. 


My Lord, “ Britannia,” in Beicos Bay, December 28, 185d, 


WITH reference to your Excellency’s former correspondence (to which 
you refer me to-day), and the conferences that had been held on the subject of a 
part of the squadron under my command proceeding, in conjunction with that 
of the French, into the Black Sea, I have the honour to state that it does not 
appear to me at all clear, by your Excellency'’s despatch of the 27th instant 
(received this evening), if it is intended that the whole of the combined squad- 
rons should leave the Bosphorus unprotected, and proceed in execution of the 
service pointed out in that despatch. 

Admiral Hamelin called upon me this evening, when I had proceeded thus 
far in my letter to your Excellency, and informed me that the despatch he had 
received from his Ambassador left him equally in doubt with myself on this 
point. Under these circumstances, | have to request your Excellency will 
inform me whether you intend the whole of my squadron, or the part of it 
hitherto contemplated, to proceed to sea, in order that your instructions may be 
carried out without delay, 

And I beg to acquaint you that the draft of your letter, which your 
Exeelleney has instructed me to copy, sign, and forward to the superior officer 
in command at Sevastopol, shall be sent by the “ Retribution” as soon as I 
receive your reply. 

I have,

Fice-Admiral Dundas to Lord Stratford de Redeliffe. 


My Lord, “ Britannia,” in Beicos Bay, December 80, 1853. 

I HAD the honour to receive your Excellency’s letter of the 29th instant 
yesterday evening, and it is my intention to put to sea with five sail-of-the-line 
and six steam-vessels as soon as possible, in execution of the instructions | have 
received from you to that effect. 

Vice-Admiral Hamelin will accompany me with the same, or nearly the 
same foree, and the “Retribution” will proceed to Sevastopol as soon as the 
squadrons shall have entered the Black Sea. 

Linelose for your Excellency’s information a copy of a minute of a letter 
I had purposed sending to you, pointing out my intentions, and in which 
Admiral Hamelin entirely coincided; but as he received early this morning an 
express intimation from his Ambassador that a larger foree than the one 
proposed should be sent to sea, | have neceszarily been obliged also to send 
an increased and mixed force of sailing and steam-ships, which cannot but 
embarrass our operations at this season. : 

I have, &c. 
(Signed) J. W. D, DUNDAS. 


Inclosure 16-in No. 615. 


Draft of a Letter proposed to have been sent by Viee-Admiral Dundas to 
Lord Stratford de Redeliffe. 


My Lord, “Britannia, Bosphorus, December 59 1853, 

IT appearing by your Excellency's despatch of the 27th instant, that the 

object of the squadrons in going to sea is to protect the Ottoman territory 
against every aggression on the part of the Sultan’s enemies, and also by your 
letter to me of the 29th instant, in answer to one from me of the day before, 
that you mean that Vice-Admiral Hamelin and myself should send the whole or 
such portion of the squadrons as we ‘‘ may agree in thinking sufficient for the 
yrotection of the Ottoman territory against any amount of force which the 
Russian authorities may be able to send out from Sevastopol, according to the 
information which I have already communicated to you,” | now beg to nequaint 
your Excellency, that on account of the very extensive line of coast (upwards of 
800 miles) to be protected and watched over, especially at this season; and 
considering the great foree that Russia could send forth from Sevastopol on any 
given point at very short notice, not only from the great advantages it possesses 
from its weatherly and central position, but from the great superiority of its 
information on every movement that takes place at Constantinople and else- 
where, while we are completely deprived of similar advantages, we cannot 
undertake with the forees we command to ensure the full object proposed in 
your Excellency’s despatch of the 27th instant, but we are of opinion that the 
plan which appears to us to afford the best chance of success is to send ocea- 
sionally a strong steam squadron, eanbaing of three screw line-of-battle ships 
and eight powerful steamers, to run along the coast of the Ottoman territory, 
with a view to its protection, and by means of despatch vessels left on obser- 
vation at Varna and Sinope, to give instant information of any hostile attempt 
to the main body of the combined squadrena in the Bosphorus, which could 
then proceed to any known point that might be attacked or threatened, either 
in Europe or Asia, and the force thus remaining in the Bosphorus would also 
secure Constantinople, as well as the important command of the Dardanelles. 

I confidently believe that by adopting these measures we should more 
effectually protect the Ottoman territory than by sending a force of heavy suil- 
ing ships to sea in the winter, without a precise object or destination, and liable 
to certain damage, more or less serious, by which their real efficiency in the time 
of need would be materially impaired ; and | have therefore in obedience to 
your Lordship’s instructions, and in full accordance with my colleague, Vice-

Inclosure 2 in No. 616. 
Vice-Admiral Dundas to Lord Stratford de Redeliffe. 


My Lord, « Britannia,? in the Bosphorus, December 25, 1853. 


1 HAD the honour to receive at 4-30 pow. yesterday your Excellency’s con- 
fidential depatch of the 99rd instant, and on the points to which you have 
requested a distinct and early reply, I heg to state : 

1. It appears by the list of the Russian fleet, inclosed in your letter, that 
it consists of fifteen or sixteen gail-of-the-line, seven frigates, ten or twelve steam 
vessels, and numerous corvettes, bris, &c., &e, and I do not consider that the 
steam forees of the combined squadrons could ensure the Ottoman territory in 
Europe and Asia feom any Russian hostile aggression, as the screw line-of-battle 
ships, and many of the steamers, cannot carry coals to last for any extended 
period, and, therefore, could not move speedily from eoast to eoast in search of 
an invading force. 

9, | have frequently stated by letter, and at the various conferences which 
have been held, and in whieh Admiral Hamelin perfectly coincided, that a cruize 
in the Black Sea would at this season too probably impair the efficiency of the 
fleet; but 1 am ready to proceed to sea, even alone, with my squadron, if called 
upon by your Excellency to do so by vecise instructions to that effect, and 1 
have no hesitation in saying, that should we be at war with Russia, | will do my 


best to bring the Russian fleet to action, notwithstanding the superiority of 
their force. 

L must, however, again suggest to your Excellency that two steamers 
stationed at Varna could bring us vapid intelligence of any aggression of Europea 
Turkey, and enable the combined forces to act with promptitude on any known 

yoint, as the steamers would then have sufficient coals for extended operations, 
and the ships of the line be efficient for any Service. 

With reference to anchoring my squadron in Sinope Bay, as your Excellency 
suggests, I gather from the opinion of Captain the onourable J, Drummond, 
that the anchorage is not safe for heavy vessels at this season, especially now 
that it 1s encumbered with the anchors, chains, and wrecks of the ‘Turkish 
squadron ; therefore, 1 should not be justified in exposing Her Majesty's ships 
there, even should it be deemed advisable to remove the British squadron to 4 
point so distant from Varna and the Bosphorus. 

The French Admiral fully accords with me in my reply to your Excellency’s 
first question, and you can readily conceive that I have not even alluded to the 
second, which contemplates & separation of the cambined forces of France and 

Fingland. 
| have, &c. 
(Signed) J. W. D, DUNDAS.

_ ON the 18th November the “ Medari Tidjaret,” an Ottoman steamer, was 
seized by a Russian steamer and carried away a prize. On bourd the captured 
vessel were two Englishmen, serving 28 engineers; the one 1s my brother-in-law 
Alex, Cleland, the other, Archibald Morrison, is a friend. As the vessel was i 
trader without guns and completely unarmed, bringing a freight from one 
urkish port to another, there can be no legal grounds for detaining these men 
more especially as the English nation, to which they belong, is at peace with 
Russia, and no notice has been yet given by the Consulate to the English 
engincers serving I the Ottoman Steam Navigation Company. } 
The very name of the vessel implies its commercial character; and it 
appears to have been employed, when taken, solely in commercial objects

Inclosure 3 in No. 617. 


Lord Stratford de Redcliffe to Vice-ddmiral Dundas. 


Sir, Pera, December 28, 165d. 

| HAD prepared a despatch for Her Majesty's Consul-General at Odessa, 
in pursuance of which I wrote to you on the 26th instant, respecting two British 
engineers detained as prisoners of war in Russia. I have since learnt from 
Mr. Yeames that the local authorities had rejected his application for their 
release. 

Such being the present state of the case [ am opinion that it will be 
advisable to send the steamer, destined in the first instance for Odessa, direct to 
Sevastopol, and to apply to the superior naval authority there for the delivery of 
the men in question. The capture of the Turkish trading-vessel, “ Medari 
Tidjaret,” on board of which the two engineers served, having been effected by 
« Russian steam-frigate, it is presumable that the commanding officer of this 
vessel depended on the Admiral at Sevastopol, and that the prize was carried 
into that harbour, | 

I have in consequence to request that you will direct the officer in command 
of the steam-vessel selected by you for the service in question to apply at 
Sevastopol for the release and delivery to him, if they are willing to embark, of 
the engineers, named Alexander Cleland and Archibald Morrison, taken 
prisoners, as stated above; and in the event of his demand not being complied 
with, to obtain an official statement of the grounds of refusal for the information 
of Her Majesty's Government. 

| have already communicated to you the particulars of the case, and I 
repeat that the detention of the men appears to be an arbitrary act; and even 
that the capture of the vessel in which they served, was not warranted by 
circumstances at the time when that occurrence took place. 

I have, &e. 
(Signed) STRATFORD DE REDCLIFFE, 


Inclosure 4 in No, 617. 


Lord Stratford de Redcliffe to Vice-Admiral Dundas. 


Sir, Pera, December 28, 1853. 

AS the squadrons are directed to go into the Black Sea it is necessary to 
execute an instruction provided by Her Majesty's Government for that con- 
tingency, namely, to notify the general object of their movement at Sevastopol. 
The French Ambassador acts on the occasion in concert with me, and will cause 
a cammunication identical with mine to be addressed to the proper authority 
there, who, I presume, is the Admiral commanding in chief the Russian naval 
forces in the Black Sea. | ' 

You will, therefore, take advantage of the steam-vessel ordered to Sevas- 
topol for another purpose to address that commander in the terms adopted by 
General Baraguay and myself iu pursuance of our respective instructions, and 
now inclosed to you herewith. The draft has been drawn up in French as a 
convenient means of communication between two commanders-in-chief not likely 
to be acquainted with each other's native linguage. An officer, appointed by 
General Baraguay d' Hilliers, will be charged with the delivery of Admiral Hame- 
lin’s letter, and | have to request that you will direct him to be received and 
entertained on board the steam-vessel dispatched to Sevastopol. The officer in 
command of the vessel will, of course, take charge of any answer which the 
Russian Admiral may think proper to return to your letter of notification. 

I have, &e. 
STRATFORD DE REDCLIFFE,

L'ESCADRE sous mes ordres étant sur le point de paraitre dans la Mer 
Noire, de concert avec celle de la France, et Vobjet de ce mouvement étant de

aux relations amicales qui existent entre mon Gouvernement et le votre, rela- 
tions que nous désirons conserver et que vous tenez aussi, sans doute, a

No. 618. 
Lord Stratford de Redcliffe to the Earl of Clurendon.—( Received January 19.) 


(No. 1. Confidential.) 
My Lord, Constantinople, January 1, 1854, 

THE Prussian Envoy sent a Secretary to me this morning with a copy of 
an instruction respecting the combined squadrons, as forwarded to your Lordship 
confidentially with one of my preceding despatches. I asked whether the 
communication was meant to be official, observing that 1 was not aware of any 
title which his Excellency had to interfere with the movements of the squadrons, 
The Secretary said that the communication was private (particuli¢re). I 
replied, that if he would have the goodness to leave the paper, | would read it 
at my leisure. He said that he wus directed to read it to me, and not to leave 
it. J answered that in that case 1 should decline receiving the communication, 
not from any want of respect towards the Envoy and his Court—far from it; but 
because I thought it desirable to avoid a position which might require the 
expression of remarks less consonant than T could wish to the harmony which 
had prevailed in all that related to our recent negotiations for peace. He per- 
sisted in not leaving the paper, aud went away, . 

In the course of the morming a Secretary arrived with a similar com- 
niunication fram the Internungio. 1 gave the same answer, and a similar result 
ensued, 

The manner in which T explained myself, was intended to avoid, though | 
know not how successfully, every cause of offence or misunderstanding, and I 
hope your Lordship will think that I took a suitable course under the cireum- 
stances. 

| am ignorant whether similar communications have been proposed to the 
French Ambassador, and ifso, whether or in what manner they have been 
received by lis Excellency. 

I have, &e. 
(Signed) STRATFORD DE REDCLIFFE, 


P.S.—Jonuary 2. 1 have just learnt from the French Ambassador that, 
although he read the instructions communicated to him by the Austrian and 
Prussian Seeretaries, he gave, in substance, to each an answer similar to mine.

view, and her wish that the smaller States should be informed of the present

Austrian Cabinet appear to have urged the necessity, in the event of hostilities 
between England and France with Russia, of consolidating the whole of central 
Europe in one neutral body, whose numerical military foree would be enabled to 
withstand any attack from any quarter. 

Baron Manteuffel informed me that he had declined this invitation, stating 
that the eoneert and union which was most efficacious was: that of the Four 
Powers, and which was at present most completely attained in the Conference at 
Vienna; that in his opinion this union of the Four Powers was the surest way 
to preserve peace, and that nothin should be done which could, in any way, 
separate their collective action; and that on these grounds he did not consider 
it necessary or advisable to assent to the proposition of the Austrian Cabinet. 

Baron Manteuffel (who was little discursive upon this subject further than 
communicating to me the simple facts) told me that a despatch which he had 
written this day in the above sense had been approved hy the King, and would 
be immediately transmitted to Vienna. 

His Excellency remarked to me that the object of the Austrian Cabinet was 
of similar purpose and intent as the invitation submitted some months ago to 
invite a declaration of neutrality on the part of the Germanic Diet. 

I think that 1 may safely inform your Lordship that the decision of the 
Prussian Government on this subject isa fixed one, and that it is not likely to 
be recalled. 7

(No. 12:) 
My Lord, Vienna, January 11, 1854. 

COUNT BUOL has received a telegraphic message from Semlin, 
announcing the arrival in that place of the communications he has been 

expecting from Constantinople, and which have been forwarded from thence 
by messenger, who is expected to arrive to-morrow. ean 

* ‘He mentioned the hope he entertained, from the telegraphic communication 
he had received from the Internuncio, that, the reply of the Porte to the Repre- 
sentatives, which was now transmitted, might be of a satisfactory nature; he 
intended, therefore, as IT have reported in my despatch No. 5, to communicate it 
immediately to the Conference, and, after consultation, and in accordance with 
them, to transmit it by Count Esterhazy to St. Petersburgh, with directions to 
make every possible effort to obtain tts acceptance, ; 

I told Count Buol that your Lordship felt that some collective form of 
communication would be necessary, as otherwise the action of the Four Powers 
in this important transaction would be set aside; and as the first step which 
had heen taken in this negotiation had been made known to the Cabinet of 
St. Petersburgh by the communication through Baron Meyendorff of the note to 
Reshid Pasha, and the Protocol, it, would be naturally expected by Russia that 
the opinion of the Four Governments upon the present propositions should be 
made known to her. + 

Count Buol concurred entirely in this view; he was ansious the opinions 
of the Four Powers should be communicated to the Cabinet of St. Petersburgh, 
and he intended to employ the decision the Conference might come to 4s the 
strongest argument in favour of the proposals he should advocate, He stated 
that, with respect to the line he meant to adopt in transmitting, without delay, 
the communications he should receive from the Internuneio, he had_ fully 
explained it in his communications to Count Colloredo for your Lordship’s 
information, by a messenger he had forwarded on Sunday last to Paris and 
London. 

After Lhad held this conversation with Count Buol, | learnt trom M, de 
Bourqueney that he had received a telegraphic despatch, transmitting to him a 
form of Protocol, which he was directed to sign after the Conference should have 
approved of the communications from Constantinople, and which should be 

laced in the hands of Count Buol, and shortly afterwards 1 received your 
Vordahipts instruction to sign the same document. Baron de Bona neney has 
not thought it advisable to communicate this Protocol to Count Buol until he 
shall have called the Conference together for the purpose of taking into consi- 
deration the answer from the Porte; and as I consider this document to be 
subject to his control, T have tiot taken any steps with regard to it, except to 
inquire of your Lordship, by my telegraphic message of yesterday, whether I 
was to retain it, after signature, till Thad received from your Lordship your 
further instructions with respect to it. 
I have, &c.

(No. 13:) 
My Lord, Vienna, January 11, 1854, 


ACCORDING to the instructions contained in your Lordship’s despatch 
No. 426, I stated to Count Buol the regret of Her Majesty's Government at the 
presence of the Austrian Chargé d’Affaires at a religious ceremony performed at 
the Winter Palace in St. Petersburgh, to celebrate a victory attained by the 
Russians over the ‘Turks, and the bad effect that such presence might produce. 
Count Buol replied, that this had taken place in the absence of any instructions 
on the subject from the Government at Vienna, and simply as complymg with 
an invitation received by M, de Lebzeltern from the Russian Court. Under the 
circumstances he had not thought it necessary to make any particular remark 
with regard to M, de Lebzeltern’s conduct, 

The Turkish Ambassador here has not made any representation upon this 
subject, and it is probable that (as Sir H. Seymour remarks) the Government of 
the Sultan may be too sensible to regard any trifling circumstances of this kind 
with suspicion, as they are aware that the Austrian Goyernment are using their 
best efforts for the attainment of a just and honourable settlement of the differ- 
ences now existing between themselves and Russia.

No, 630, 
The Earl of Westmorland to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received January 17.) 
(No. 16.) 
My Lord, 


Vienna, January 12, 1894. 

AT the Conference held this day, Count Arnim stated that he had received 
a despatch from M. de Wildenbrach, the Prussian Minister at Constantinople, 
by which it appears that Reshid Pasha had made to him a communication to the 
effect that the entry of the allied fleets into the Black Sea had been decided 
upon with the approbation of the Four Powers. M. de Wildenbrach had con- 
sequently though it his duty to address a note to Reshid Pasha, declaring that 
the Prussian Government was in no way a party to that measure. 

Count Buol stated, that he also had received a despatch from the Inter 
nuncio, informing him he had received the same communication from Reshid 
Pasha, and that he had equally declared to that Minister that his Government 
had had no share in the adoption of the orders to the fleets, and that he did not 
consider them to be in accordance with the arrangements agreed upon by the 
Representatives, his colleagues, on the 12th of December. 

January 13th.— Count Buol read this day to the Conference the despatch 
above referred to, which the Internuncio had addressed to Reshid Pasha, a copy of 
which he will transmit to Count Colloredo for communication to your Lordship.

No. 632, 
The Earl of Westmorlond to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received January 18.) 


No. 183) 
Ne Lord, Vienna, January 13, 1854. 

1 HAVE already reported to your Lordship by telegraph that I, ue day, 
in conjunction with the other members of the Conference, signed the xatone 
which was (with the addition of a preamble) drawn up im accordance ee t 9 
one proposed by M. Drouyn de Lhuys and transmitted to M. de Bourqueney. 
[ have the honour of inclosing a copy of this document, as well as of the note of 
Reshid Pasha which is annexed to it. This Protocol is marked No. 2, for the 
purpose of showing that it is a continuation of the acts of the Conference a4 
recorded in the first Protocol, which had been signed on the Sth of December, 

After this document had been agreed upon, Count Buol read to the Confer- 
ence the despatch he had drawn up, and which he intended to address to Baron 
Lebzeltern, with an order to place a copy of it in the hands of Count Nesselrode. 


oO] 


He at the same stated, that his first intention had been to transmit this document 
by Count Valentin Esterhazy, the pen eroinied Minister to the Court of 
St. Petersburgh; but that, as he was too unwell to be able immediately to under- 
take the journey, and as he thought it was of the utmost consequence that the 
communication should not be delayed, he had determined to send it at once by a 
messenger, who would leave Vienna this evening. 

This despatch to Baron Lebzeltern will, without delay, be communicated to 
Count Colloredo for your Lordship's information, but in the mean time I feel it 
my duty to state, that it was most highly approved by the members of the 
Conference; that it was considered as doing full justice to the anxiety with 
which the Four Powers liad laboured to obtain from the Government of the 
Sultan such proposals for the re-establishment of peace, as, while honourable to 
themselves, would equally be so to the Emperor Nicholas; as explaining that, in 
consequence of the non-arrival in time of the phe by the Conference of 
of Vienna, those which, in the same sense, had been proposed to Reshid Pasha 
by the Representatives at Constantinople liad been adhered to; and lastly, as 
bringing before the Imperial Government the opinion of the allied Governments 
as contained in their Protocol, that the proposals of the Porte were conformuble 
to the views they entertained, as stated in the Acts of the Conference of the Sth 
of December, and consequently, that they were such as they confidently expected 
the Emperor of Russia would accept as the basis of a negotiation which offered 
to both parties the mode of terminating with honour the unfortunate state of 
war at present existing, and which, in the unanimous conviction of the Four 
Powers, is 50 deeply to be deplored. 

The tone of this despatch is full of friendly interest for the Emperor 
Nicholas, but it does not fail to point out to him the anxious expectation of the 
Austrian Government that, in pursuance of that respect for the maintenance of 
the tranguillity and independence of the States of Europe by which his policy 
has been distinguished, he will seize this opportunity of putting an end to a state 
of things which, by being prolonged, might compromise all those interests which 
he has hitherto so eminently cooperated in maintaining. 

IT have, &c. 
(Signed) WESTMORLAND.

differences between Russia and the Porte.

Austria in negotiation, they acted independently of her im protecting the 
Sultan's territory from ageression, Count Buol, Psaid, was well aware that the

(No. 11.) 
My Lord, St. Petersburgh, January 7, 1854. 

I HAVE the honour of acknowledging the receipt of your Lordship’s 
despatch No. 345 of the 27th ultimo, which was delivered to me on the morning 
of the 4th instant by the messenger Haviland. 

Your Lordship will, I trust, allow me to express the warm satisfaction with 
which | have learned the measures which have been concerted between Her 
Majesty’s Government and that of the Emperor of the French for preventing a 
repetition of such acts as. that which occurred at Sinope—from putting an end 
to the naval resources of Turkey. 

No impartial judge can, I apprehend, be of opinion that either of the 
Allied Powers haye been wanting in conciliatory conduct towards Russia, and if 
their pacific dispositions are not proof against any further trials, it ts only to be 
ascribed to the insolent and pernicious policy of a State which, while constantly 
declaring its eagerness to preserve the existence and independence of a weakened 
neighbour, is only endeavouring to endanger the one, and to annihilate the 
other. 

In the midst of the excitement which recent transactions must have oeca- 
sioned to all those who have been in any way connected with them, I have 
endeavoured to preserve that impartiality which is so essential for a right judg- 
ment of affairs, and althouyh Tam the first to admit that the information which 
L have transmitted to your Lordship may have been eccasionally incorrect, as it 
has been, Lam certain, constantly incomplete, L can safely assert that I have 
neither sought to exaggerate or to extenuute the circumstances which have come 
under my observation. 

With this preface I will again state to your Lordship, that with regard to 
the late dreadiul catastrophe at Sinope, all that comes to my knowledge tends 
to strengthen my belief of the Russun Government being chargeable rather 
with areckless pursuit of their own object than with any wish to set at defiance 
those of England and France, 

The Imperial Government are perfectly aware that a fire may readily be 
lighted up on their south-eastern [rontiers which months and years of costly 
exertion may be insufficient to extinguish ; and looking to this danger, I believe 
that (he uttention of the naval officers at Sevastopol had been especially directed 
to the attempt which would be made from Constantinople for affording assist- 
ance to thse hardy tribes which under the most adverse circumstances have 80 
long maintained their independence against the eile might of Russia,

My Lord, St, Petersburgh, January 9, 1854. 
SUCH is the gross ignorance with regard to England which prevails here, 

even among comparatively well-educated persons, thut it ts commonly received 

that we are unable to engage in war with Russia ; and that, were such a misior- 

tune to befall us, it could hardly fail of reducing England to. a state of bank- 


ruptey. a 
Eteae of this opinion being held by persons who, from the position which 

they hold, ought to be supposed possessed of at least some rudimentary know- 

ledge of finance and commerce. ee oP 

What the financial state of England may be after a war with Russia remains 
to be proved ; but that the financial difficulties of Russia have commenced hefore 
she has exchanged a shot with a Power of her own magnitude ts very evident. 
She may possibly be able to satisfy her religious prejudices and her ambitious: 
designs, but it is very certain that she will pay dearly for the gratiheaton. 

The want of funds is already sensibly felt by the Government ; and, as I 
understand, the Finance Minister has it in contemplation to cover the difficulties 
of the moment by the issue of exchequer bills to the amount of 60,000,000 of 
silver roubles, or about 10,000,0001. sterling. 

f am assured that the Government intend to treat this'as a currency ques- 
tion, and to state that as, as in other countries, the deposits of gold do not exceed 
a fifth of the circulation, the immense stores of specie in the fortress admit of 
a very extended paper issue. ; nd ee 

This may possibly be so. It is easily proved that very large sums have been 

eposited at the fortress, but it would be very dificult for any one not initiated 
in the secrets of the Finance Department to state with precision what amount 
has been withdrawn from the deposit.

TT ite ta the fair half of the responsibility should be incurred by

®8th ultimo received here from M. de Kisseleff. M. de Kisseleff, as 1 under-

Government were continually urging him forward, and that some mensure was 
in consequence likely to he taken with regard to the two fleets. 

It is so much the object of the Russians to sow mistrust between the 
English and French Cabinets, that 1 look with some suspicion upon M, Kisseleff’s 
statement. 

With regard to the last accounts from Baron Brunnow, I do not seruple to 
say, cither that he is imperfectly informed as to the intentions of Her Majesty's 
Government, or that he is chargeable with a suppression of a part of the truth. 
Writing on the 27th or 28th ultimo, M. de Brunnow acquaints Count Nessel- 
rode that it is the intention of the allied forces to prevent Turkish vessels of war 
from putting to sea, but he makes no allusion to the restraint which it is 
intended to put upon Russian ships of war. 

The report accordingly has given pleasure here, and will inerease the 
feelings of soreness with which the communication which Tam charged to make 
to Count Nesselrode will be received, 

It is with considerable surprise that I have read in the Prussian “ Staats 
Anzeiger,” I believe in the number of the first day of the year, a ety faithful 
account of the orders despatched to the English and French Admirals. This 
announcement increases the ditheulties of the moment, and makes it the more 
essential that the communication to be made to Count Nesselrade should be 
delayed as little as possible. 

The non-arrival of the Paris despatches is im all probability to be ascribed 
to the accumulation of snow in Belgium and France. ‘The communications 
appear to be interrupted, the latest intelligence received here from Paris and 
London being of the date of the 28th ultimo. 

Lhave settled with General Castelbajac that as soon as he receives his 
instructions we shall write to Count Nesselrode to ask for-an interview, at which 
will be made respectively the communication respecting the orders sent to the 
French and English Admirals,

three days of the state of Prince Woronzow’s health, it has been decided that he

leave of absence as soon as peace shall be restored. 

Tt is now well known that Prince Woronzow had asked for reinforcements 
some months ago, and that he had been placed in a very critical position from 
not having received them. Little doubt exists that if the Turkish Generals had 
acted with more energy, Tiflis and the whole of Georgia must have been 
evacuated by the Russian forces, 

lt is only fhir to state, that there is considerable reason for believing that 
the Emperor had not been insensible to the risks to which Tiflis and the 
adjacent country was exposed, but that the fear of alarming Murope by the 
extent of military preparation had, in his view, outweighed other considerations ; 
pcrably too the amount of resistance which the Turks were capable of making 
md been miscalculated.

to your Lordship, as the opinion of some of the leading military men of Russia, 
that, like his colleague in Asia, Omer Pasha has been deficient in enterprise, and

Lord A. Loftus to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Recetved January 20.) 


(No. 35.) 
My Lord, Berlin, January 18, 1854. 

| HAVE not been able to see Baron Manteuffel to-day, but am privately 
informed that the reports received from General Rochow state that the Emperor 
Nicholas, accompanied by the Grand Duke Hereditary of Russia, had had a 
protracted conterence with Count Nesselrode subsequently to the communi- 
cations which had been made to his Exeellency by Sir Hamilton Seymour 
and the French Minister, but that the result of this conference had not trans- 
vired. He is evidently of opinion that these communications will not be 
followed by any abrupt measure on the part of His Imperial Majesty. He 
appears to think that they will be replied to verbally at Paris and in London, 
and that the Emperor will await some demonstrative act of hostility in the 
Bluck Sea previous to recalling his Ministers from London and Paris. 

1 have, &e. 
(Signed) AUGUSTUS LOFTUS.

My Lord, St. Petersburgh, January 12, 1854. 
AS I have no knowledge of military matters, it is always with some’ reluc- 
tance that | address your Lordship any observations relating to such affairs. | 
would, however, venture to remark, that as itis assumed by the Russian Govern- 
ment that the Ottoman Empire, after a gradual decay, has reached that stage af 
decrepitude which renders the dissolution of the Empire inevitable (in spite of 
the wishes sincerely entertained by Russia forits preservation), it appears strange 
that an attack upon Turkey having been considered requisite, a larger force 
should have been poured into the country than was judged necessary for a similar 
invasion in 1828. . 


In 1828 the forces sent into the Principalities consisted of,— 


The 3rd corps d’armée - - 0,000 
«6th ditto - . 20,000 
‘* 7th ditto = os 15,000 


Or 65,000 
This force being subsequently reinforced by the 2nd corps d’armée and part 
of the Guards, in numbers 32,000, which brought the whole available force to 
97,000. 
"In the autumn of 1853, Prince Gortehakoff erossed the Pruth with— 
The 4th corps d'armée, or — - - - . = - 60,000 
A division of the Sth corps d’armée under General Liiders 12,000 


To which are to be added some 10,000 Cossacks of the 
80,000 always available - 


. - . 10,000 

And the 3rd corps under General Osten-Sacken, 55,000 
or 60,000 strong, say = « - - - 7 65,000 
137,000 


These facts being established, the dilemma at once presents itself; either 
the Turkish Empire instead of being weaker must be considered capable of much 


more resistance now than it was in 1828, or that more extensive and permanent 
plans are entertained now than had been indulged in by Russia at that period. 


Your Lordship will observe that Ido not endeavour to establish a compa- 


rison between the amount of Russian forces employed in Asia Minor during the 


two years, although there the difference would be more striking than with regard 
to those sent into Wallachia and Moldavia, 


I take the numbers of the Russian troops employed in 1828 from De 


Moltke’s work, which is considered a high authority. 


I have, &e. 
(Signed) G. H. SEYMOUR.

This opinion, I replied, was entirely shared by Her Majesty’s Government, 
and, as [ had before stated, nothing of the sort would have happened but for 
the attack upon Sinope and the dreadful incidents by which this attack had been 
attended; Her Majesty’s Government were nevertheless still intent upon peace 
if it were attainable. 

As I saw that Count Nesselrode was too ill to carry on a longer conversa- 
tion, I rose to take leave of him, when he said that he could not at present make 
uny reply to my communication beyond this, that it would be his duty to bring 
it as soon as possible to the Emperor's knowledge, and to take His Majesty's 
orders upon the subject. : . 

1 said, M. le Comte, allow me then to take this opportunity of saying that, 
whatever comes of this affair, I shall leave St. Petersburgh, when the time 
arrives for doing so, with a feeling of sincere good-will towards you—a feeling 
which I am willing to believe will in some measure be corresponded to on your 
side. Let me however add that private feelings of this nature have nothing todo 
with the conduct of public affairs; all that your Government, like my own, have 
to look to is its own interests and dignity. | 

Upon public grounds I am most anxious that everything should be arranged 
amicably, but at the same time I will not conceal from you that my position 
here has been so long a painful one that personally the decision about to be 
taken will very little affect me. a 

I have only to add that,.in consequence of a slight misunderstanding, 
Jeneral Castelbajac was introduced into the Chancellor's sick-room on the 11th 
instant, when his Excellency was still so indis nosed ‘as to be unable to speak to 
him upon public business. Last might his Excellency apprised my colleague, 
by a note, that he would see him as soon as he was capable of the exertion ; but 
he is aware that the communication he is to receive is a matter of form, as it is 
a mere repetition of that already made on the part of Her Majesty's Govern-
