Sir G. H. Seymour to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received January 20.) 


(No. 37. Secret and Confidential.) 
My Lord, St. Petersturgh, January 13, 1854. 


I LEARN upon unquestionable authority that a very warm altercation 
took place on the 7th instant between the Emperor and Count Nesselrade, who 
was reproached sharply by His Imperial Master with the manner i which he 
had conducted himself during the lute transactions with the English and French 
Governments. 
ne This much may be considered as certain; that which is less so, but which 
there i reason for believing is, that at the same conversation the Emperor 
alluded to the instructions which the English Minister was known to have 
received, whilst none of the same kind had reached the French Mission. | 

From this fact His Imperial Majesty deduced the proof of his having been 
correct in his opinion that there was no cordiality of feeling between England 
and France, and that the latter would not take the resolution which appeared 
to have been adopted by Her Majesty's Government with regard to the Black 
Sea. ee 

It is further understood that Count Nesselrode did not give up his opinion, 
and expressed his confidence that France and England were about to act upon 
a common system, , fa | 

L apprehend that this painful conversation has contributed to bring on the 
indisposition from whieh Count Nesselrode has since been suffering. — 

In consequence of a sort of misunderstanding the French Minister was 
admitted on the L1th instant to Count Nesselrode’s sick room, and the Chan- 
cellor, after observing that he felt too ill to enter upon a discussion of political 
affairs, added, ‘ ‘The fact is, that this Eastern question will be the cause of my 
death,” 


a2] 


When J waited upon the Chancellor I found him so weak and reduced that 
it was manifestly painful to him to converse, and the Emperor, who had been 
anxious to know what had passed at the interview which I had just had of his 
Excellency, went to his hotel for the purpose of hearing his report. 

I have, &c. 


(Signed) G, H. SEYMOUR.

Inclosure in No. G62. 
Consul-General Yeames to Lord Stratford de Redcliffe. 


My Lord, Odessa, December 13, 1853. 

I BELIEVE that the whole military force of this Empire is about to be 
placed on the war-footing, Large masses of troops are in motion, and Lam 
told that the 6th corps d'armée always stationed about Moscow, and considered 
as a reserve, will soon be on its march, not asT should have supposed towards the 
Caucasus, but directed to this quarter. To my surprise | learn that one of the 
divisions of infantry of the Ist corps d'armée now in Poland, is destined for the 
Caucasus, and I know that the reserve division of infantry stationed at the 
head of the Asoph is to break up its cantonments on the Ist day of January 
for its march to Sevastopol. Your Excellency is already aware of the advance 
of the 3rd corps d'armée under the command of General Osten-Sacken, and the 
head of its first column of infantry was on the Sth or 6th instant to have 
reached Seculani on the Pruth. I have not yet heard that an extmordinary 
conscription has been ordered, which if present operations be continued vill 
become indispensable, If such a measure has been rumoured, it arises no doubt 
from the severity with which the conseription in arrear has been enforced, 

Great exultation has been created here by the Russian victory, or, to speak 
more correctly, of the Turkish disaster in the roads of Sinope. No vessel was 
on that oceasion carried away, and but o very few prisoners. Osman Pasha 


522 


and other wounded are in Sevastopol, and on Saturday the 10th instant were 
brought here 207 prisoners. that had been taken off Sinope, and in the two 
steamers previously captured. ‘There are three English engineers, Bell, Morrison, 
and Cleland among them. ‘The first was on the Egyptian war-steamer « Parvis 
Bahri,’ and the others in the merchant-steamer ~ Moedari Tidjaret.” ‘The 
capture of the last vessel may be qualified as an act of piracy if the Ministerial 
Russian proclamation means anything, when the term is stated to be the 22nd 
November, before which no Turkish merchant ships met at sea, are to be seized, 
| have, however, applied to the Acting Governor-General fruitlessly in favour of 
our countrymen, and they with two Maltese stokers, and two lonians, are to be 
marched up far into the country. Five Egyptian officers were sent off this 
morning for St. Petersburgh, where no doubt niuch will be made of them; all 
the prisoners are in truth well treated. 

1 have 2 letter from Sir Hamilton Seymour of the And in whieh he alludes 
to the fresh attempt now made at Constantinople for a pacilic adjustment, for 
the suecess of which itis impossible to feel sanguine, ** We are,’ he says, 
“very conciliatory, a8 We have been, Heaven knows, throughout; but there are 
limits which we shall not and cannot pass by one hair's breadth.” 

There is much yulger exasperation here against the English, while the 
French seem not to be named. A fray with England is an astounding novelty. 
I feel it necessary and prudent to keep within doors, notwithstanding which I 
have acquired a bad name, and aii indirectly threatened that my Government 
ic to he required to call me away from here. My correspondence by post is of 
course seen, and displeases however cireumspect it may be. 

The danger to # maritime expedition by the ‘Turks from the Bosphorus to 
the most distant coast of the Black Sea was to be foreseen, and | should be 
unhappy to know that a squadron of our own should come into this Sea in- 
sufficiently strong to command respect; for the moment may be at hand when 
all scruples cense. 

We have news here of 4 battle fought on the o6th ultimo near Akhalchik, 
which appears to have been abstinately contested, having cominenced at SUNISe 
and continued the whole of the day, We are fold that it terminated in the 
defeat of the Turks, whose logs is reported to have heen about 1,000 killed, 120 
prisoners, among whom, it ia boasted, there were Mullah and a Pasha’'s Seere- 
tary, LO field-pieces, 2 mountain guns, and 2 cannon of position, and a large 
quantity of provisions found in their captured camp. Of the forces on cither 
cide there is nO enumeration the Russians were under the command of Lieute- 
nant-General Prince Andronikolf, 

There are rumours of other affairs in the Caucasus and at sea, of which we 
have no explanation and that are too vague to be repeated. 

The public prints have of late said much of the mvasion of Khiva. I myself 
know of no further progress of the Russians than to Ak-Mecheh on the Syr- 
Daria, 1 beg leave to refer to my letter of the 22nd Oetober, 1891, en that 
subject. In the vain expectation of further accounts I have not wiitten so much 
ta the Foreign Office, which Ido now regret; for my vigilance will be accused to 
have been at fault. 

The winter has set in with early severity, and to day we have a snow-storm, 
which upon these steppe lands are perilous to travellers and to troops on their 
march, 

1 have, *c. 
(Signed) JAMES YEAMES.

Lord Stratford de Redelijfe to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Recetved January 21.) 


(No, 6.) 
My Lord, Constantinople, January 4, 1854. 

I WAS surprised the day before yesterday by receiving the official note of 
which a copy is herewith inclosed, from the Prussian Envoy here. Your Lord- 
ship will perceive that it relates to the subject of my despatch No. 1 of this year. 
I have made a point of replying to it with a degree of moderation ill deserved, 
though it is evident that M. de Wildenbruch’s interference with the movements 
of the squadron was as injudicious as it was “spontaneous” and uncalled-for. 

A copy of my answer to his note is inclosed herewith. 

Baron de Bruck received from me exnetly the same answer which I had 
gent to the Prussian Envoy, but Tam not aware that he has taken it amiss; at 
least he has sent me no retort, 

The step taken at the Porte by his Excellency and his Prussian colleague 
occasioned a report that the combined squadrons had heen restrained from going 
into the Black Sea by the remonstrances of those two Ministers. 

1 have, Xe. 
(Signed) STRATFORD DE REDCLIFFE. 


P.S.—I am informed on good authority that the Internuncio carried his 
anxiety on the subject of the squadrons so far as to request that Reshid Pasha 
would use his influence with me and the French Ambassador to dissuade us 
from sending them out! I am the more surprised at this palpable absurdity, a8 
it is generally believed that the Austrian Government will be glad to know that 
the combined squadrons are in the Black Sea,

Londres, 3 Rebiul-Akhir, 1270. (Le 3 Janvier, 1854.) 

LES Représentants des Quatre Puissances ayant adressé derni¢rement a la 
Sublime Porte des notes officielles identiques, relatives 4 un projet d’arrange- 
ment pacifique, et le Gouvernement Impérial leur ayant remis, de son cbté, une 
note responsive par laquelle il leur communique son adhésion, je vous envoie 
ci-jointes, pour votre information, les copies des piéces échangées. 

Ainsi que vous le remarquerez par la lecture de notre réponse, les notes A 
adresser aux Puissances, conjointement avec les firmans [mpériaux confirmatifs 
des priviléges spirituels des communautés de tous les sujets non-Mugsulmans de 
la Sublime Porte, seront rédigées dans des termes généraux et uniformes; c'est a 
dire, qu’elles auront pour objet de communiquer A chacune de ces Puissances 
ensemble de l'état de choses sans qu'il y soit fait mention des noms d’aucune 
communauté ou religion quelconque, et sans que rien de plus y soit ajoute par 
les Puissances en faveur d'une de ces communautés, |

modifications de certains passages ¢taient de nouveau proposées A la Sublime

De méme, si, par exemple, aprés l'adhésion du Cabinet de Russic aux bases de

quelque forme que ce soit, dans la note A adresser & ce sujet, une mention 

uelconque de la religion Greeque, étaient mises en ayant dans la Conférence 
urant les négociations, il est évident i s négociations seraicnt rompues.

‘No. 20.) 
My Lord, Vienna, January 16, 1854. 

COUNT BUOL assembled the Conference this day, for the purpose of 
stating that the ‘Turkish Ambassador had yesterday communicated to him a 
letter from Reshid Pasha, dated the ord instant, which recupitulated the terms 
of negotiation upon which the Porte was ready to treat for peace, and which 
were detailed in the letter he lad addressed to the Four Representatives at 
Constantinople. Count Buol had caused a translation to be faa af this doct- 
ment, which he read to the Conference ; the original, in the ‘Turkish language; 
ve had returned to the Ambassador, 

Count Buol characterized this despatch as being entirely inopportune; it 
puts sach a limit to negotiation as almost to invalidate the consent to treat, 
which was consigned in the answer to the Four Powers ; for it decided before- 
hand almost every question which might be brought into discussion. But his 


= + 


vyeat objection to it was the peremptory manner 1D which it refuses ever to 


admit the indication of the Greck religion; this had never before been refused 


hy the Government of the Sultan, and it was, therefore, puttin forward a 


pretension leyond the engagements which had been taken by the four Powers 
in the Protocol of the Sth of December last, by which the Porte shoulil not be 


required to agree to any stipulation which she had already refused, 


Count Buol also objected to the passage in which it was stated that the 
honour of the Four Powers was engaged to obtain all the pretensions which were 


put forward in this despatch. 
Count Buol looked upon this document as likely to create the most 


unfavourable impression if itwas known at St. Petersburgh, and it might prevent 
the acceptance of the negotiation whieh had now been proposed, He therefore 


requested the members of the Conference, as he had done the ‘Turkish Ambir 


aador, to keep it entirely secret. 


529 


_ He also requested that the members of the Conference would consult 
their Governments, whether it would not be advisable that they should take 
this document into deliberation, in order to examine whether it accorded with 
the intentions and decisions of the Four Governments as stated in the Protocol 
of the 5th of December last; and if (as Count Buol believes) it did not do so, 
that the Conference should be authorized to state this in a Protocol, and should 
declare that they did not, in consequence, consider it as a document whieh could 
be recognized as being im accordance with, or as bearing upon the negotiation 
which they hoped might shortly be established. : | 
we As, at the end of this despatch to the Turkish Ambassador, it is stated that 
it will be communicated to the Governments of the Allied Powers, I have no 
doubt it 1s already in your Lordship’s hands; and I have only to add, that Count 
Buol hopes that your Lordship’s reply to this communication may not be 
delayed. : | aX 

Count Buol conceives that this document, if it become known, would have 
ais disastrous an effect upon the pending negotiations as the despatch of Count 
Nesselrode on the Turkish modifications of the Vienna note had exercised upon 
a former oecasion in preventing the adoption of that document. |

Inclosure 2 in No. 670. 
M, E. Pisani to Lord Stratford de Redeliffe. 


\iv Lord, Pera, January 4, 1854, 

" IN conformity with your Excellency’s instruction of this day’s date, | 
waited upon Reshid Pasha and informed him that you have instructed Admiral 
Dundas to protect the Porte's shipping as well as territory in the Black Sea. 
His Highness told me that a similar communication has also been received from 
the French Embassy, and requested me to express his heartfelt ratitude for this 
important information, and nequaint your Excellency that he will lose no time in 
conveying the same to his Imperial master. 

Phe five Turkish war-steamers, which for some days were preparing to go 
‘to the Black Sea, left this morning with a number of troops and with ammu- 
nition for Trebizond, Should any more ‘Turkish ships go in that direction, the 
Porte will not fail to acquaint the limbassy beforehand of such an intention, 
The Capoudan Pasha has been accordingly officially directed to abstain from any 
steps whatever without the previous knowledge of the Embassy, and without the 
concurrence of the British and French Admirals. 

T have, &c. 
(Signed) ET. PISANI,

No. 671. 
The Earl of Clarendon to Lord Stratford de Redcliffe. 
(No, a1.) 
My Lord, Foreign Office, January 24, 1854. 


| HAVE received your Excellency’s despatch No. 6 of the 4th instant, 
inclosing copies of a correspondence with the Prussian Minister on the subject 
of your refusal, reported in your despatch No. | of the lst, to receive from his 
Secretary the unofhicial communication of a letter which he had written to the 
Porte respecting the entrance of the combined squadrons into the Black Sea. 
The Internuncio, it would seem, did not regard in the same light with his Prussian 
colleague a zimilar refusal on your Excellency’s part as applied to himself, 

Hier Majesty's Goverement have learnt with regret the steps taken by the 
Internuncio and the Prussian Minister, as reported in your peveral despatches, 
winich they apprehend may impair that union and friendly. feeling between the 


531 


fos eaten at Constantinople which exist between their respective Courts, 
and which it is of essential importance to maintain. 

On the receipt of your first reports on this subject, | directed the Earl of 
Westmorland and Lord Augustus Loftus to request explanations of the Austrian 
and Prussian Governments as to the course pursued by their Representatives ; 
but [ was subsequently led by the despatch from the Earl of Westmorland, of 
which I inclose a copy,* to direct them to suspend A the instruction. 
It appeared from Count Buol’s statement to the Earl of Westmorland, that the 
notes of the Austrian and Prussian Representatives to the Porte were ealled 
forth by a communication made to them respectively by Reshid Pasha, to the 
effect that the entry of the allied fleets into the Black Sea had been decided upon 
with the approbation of the Four Powers. 

But it would seem from M. de Wildenbruch’s letter, inclosed in your 
despatch No. 6, that his communication, and it may be inferred that of the 
Internuncio also, originated entirely with themselves ; and, therefore, in trans- 
mitting to Lord Bloomfield a copy of that sespale I have directed him to 
express to Baron Manteuffel the regret of Her Majesty's Government that M. de 
Wildenbruch should have thought it his duty to interfere respecting the entrance 
of the combined fleets into the Black Sea, which was a measure rendered indis- 
ensable by the disaster at Sinope, and the danger of aggression upon the 
Turkish territory, which England and France had declared their determination to 

rateat. 

: Lord Westmorland will be instructed tomake a communication to the same 
effect to Count Buol; and both Lord Bloomfield and Lord Westmorland will be 
directed to express the earnest desire of Her Majesty's Government that the 
same cordiality of feeling which exists between England and the Courts to which 
they are respectively accredited, should be maintained by their Representatives 
at Constantinople. 

I am, 


ke. 
(Signed) CLARENDON.

My Lord, Foreign Office, January 24, 1854. 

| HAVE to acquaint your Excellency, in reply to your despatch No. 4 of 
the 3rd instant, that Her Majesty’s Government approve of the alteration which 
you made, as stated in that despatch, in the letter to be addressed by Vice- 
‘Admiral Dundas to the Russian naval authorities at Sevastopol; the effect of 
that alteration being, that the protection to be afforded by the presence of the 
combined squadrons in the Black Sea was to apply as well to the Ottoman flag 
as to the Ottoman territory. . 

[ conclude that a similar course has been taken by General Baraguay d’Hil- 


liers in regard to the communication to be made by the French Admiral to the 
Russian authorities.
